On September 30, 2026, Senator Capito, on behalf of herself, Senator Heinrich, Senator Lee, and Senator Whitehouse, introduced S. 5653—the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). BAAJA contains seven titles within two divisions, each with some provisions that directly or indirectly relate to energy infrastructure or permitting. The bill would reform certain federal environmental review and permitting processes to potentially expedite infrastructure projects.
The bill is organized according to two divisions.
Division A—Committee on Environment and Public Works—has four titles:
Division B—Committee on Energy and Natural Resources—has three titles:
This report identifies the provisions contained within BAAJA, with abbreviated information about their content and the citations to relevant existing law, where applicable.
On September 30, 2026, Senator Capito, on behalf of herself, Senator Heinrich, Senator Lee, and Senator Whitehouse, introduced S. 5653—the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The bill would address numerous aspects of infrastructure permitting—especially for electricity and energy projects—including federal processes for environmental considerations and historic preservation.
This report provides a short summary of each provision of BAAJA as introduced; citations to relevant existing law that would be amended by the provisions, where applicable; relevant CRS background reports, where applicable; and CRS experts and points of contact that congressional clients may contact for additional information. For provisions with affected U.S.C. citations, the citations are listed in order of appearance in the bill.
Summary of provision. Section 1101 would amend the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA; 42 U.S.C. §§4321 et seq.) to specify that it prescribe a procedure to inform the public about environmental effects of major federal actions and require the result of the NEPA process to be an informational document used in federal decisionmaking. It would state that NEPA does not mandate a particular outcome in decisionmaking.
Affected U.S.C. citation. The provision would amend the following section of the U.S. Code:
CRS product. For related information, see the following CRS product:
CRS contacts. For additional information, congressional clients may contact the following CRS staff:
Summary of provision. Section 1102 would reorganize NEPA's definitions from Section 111 to a new Section 3 and make them applicable to both of NEPA's titles.2 It would remove two existing definitions, modify several existing definitions, add 15 new definitions, and make conforming amendments. For example, it would expand the list of exclusions in the definition of "major federal action," remove the definition of "participating Federal agencies," and add definitions for terms such as "authorization" and "make public."
Affected U.S.C. citations. The provision would amend the following sections of the U.S. Code:
CRS products. For related information, see the following CRS products:
Summary of provision. Section 1103 would require each federal agency to revise its NEPA regulations, procedures, or policies within 180 days after enactment of BAAJA and would direct the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) to promote standardized implementation of NEPA across federal agencies.
Summary of provision. Section 1104 would require that federal agencies' methods and procedures for implementing NEPA be consistent with minimum functional requirements and data and technology standards for agency implementation of eNEPA technologies (see Section 1121 for more information). It would also replace "responsible official" with "lead agency," replace "proposal" with "proposed agency action," and make other terminology and cross-reference changes.
Summary of provision. Section 1105 would amend the process for determining whether an action requires an environmental document (i.e., a threshold determination) and which level of review applies. It would authorize the use of two or more categorical exclusions (CEs) on a proposed agency action—excluding overlapping CEs based on size, acreage, or dollar amount thresholds—and recognize statutory CEs; it would add state, tribal, and non-NEPA federal reviews that are functionally equivalent to NEPA reviews as threshold grounds for not preparing an environmental document; it would allow a sponsor to request an environmental impact statement (EIS) in place of an environmental assessment (EA); and it would bind other agencies to a lead agency's threshold determination.
Summary of provision. Section 1106 would revise and expand NEPA Section 107, which currently governs many of the procedural elements of agency environmental reviews. Section 1106 would expand requirements governing roles and responsibilities of lead, joint lead, and cooperating agencies for federal decisions "relating to an authorization." Among other changes, the section would expand lead agency duties in managing a schedule for environmental review and needed authorizations; specify aspects of CEQ's role in resolving disputes associated with participating agencies and deadlines; and add interagency scheduling and coordination requirements. The section would also eliminate consideration of certain alternatives to a proposed action; place limitations on when an agency is required to consider new scientific or technical research; and facilitate the use of state and tribal environmental review documents.
Additionally, Section 1106 would limit the scope and timing of cooperating agency comments and prescribe certain public comment periods for environmental impact statements. The section would establish deadlines for authorization decisions following completion of the NEPA process, and it would provide administrative consequences if an agency misses a deadline for environmental reviews and authorizations. The section would expand judicial review for missed deadlines for NEPA and related authorization decisions.
It would specify annual reporting requirements for agencies and CEQ that include information related to missed deadlines for environmental documents, progress toward adhering to deadlines year over year, and recommendations on how to improve agency adherence to deadlines.
Summary of provision. Section 1107 would extend the timeline for reliance on programmatic environmental documents from 5 years to 10 years.
Summary of provision. Section 1108 would require agencies to report CEs to CEQ within 30 days of the enactment of BAAJA and would require that CEQ maintain a central public record of all CEs across federal agencies, including those established by Congress. It would authorize the adoption by another agency of any CE listed on CEQ's central public record, provided that certain requirements are met.
Summary of provision. Section 1109 would replace NEPA Section 110—which required CEQ to conduct a study and report to Congress on developing a permitting portal—with new requirements governing applications for federal authorizations. Section 1109 would add requirements for project sponsors to submit specified permitting, stakeholder engagement, and project information in addition to other application information required by a federal agency. It would also establish deadlines for agencies to assess application completeness and determine the applicable level of NEPA review.
Summary of provision. Section 1110 would affect the timing, venue, available remedies, and other considerations associated with judicial review of NEPA and potentially related claims. This would include a statute of limitations to file a claim of NEPA noncompliance 150 days after an EIS is published in the Federal Register or an authorization is "made public"; limits on who can file a claim; requirements that claims be filed in a federal court of appeals; and a general prohibition on any judicial remedy awarding vacatur or injunctive relief unless certain criteria are met beyond finding of a NEPA violation.
Affected U.S.C. citation. The provision would make the following change to the U.S. Code:
CRS contact. For additional information, congressional clients may contact the following CRS staff:
Summary of provision. Section 1121 would establish a statutory framework for and direct CEQ to lead development of electronic tools for federal environmental reviews (i.e., "eNEPA technologies") and authorizations. It would direct the CEQ chair to, among other things, establish data standards and minimum technological functions, require "key permitting agencies" to begin implementing those functions, establish an interconnected federal data system (i.e., "ePermit unified interagency data system") with a common authorization portal, provide public access to certain information, and require "key permitting agencies" to submit biannual reports on the status of meeting the implementation requirements. It would also direct the CEQ chair to develop performance measures for agencies and personnel, authorize contracts supporting implementation, and require annual reports to certain congressional committees.3 It would also amend NEPA to increase the authorization of appropriations from $1 million to $5 million annually.
Summary of provision. Section 1131 would define terms for the federal permitting improvement subtitle including "applicable deadlines," "applicable schedule," "NEPA terms," "tracker," and "transparency project."
Affected U.S.C. citations. Not applicable (N/A).
Summary of provision. Section 1132 would require CEQ, in coordination with the General Services Administration (GSA), to maintain an online database tracking environmental reviews and authorizations for transparency projects. A "transparency project" would be defined in Section 1131 as any proposed agency action requiring an EIS or any proposed agency action requiring an EA that has not been completed by 13 months after the deadline established in Section 107(g) of NEPA, as amended by BAAJA. Entries on the tracker would identify information such as project location, major features, purpose and need, agency contact information, schedule and compliance status, and description of any litigation directly related to the project.
Affected U.S.C. citations. N/A.
Summary of provision. Section 1133 would establish a Permitting Improvement Fund and authorize $20 million annually for FY2027 through FY2033. The fund would be authorized for CEQ's chair to administer for the purpose of "improv[ing] the performance of key permitting agencies with respect to timely environmental reviews and authorizations required under [NEPA]."
Summary of provision. Section 1201 would formally require the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to issue water quality criteria through notice and comment rulemaking. It would specify the judicial review provision applicable to issuance of water quality criteria and regulations defining the scope of "waters of the United States."
Summary of provision. Section 1202 would amend the Clean Water Act (CWA; 33 U.S.C. §§1251 et seq.) Section 401 to narrow the scope of what certifying authorities (typically states) could consider in their water quality certification reviews and the scope of conditions they could include when granting certifications generally. It would further narrow the scope of certification reviews and conditions for certain projects, including interstate transmission line and natural gas pipeline projects. It would also narrow the bases on which certification may be denied and would amend several aspects of Section 401 certification timelines, processes, and judicial review.
Summary of provision. Section 1203 would extend the permit term limit for National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permits from 5 years to 10 years.
Summary of provision. Section 1204 would limit the period of time during which EPA could issue a Section 404(c) "veto" of a Section 404 permit for the discharge of dredged or fill material into waters of the United States. It would extend the permit term limit for Section 404 general permits from 5 years to 10 years. It would specify that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) consideration of environmental effects for general permits be limited to "water quality requirements," which would be newly defined in the bill, and that any adverse effects of discharges of dredge or fill material into less than two acres of waters of the United States would be considered minimal. It would require USACE to maintain certain nationwide permits and would raise the threshold of allowable impacts for coverage under these permits.
Summary of provision. Section 1205 would impose a 150-day statute of limitations for lawsuits challenging Section 404 permits and certain other actions taken pursuant to Section 404 of the CWA. It would limit the availability of judicial review to parties that commented on an issue related to the lawsuit during the public comment period. It would limit the ability of courts to vacate permits or other agency actions found to be unlawful and would require courts to set and enforce specific deadlines for agencies to act on remand.
Summary of provision. Section 1301 would define the terms "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available" under the Endangered Species Act (ESA; 16 U.S.C. §§1531 et seq.).
These terms would
(A) mean all relevant and objective scientific and commercial information available at the time of the agency action; and
(B) include credible and reliable data, quantitative analyses, conceptual and numerical models, and model results that—
(i) account for known or potential sources of error;
(ii) are applied using prevailing principles, methods, tools, and professional standards of practice; and
(iii) are impartially gathered and objectively applied without presumptions or policy prescriptions that bias the application.
Section 1301 would replace "the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands" with "the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands" in the definition of "state."
Summary of provision. Section 1302 would change the deadline for formal consultation under Section 7—which requires federal agencies to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) and National Marine Fisheries Service as to the effects of certain federal actions on listed species and critical habitat—from 90 days to 60 days. It would shorten the time frame for extensions of the consultation period that require only a written explanation to a relevant applicant from 150 days to 100 days. It would also shorten the time frame after which the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce would be required to obtain a relevant applicant's consent for extensions of the consultation period from 150 days or more to 100 days or more.
Section 1302 would authorize a permit or license applicant to sue if the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce and the consulting federal agency propose to extend the consultation period beyond 145 days and do not provide a written statement to or obtain consent from the applicant, as applicable.
Section 1302 would require that Section 7 consultation be finished no later than the date of completion of any NEPA documentation required for the federal action, unless the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce approves an extension due to "extraordinary circumstances beyond the control, and not due to any action, of the consulting parties."
Summary of provision. Section 1303 would provide that any project categorically excluded from NEPA pursuant to Section 1316 of P.L. 112-141 (i.e., projects to be undertaken in existing operational rights of way related to roadways) would be exempt from Section 7 consultation.
Summary of provision. Section 1304 would direct the Secretary of the Interior to establish a program that would allow the Secretary to assign the consultation responsibilities of the Secretary to states, at the state's election, under certain conditions. (This program would apply only to consultations conducted by FWS.)
Section 1304 would not allow for the assignment of consultation responsibilities for projects or other agency actions that exceed the boundaries of a state. If the project or agency action would occur within one state but affect an area outside that state's boundaries, the bill would require the state to consult with the other affected states, if they have assumed consultation responsibilities, or with the Secretary, if the states have not assumed such responsibilities.
Section 1304 would require the Secretary to issue proposed regulations to establish the program and ensure states adequately carry out assumed consultation responsibilities within 270 days of the enactment of BAAJA and a public comment period of not less than 60 days.
Section 1304 would require a participating state to verify, before assuming Section 7 consulting responsibilities, that it (1) had the financial, personnel, and legal resources to carry out Section 7 consultations; (2) waived sovereign immunity for the responsibilities assumed by the state; and (3) provided for public comment on the state application for consultation consistent with the bill's public notice and comment requirements. Section 1304 would require the Secretary to (1) respond to the state in writing if an application to assume consultation responsibilities is denied, identifying the reasons for denial; and (2) provide technical assistance to the state in addressing those reasons, if requested. It would direct the Secretary to approve a state application for consultation responsibilities within 180 days if the Secretary determines that the state demonstrated legal, financial, and personnel capability to conduct consultations; otherwise met the requirements in statute and regulation for the program; and entered into a written agreement with the Secretary that met certain requirements and was executed by the governor or head of the responsible state agency.
Section 1304 would give the district courts of the United States exclusive jurisdiction over any civil action against a state for failure to carry out any responsibility of the state under the program and would direct that such actions be governed by "the legal standards and requirements" that would apply to an action taken by the Secretary.
Section 1304 would authorize a permit or license applicant to elect to consult with the Secretary regardless of state assumption of consultation responsibility.
Section 1304 would direct the Secretary to conduct audits and monitoring of state implementation of the consultation responsibility. It would also require the Secretary to submit an annual report to certain congressional committees.6
Section 1304 would provide for the termination of state assumption of consultation responsibilities by either the Secretary or the state, subject to notice requirements and other criteria.
Summary of provision. Section 1305 would direct any person seeking judicial review of any biological opinion issued by the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce under subsection (b) of ESA Section 7 to do so in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit by filing in such court no later than 150 days after the date on which the biological opinion is made public.
Summary of provision. Section 1306 would require the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce, as applicable, to accept and integrate state-collected data that meet the definition of "best scientific and commercial data available" found in Section 1301 in making determinations to list or delist a species pursuant to the ESA.
Summary of provision. Section 1307 would authorize appropriations of $150 million for each fiscal year from FY2027 through FY2031 to carry out ESA Section 7 and support state participation in the consultation program.
Affected U.S.C. citation. N/A.
Summary of provision. Section 1308 would establish a National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (NFWF) Coastal State Fund to award formula-based grants to coastal states to support programs and activities intended to improve understanding of and use of coastal resources, infrastructure, and ecosystem services.
Section 1308 would authorize appropriations of $50 million for each of the fiscal years FY2028 through FY2032 and would authorize NFWF to use additional amounts as may be available to carry out the program.
Summary of provision. Absent certain exceptions, Section 1401 would prohibit a federal agency from revoking, rescinding, withdrawing, terminating, suspending, amending, or altering a federal authorization or permit in effect on or after September 16, 2026, that is necessary for project construction or "operation at full capacity," or from taking "other action to interfere with or prevent construction or operation at full capacity" of a project that has secured all necessary federal authorizations or permits. Exceptions would include actions directed by court order; violation by the authorization or permit holder of federal law or material breach of permit conditions; fraud in obtaining the authorization or permit; request by the permittee, holder of the federal authorization, or nonfederal project sponsor; and certain measures to protect life, property, national security, or defense. Section 1401 would provide for judicial review of alleged rescission, suspension, or modification of a federal authorization or interference with a fully permitted facility, with remedies to the permit holder, including injunctive relief and a portion of project costs (to be paid from the Judgment Fund).
Summary of provision. Section 1402 would provide a cause of action and remedies for developers of "covered projects" for which federal authorizations or permits were "improperly denied" or "unreasonably delayed" due to "a pattern of disparate treatment," meaning a "substantial increase" in rates of unreasonable delay or improper denial, compared to the preceding five years, that result from "an intentional course of action by the Federal Government to create such a pattern." It would entitle prevailing plaintiffs to injunctive relief, attorneys' fees, economic damages, and additional compensation for costs of construction up to full project costs (to be paid from the Judgment Fund). It would specify what types of projects are "covered" based on listed sectors, resources, and technologies.
Section 1402(c) would establish a one-year deadline for agencies to issue decisions on authorizations for covered projects that do not require an EA or EIS.
Summary of provision. Pending certain exceptions, Section 1403 would provide for judicial review of an agency's failure to comply with a deadline established in Section 1402(c), which requires federal agencies to act within one year of a covered application for a permit or authorization for which an EA or EIS is not required being deemed complete. It would direct reviewing courts to compel agencies to act on applications within 60 days.
Summary of provision. Section 2101 would amend the process by which the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) may issue construction permits for certain interstate electricity transmission lines. It would expand FERC siting authority to include certain offshore and international transmission lines.
Summary of provision. Section 2102 would establish a CE for certain activities to maintain or increase electric capacity on existing electricity transmission, distribution, or associated infrastructure. It would establish a CE for maintenance of, updating, and other activities on existing interstate natural gas pipelines.
Affected U.S.C. citations. The provision would make the following changes to the U.S. Code:
Summary of provision. Section 2103 would direct the Department of Energy (DOE) to issue a report every three years on electricity transmission capacity constraints and congestion. DOE would be required to provide an opportunity for comment to affected states and tribes. Additionally, Section 2103 would provide specific instructions for DOE's study of transmission constraints and congestion in the state of Alaska.
Section 2103 would require certain utilities to participate in regional and interregional transmission planning, with specific elements to be included as part of the transmission planning processes.
Transmission projects selected under a regional or interregional transmission planning process would be considered to satisfy certain criteria needed for a FERC-issued construction permit (as amended by Section 2101).
Summary of provision. Section 2104 would direct FERC to establish procedures by which states could refer utilities to FERC for an investigation into local processes for planning and developing local transmission facilities. Upon receiving a referral, FERC (along with state representatives) would investigate the utility's processes. If the investigative team finds that local processes "are not resulting in the selection of the more efficient or cost-effective local transmission facilities" or "are interfering with the processes of the relevant transmission planning region for planning and developing regional transmission facilities," FERC would be required to issue remedies it determined to be appropriate. FERC remedies could include requiring changes to local processes, reducing the return on equity of the utility, or issuing fines payable to the referring state.
Summary of provision. Section 2105 would prohibit FERC from allowing a federal right of first refusal in its regional and interregional transmission planning regulations.
Summary of provision. Section 2106 would direct FERC to issue a rule requiring transmission planning regions to develop consolidated generation interconnection and transmission planning processes.
Summary of provision. Section 2107 would direct FERC to change its policy regarding how transmission costs are charged to "computational load owner[s]" and "computational load operator[s]," as defined in Section 2107, and direct utilities to implement the revised policy.
Section 2107 would affirm that states have authority to implement certain policies regarding electricity rates for new data centers or high-density computing facilities.
Summary of provision. Section 2108 would require wholesale electricity markets in FERC's jurisdiction to allow participation of qualifying behind-the-meter (BTM) distributed energy system (DES) facilities. "Qualifying BTM DES facility" is defined in Section 2108 as a facility with a rated capacity of not less than five kilowatts that (1) uses an energy storage system, a fuel cell, a generator, or other resource; (2) can be brought online within 15 minutes and the output of which can be controlled by a grid operator; (3) is located behind the meter of a retail customer of a distribution utility; and (4) maintains metering and telemetry capabilities that are sufficient for dispatch and communication. As defined in Section 2108, the metering and telemetry capabilities are not required to include equipment owned or installed by the distribution utility.
Section 2108 would prohibit distribution utilities from interfering with the market participation of BTM resources.
Section 2108 would direct DOE to establish a program to further develop, expand, and support the adoption of a voluntary streamlined permitting and inspection process for authorities having jurisdiction over the permitting of qualifying distributed energy resources. It would authorize appropriations of $20 million annually from FY2026 through FY2031 for the DOE program.
Summary of provision. Section 2109 would direct FERC to require the use of advanced transmission technologies and best-available transmission conductors (to be determined by FERC in consultation with DOE) for new and modified transmission facilities under its jurisdiction.
Section 2109 would direct FERC to require utilities to conduct recurring evaluations related to deploying advanced transmission technologies and to determine penalties for failure to deploy advanced transmission technologies that have a benefit-cost ratio greater than one.
Section 2109 would amend the definition of "advanced transmission technology" to include additional technologies.
Summary of provision. Section 2110 would direct FERC to initiate a rulemaking within one year after enactment of BAAJA to require utilities to share and employ, as appropriate, the use of computing technologies (e.g., artificial intelligence) to expedite interconnection studies.
Section 2110 would direct FERC to reopen the rulemaking at least once every four years to determine whether additional steps are needed to ensure adequate use of advanced computing technologies.
Summary of provision. Section 2111 would direct certain transmission providers to obtain, assemble, maintain, and use "grid data," as defined in Section 2111, for generation or load interconnection studies, facilities studies, feasibility studies, or affected-system studies.
Section 2111 would direct FERC and DOE to publish a reference specification identifying data needed to fully automate interconnection studies, including system impact studies.
Summary of provision. Section 2112 would direct power marketing administrations to develop compensation plans for employees. Plans would be required to meet specified criteria and be reviewed and updated, as appropriate, annually by the power marketing administrator.
Summary of provision. Section 2113 would require FERC, at least every five years, to review whether its fees and charges are sufficient to allow it to expediently handle its workload. It would require FERC to submit a report on the review and results to certain congressional committees.9
Summary of provision. Section 2114 would define "data center entity" to mean
an end-user, or group of co-located end-users, the primary purpose of which is to house computing, networking, or data storage equipment used to process, store, or transmit digital data, including equipment used for—
(A) artificial intelligence training or inference;
(B) cloud computing or data hosting; or
(C) cryptocurrency mining or other distributed-ledger or digital-asset computation.
Section 2113 would also direct the U.S. Energy Information Administration to collect electricity demand information from those entities.
Summary of provision. Section 2115 would make conforming amendments and specify that nothing in Division B, Title I, of BAAJA grants FERC authority over retail electricity sales or the local distribution of electricity.
Summary of provision. Section 2201 would create a 150-day statute of limitations to seek judicial review of a covered authorization, which includes "lease sales, permits, rights-of-way, or plans required to explore for, develop, or produce energy or minerals" under specified statutes for specified infrastructure and fuels reduction projects. It would provide "expedited" consideration for judicial review of a decision to grant or deny an authorization; provide for expedited treatment by the agency of the authorization on remand (if ordered); and treat supplemental or revised NEPA documents as separately reviewable actions from the grant or denial of an authorization.
Summary of provision. Section 2211 would exclude oil and gas activities from the requirement to obtain an approved federal application for permit to drill (APD), provided the well is located on nonfederal land and (1) the federal government owns less than 50% of the subsurface estate, (2) the well overlies a nonfederal mineral estate but the wellbore enters and produces from the federal mineral estate, or (3) the wellbore traverses but does not produce from the federal mineral estate. It would prohibit the Secretary of the Interior from imposing certain requirements (e.g., bonding) on leases that meet these criteria. This exclusion from requiring an APD would not apply to Indian land as described in this section. Section 2211 would require federal mineral lessees to submit copies of state APDs to the Secretary of the Interior if activities would "impact or extract oil and gas owned by the Federal Government."
Summary of provision. Section 2112 would authorize a Tribe to grant rights-of-way across its tribal land without approval by the Secretary of the Interior provided that the Tribe issues regulations approved by the Secretary governing the Tribe's process to grant rights-of-way. It would require the tribal rights-of-way regulations to meet certain criteria, such as including an environmental review process.
Summary of provision. Section 2213 would establish various deadlines related to applications for rights-of-way under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) for renewable energy development, including notifications of completeness or incompleteness, grants or denials, and steps to be completed by applicants or federal agencies. It would require the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture to each develop or adopt one or more CEs for certain low-disturbance activities related to renewable energy development.
It would require the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to promulgate renewable energy project review standards to be adopted by regional renewable energy coordination offices.
Summary of provision. Section 2214 would require the Secretaries of the Interior and Agriculture to each develop or adopt one or more CEs covering activities related to the placement of electricity transmission or distribution lines or certain modifications of existing transmission or distribution facilities and associated infrastructure. The CE would apply to activities within existing right-of-way corridors or on previously disturbed or developed land.
Summary of provision. Section 2215 would allow for proprietors of mines to locate and include as many mill sites from public land as "reasonably necessary" for their plan of operations. These mill sites would convey no mineral rights, and claim holders would be required to pay an updated annual claim maintenance fee of $400 per site.
Section 2215 would amend the definitions of and references to "hardrock minerals" in existing mining laws, including adding hardrock minerals to the list of deposits subject to leasing.
Section 2215 would direct claim maintenance fees collected from mill sites and receipts from leases of hardrock minerals into the newly established Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund in the Treasury. The fund would carry out the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program established via Section 40407 of Title VII of P.L. 117-58.
Summary of provision. Section 2221 would require the Secretary of Agriculture (for National Forest System land) and the Secretary of the Interior (for public lands) to each develop a CE for geothermal observation test projects.
Affected U.S.C. citations. The provision would make the following change the U.S. Code:
Summary of provision. Section 2222 would revise the timeline for calculating royalty rates for geothermal energy production. The timeline would be based on the in-service date of individual turbines (as new turbines may be added to a site as separate operating units) instead of being based on the initial in-service date of the site as a whole.
Summary of provision. Section 2223 would require BLM to hold geothermal lease sales every year instead of every two years, where there are nominated lease parcels. It would establish deadlines for considering geothermal drilling permit applications, notifying applicants of incomplete applications or of steps needed to complete the permit review, and approving or deferring decisions pending completed reviews.
Summary of provision. Section 2224 would create a BLM ombudsman, appointed by the Secretary of the Interior, to work with the BLM director, various BLM offices, and other federal entities to facilitate geothermal energy permitting. It would create a task force, headed by the ombudsman, to coordinate with Department of the Interior (DOI) offices and staff to support geothermal permitting. The ombudsman would be required to submit an annual report to certain congressional committees that describes the activities of the task force and the effectiveness of the permitting process during the preceding year.11
Summary of provision. Section 2225 would exclude geothermal exploration and production activities on nonfederal land from being required to obtain a federal permit, provided the federal government owns less than 50% of the subsurface estate and the activity is authorized by a state permit. This exclusion would not apply to Indian land as described in this section.
Affected U.S.C. citations. The provision would make the following change to the U.S. Code:
Summary of provision. Section 2226 would require any federal authorization related to a geothermal lease application to be approved and issued or denied within 60 days of the Secretary of the Interior having completed all requirements under federal law, including environmental review. Pending civil court actions would not alter this requirement unless a federal court vacated or provided injunctive relief for the authorization.
Summary of provision. Section 2227 would allow the Secretary of the Interior to require an applicant or holder of a geothermal lease to reimburse the United States for all reasonable costs relating to processing an application and for administrative actions related to permitting, as well as for inspecting and monitoring activities. Within five years after enactment of BAAJA, the Secretary would have to submit a report to certain congressional committees on the effects of this section and any recommendations for reauthorization of it, taking into consideration feedback from the geothermal industry and others.12
Summary of provision. Section 2228 would require the Secretary of the Interior to identify standard procedures and guidelines for efficient and environmentally responsible geothermal leasing and permitting and to publish an updated handbook—the "Gold Book"—reflecting any changes. It would also direct the Secretary to rename the Gold Book as appropriate and to update it at least once every five years.
Summary of provision. Section 2229 would revise an existing CE that applies to certain low-disturbance oil and gas activities to include the same activities for geothermal energy. It would extend the time period in which a previous right-of-way corridor approval allows the CE to apply to a pipeline placement, and it would allow for the similar application of the CE to the placement of transmission or distribution lines to serve geothermal development.
Summary of provision. Section 2231 would require FERC to issue a report on hydropower market barriers to certain congressional committees.13 In preparing the report, FERC would be required to solicit public input by convening a technical conference and providing an opportunity for public submission of written comments on the draft report.
Summary of provision. Section 2232 would amend the section of the FPA that grants FERC the authority to issue hydropower licenses by adding that the conditions of a license for a reservation are to be reasonably related to the effects of the project.
Summary of provision. Section 2233 would amend the FPA to direct FERC to require prior approval of a "substantial alteration or addition" to a hydropower project. FERC approval would not be required for an alteration or addition that is pursuant to the findings of the rulemaking described in this section.
Section 2233 would require FERC to undertake a rulemaking to establish (1) the standards for determining a "substantial alteration or addition,'' ''nonsubstantial alteration or addition,'' and ''routine maintenance, repair, or replacement'' to a hydropower project; and (2) a formal process for determining whether a proposed alteration or addition constitutes a ''substantial alteration or addition."

Pensacola, Florida – Akeem Cornell Shaw, 39, of Pensacola, Florida, was sentenced to six and a half years in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to possession of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and cocaine with intent to distribute, possession of firearms in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense, possession of firearms by a convicted felon, and possession of a short- barreled rifle. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office, with support from our federal law enforcement partners, continues to strike back against the armed criminals flooding our streets with drugs. As this defendant has learned, my office is committed to aggressively prosecuting drug-peddling criminals, and we’ll continue to do so until we deliver the safe, drug-free communities that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that law enforcement executed a search warrant at the defendant’s residence in February of 2025. During a search of the defendant’s bedroom, investigators located three firearms, one being a short-barreled rifle, fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, ammunition, and other items indicative of drug distribution. The defendant has multiple prior felony convictions and cannot legally possess firearms and ammunition.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Jessica S. Etherton.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

EPA Finalizes First-of-Its-Kind Air Quality Plan to Promote Clean Air and Facilitate Economic Growth in Maricopa County
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) took a historic step by approving a first-of-its-kind air quality rule that will enable the building and expansion of manufacturing, power plants, and other critical industries without increasing emissions in Maricopa County, Arizona. Known as “Rule 205,” Maricopa County’s Air Quality Department’s innovative air regulation will unlock a new source of emission reduction credits (ERCs) for businesses to offset emissions, as is required for the area under the Clean Air Act (CAA). By providing a new avenue for businesses to be able to build in the County, while still meeting federal air requirements, EPA is working in partnership with Maricopa County to bring new economic investment and good-paying jobs to the community. The final action proves once again that there does not have to be a binary choice between protecting the environment and growing the economy.
“When states, that know their economies and environment best, come up with a creative way to grow their economies while working within environmental requirements, EPA should work with them to get it across the finish line. The Trump EPA is proud to approve this commonsense win for Maricopa County and businesses throughout the area,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. “EPA will continue to work with our regulatory partners to find ways to protect our environment while making sure regulations work under real world conditions.”
“Maricopa County has developed a practical, market-based tool that allows business to build and expand while keeping Clean Air Act protections in place,” said EPA Pacific Southwest Regional Administrator Mike Martucci. “EPA’s approval of Rule 205 reflects our commitment to working with local partners to support economic growth and protect health in Arizona.”
Portions of Maricopa County are currently designated as “Moderate” nonattainment for the 2015 Ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). As a result, major stationary sources, including power plants and manufacturing facilities, must obtain a preconstruction permit from the County and offset any increase in emissions, per the CAA, to build or expand in a nonattainment area. Today’s final action will allow mobile source owners and operators who permanently reduce nitrogen oxide or volatile organic compound emissions to trade those reductions as ERCs to stationary sources wishing to build or expand in the County’s nonattainment area. Historically, ERCs have only been generated and traded between stationary sources. However, EPA has found that this new plan meets statutory requirements under CAA section 173 and will enable the stationary sources to meet all CAA building requirements for an area in “Moderate” nonattainment for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS. EPA does not expect this rule to increase air emissions in the area.
The Trump EPA firmly believes its local and state regulatory partners are best positioned to understand the unique needs of their regions. Through this final action, Maricopa County and Arizona have worked within federal requirements to find a unique, market-based regulatory structure that meets the area’s economic and environmental needs. Through cooperative federalism, the Trump EPA worked with Maricopa County and Arizona to promote prosperity while fulfilling the agency’s core mission of protecting human health and the environment.
Background
In October 2026, while in Maricopa County, Administrator Zeldin a second innovative air quality rule by Maricopa County, Rule 204, covering ERCs from nonroad engines.
On March 23, 2026, EPA finalized a determination not to reclassify the Phoenix-Mesa area from “Moderate” to “Serious” nonattainment under the 2015 NAAQS. Consistent with CAA section 179B, EPA found that the Phoenix-Mesa area would have met federal ozone air quality standards by its August 3, 2024, deadline had it not been for emissions coming to the area from outside the United States.
Under the CAA, EPA established the 2015 Ozone NAAQS at 70 parts per billion.

WASHINGTON – Deaundre Blount, 33, of the District, was found guilty today in connection with his role in a violent multi-state robbery crew that targeted pharmacies and cell phone stores in the District, Maryland, Virginia, and New Jersey, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

Following about a week of trial, a federal jury deliberated for only a few hours before finding Blount guilty of all counts: Conspiracy to Interfere with Interstate Commerce by Robbery (Hobbs Act Robbery), Conspiracy to Distribute and Possess with the Intent to Distribute Controlled Substances from the pharmacy robberies, and three individual counts of Hobbs Act Robbery.

“This defendant was a member of a violent robbery crew that terrorized pharmacy employees and retail workers from Virginia to Northern New Jersey, showing no regard for the safety of workers or the communities they harmed,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Today’s guilty verdict demonstrates that if you’re in a predatory crew you will be identified, prosecuted, and brought to justice.”

“This defendant was a member of a violent robbery crew that terrorized pharmacy employees and retail workers from Virginia to Northern New Jersey, showing no regard for the safety of workers or the communities they harmed,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Today’s guilty verdict demonstrates that if you’re in a predatory crew you will be identified, prosecuted, and brought to justice.”

U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson scheduled sentencing for March 2, 2027.

According to court documents, from May 9, 2020, through May 26, 2021, Blount and his co-conspirators targeted pharmacies and cellular retail stores in the mid-Atlantic region, seeking to rob the businesses of prescription drugs and cellphones that they could then resell in the District.

Blount was found guilty in connection with his role in three of the robberies: the May 9, 2020, robbery of the Walgreens Pharmacy on State Road 33, in Neptune, New Jersey; the June 8, 2020, robbery of a CVS Pharmacy on E. Joppa Road, in Nottingham, Maryland; and the June 9, 2020, robbery of a T-Mobile store on Baltimore Avenue, in College Park, Maryland.

Surveillance photo of the May 9, 2020, robbery of the Walgreens Pharmacy in Neptune, NJ.

Multiple co-defendants already have been sentenced.

Conspiracy co-leader, Ashley Gause, 33, of the District, was sentenced on October 13 to 140 months for conspiracy to interfere with interstate commerce by robbery (Hobbs Act Robbery), conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances from the pharmacy robberies, and eight individual counts of Hobbs Act Robbery.

Conspiracy co-leader D’Marrell Mitchell, 36, of the District, was sentenced June 18 to 192 months for conspiracy to interfere with interstate commerce by robbery (Hobbs Act robbery), of conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, and of nine counts of Hobbs Act Robbery.

Floyd Neal, 32, of the District, was sentenced to 157 months in prison after pleading guilty to multiple counts of interstate commerce by robbery and possessing a firearm during a drug trafficking offense.

Ashawntea Henderson, 33, of the District, was sentenced to 57 months in prison after pleading guilty to interference with commerce by robbery and aiding and abetting.

Glenn Dolford, 32, of the District, who pleaded guilty to one count of interference with interstate commerce by robbery, was sentenced to 38 months to be served concurrent with a 42-month sentence out of DC Superior Court Case for an aggregate term of 80 months. Dolford is also serving a 22-year sentence for murder.

Terrance Branham, 36, of the District, was sentenced to 78 months in prison for conspiracy to commit Hobbs Act Robbery, conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, one count of Hobbs Act Robbery, and one count of carrying a firearm during a crime of violence.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Washington Field Office Violent Crimes Task Force with valuable assistance from the Metropolitan Police Department, Alexandria Police Department, Anne Arundel County Police Department, Baltimore County Police Department, Henrico County Police Division, Laurel Police Department, Montgomery County Police Department, Neptune Township N.J. Police Department, and Prince George’s County Police Department.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Levy and Michael Lee.

Surveillance photo of the June 9, 2020, robbery of the CVS in Nottingham.

ABERDEEN PROVING GROUND, Md. — The U.S. Army Communications-Electronics Command held a hybrid worldwide town hall on Oct. 28 to update the workforce on senior leadership transitions, civilian personnel policies, technological modernization, and upcoming performance management milestones.
CECOM Executive Director Nicholaus Saacks led the town hall alongside Command Sgt. Maj. Jay High and Command Chief Warrant Officer 5 Kevin Banks. Jacob Grenoble of the CECOM G-1 personnel directorate also addressed employees regarding the annual appraisal and contribution cycle.
Welcoming incoming leadership
Opening the town hall, Saacks discussed the command's upcoming leadership changeover. On Nov. 16, Brig. Gen. Marne Sutten will assume command of CECOM during a ceremony at Aberdeen Proving Ground.
"I’m thrilled to be here as your executive director, but the thing I’m most excited about is that I will soon go back to being the deputy to the commanding general," Saacks said, encouraging personnel at the installation and across global operating locations to attend or tune in to welcome Sutten and her family.
Workforce policies: Hiring freeze, maxi-flex, and reasonable accommodations
Saacks addressed key civilian personnel topics following recent policy updates from higher headquarters. Although Department of the Army guidance formally announced the end of the civilian hiring freeze, Saacks cautioned that hiring remains constrained by full-time equivalent authorization caps. However, the change permits CECOM to move away from temporary details and begin filling permanent positions.
Regarding work schedules, the ongoing maxi-flex pilot program will run through the end of the calendar year. Saacks encouraged participating supervisors and employees to submit feedback to help leadership strike the right balance between workplace flexibility and operational mission requirements.
In alignment with revised Army regulations, CECOM is also standardizing internal processes under the command's equal employment opportunity office. Standard accommodation requests will continue to be handled at the direct supervisory level. High-impact requests, such as full-time telework exceeding six months, substantial equipment expenditures, or formal job reassignments, will require approval from senior executive service or general officer leadership.
Sustaining the fight: 'How the Army Fights' and Soldier honors
High praised the workforce's reputation across Army Materiel Command before showing a video debuted at the recent Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting titled "How the Army Fights." High underscored that CECOM’s command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and medical mission supports all four Army warfighting focus areas — convergence, strike, close battle, and endurance.
"What we're doing for the C5ISR community layers through every single one of those four buckets," High said. "More importantly, we are solidly in the endurance bucket, sustaining all things that we do to sustain the fight."
High also recognized Spc. Kwesi Cook of the U.S. Army Medical Materiel Center-Europe, who represented the command in the AMC Best Squad Competition at Fort Benning, Georgia, noting his recognition alongside his family during AUSA.
Modernization priorities: AUSA takeaways
Banks summarized key observations from the AUSA gathering in Washington, which drew more than 40,000 defense attendees and 750 industry exhibits, and noted how senior defense leaders placed an emphasis on accelerating the fielding of autonomous, space-enabled, and first-person-view drone capabilities directly to operational units.
CECOM also showcased its own technical initiatives at AUSA, including the Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Maintenance tool, where command representatives conducted 15 targeted senior-leader engagements. Banks also mentioned a scheduled visit to Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, to align AIAM with Project Meridian, an Army G-4 effort modernizing legacy sustainment systems.
Citing praise from the Secretary of the Army for low code and application programming interface development, Banks detailed how Project Gatekeeper aims to compress software authority-to-operate approval timelines from several months to only a couple of weeks.
"That's a significant milestone for the Army — getting software integrated into our systems a lot faster than we've traditionally done," Banks said.
G-1 update: AcqDemo and evaluation timelines
Grenoble provided a broad overview of ongoing civilian appraisal cycles, highlighting the transition of AcqDemo pay pools to an organization-based structure designed to ensure greater consistency and equity across subordinate elements and staff sections. Grenoble added that overall performance recognition will be bolstered by an expanded Department of the Army Civilian awards funding pool, giving leadership greater flexibility to reward high performance throughout the command.
SES notes and legal awards
The town hall concluded with the presentation of awards and honors. Saacks recognized Civilian employees Morgan King, Drew Rehkop, and Hector Rodriguez, who were selected to attend the Army War College, as well as command legal personnel who were formally recognized as recipients of the annual AMC Attorney Awards.
"You're making a difference every single day," Saacks said in closing remarks. "We're in a great spot, and I can't wait for our incoming commander to see all the great work you are doing."
title: CECOM town hall highlights leadership transitions, workforce initiatives, and modernization priorities

COLUMBUS, Ohio – A Texas man was sentenced in federal court here today to 360 months in prison for exploitation crimes related to traveling to Ohio to have sex with a minor he met online playing Call of Duty.

In February 2025, Harrison Michael Barton, 39, of North Detroit, Texas, took a 31-hour Greyhound bus trip from Florida to Coshocton County to sexually exploit a 15-year-old girl he met online approximately one month prior.

“Barton was a registered sex offender who traveled the country to commit crimes against a minor he met online,” said U.S. Attorney Dominick S. Gerace II. “He is a predator, and his history makes clear that he poses a grave and ongoing threat. My Office will never stop pursuing those who prey on children. We will prosecute these cases to the fullest extent of the law and seek multi-decade sentences like the one Barton received today.”

Barton was arrested at the John Glenn Columbus International Airport while attempting to fly to Florida with the victim.

At the time, Barton was wanted on an outstanding parole warrant out of Texas stemming from a prior conviction for online solicitation of a minor, in which he was sentenced to 10 years in prison.

Barton admitted that, in this instant case, the teenager picked him up in Newcomerstown, Ohio. Prior to arriving at the airport, the defendant admitted to engaging in sexual conduct with the minor and to taking sexually explicit pictures of the victim.

Barton pleaded guilty in February 2026 to sexual exploitation of a minor and attempted kidnapping of a minor.

Dominick S. Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio; Jason Cromartie, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cincinnati Division; Coshocton County Sheriff Christopher Walters; Newark Police Chief Erik McKee; and John Glenn Columbus International Airport Police Chief Ronald Gray announced the sentence imposed today by U.S. District Judge Edmund A. Sargus, Jr. Assistant United States Attorneys Emily Czerniejewski and Jennifer M. Rausch are representing the United States in this case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice (DOJ) to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and DOJ Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, visit www.justice.gov/psc .

# # #
title: Repeat sex offender who rode bus from Florida to Ohio to sexually exploit teenager he met online gaming sentenced to 30 years in federal prison

JOINT BASE SAN ANTONIO-FORT SAM HOUSTON, Texas (Nov. 4, 2026) – Brooke Army Medical Center’s Pediatric Intensive Care Unit reopened Oct. 19, almost a year after it closed on Halloween 2025.
“I’m so proud of all the work the members of the PICU team have done to bring this capability back to BAMC,” said Col Kevin Kelly, BAMC’s commander. “They never gave up on the idea that they could come back. They knew how vital a PICU is to our patients and they all continued their efforts to get us to where we are today.”
A shortage of PICU nurses forced the unit to close in 2025. Several factors contributed to the scarcity of available nurses, including deployments, extended military schools and training, and a hiring freeze that prevented BAMC from hiring civilian replacements. Because PICU nurses require specialized training, BAMC could not reassign nurses from other areas to fill in the gaps.
“A lack of staffing can kill a PICU,” said Army Lt. Col. Marcus Burgess, BAMC’s chief of critical care nursing services. “A PICU’s ability to thrive is based on physician services; but their ability to survive is based on nursing services.”
Since the closure, BAMC’s PICU leadership has strengthened nurse staffing by adding civilian PICU nurses and pairing them with military nurses. Combining military and civilian staff helps maintain adequate staffing when military members deploy or are sent on training or actual missions outside of BAMC.
Air Force Maj. Hannah Gale, the PICU medical director, said the PICU also supports training functions within BAMC. Along with supporting pediatric graduate medical education and surgical services, the PICU gives BAMC’s pediatric residents more complete training.
Kimberly Bogue, the PICU’s interim clinical nurse officer in charge, said there are numerous benefits to having a PICU at BAMC.
“The PICU keeps patients here at BAMC instead of us having to send them elsewhere,” Bogue said. “We support the operating rooms. Some surgeries require the availability of a PICU to complete and for patients to have follow-on care.”
BAMC’s in-house PICU allows parents of pediatric patients to stay with their children. Also, pediatric patients can receive follow-on care in the same location, Bogue said. This helps both patients and families with continuity of care.
“This is a benefit to children with chronic medical conditions,” said Air Force Maj. Kayla Rondina, chief of child nursing services. “If patients and their parents know our staff, this becomes more of a welcoming environment for them.”
According to Rondina, pediatric patients with chronic medical conditions face a higher risk of ICU admission and readmission and they tend to stay longer. Having access to BAMC’s PICU lets patients stay with their same providers and nurses instead of having to go to other medical facilities for one set of care and a different one for ICU-type care. This lessens stress on the whole family because they are in a welcoming environment with familiar people.
PICU staff also assist Exceptional Family Member Program beneficiaries. Young EFMP patients often need specialized care , and military families need access to treatment facilities with certain capabilities – capabilities that BAMC’s PICU can provide.
The newly reopened PICU received its first two inpatients just a couple of days after reopening. Janet Castillo brought in her five-year-old daughter, Marilyn Rivera Castillo, for upper respiratory issues. When she came in, Janet didn’t know the PICU was open. She brought her daughter to the emergency department early in the morning. Doctors there determined Marilyn needed additional care and admitted her into the PICU.
“I feel good knowing that this type of care is available,” Janet said. “I was scared when I brought her in because I didn’t know what was happening. Now that we are here (in the PICU), I am comfortable knowing that she is receiving the best care here at BAMC, and it’s even better that I can stay with her.”
title: BAMC Pediatric Intensive Care Unit reopens

CAMP HUMPHREYS, South Korea — Garrison leaders, project partners, and future residents gathered Nov. 4 for a ribbon-cutting ceremony to officially open Barracks Building P-6852, a modern facility designed to enhance Soldier quality of life and operational readiness.
The five-story building features 302 private bedrooms, 151 shared kitchens, and laundry facilities on every floor. Building P-6852 is one of three new barracks projects representing a combined investment exceeding $120 million, along with $2.5 million dedicated to furnishings. The facility will exclusively house Soldiers assigned to the 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade.
Sgt. Maj. Atarius Henley, the 2nd Infantry Division/ROK-U.S. Combined Division G-4 sergeant major, noted that modern housing reflects the Army's ongoing commitment to troops stationed abroad.
“This building provides a place where Soldiers can come and they can recover,” Henley said. “They can have a place that they can call home for the time that they’re here. It shows our commitment to our Soldiers, to American sons and daughters, and to our readiness as an Army force.”
For junior enlisted personnel moving from older barracks, the facility provides an immediate upgrade in living standards and communal areas. “I’m really grateful for the opportunity to be moving into a fresh barracks,” said Pfc. Lindsay Anderson, an aviation Soldier with the 4th Battalion, 2nd Aviation Regiment, 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade. “I’m happy that leadership put in the time and effort for all the enlisted Soldiers.”
The opening underscores a continuous garrison commitment to providing safe, well-equipped accommodations that directly bolster troop welfare and mission capability across Camp Humphreys.
title: New barracks facility opens at Camp Humphreys

This report provides information on selected federal agencies that provide grants, technical assistance, training or other support targeted to state and local law enforcement agencies. This report also provides information on selected grant and loan programs with broader purposes that could potentially be used for law enforcement purposes.
Law enforcement agencies frequently contact congressional offices for information on federal assistance for a wide range of agency needs. This report provides information on selected federal agencies that provide grants, technical assistance, training, or other support targeted for state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies. It also provides information on selected grant and loan programs with broader purpose areas that could potentially fund activities related to law enforcement and public safety. Current program availability and areas of focus may depend on several factors, including appropriations, the priorities of Congress and the Administration, and award cycles. Monitoring funding opportunities through these agencies can help congressional staff track available funding for their constituents' projects.
Funding from the grant programs described in this report can be provided through formula or discretionary grant programs. Federal formula grant programs allocate funds to eligible entities (often state and local governments), which in turn may issue subgrants or contracts with other entities. Federal discretionary grant programs make awards to eligible entities directly on a competitive basis.1
This report provides resources that can help congressional staff access information for their constituents on funding via federal agency websites. Where applicable, program websites are included. This list should not be considered comprehensive.
The Office of Justice Programs (OJP), the Office of Violence Against Women (OVW), and the Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS) Office are the three agencies that administer DOJ's grant programs.2
OJP is the largest of DOJ's three grant administering agencies and administers the widest portfolio of public-safety-related grant programs. OJP is comprised of six bureaus and agencies that are responsible for administering certain portfolios of grant programs.3 The Bureau of Justice Assistance (BJA) within OJP administers the broadest range of programs, including many focusing on law enforcement. Grant opportunities recently available from BJA include support for rural police departments, immigration enforcement, law enforcement agency accreditation, forensic science improvements, and violence prevention. BJA grant opportunities have also been available for purchasing certain equipment and other support for law enforcement agencies, including body-worn cameras, fentanyl and methamphetamine detection equipment, and canines.
The largest source of federal funding to state and local law enforcement is through the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant Program (JAG)4 administered by BJA. States and some local governments are eligible to apply for JAG grants.5 Funding must be used for purposes related to one of the 11 programs areas,6 including hiring personnel, purchasing equipment and supplies, information systems, and training, among others.
For more information see https://www.ojp.gov/funding/explore/current-funding-opportunities.
The COPS Office provides grants and information to advance the practice of community policing by the nation's state, local, territorial and tribal law enforcement agencies.7 Grants awarded by the COPS Office are used to hire law enforcement officers; develop and test innovative policing strategies; and provide training and technical assistance to community members, local government leaders, and all levels of law enforcement.8
For more information see https://cops.usdoj.gov/grants.
OVW administers grant programs to "address domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking, support victims and survivors, and hold offenders accountable."9 Some OVW grants are targeted to support law enforcement agencies, and others are open to state and local government agencies, which could include law enforcement.
For more information see https://www.justice.gov/ovw/funding-opportunities.
LESO's 1033 program allows the transfer of excess DOD equipment that might otherwise be destroyed to law enforcement agencies within the United States and territories. Participation in the program requires approval by a state's governor and a memorandum of understanding regarding the requirements of program participation.
The program allows for the transfer of controlled and uncontrolled property. Controlled property includes small arms and personal weapons, night vison equipment, and demilitarized vehicles and aircraft. These items are on loan to agencies and must be returned when no longer being used.
Uncontrolled property consists of general use items that could be sold to the public. Examples include computers, digital cameras, first-aid kits and supplies, and sleeping bags. When transferred to a law enforcement agency, the equipment becomes property of the law enforcement agency and does not have to be returned to DOD.
According to DOD, most of the equipment issued to local law enforcement is uncontrolled.10
For more information see https://www.dla.mil/Disposition-Services/Offers/Law-Enforcement/
For state coordinators see https://www.dla.mil/Disposition-Services/Offers/Law-Enforcement/State-Coordinators/
The following programs are administered by a range of federal agencies and are not specifically for law enforcement agencies, but they could be used to support various activities related to public safety.
The Department of Homeland Security's (DHS's) Homeland Security Grant Program is administered by the Federal Emergency Management Administration and provides grants to state, local, tribal, and territorial entities to assist in preventing, protecting against, mitigating, responding to, and recovering from acts of terrorism and other threats. Funds may be used for organizing and planning training, scenario-based exercises, equipment purchases, and management costs.
For more information see https://www.fema.gov/grants/preparedness/homeland-security.
The U.S. General Services Administration's (GSA's) Office of Personal Property Management helps state and local government agencies and nonprofits acquire surplus federal property, which may include office equipment, furniture, and vehicles, among other items.
For additional program information see https://www.gsa.gov/buy-through-us/government-property-for-sale-or-lease/personal-property-for-reuse-and-sale/for-state-agencies-and-public-organizations.
The Public Benefit Conveyance Program allows surplus federal land, buildings, and military bases closed under Base Realignment and Closure to be conveyed to public entities at no cost. Eligible applicants for this property include states or political subdivisions or instrumentalities of states that propose to use the property for law enforcement or correctional facility purposes. Applications for these purposes are submitted to DOJ to ensure that the properties meet the statutory requirements for law enforcement or correctional use. DOJ also ensures that potential environmental impacts are assessed under the National Environmental Policy Act. Once DOJ approves the application, it is forwarded to GSA or DOD for consideration. Final approval is determined by the agency owning the property.
For more information see https://bja.ojp.gov/program/public-benefit-conveyance-program/overview.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Community Facilities Direct Loan and Grant Program provides affordable funding and grants to develop essential community facilities in rural areas.11 Funds can be used to purchase, construct, and/or improve essential community facilities; purchase equipment; and pay related project expenses. Examples of essential community facilities related to public safety include fire departments, police stations, prisons, police vehicles, fire trucks, and public works vehicles or equipment.
For more information see https://www.rd.usda.gov/programs-services/community-facilities/community-facilities-direct-loan-grant-program.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development's CDBG program provides funds to address a wide range of unique community development needs. CDBG-funded activities must be tied to one of three national objectives: (1) principally benefit low/moderate-income persons, (2) aid in preventing or alleviating blight, and/or (3) address some kind of "imminent threat" to health/safety. Crime prevention and public safety may be considered an eligible public service activity. Certain police equipment and facilities may be eligible for funding under the Public Facilities and Improvements category of the program. Funds are administered at the state and local levels.
For more information see https://www.hudexchange.info/programs/cdbg/
Several agencies support training and technical assistance activities and training centers to aid law enforcement agencies in preparing for and responding to issues such as terrorist threats, hate crimes, and active shooters, as well as crime prevention, conflict resolution, and officer safety and wellness efforts.
The BJA NTTAC provides access to resources for free training and technical assistance to law enforcement agencies, prosecutors' offices, corrections departments, and city or county commissioners on a wide variety of criminal justice issues. Examples of available training and technical assistance programs include critical response training, forensic science support, peer support for police, and survivor programs for families of officers killed in the line of duty. Training can be provided in person or virtually.
For more information see https://bja.ojp.gov/training-technical-assistance.
OJJDP's NTTAC provides no cost training and technical assistance to juvenile justice practitioners, providers, and communities. Topics covered include combating gangs, mentoring youth, preventing violence, reducing youth drug use and more.
For more information see https://ojjdp.ojp.gov/national-training-and-technical-assistance-center.
The focus of this BJA initiative is to improve officer safety, wellness, and resiliency. The program provides comprehensive training on officer safety, suicide prevention, and resiliency. Services are provided at no cost.
For more information see https://bja.ojp.gov/program/valor/overview#3-0.
BJA's SLATT program offers free targeted training to law enforcement on terrorism and violent extremism. Programs focus on providing law enforcement with the necessary skills and knowledge to prevent, detect, and investigate attacks.
For more information see https://www.slatt.org/.
The COPS office oversees the CRI-TAC program, which provides a variety of no-cost resources, training, and technical assistance to state, local, territorial, and tribal law enforcement agencies. Topics are identified by participating agencies based on local needs.
For more information see https://cops.usdoj.gov/critac.
The DOJ Community Relations Service provides free training, consultation, mediation, and other support to law enforcement agencies to improve community relations, conflict resolution, and cultural awareness.
For more information see https://www.justice.gov/crs.
In conjunction with the International Association of Police Chiefs (IACP), MVAI assists law enforcement agencies in communities that have experienced incidents of mass violence. The program offers peer-to-peer support to law enforcement leaders from professionals who have also experienced mass violence incidents. Teams include law enforcement leadership, faith-based and community representatives and psychological service providers. Services are free to communities in need.
For more information see https://bja.ojp.gov/program/mass-violence-advisory-initiative/overview.
OSLLE coordinates and partners with state, local, tribal, territorial, and campus law enforcement agencies to disseminate information and ensure two-way communication regarding the formulation of DHS policies, programs, initiatives and operations. OSLLE issues guidance and conducts compliance reviews focused on terrorism prevention activities funded through DHS grants.
For more information see https://www.dhs.gov/office-state-and-local-law-enforcement.
title: Connecting Constituents to Federal Assistance for Law Enforcement
