Rep. Joe Neguse Announces Candidacy for Assistant Speaker
Washington, D.C. — Today, Colorado Congressman Joe Neguse announced his candidacy for the position of Assistant Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Neguse currently serves as Assistant Democratic Leader, and at Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ request, served as Chair of House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force in the 119th Congress.
If elected, Neguse will become the youngest lawmaker in the history of the Congress to assume the role of Assistant Speaker, a position previously held by leading voices in the Democratic Party, including Whip Katherine Clark and Senator Ben Ray Luján.
In a letter sent to his colleagues, Neguse cited efforts to ensure voices from across the House Democratic Caucus are uplifted, included, and heard. He pointed to the broad constituency of his own large congressional district in the Rocky Mountain West—spanning rural, suburban, and urban areas—as a demonstration of this ability. The millennial Congressman, 42, is the only non-coastal member of senior House Democratic leadership, and the youngest member of the team.
Neguse also highlighted his team’s work to expand support for Members, specifically by assisting new Members with their transition to Congress, enhancing staff assistance programs, and assessing and addressing the needs of congressional offices across the country. He also pointed to his successful efforts as Chair of the Litigation Task Force as an example of how he would continue to use his leadership skills to assist Committee leaders and fellow Members in fighting back against the Trump administration’s rampant lawlessness.
During the 119th Congress, the Litigation Task Force was responsible for taking unprecedented steps to stand up for the American people, filing dozens of legal challenges in federal courts across the country and paving the way for judges to strike down disastrous and unconstitutional directives from the Trump White House, including illegal tariffs, restrictions on voting by mail, stripping individuals born on U.S. soil of the guarantee to birthright citizenship, and unlawful impoundments of taxpayer funds.
Read Neguse’s entire letter to his colleagues HERE and below.
November 5, 2026
Dear Colleague:
It has been an honor to serve as Assistant Democratic Leader, and to work alongside each of you during the 119th Congress. I remain deeply inspired by the talent, commitment, and tenacity our caucus has consistently shown. With our decisive and overwhelming victory this week, it is more important than ever for the House Democratic Caucus to be unified in the 120th Congress, and to repay the faith that the American people have put in us to lower costs, end corruption, and deliver for working families. To that end, and as we embark on that road together, I write to respectfully request your support for Assistant Speaker.
I’m deeply grateful to have had the opportunity to serve our caucus in House Leadership, mostly recently as Assistant Democratic Leader and previously as a Co-Chair and Chairman of the DPCC, DCCC Recruitment/Red-to-Blue Co-Chair and National Finance Co-Chair. In each position, I’ve worked to engage everyone in our caucus, firmly rooted in my belief that every member has much to offer to the House and to the country. As someone who represents a large rural, suburban, and urban district (with agricultural communities extending all the way to the Wyoming border), I’ve long worked hard to effectively serve a broad constituency — and I’ve adopted that same approach as a member of the leadership team, ensuring voices from across our caucus and the ideological spectrum are elevated, included, and heard.
As Assistant Leader, my focus has been on serving our caucus — by expanding opportunities for members, enhancing staff assistance programs, and ensuring our office is addressing your technical needs. With your help, we launched the successful New-Member ADL Mentorship Program to assist new members with their transition to the Congress. We also worked to uplift each and every member of the broader caucus, including through monthly ADL press conferences and corresponding special order programming — elevating your talents and expertise for the benefit of the country. And through our office’s management of House Democrats’ District Director Services Program, our team has worked to assist your District staff with their everyday needs, including via our weekly roundtables, technical assistance programs, annual Conference & Fly-In, and the new District Director Mentoring program we launched earlier this year.
Finally, at the request of Leader Jeffries, I was proud to serve as Chair of the Litigation Task Force for House Democrats, and in so doing, provide Members with opportunities to weigh-in on over twenty lawsuits against the Trump Administration's lawlessness. From our successful amicus briefs in multiple cases, our groundbreaking lawsuit against ICE, and regular programming opportunities for member engagement with legal experts, I’m deeply grateful to the many members of our caucus who made the Task Force’s work so consequential and impactful. And with your support, I would be honored to continue that work with each of you and our talented Committee leaders in the 120th Congress.
If elected Assistant Speaker, my goals would be straight-forward — to prioritize direct member services for every member of our diverse and talented caucus, and to assist Speaker Jeffries and our incredible Democratic Leadership team. In addition to continuing the existing programming of the Assistant Leader’s Office, I’d relish the opportunity to launch multiple new programs, including expanding training programs for our District Directors, launching a new technical assistance program for subcommittee chairs, and enhancing the mentorship and transition programming for new members. All in all, I believe such efforts will ensure that every member and their office has the resources they need to succeed.
In sum, it has been such a privilege to work alongside each of you over the past several years, and it would truly be an honor to serve our caucus, the Congress and the country as Assistant Speaker. I look forward to continuing the conversation with you about my candidacy and ideas, and thank you so much for your consideration.
Sincerely,
###
title: Rep. Joe Neguse Announces Candidacy for Assistant Speaker

Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Two-Year Sentence for Distributor of Cocaine and Fentanyl in Seattle Homeless Encampments
Defendant Possessed Firearm While Distributing Drugs in the Chinatown International District and the "Jungle"
SEATTLE – A 46-year-old Seattle man was sentenced late yesterday in U.S. District Court in Seattle to two years in prison for his role in a drug trafficking organization that sold cocaine and fentanyl in Seattle homeless encampments and in the Chinatown International District. Sang Su has been in custody since his arrest in August 2025. Su was heard on a wiretap investigation discussing cocaine distribution and obtaining ‘samples’ of fentanyl powder. At the sentencing hearing U.S. District Judge Tana Lin said, “It is aggravating that you were selling significant amounts of cocaine and fentanyl to some of the most marginalized members of our community.”
“Drug traffickers who distribute fentanyl and cocaine to vulnerable communities put lives at risk and fuel addiction, violence, and instability,” said Robert A. Saccone, Special Agent in Charge, DEA Seattle Field Division. “Sang Su’s role in this organization helped extend the reach of these dangerous drugs and threatened public safety. DEA remains committed to working alongside our federal partners through the Homeland Security Task Force to dismantle drug trafficking organizations, hold those responsible accountable, and protect our communities as we work toward a Fentanyl Free America.”
“Our goal with the Homeland Security Task Force is to remove dangerous criminals from our community – especially in neighborhoods that have been disproportionately victimized like the Chinatown International District.” said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd. “Whether you are a low-level distributor or a high-volume dealer, we will prosecute you. Mr. Su was a repeat offender selling drugs while armed and preying on the vulnerable population in the international district. He has earned his time in prison which will hopefully break his cycle of crime.”
“As a redistributor, Mr. Su contributed to the high volumes of deadly and addictive drugs this drug trafficking organization poured into our most vulnerable communities,” said W. Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Seattle field office. “He directly interacted with the group leader and further endangered the public by possessing a loaded firearm to protect the proceeds of the trafficking. The FBI and our partners will continue to hold each of these conspirators, and others like them, responsible for the damage they do to our communities.”
According to records filed in the case, in 2023, after incidents of drug trafficking-related violence in and around homeless encampments in Seattle’s Chinatown-International District and the greenbelt adjacent to Interstate-5, commonly known as the “Jungle,” the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”) and the Seattle Police Department (“SPD”) began a narcotics trafficking investigation into individuals distributing controlled substances in these areas.
On May 29, 2025, law enforcement executed 16 search warrants in Federal Way, Vancouver, Everett, Pacific, Tukwila, Kent, Issaquah, Seattle, Woodlake California and Beaverton, Oregon. Investigators seized more than seven kilograms of cocaine, 18 kilograms of methamphetamine, more than 57,000 fentanyl pills, and 17 firearms. They also seized more than $353,000 in cash.
Sang Su was not arrested during the execution of the May 2025 warrants and was sought by law enforcement until his arrest on August 18, 2025.
Sang Su was initially contacted by law enforcement as part of the investigation in October 2024. Su had just made a drug purchase from the organization leader at a market on Beacon Hill in Seattle when he was stopped by law enforcement and the drugs and a firearm were seized from his car.
Su pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance on July 2, 2026.
In asking for a 30-month sentence, prosecutors noted that Su had ignored police interventions that could have put him on a better path writing, “However, between 2002 and 2025, Su had multiple contacts with law enforcement, which include multiple arrests for assault, controlled substances violations, and carrying loaded firearms. While these arrests were either later dismissed or charges were never filed, it is concerning the number of contacts that Su has had with the criminal justice system. Despite benefiting from charges never being filed or later being dismissed, these law enforcement interventions failed to curtail Su’s criminal acts.”
Judge Lin ordered Su to be on three years of supervised release following prison.
The investigation was led by the FBI, Seattle Police Department and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with significant assistance from the Internal Revenue Service - Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program (HIDTA), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and Washington National Guard Counterdrug Program. Investigators also worked with the Oregon State Police and Clark County, Washington Sheriff’s Office.
This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Seattle comprises agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), The United States Marshals Service (USMS), the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), the Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigations (IRS-CI), the United States Secret Service (USSS), U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the U.S. Coast Guard Investigative Service, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington.

U.S. Marshals Arrest Richmond Man Wanted for Child Assault Charges
For immediate release
Wesley Watkins, Deputy U.S. Marshal
LEXINGTON, Ky. – U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) Central Kentucky Fugitive Task Force (CKFTF) on Tuesday arrested a man wanted for second-degree assault, domestic violence (child) and criminal abuse/neglect first-degree- child under 13 years of age.
An arrest warrant was issued Tuesday for Daniel Keate, 37, out of Madison County by the Richmond Police Department after a forensic interview with Keate’s two children. Keate allegedly squeezed his 5-year-old daughter’s rib cage on Aug. 13 to the point it caused severe pain and was later confirmed by UK Children’s Hospital to have resulted in a broken rib.
The USMS CKFTF adopted the warrant upon issuance due to the violent nature of the offense.
During the fugitive investigation CKFTF developed information that Keate had traveled from London and was possibly at an apartment in the 100 block of Logan Court in Berea. While conducting surveillance operations investigators developed information that confirmed Keate was at the address.
CKFTF executed an operational arrest plan at Logan Court and Keate was taken into custody without incident with the assistance of the Richmond Police Department in the evening of Nov. 3. 
The U.S. Marshals Service provides assistance and expertise to other federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies in support of their fugitive investigations and apprehending violent offenders.

SCRANTON - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Scotch Bruce Hanning, age 46, of Selinsgrove, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on November 3, 2026, to 204 months’ imprisonment by Chief United States District Judge Matthew W. Brann for possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine base (crack), in both Snyder and Union Counties, and elsewhere.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, on January 3, 2023, law enforcement conducted a traffic stop on Hanning in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania. A search of Hanning’s person revealed 1.89 grams of fentanyl, .79 gram of buprenorphine, and 3.50 grams of crystal methamphetamine. A police canine alerted to narcotics in the vehicle and 3.98 grams of fentanyl, 4.1 grams of cocaine base (crack), and 13.9 grams of crystal methamphetamine were discovered. Law enforcement then obtained a search warrant for the property in which Hanning was living where they recovered .32 gram of cocaine base and .14 gram of fentanyl.

The FBI Philadelphia’s Scranton Resident Agency, the Pennsylvania State Police, and the Lycoming County Narcotics Enforcement Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Luisa Honora Berti prosecuted the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA; S. 5653) was introduced on September 30, 2026. The bill, as introduced, contains seven titles within two divisions that aim to reform certain federal environmental review and permitting processes to expedite a wide range of project types, with an emphasis on energy-related projects.
Some Members of Congress have shown interest in amending the nation's permitting laws to facilitate energy production and expedite a variety of projects and actions (e.g., transportation infrastructure, energy, data center development, ecological restoration, and water conveyance). Some bills have addressed permitting requirements under the Endangered Species Act (ESA; 16 U.S.C. §§1531-1544), notably Section 7 consultation under the act. For example, H.R. 1897 in the 119th Congress would narrow the scope for consultation and potentially increase exemptions from Section 7 consultation.
The ESA aims to conserve species in danger of or threatened with extinction that are listed as endangered or threatened under the act. Species of animals and plants can be listed under the ESA as either endangered or threatened, according to an assessment of the risk of their extinction. Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (ESA; 16 U.S.C. §1536) requires federal agencies to ensure that actions they undertake, authorize, or fund are not likely to jeopardize threatened or endangered species (i.e., listed species) or adversely modify designated critical habitat for listed species. Section 7 generally requires federal agencies to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) (in the Department of the Interior) or the National Marine Fisheries Service (in the Department of Commerce) when their proposed actions may affect listed species or critical habitat.
This report analyzes the provisions in BAAJA specific to the ESA (Division A, Title III of BAAJA). These provisions include sections that would define "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available" (Section 1301) to mean all existing scientific and commercial information available at the time of the agency action and to include data, analyses, and models that are applied using existing standards of practice and without presumptions or policy prescriptions that bias the application. Sections 1302 and 1303 would shorten timelines for consultation and exempt certain transportation projects from consultation. Section 1304 would authorize the Secretary of the Interior to establish a program that would allow states to take on the consultation responsibilities of the Secretary if they can verify that they have the financial, personnel, and legal resources to carry out Section 7 consultations, among other factors. This section would apply to consultations done by the FWS and to projects and actions that occur within the boundaries of a state. Section 1305 would amend judicial review for biological opinions issued during consultation. Section 1306 would allow for state data to be accepted and integrated into species listing or delisting determinations pursuant to the ESA. Section 1307 would authorize $150 million in appropriations for Section 7 consultation and the state program authorized under Section 1304 from FY2027 to FY2031. In addition, "project certainty" provisions in BAAJA (Division A, Title IV) would prohibit a federal agency from removing, terminating, suspending, amending, or altering certain federal authorizations or permits (including an applicable biological opinion or incidental take statement) in effect on or after September 16, 2026, absent certain exemptions. Such provisions could have implications for Section 7 consultation under ESA, notably for changing or amending a biological opinion and incidental take statement.
BAAJA is organized according to two divisions:
This report examines the following sections in BAAJA specific to the ESA (Division A, Title III):
The report provides an overview of the ESA and background on parts of the ESA that would be addressed by BAAJA. The report then summarizes provisions that BAAJA would amend or add to the ESA, compares each ESA-related provision in BAAJA to existing law, and analyzes selected changes to the ESA that the bill would make if enacted. Further, the report discusses the potential implications of Section 1401 of BAAJA on the ESA Section 7 consultation process.
The ESA aims to conserve species in danger of or threatened with extinction that are listed as endangered or threatened under the act.1 Under the ESA, it is the policy of Congress that all federal agencies shall seek to conserve threatened and endangered species, use their authorities in furtherance of the ESA, and cooperate with state and local agencies to resolve water resource issues in concert with conserving endangered species.2 The ESA is administered by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) and the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) (together, the Services).3 Domestic and foreign species of animals (both vertebrate and invertebrate) and plants can be listed under the ESA as either endangered or threatened, according to an assessment of the risk of their extinction.4 Listing determinations are to be made "solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available."5 When a species is listed, the ESA directs the Services—"to the maximum extent prudent and determinable"—to simultaneously designate critical habitat for the species based on the "best scientific data available," accounting for economic impacts, national security impacts, and any other relevant impacts.6 Once a species is listed, the act provides tools to aid its conservation and recovery and to protect the species and its habitat. Among these tools are the ESA's prohibition on take (e.g., killing or harassing) of and other activities involving endangered species without a permit; its requirement that the Services extend such prohibitions by regulation to threatened species as they deem "necessary and advisable" for the species' conservation; and its requirement that federal agencies, in consultation with FWS or NMFS,7 as applicable, ensure their actions are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or result in destruction or adverse modification of designated critical habitat.8
The BAAJA addresses several components of the ESA, namely the meaning of "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available," Section 7 consultation, and judicial review. An overview of these concepts under current law is provided below.
Pursuant to statutory requirements, the Secretary (of either the Interior or Commerce depending on the species) must decide whether to list species based only on the best available scientific and commercial data, using information to which the agency has access and information obtained from the public through the agency rulemaking process.9 The statute does not define the phrase "best available scientific and commercial data," and the Services have not interpreted this phrase through regulation. The Services are also directed to use the best available scientific and commercial data to make several other determinations under the ESA, for example designating critical habitat,10 formulating a biological opinion (BiOp) during Section 7 consultation,11 and delisting a species.12
Section 7 of the ESA requires federal agencies to ensure that their discretionary actions,13 including authorizing (e.g., issuing a permit) or funding actions of nonfederal parties, are "not likely to jeopardize the continued existence" of any endangered or threatened species or adversely modify or destroy critical habitat.14 Federal agencies undertaking actions (action agencies), whether directly or through federal approvals, permits, or funding for nonfederal parties,15 must consult with the Services, as appropriate, if those actions might affect a listed species or designated critical habitat. This process is referred to as Section 7 consultation (consultation). Action agencies are, in the first instance, to evaluate possible effects of proposed projects on listed species or designated critical habitat. For major construction activities, this evaluation is known as a biological assessment (BA). If the action agency concludes that the action may adversely affect listed species or critical habitat, it initiates formal consultation with the Services. The Services' goal in conducting formal consultation is to determine whether the agency action is likely to jeopardize listed species or adversely modify or destroy their critical habitat and, if so, whether there are reasonable and prudent alternatives (RPAs) that would avoid those outcomes. To conclude formal consultation, the Services publish a BiOp articulating their findings with respect to jeopardy and RPAs. So long as the Services determine the action is not likely to jeopardize listed species or there are RPAs, the Services issue an incidental take statement (ITS) with a BiOp authorizing a certain amount of unintentional (i.e., incidental) take expected to result from carrying out the action.16 If that number is exceeded, the action agency must reinitiate consultation.17 According to a study, the majority of consultations result in no jeopardy opinions, and nearly all of the rest identify RPAs that permit the action agencies to go forward with the proposed actions.18
The Services generally must conclude consultation within 90 days of receiving an action agency's request for consultation, unless the Services and the action agency mutually agree to a longer period.19 For consultations involving a nonfederal party (e.g., a permit applicant), the 90-day period may be extended up to an additional 60 days without the nonfederal party's permission; the Services and action agency are to provide the nonfederal party with a written explanation for the delay, any information required to complete consultation, and the estimated time frame for completion.20 The Services and action agency must obtain the nonfederal party's permission to extend the consultation beyond 150 days from its initiation.21
The ESA does not specify a particular venue or time frame for legal challenges to BiOps issued by the Services under Section 7. Instead, Section 11(c) assigns federal district courts jurisdiction over "any actions arising" under the ESA, which would include challenges to BiOps.22 Section 706 of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) supplies the standards of review for challenges to BiOps issued by the Services.23 Such actions are subject to a six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. §2401(a).
Table 1Table 1.
Table 1. Summary of Selected Provisions of BAAJA as Introduced that Would Amend or Address the Endangered Species Act (ESA)
Sources: S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), and the Congressional Research Service.
Notes: ESA = Endangered Species Act.
a. For example, see FWS and NMFS, Endangered Species Consultation Handbook: Procedures for Conducting Consultation and Conference Activities Under Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act, March 1998, Chapter 2, pp. 2-16 at https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/endangered-species-consultation-handbook.pdf.
BAAJA's ESA-related provisions propose several amendments to the ESA and would change aspects of its implementation. This section discusses selected changes to the ESA proposed by BAAJA and provides related stakeholder perspectives and potential congressional considerations. The BAAJA provisions discussed include Section 1301 on the definition of the phrases "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available," Section 1304 on the state assumption of consultation responsibilities, and Section 1305 on judicial review. Section 1401, which may affect the ability to modify or revoke BiOps and ITS under Section 7 of the ESA, is also discussed in this section.
BAAJA would add a definition of the phrases "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available." The phrases would be defined to mean
all relevant and objective scientific and commercial information available at the time of the agency action; and include credible and reliable data, quantitative analyses, conceptual and numerical models, and model results that account for known or potential sources of error; are applied using prevailing principles, methods, tools, and professional standards of practice; and are impartially gathered and objectively applied without presumptions or policy prescriptions that bias the application.24
Some stakeholders contend that this definition would "raise the evidentiary burden" for protecting listed species under the ESA by lowering the ability of FWS and NMFS to make decisions accounting for scientific uncertainty.25 Some other stakeholders assert that this definition would allow project applicants to work from a "standard set of facts" when completing Section 7 consultations.26
While "best scientific and commercial data available" and "best scientific data available" lack a statutory definition in the ESA as currently enacted, the federal courts have construed these terms for decades. As a general matter, courts have held that these phrases require the Services to consider scientific and commercial data available at the time the agency makes its decision,27 prohibit the Services from ignoring available studies even if they discount or discredit such studies,28 and do not require an action agency to conduct new tests or generate new data that do not already exist.29 Some courts have also held that these phrases include a "benefit of the doubt in favor of the species" under conditions of uncertainty,30 but other courts have rejected this reading of the phrases.31 The Supreme Court has never explicitly addressed whether the best available science standard includes a "benefit of the doubt" or presumption. In the 1997 case Bennett v. Spear, the Court appeared to cast doubt on interpreting the phrase to include that kind of presumption.32 The Court wrote, albeit discussing a separate legal issue, that the purpose of the best available science standard
is to ensure that the ESA not be implemented haphazardly, on the basis of speculation or surmise. While this no doubt serves to advance the ESA's overall goal of species preservation, we think it readily apparent that another objective (if not indeed the primary one) is to avoid needless economic dislocation produced by agency officials zealously but unintelligently pursuing their environmental objectives.33
Given the disagreement among courts about the existence of any kind of presumption or benefit of the doubt in favor of the species, it is difficult to predict whether the definition proposed in BAAJA would meaningfully change the kind of data the Services are required or permitted to incorporate into some of their decisions under current law. Under one interpretation, the definition would limit the Services' ability to adopt a presumption favoring species protection in situations where data are lacking. Whether this would be a change from current law is contested.34 The ESA itself contains no explicit language supporting a presumption in favor of species protection in all cases of uncertainty, and even courts that have adopted the "benefit of the doubt" standard demand that the Services justify their decisions based on the particular strengths and gaps in the data relevant to a particular species.35 There appears to be little to no support in case law applying the ESA for a reflexive presumption in favor of the species in every instance of uncertainty about the future survival of a species.
Members of Congress may have various considerations related to this proposed definition. For example, Members may consider whether this definition would restrict, maintain, or improve the quality and availability of data currently used to make decisions under the ESA. Congress might question whether this definition would change current practices related to collecting and applying the best scientific and commercial data available. Specifically, Members could consider whether this definition would clarify, standardize, or improve the quality of data used to make decisions under the ESA. Members also may consider whether the definition should be changed to apply solely to the data collected, analyses, and models, as compared to the Services' application of that data to decisionmaking.
BAAJA would require the Secretary of the Interior to establish a program that would allow states to assume the responsibility for Section 7 consultations (consultation) under the ESA for projects and actions within their state boundaries.36 States would apply to the Secretary to assume consultation responsibilities under the program and would have to verify that they have the financial, personnel, and legal resources to carry out consultation.37 States in the program would take on the role of FWS for consultation regarding potential impacts on species managed by FWS and would have to adhere to Section 7's requirements. States would also have to waive sovereign immunity for consultation responsibilities, meaning that their actions pursuant to the assumption of Section 7 consultation could be challenged by private citizens in federal court. Licensees or permittees involved with federal agencies for consultation would have the choice of whether to consult with the state or FWS. The Secretary would conduct audits of states participating in the program for the first four years and monitor the program thereafter. The Secretary or the state may terminate the delegation of consultation responsibilities, subject to certain notice and other requirements.
Some stakeholders assert that this program would give states a larger role in consultation.38 Further, some in favor of the bill contend that states might have a better understanding of listed species and their critical habitat within their state, and a better understanding of how proposed actions affect species and critical habitat, compared with FWS.39 Other stakeholders who oppose this program contend that there would be inconsistency among states handling consultation for projects and actions that affect the same species. They assert that this may lead to varying levels of protection for the same species located in different states.40 Further, some argue that states do not have the expertise, financial resources, or personnel to handle Section 7 consultation.41 Some of the same stakeholders contend that states may be pressured to favor economic interests over the protection of listed species when conducting consultations.42 Further, these stakeholders assert that states might be pressured to defer to local interests when conducting consultations.43 For example, some developers might contend that some states could show bias against development when carrying out a consultation program, using consultation to place onerous conservation measures on proposed actions related to projects that would affect listed species and critical habitat.
Some critiques of the proposed program noted above are broadly addressed by BAAJA. The bill would require states to verify that they have the financial, legal, and personnel resources to conduct consultations.44 Further, the bill would direct the Secretary to conduct outreach, education, and capacity building to support state consultation efforts.45 The Secretary would also be directed to audit and monitor the program, which could provide the Secretary the opportunity to conduct oversight over how states are handling consultation responsibilities and whether the states' resources are adequate in practice.46 The bill would further give the Secretary the option to terminate a state's assumption of consultation responsibilities if the state is not adequately carrying out its responsibilities, subject to certain conditions. The Secretary may clarify the details of how the program is implemented within regulations required by the bill.47
Congress may consider several questions about establishing a program that allows states to take over consultation responsibilities from the Secretary of the Interior. Members may consider how many states are willing to enter such a program and whether those states would have sufficient resources to conduct consultations. States that consider entering the program might weigh the costs of consultation against the benefits. For example, conducting consultations could require greater financial and personnel resources from states than already exist. Further, states would be required to waive sovereign immunity and could be sued due to their consultations. In contrast, states may welcome the opportunity to consult on species within their boundaries and prescribe conservation measures that balance their perceived needs for conservation and development. Congress might also consider expanding this program so that consultations of projects and actions on species addressed by the Secretary of Commerce could also be done by states.
Members may question whether this program would increase or decrease the time it would take to complete consultations. Having states responsible for certain consultations could lower the burden for completing consultations on FWS and potentially lower consultation times. However, if states lacked the expertise or institutional knowledge for conducting consultations, or if states needed to consult with neighboring states or FWS, delays could ensue. The bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to conduct training and outreach to states, which might increase states' capacity to conduct consultations.
Members also may consider whether states can and would conduct informal consultations as part of assuming consultation responsibilities.48 According to one study, informal consultations greatly outnumber formal consultations under Section 7.49 If states are unable to conduct informal consultations in an efficient manner, license and permit applicants might opt to conduct consultations with FWS, particularly if FWS has an established process for conducting informal consultations. This option would not be given to federal agencies consulting with participating states under BAAJA.
The ESA does not specify a particular venue for legal challenges to BiOps issued by the Services under Section 7; instead, 16 U.S.C. §1540(c) assigns federal district courts jurisdiction over "any actions arising" under the ESA. BAAJA Section 1305 would assign challenges to BiOps issued by the Services to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. Challenges to federally issued BiOps would have to be brought within 150 days after the publication of the BiOp.
With respect to challenges to BiOps issued by state authorities, the bill would assign jurisdiction to the U.S. federal district courts where projects are located. Under BAAJA Section 1304(e)(2), claims challenging state compliance with the ESA would "be governed by the same legal standards and requirements that would apply" in an action against the Secretary of the Interior had the Secretary issued the BiOp. BAAJA Section 1304 includes no explicit statute of limitations for claims brought against states, unlike BAAJA Section 1305, which would require claims against the Secretary to be brought within 150 days of the BiOp being made public. It is possible this means actions challenging state BiOps could be subject to the standard six-year statute of limitations under 28 U.S.C. §2401(a). However, it is also possible that the provision in BAAJA Section 1304 imposing the same "legal standards and requirements" on suits against states as would apply in a suit against the Secretary could effectively import the 150-day filing limit for federal BiOps from BAAJA Section 1305, if a court determined that such time limit were a "legal standard or requirement." Because that determination would likely be made by federal district courts considering challenges to state actions, it is possible that courts in different circuits could draw different conclusions.
Title IV of BAAJA, titled "Project Certainty," contains provisions that could affect ESA implementation. Among other things, BAAJA Section 1401 would prohibit a federal agency from revoking, rescinding, withdrawing, terminating, suspending, amending, or altering a BiOp or ITS, or other applicable federal authorization or permit in effect on or after September 16, 2026. This prohibition would be subject to five statutory exceptions.50 Further, BAAJA Sections 1402 and 1403 would generally require federal agencies to render a decision on certain complete applications for federal authorizations or permits within one year after the date on which the latest of the covered applications is deemed to be complete. This requirement would apply to federal authorizations or permits for which an environmental impact statement (EIS) or environmental assessment (EA) is not required.51 It would apply to actions that require a BiOp but not an EIS or EA. This may include projects or actions where the scope or magnitude of the action's impact may be considered minor, or projects or actions that are granted categorical exclusions under the National Environmental Policy Act.52 Environmental analysis under Section 7 consultation typically is still required for determining any potential impacts of the activity on ESA-listed species.53 Sections 1401-1403 of BAAJA would provide for judicial review of the application of any exception, of any "improperly denied" authorization, or of an agency's failure to comply with a one-year decision deadline. Under particular circumstances, the bill would provide remedies to the permit holder or applicant, including injunctive relief and monetary damages up to the full project costs in certain situations.
Under regulations promulgated pursuant to the ESA, the Services must reinitiate formal consultation or reissue a BiOp under certain circumstances.54 Reinitiation of consultation is triggered by any one of four possibilities: (1) when the amount or extent of take specified in an incidental take statement is exceeded; (2) new information on the species or the action shows an effect on the species or its critical habitat that was not considered in the BiOp; (3) the action was sufficiently modified that it would cause an effect on species or critical habitat not considered in the BiOp; or (4) the listing of a new species or designation of critical habitat that may be affected by the action.55 In addition to the Services reinitiating consultation, legal challenges to BiOps may result in court orders requiring changes to or reissuance of a BiOp.
Although BAAJA Section 1401 would generally prohibit an agency from amending a federal authorization, several exceptions contained in the provision may apply to the reinitiation of consultation or to court orders requiring amendments to a BiOp. BAAJA Section 1401 likely would not limit agency action pursuant to a court order, nor would its prohibitions likely apply where a permit holder (in this case, the holder of an ITS) violates the terms of the permit or otherwise violated federal law. BAAJA Section 1401 also would allow for otherwise prohibited action by the agency if it is needed to prevent "specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage to life, property, national security or defense" in light of new information not considered in the environmental review process or final agency action. These exceptions likely would permit the Services to amend and reissue a BiOp pursuant to a court order or where the take of listed species has exceeded (i.e., violated) the limits set out in the ITS. It is unclear, however, whether the other triggers for reinitiation of formal consultation could fall within the exception for urgent harm.
Regarding reinitiation and the urgent harm exception, some stakeholders suggest that BAAJA might prevent the reinitiation of consultation for a BiOp addressing a project or action that meets the conditions under Section 1401.56 If damage to life and property is considered to include damage to the species and critical habitat, reconsultation could occur. However, some stakeholders have raised concerns that these circumstances may not specifically include environmental harm;57 others collectively summarize these exemptions under the classification of "significant newly discovered risks" or "urgent harm."58 Some stakeholders with mixed views of the provision note that it is intended to provide more durability and predictability for projects that have received federal approvals (e.g., wind and renewable energy projects; pipelines) and to prevent politicized revocation of approved projects.59 Others have expressed concerns about potential effects to the use of adaptive management approaches, such as in BiOps.60 Relatedly, some also note that agencies would be responsible for establishing an exception based on specific evidence, which some may interpret as agencies specifying particular factors requiring reinitiation of consultation.61
Members may consider how the project certainty language in BAAJA (as introduced) may affect reinitiation of Section 7 consultation for projects and actions, and other provisions or regulations of the ESA. Congress might consider whether these provisions would prevent or allow reinitiation of consultation if there were a change in a project or action if a newly listed species or newly designated critical habitat were affected by the project or action. Members may also consider if Section 1401(b) of BAAJA would restrict or allow for changes to a BiOp if "such action is necessary to prevent specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage to life." The terms "life" and "harm" are undefined in BAAJA.62 Further, Members may consider if the Services' lack of a definition for harm under the ESA and its regulations may affect implementation of BAAJA's project certainty provisions with respect to any allowable changes to a BiOp.63 Such considerations may include whether the use of the term "harm" would apply to factors triggering reinitiation of consultation. Congress also may examine how BAAJA's proposed limitations for modifying or revoking a BiOp or ITS may affect ESA provisions allowing for an exemption of Section 7 consultation requirements by the Endangered Species Committee (ESC).64 For example, in a March 2026 decision, the ESC (composed of multiple federal agency representatives) granted an exemption from the requirements of the ESA for agency actions analyzed in a 2025 NMFS BiOp and in 2018 and 2025 FWS BiOps based on matters related to national security.65 Members may consider the degree to which national-security-related exemptions under BAAJA might apply to this type of situation.
Members may consider the potential advantages of including project certainty provisions, such as the benefits of formalizing guardrails to limit an Administration's ability to prevent a federally approved project from occurring or to broadly modify the terms of a given permit. Members also may weigh how these project certainty directives might allow for efficiencies in evaluating future proposed projects by constraining recurrent agency attention on previously approved projects.
title: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA): Analysis of Endangered Species Act Provisions

text:
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P)
Overview
On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued the Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) proposed rule. This rule proposes regulatory revisions to the Conditions of Participation (CoPs), Conditions for Coverage (CfCs), and Requirements for Participation for Medicare- and Medicaid-participating providers and suppliers (collectively referred to as CoPs). These revisions would reduce costs, increase transparency, enhance flexibility for providers to deliver innovative patient care, and streamline existing regulations. It also proposes to rescind certain Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers.
Background
CMS conducted a comprehensive review of the CoPs for all 21 provider and supplier types, as well as some payment policies, to identify opportunities to reduce administrative burden while maintaining patient safety and quality care. The agency identified obsolete, outdated, and excessively burdensome regulations that CMS proposes to eliminate or reform to enhance the effectiveness of facility operations and reduce unnecessary burden or other costs, with a particular focus on freeing up resources that healthcare providers could otherwise use to improve patient health and safety. Collectively, CMS estimates the proposals would save $320 million, returning more than 3.26 million hours of staff time to providers.
This proposed rule would alleviate unnecessary regulatory burden through deregulation in the following ways:
Hospitals
- Remove the staff training requirements for transfer protocols and emergency services readiness (both currently effective), and obstetric (OB) care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027).
- Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027).
- Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by hospitals that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons.
Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs)
- Remove the staff training requirements related to emergency services readiness (currently effective) and OB care (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027).
- Remove the OB care-specific Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements (otherwise effective Jan. 1, 2027).
- Propose to establish new requirements regarding patients’ rights related to birth tissue collection by CAHs that provide OB care services, including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious, or personal reasons.
- Revise regulations to clarify current CMS policy that CAH distance eligibility determinations are based on proximity to hospitals that provide acute care inpatient services or another CAH.
- Implement new statutory requirements to allow CAHs that meet certain qualifying criteria, as defined by the statute, to be exempt from the distance eligibility requirements.
Long-Term Care (LTC) Facilities
- Remove the COVID-19 vaccine requirements related to educating staff about the benefits and risks, offering the vaccine, and documenting these actions.
- Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for residents.
- Remove the continuing respiratory illness data reporting requirement while retaining the requirement for specific reporting during a future Secretary-declared public health emergency (PHE).
- Modify the requirement for LTC facilities to provide a state ombudsman with notice of resident transfers related to emergent care.
- Revise the requirements for the active involvement of representatives of direct care staff in conducting the LTC facility assessment.
- Revise the physical environment requirements to exempt existing facilities from the room occupancy and bathroom facility standards.
Intermediate Care Facilities for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (ICFs/IID)
- Remove the requirements related to educating staff about the COVID-19 vaccine and its benefits and risks, offering it to them, and documenting these actions.
- Streamline the remaining COVID-19 vaccine requirements for clients.
Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs)
- Remove expired COVID-19 and seasonal influenza reporting requirements related to ongoing data reporting and staff vaccination.
- Remove REH data reporting requirements during a PHE.
Physical Environment
Life Safety Code (LSC) and Health Care Facilities Code (HCFC) Updates and Emergency and Standby Powers Systems (ESPS) Codes
- Adopt the 2024 editions of National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) LSC and HCFC and the 2022 edition of the ESPS Codes.
Outside Window or Door Requirement
- Remove the requirement that patient care areas have access to natural light and ventilation through exterior windows and doors for hospitals, CAHs, and other providers with similar regulations (Religious Nonmedical Health Care Institutions, LTC facilities, ICFs/IID and hospice inpatient care facilities).
Waiver Authority
- Codify in the regulations CMS’ authority to permit facilities to comply with specific provisions of a newer edition of the LSC or HCFC.
Medicaid Payment Transparency for Nursing Facilities and ICFs/IID
- Rescind the following Medicaid institutional payment transparency reporting requirements to reduce burden for states and institutional providers:
  - The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for direct care workers,
  - The percentage of Medicaid payments for nursing facility services spent on compensation for support staff, and
  - The percentage of Medicaid payments for ICFs/IID services spent on compensation for support staff.
Comment Solicitations
CMS is including comment solicitations in this proposed rule to obtain input from interested parties related to the following topics:
- Allowing LTC facility residents to opt-out of having a discharge notice sent to the state ombudsman office;
- Strategies to minimize burden for hospitals and CAHs to comply with ongoing respiratory illness and PHE infectious illness data reporting requirements;
- Approaches to allow flexibility for providers regarding the requirement for physician supervision of certified registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs);
- Expanding the scope of practice of physician assistants and nurse practitioners providing care in LTC facilities, especially as it pertains to performing visits currently required by a physician;
- Revising criteria for transplant program initial certification to reduce barriers to entry for new transplant programs while maintaining patient safety and ensuring the transplant program’s competence; and
- Future policies to address Medicaid institutional workforce shortages and strengthen the institutional workforce.
View the final rule on the Federal Register at: https://www.federalregister.gov/public-inspection/2026-22812/medicare-and-medicaid-programs-cutting-administrative-requirements-for-excellence-in-patient-care.
title: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Cutting Administrative Requirements for Excellence in Patient Care (CARE) (CMS-3484-P)

ALBUQUERQUE – Today, the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico announced its immigration enforcement statistics. These cases are prosecuted in partnership with the El Paso Sector of the U.S. Border Patrol, along with Homeland Security Investigations El Paso, and assistance from other federal, state, and county agencies.

In the four-week period ending October 30, 2026, the United States Attorney’s Office brought the following criminal charges in New Mexico:

249 individuals were charged with Illegal Reentry After Deportation (8 U.S.C. 1326)

27 individuals were charged with Alien Smuggling (8 U.S.C. 1324)

139 individuals were charged with Illegal Entry (8 U.S.C. 1325)

285 individuals were charged with Illegal Entry (8 U.S.C. 1325), violation of a military security regulation (50 U.S.C. 797) and Entering Military, Naval, or Coast Guard Property (18 U.S.C. 1382), arising from the newly established National Defense Area in New Mexico.

Many of the defendants charged pursuant to 8 U.S.C. 1326 had prior criminal convictions for drug trafficking, assault with a deadly weapon, disorderly conduct, unlawful weapons possession, domestic violence by strangulation, possession of a stolen vehicle, robbery, burglary, larceny, counterfeiting, child abuse, aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, criminal damage to property, narcotics trafficking, alien smuggling, and prior immigration offenses.

These cases are part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

These statistics represent prosecutions by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico only. The numbers do not include individuals apprehended by immigration enforcement officials and subjected solely to administrative process.

Under current leadership, public safety and a secure border are the top priorities for the District of New Mexico. Enhanced enforcement both at the border and in the interior of the district have yielded aliens engaged in unlawful activity or with serious criminal history, including human trafficking, sexual assault and violence against children.

The District of New Mexico consists of 33 counties and shares 180 miles of international border with Mexico. Assistant U.S. Attorneys from Albuquerque and Las Cruces work directly with our federal, state and local law enforcement partners to prosecute immigration-related and other federal offenses.
title: U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico Weekly Immigration and Border Crimes Report

CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT Urge Critical Infrastructure To Strengthen Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems Cybersecurity
WASHINGTON – Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DOT) published a fact sheet that warns organizations of ongoing cyber threat activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems. Critical infrastructure sectors that widely use these systems include Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems.
Globally, malicious cyber actors are targeting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system. The fact sheet provides recommended best practices and protections against this threat activity such as:
- Remove control system devices and/or systems from the internet.
- Change default passwords and strengthen passwords.
- Apply patches and keep devices and systems updated.
- Identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that the vendor no longer supports.
“In close collaboration with our government, industry and international partners, CISA is actively tracking this threat activity,” said CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target. We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps.”
“Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk. This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations. The FBI urges every organization that relies on these systems to review our guidance, implement the recommended mitigations, and report any suspicious activity to the FBI.”
For more information on how to protect against cyber threats, visit Cybersecurity Best Practices.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
title: CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT Urge Critical Infrastructure To Strengthen Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems Cybersecurity

DES MOINES, Iowa – The Department of Justice has recognized Assistant United States Attorney Kyle Hanson of the Southern District of Iowa for his outstanding appellate advocacy. Hanson received a Director’s Award from the Executive Office for United States Attorneys (EOUSA) during an awards ceremony held on October 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C.

Hanson’s exemplary efforts have secured favorable results in significant cases involving a wide range of legal issues. Hanson also serves as an invaluable resource for the district’s trial attorneys facing complex and novel legal questions.

“We are proud to work alongside AUSA Kyle Hanson in the Southern District of Iowa. Kyle provides exceptional appellate advocacy and rigorous legal analysis in every case. This national recognition reflects Kyle’s outstanding achievements over the past year and his ongoing dedication to the mission and values of the Department of Justice,” said United States Attorney David C. Waterman.

Under the direction of the Deputy Attorney General, EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 93 United States Attorneys’ Offices around the country. For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao .

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration is reminding eligible businesses, private nonprofit organizations, homeowners, and renters in West Virginia of the Dec. 7 deadline to apply for low-interest federal disaster loans to offset physical damage caused by severe storms and flooding occurring Aug. 14 –18.
The declaration covers West Virginia primary counties of Fayette, Harrison, and Kanawha, which are eligible for both physical damage loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA. Small businesses and most private nonprofit organizations in the following adjacent counties are eligible to apply only for SBA EIDLs: West Virginia counties of Barbour, Boone, Clay, Doddridge, Greenbrier, Jackson, Lewis, Lincoln, Marion, Nicholas, Putnam, Raleigh, Roane, Summers, Taylor, Upshur, and Wetzel.
Businesses and private nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against high wind damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
“One distinct advantage of SBA’s disaster loan program is the opportunity to fund upgrades reducing the risk of future storm damage,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “I encourage businesses and homeowners to work with contractors and mitigation professionals to improve their storm readiness while taking advantage of SBA’s mitigation loans.”
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 3% for homeowners and renters, with terms of up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due, until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return applications for physical property damage is Dec. 7. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 7, 2027. However, after the deadline has passed, there is a 60-day grace period in which SBA will accept applications.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Relief Still Available to West Virginia Businesses, Private Nonprofits, Residents Affected by Severe Storms and Flooding

Moore, Chu Reintroduce EITC Age Parity Act to Expand Tax Credit to Younger and Older Workers
Representative Gwen Moore (WI-04) and Representative Judy Chu (CA-28) introduced the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) Age Parity Act to eliminate a barrier preventing younger and older workers without children from accessing the EITC.
Last year, 24 million workers and families received the credit, pulling millions out of poverty. But under current law, workers under the age of 25 and over the age of 65 without children are not eligible for the credit. The EITC Age Parity Act expands this credit’s eligibility so these workers can finally receive permanent support.
“At a time when American families and workers are struggling with higher costs for just about everything, our tax laws should not be taxing workers into poverty. That is why I have long championed updates to the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), one of our nation’s largest anti-poverty tools. While the American Rescue Plan Act made important changes to the EITC, including allowing younger and older adults without children to benefit from this refundable credit, those temporary changes expired, depriving some of our most vulnerable workers of critical assistance. The EITC Age Parity Act would permanently allow younger and older workers to benefit from the EITC, a crucial first step in ensuring that our tax code can better serve all our workers,” said Rep. Moore.
“The EITC is one of the most impactful and transformative anti-poverty tools we have at our disposal. Unfortunately, arbitrary age limits exclude millions of hardworking Americans who could benefit from it greatly,” said Rep. Chu. “Right now, a 23-year-old stocking shelves and a 66-year-old still working to make ends meet, neither with children at home, are shut out of the EITC for no reason other than their age. I’m proud to reintroduce the EITC Age Parity Act with Rep. Moore to lift more families out of poverty and put more money back in the pockets of millions of workers.”
Congresswoman Moore remains a champion for enhancing the EITC. In addition to introducing the EITC Age Parity Act, Congresswoman has introduced legislation, the Worker Relief and Credit Reform Act (the WRCR Act), which would expand the EITC to provide more support for more people by increasing the maximum credit for all filers, changing age limits to benefit young and older workers without children, as well making low-income students and certain unpaid caregivers eligible for the credit.
title: Moore, Chu Reintroduce EITC Age Parity Act to Expand Tax Credit to Younger and Older Workers

DENVER – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado announces that James Zachary Heath, 27, Castle Rock, was sentenced to 450 months in federal prison and a lifetime of supervised release after pleading guilty to one count of production of child pornography and one count of distribution of child pornography.

According to the plea agreement and facts established at sentencing, the defendant came to the attention of law enforcement in July 2024 when a foreign law enforcement agency located an explicit video on the dark web of a man sexually abusing a toddler. In September 2024, the foreign law enforcement agency found a longer compilation video that depicted the sexual abuse and exploitation of the minor and which ultimately led to the defendant being identified.

“This lengthy prison sentence demonstrates how seriously the American justice system takes these horrendous crimes,” said United States Attorney Peter McNeilly. “And I am glad this predator is out of our community for a very long time.”

“Child sexual abuse material impacts not only the initial victims and their families, but it also feeds the abominable marketplace for the images and videos,” said FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski. “Child predators be on notice: The FBI and justice will find you. There is no place in our society for child exploitation.”

The FBI Denver Field Division handled the investigation. Assistant United States Attorney Alecia L. Riewerts handled the prosecution.

United States District Judge S. Kato Crews presided over the sentencing.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc. For more information about Internet safety education, please visit www.justice.gov/psc and click on the "Resources" tab on the left of the page.

Case Number: 1:24-cr-00309-SKC
title: Castle Rock Man Sentenced to 450 Months In Prison After Pleading Guilty To Producing Child Sexual Abuse Material And Distribution

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Kelong Han, 43, of Paoli, Pennsylvania, entered a plea of guilty before United States District Judge Kelley Brisbon Hodge this week to two counts of filing a false tax return.

The defendant was charged by information in September; with his plea, he has waived prosecution by indictment.

As detailed in court filings and statements, Han willfully made and filed a United States Individual Income Tax Return Form 1040 for the calendar year 2020 and 2022, verified by a written declaration that it was made under the penalty of perjury, which he knew was not true and correct. Han created two fictitious businesses and filed Schedule Cs concerning those fake entities, claiming that his wife and young children worked at those false businesses and earned wages. In reality, his family did not receive wages, nor did the businesses earn any revenue.

For 2020, Han’s return reported taxable income of $9,531, when, in fact, as Han knew, his actual taxable income was approximately $1,028,524. Similarly, for 2022, Han reported taxable income of $115,053 when, as he knew, his taxable income was substantially higher, approximately $1,002,173.

Han also fraudulently applied for Paycheck Protection Program loans for the fake businesses and received approximately $220,000. As part of his plea agreement, Han will pay $1,723,658 in restitution for his criminal acts.

The defendant is scheduled to be sentenced on March 31 and faces a maximum possible term of six years in prison and a $500,000 fine.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

This case was investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation and is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Eric D. Gill.
title: Chester County Man Pleads Guilty to Tax Fraud

JOINT BASE LEWIS-McCHORD, Wash. — For Signal Intelligence Analysts, daily duty typically revolves around high-frequency antennas, data terminals, and secure workspaces. But across the vast littoral expanses of the Pacific, combat operations do not begin or end at a desk.
To bridge that gap, combat support enablers assigned to 1st Special Forces Group (Airborne) recently took to the frigid waters of the Puget Sound to complete the Maritime Operations (MAROPS) Familiarization Course, learning how to assemble, launch, navigate, and maintain inflatable boats. The course is just one of many courses offered by 1st SFG(A)’s Special Forces Advanced Skills Company (SFASC).
Cadre members assigned to SFASC emphasize that an enabler’s proficiency in waterborne activities only improves mission survivability and success. The course is therefore open to all enablers within the organization to attend.
“When a Soldier is attached to an ODA [Operational Detachment-Alpha] they have to be prepared to embed with a team throughout a mission,” said a cadre member. “By offering this training to our enablers we can arm our ODAs with an additional capability, and ensure the entire team remains safe.”
For the detachment of 35N Signals Analysts participating in the MAROPS training, the transition to the maritime domain was an eye-opening departure from routine duties.
"I didn’t really know what to expect,” one of the analysts said. "35Ns are often attached to ODAs, and if we ever are in the future, it is very useful training. Additionally, it helps intelligence Soldiers understand how our own forces move and operate so we can better understand what’s important in a maritime environment."
The curriculum challenges Soldiers from open-water swimming and small-boat helmsmanship to troubleshooting outboard engines. For support personnel accustomed to strict processes, the water provided an immediate, unforgiving classroom in attention to detail.
"I found assembling the boat to be challenging, as there are a lot of steps to the process that must be done in order," the analyst explained. "This training reinforces the importance of attention to detail in every task and doing the right things in the right order. Going back and having to disassemble a boat because one of the first few steps was done wrong is definitely strong encouragement to do it right the first time.”
A cadre member explained that cross-training enablers is fundamental to distributed operations throughout U.S. Pacific Command.
"In the Pacific, our teams operate across isolated islands and contested coastlines-there are no passengers in a Zodiac," said a cadre member. ”When an enabler understands boat mechanics, navigation, and small-team safety, an ODA doesn't have to slow down. They plug right in, pull their weight, and make the entire detachment more lethal."
Having enablers who are confident on the water ensures 1st SFG(A) can deploy specialized technical capabilities into austere littoral environments without sacrificing operational speed or survivability.
For the analyst, the course reinforced mutual trust between Units of Action and the enablers supporting them.
"My advice to anyone nervous about the training is that they shouldn’t be," the analyst added, crediting the dedication of the cadre for preparing the class. "The instructors are not going to put you in any danger. Also, you are not going to sink in a wetsuit.”
title: 1st SFG(A) enablers take to the water

Applicants and employers crowded the Swabian Event Center on U.S. Army Garrison Stuttgart’s Patch Barracks Oct. 28 for a day of events designed to help military spouses, transitioning personnel and more find the next steps of their careers.
USAG Stuttgart’s Transition Assistance Program, part of the Directorate of Human Resources, coordinated with the non-profit organization Hiring our Heroes to bring classes and employers directly to potential employees.
"We've got an amazing pool of qualified candidates, and it is a huge win to be able to connect them with opportunities both local and throughout the globe," USAG Stuttgart Director of Human Resources James Hill said. "It's about them, the people seeking jobs, to give them opportunities."
Capt. Patrick Gendron attended the career fair in preparation to retire from the Navy next spring. As he looks for a job that keeps him in Europe or Japan, he said that events like this one are key for transitioning service members
“The best thing that people can do is go out early and see what’s available to them,” Gendron said. “The transition process is a little daunting, but it doesn’t have to be. The more you know the better prepared you can be.”
Creating opportunities for military spouses, reshaping the workforce and connecting available applicants with roles that help support the future objectives of the Army and Department of War starts with events like the USAG Stuttgart Career Summit, according to Hill.
“We get to support our community members, it’s what we’re here for, to serve people,” Hill said. “But the larger picture is that we make sure our mission partners and the greater organization retain talent and experience, even if it is at another location. This summit is a win, locally and globally.”
Approximately 150 jobseekers attended the USAG Stuttgart Career Summit, where dozens of employers were able to meet them.
title: USAG Stuttgart partners with Hiring our Heroes for Stuttgart Career Summit
