The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Buffalo District, completed dredging on Nov. 5 of approximately 109,000 cubic yards of sediment from Sandusky Harbor, ensuring safe and navigable waterways for Great Lakes commercial vessels, recreational boaters and other harbor users on Lake Erie.
The work was completed under a $628,000 contract, with the majority of the sediments dredged placed in a nearshore site, allowing local currents to deposit the material along the coastline, mimicking natural nourishment processes.
- 100,000 cubic yards of dredged sediments placed in nearshore site, nourishing Ohio’s coastline.
- $628K project maintains safe navigation for commercial ships and recreational boats.
- Sandusky Harbor supports more than $322M in economic impact annually.
- Photos & B-roll available here.
“Completing dredging in Sandusky Harbor is another mark of the Corps of Engineers’ dedication to efficiency, good stewardship of American taxpayer dollars, and delivery of a critical mission the Corps of Engineers is known for,” said Lt. Col. Aaron Anderson, commander of the Buffalo District. “This work ensures vessels remain safe, ports across Ohio and the Great Lakes keep thriving, and the U.S. economy stays strong.”
Work started Oct. 6 and was completed under a $628,000 contract awarded in July 2026 to Michigan-based Morrish-Wallace Construction Co.
Approximately 109,000 cubic yards of sediment was mechanically dredged from the federal navigation channel in the Moseley and Straight Channels. 9,000 cubic yards of material was placed in a designated open-lake site, and 100,000 cubic yards was placed in the nearshore site.
The harbor was last dredged in 2025, when approximately 9,000 cubic yards of material were removed and placed in the open lake. Sandusky Harbor is dredged annually depending on shoaling conditions, funding availability and federal navigation priorities.
Sandusky Harbor is a deep draft commercial harbor which handled 2.6 million tons of cargo, including coal & lignite (90%), petroleum coke (5%), and coal coke (4%) in 2023. Waterborne transportation facilitated by the harbor supports $266.8 million in business revenue, 864 direct, indirect, and induced jobs, and $55.5 million in labor income to the transportation sector.
Authorized depths within Sandusky Harbor range from 21 to 26 feet, with the shallowest depths in the Straight Channel and the deepest depths in the Moseley Channel. The Corps of Engineers maintains these depths to support safe and efficient navigation for large vessels.
Operation, maintenance and dredging of harbors like Sandusky by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers is critical to the economy of Ohio, the Great Lakes region, and the United States.
Photos of dredging in Sandusky Harbor are available at: https://www.flickr.com/photos/buffalousace/albums/72157714753598288/
The Buffalo District delivers world class engineering solutions to the Great Lakes Region, the Army and the Nation to ensure national security, environmental sustainability, water resource management, and emergency assistance during peace and war. Learn more at www.lrd.usace.army.mil/buffalo.
title: Sandusky Harbor Dredging Completed; Benefits Local Beach Nourishment

text:
The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states recently filed an updated version of their complaint against Amazon with unredacted details about Amazon’s alleged use of deceptive and unfair practices to secretly inflate prices in its online search advertising auction.
Details in the updated version of the complaint show substantial harm to advertisers as well as the direct statements Amazon made to mislead advertisers about the true cause of the price increases resulting from its scheme.
In August, the FTC and its state partners sued Amazon in the Western District of Washington, arguing that the online retailer harmed advertisers by covertly and substantially increasing the prices charged to them for advertising on Amazon’s platforms. The new filing makes public factual details that had previously been redacted.
The unredacted portions of the complaint allege that Amazon secretly raises advertising prices by as much as 50% above auction results on ordinary days and by as much as 250% on major shopping days like Prime Day or Black Friday.
Amazon’s efforts led to significantly higher advertising prices during high-volume shopping days. Newly unsealed portions of the complaint allege that during the 2021 holiday season, Amazon increased advertisers’ average cost-per-click by 20%, with some advertisers experiencing increases of over 200%. Similarly, during the 2022 holiday shopping season, Amazon secretly and successfully raised its surcharges to increase its revenue by $87 million worldwide.
Neither small businesses nor large and sophisticated customers were spared from the surcharges. One large food and beverage advertiser, for example, was subjected to price increases of more than 100% during Prime Day in 2023. Internally, Amazon acknowledged that its price increases led to decreases in the advertiser’s return on ad spend that were “destroying campaign performance.”
The unsealed allegations also demonstrate that Amazon used its hidden surcharges to meet revenue goals. In 2023, Amazon executives discussed the need to find an additional $40 million in revenue to meet corporate financial targets, according to the complaint. Per the complaint, the head of Amazon Ads told Amazon’s senior vice president of ad products and technology in an email that, “I’d like to pull out all of the stops (without doing unnatural acts) to close our gaps to plan. I suspect that the entire gap won’t be closed, so whatever can be done with reserves (ideally at least $40MM would be helpful).”
As alleged in the unredacted portions of the complaint, when advertisers facing prices inflated by Amazon’s hidden surcharges asked if “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process,” Amazon falsely reassured them the price increases were the result of increased competition.
In one instance, for example, after being directly asked by an advertiser whether “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process, either by design or mistake,” an Amazon account manager falsely stated, “After reaching out to the product specialist team we were informed there is not a bug, or a change in auction style, so no worries there. This year the marketplace is even more crowded than any year previous, and we are seeing the spike in CPCs [costs-per-click] as a direct reflection.”
The attorneys general of Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont and Washington joined in filing the now-unredacted complaint.
The Federal Trade Commission works to promote competition and protect and educate consumers. The FTC will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise you a prize. Learn more about consumer topics at consumer.ftc.gov, or report fraud, scams, and bad business practices at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Follow the FTC on social media, read consumer alerts and the business blog, and sign up to get the latest FTC news and alerts.
title: New Details Emerge in Amazon Ads Auction-Rigging Case

text:
TROY, N.C. — To a camper settling in for the night or a hunter waiting for dawn, Uwharrie National Forest is a place where they can find solitude in the woods of central North Carolina. But this October, the forest has another story to tell. Beneath the full moon, hidden under its canopy among the calls of owls and the distant howls of coyotes, U.S. Green Berets assigned to 3rd Special Forces Group (Airborne) put their combat skills to the test during War Horse, the Group’s baseline lethality training exercise.
Under the uneven glow of the full moon, light slips through the canopy in scattered patches, leaving stretches of the forest cloaked in darkness to the naked eye. The crunch of leaves beneath boots breaks the silence of the night, a gentle reminder that even the smallest of movements could compromise a Soldier’s position. Moving with rucksacks, weapons and night-vision devices, the Green Berets strategically navigated the steep and densely vegetated terrain, working to remain undetected by the civilian population they shared the forest with for two weeks.
The training conducted in Uwharrie is a part of a larger training objective for exercise War Horse. Multiple Operational Detachments Alpha, the 12-man team that forms the basic construct of the Green Berets, tested their skills across a series of objectives designed to challenge their ability to operate in the most demanding environments, both individually and as a team.
Each ODA spent 72 hours in the forest, quietly moving between three key objectives over the course of the training. The 30-kilometer movement across mountainous terrain required Green Berets to navigate steep, rugged terrain under heavy packs while maintaining tactical movement and remaining undetected. With only 24 hours dedicated to each objective, the teams had to move quickly to complete their assigned missions before advancing to the next stage.
For the 12 highly trained Green Berets, the mission began at 8 p.m. as the sun fell and temperatures began to plunge. Under the cover of darkness, the small team moved into the uneven terrain of Uwharrie National Forest, using the night to conceal their movements as they made their way toward the first objective. With two more objectives ahead, the first night marked the beginning of their three days in the forest.
Upon reaching their initial objective area, the team halted, sinking into a perimeter defense to establish an objective rally point, a location outside of sight and sound from the objective. Hand and arm signals replaced spoken commands. Within minutes, a two-man reconnaissance element broke away, headed toward the wood line, watching every step to avoid the quick sounds of twigs breaking beneath their muddy boots. While one Green Beret knelt in the damp undergrowth to establish security, the other began to set up the team’s surveillance equipment. Working only by touch, eyes illuminated under the iridescent glow of his night vision equipment, he set up specialized surveillance equipment. With the device in place, the pair slowly retreated back into the shadows to reconvene with the rest of the ODA. Without a sound, the first mission was complete.
Mission two brought new challenges: an asphalt road bisecting the ODA’s route to a suspected drop zone. With a timeline to meet, the team carefully maneuvered through exposed ground. After descending a steep hill, guided only by hand and arm signals, three Green Berets quickly maneuvered across the moonlit street, disappearing into the trees that lined the road. Once in place, two Soldiers established security as the third crept onto the perimeter of the wide-open area. Staying low against the dew-soaked grass, he began to take measurements, gauging tree heights and other obstructions that could prevent the deployment of supplies or troops. With just hours before dawn, the three-man element pulled back, vanishing just as swiftly and as quietly as they appeared.
By the third night, the fatigue of carrying 80-pound rucks for nearly three days was setting in, but the ODAs had one final mission: establish tactical communications. After reaching their designated clearing, the ODA dispatched a two-man element to complete the final mission. As security kept watch on the surrounding ridge, the Special Forces communications sergeant, an expert in tactical communications, assembled the equipment, ensuring the transmission could penetrate through the dense vegetation. With the burst transmission sent, the gear was broken down and repacked, leaving no trace of the secretive mission.
By 6 a.m., a shimmer of light began to pierce the pine trees that covered the forest. Punctual to the second, the rumble of a brandless white moving truck rolled down the gravel road. As the truck began to back into the woods, the rear roll-up door opened. After a few short seconds, Green Berets emerged from the brush. Weighted down with heavy rucks, eyes glowing under the night vision and rifles at the low ready, each man quickly climbed into the truck. After a tap on the shoulder as each Green Beret climbed in, the door rolled down and the truck began to drive off, marking the end of the ODA’s 72-hour mission in Uwharrie.
While the training in Uwharrie represents one part of a larger effort, its purpose extends beyond completing individual objectives. Through exercise War Horse, 3rd Group is working to strengthen its baseline lethality, reinforce existing capabilities and adapt its training to the demands of large-scale combat operations. By testing Green Berets in demanding field environments, the Group is sharpening its ability to operate in unfamiliar and austere conditions, ensuring its Green Berets remain prepared for the challenges of future deployments.
title: Quiet professionals train in the shadows of Uwharrie

Earlier today, an indictment was unsealed in federal court in Brooklyn charging Andrew Reyes, a former Special Agent with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), with willfully depriving an individual of his constitutional rights while acting under color of law and making false statements. Reyes was arrested this morning and is scheduled to be arraigned this afternoon before United States Magistrate Judge Clay H. Kaminsky.

Joseph Nocella, Jr., United States Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, and Ryan T. Geach, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General’s Northeast Region, announced the arrest and charges.

“As alleged, the defendant was driving his government vehicle the wrong way on a major Brooklyn thoroughfare, blew through a red light, struck a pedestrian, and then fled the scene without rendering aid to the severely injured victim or reporting the incident,” stated United States Attorney Nocella. “The defendant’s alleged conduct demonstrated a shocking disregard for human life and his sworn oath to uphold the law. The charges announced today send the clear message that no one is above the law and those who abuse their position of trust and deprive citizens of their constitutional rights will be prosecuted.”

Mr. Nocella expressed his appreciation to the New York City Police Department, the United States Department of Justice Civil Rights Division for their work in this case, and the FBI, New York Field Office, for their cooperation and assistance.

As alleged in the indictment, on February 3, 2026, Reyes was driving his FBI‑issued vehicle in Brooklyn with the emergency lights activated. As Reyes approached the intersection of Ocean Parkway and Beverley Road, he drove on the wrong side of the road—northbound on Ocean Parkway in the southbound lane of traffic—and through a red light. Reyes’s car struck a pedestrian crossing the street, knocking him to the pavement. After stopping his car, Reyes approached the unconscious victim and dragged him from the street, across the sidewalk, and placed him on a bench. Reyes also retrieved the unconscious victim’s bag and placed it next to him on the bench. Reyes then returned to his vehicle, which still had its emergency lights engaged, and drove away from the scene, leaving the victim severely injured and unattended. Reyes did not alert medical authorities or report the incident. When later asked by federal agents whether he had ever hit a person with his FBI-issued car and not reported it, Reyes falsely stated that he had not.

The charges in the indictment are allegations. and the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. If convicted, Reyes faces up to 10 years in prison.

The government’s case is being handled by the Office’s Human Trafficking and Civil Rights Section and its Public Integrity Section. Assistant United States Attorneys Miranda Gonzalez and Gilbert M. Rein are in charge of the prosecution, with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Daniel Arakawa.

The Defendant :

ANDREW REYES Age: 30 Brooklyn, New York

E.D.N.Y. Docket No. 26-CR-306 (DLI)
title: Former FBI Special Agent Charged with Federal Civil Rights Violation and Making False Statements

Department of Justice Launches Super Intelligence Task Force
The U.S. Department of Justice is announcing the formation of its Super Intelligence (SI) Task Force (DOJ-SITF). President Trump has made clear that “America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence,” and the Department will be a leader in safeguarding against malicious SI actors.
Led by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss, the DOJ-SITF will ensure that America's leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.
“SI development will continue to be powered by American innovators,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The SI Task Force at the Department of Justice will facilitate our partnership with SI Force Chair Jay Clayton as we ensure critical SI technologies serve the American people and are not manipulated by bad actors at home or abroad. The Department of Justice will continue identifying and prosecuting individuals whose use of SI violates the law, including by maliciously targeting American taxpayers, critical U.S. infrastructure, or other aspects of our national security.”
“As technological capabilities evolve, the DOJ-SITF will advance the Department’s mission to make America safe,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. “Our comprehensive effort will promote innovation and prevent the misuse of Super Intelligence.”
“The creation of the DOJ-SITF marks an important moment for the Department to help advance SI technologies and, at the same time, protect American innovation," said Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss. "The Department also has a responsibility to utilize law enforcement tools at our disposal to deter improper use of SI, harden regular reporting on SI risk and response, and ensure companies exercise vigorous internal controls so that SI technology behaves as intended. The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests.”

HONOLULU, HI – This week, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon visited Hawaii on her Returning Education to the States Tour, her 49th state visit.
On Wednesday, Secretary McMahon began at Admiral Arthur W. Radford High School, exploring its classes before meeting with military students at the Student Transition Center. Next, she toured Mokapu Elementary School – the state's only school on a Marine Corps base – and joined a Literacy & Military Education Roundtable focused on helping military children navigate frequent relocations and deployments.
Her tour continued at Keiki Roots, a nature-based homeschool enrichment co-op along Kāneʻohe Bay, where she explored outdoor learning spaces and read to the program’s young students. She concluded her tours on Wednesday with a visit to the University of Hawaii’s Institute of Marine Biology to see the Marine Science Research Learning Center and the Coral Resilience Laboratory.
To conclude the trip, Secretary McMahon today participated in a Returning Education to the States Roundtable with members of the Hawaii State Legislature and toured Ka Waihona o Ka Na’auao, a K-8 Hawaiian language immersion charter school.
“The 49th state tour stop in Hawaii highlighted the incredible work that happens when education is designed around a community's specific geography and heritage. Whether it's the specialized military support at Mokapu Elementary, the coral resilience research at the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology, or the deep cultural preservation at Ka Waihona o Ka Na’auao Hawaiian language immersion school, these uniquely tailored programs reinforce why Washington should never impose a one-size-fits-all model,” said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon. “States require the autonomy to innovate, and Hawaii is demonstrating that by building classrooms that honor its people and environment.”
Background:
On her Returning Education to the States Tour, Secretary McMahon is traveling to all 50 states to hear directly from teachers, parents, students, and community leaders about what is working in their communities and to compile a toolkit of best practices to share with states across the nation. Learn more about Secretary McMahon’s Returning Education to the States Tour here.
title: U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon Visits Hawaii on Returning Education to the States Tour

Release Number 9323-26
CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation
November 05, 2026
WASHINGTON — The Commodity Futures Trading Commission today issued an interpretation (“Interpretation”) of the requirement that designated contract markets (“DCMs”) provide competitive, open, fair, and impartial access to their members and persons with trading privileges under Commission Regulation 38.151(b) (“Impartial Access Requirements”).
“Derivatives markets must operate on a uniform basis at a national scale in order to achieve the purposes set out in the Commodity Exchange Act,” said Chairman Michael S. Selig. “Geographic access restrictions are inconsistent with those purposes and the Act’s impartial access requirements.”
DCMs must cease domestic geographic restrictions that violate the Impartial Access Requirements within 30 days, or else submit to the Division of Market Oversight (“Division”) an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. Further, within 30 days, DCMs should ensure that intermediaries accessing their markets are not impeding and are complying with the DCM’s Impartial Access Requirements, or else submit to the Division an explanation for why such compliance is not feasible. The Commission will consider the facts and circumstances of any particular case in connection with potential Commission action.
-CFTC-
title: CFTC Issues Impartial Access Requirements Interpretation

ATLANTA - Hugh A. Brown, Jr. was sentenced to federal prison today for fraudulently obtaining roughly $1.25 million in pandemic relief and auto loans.

“This defendant shamelessly fleeced federal taxpayers and financial institutions over half a decade through various loan fraud schemes,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “My office will continue to prosecute and seek prison time for anyone who abuses government relief programs.”

“Submitting false information to obtain federal pandemic relief funds, using fraudulent documents and deliberate misrepresentations to secure loans from banks and credit unions, are serious offenses that undermine the integrity of our financial institutions and erode public trust,” said Acting Assistant Special Agent in Charge Patrick M. Palmer, IRS Criminal Investigation, Atlanta Field Office. “IRS Criminal Investigation remains steadfast in its commitment to identifying and investigating financial fraud. Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners and the U.S. Attorney’s Office, we will continue to protect taxpayers, safeguard the integrity of our financial system, and ensure that individuals who exploit these institutions for personal gain are held accountable under the law.”

“The U.S. Postal Inspection Service sees firsthand through investigations how devastating fraud and deception can be on our communities. That’s why we commit, every day, to bring criminals that choose to undermine the integrity of our financial system and betray the trust of lenders to justice,” said Rodney M. Hopkins, Inspector in Charge of the Atlanta Division of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. “The defendant in this case stole money earmarked to help people in a time of economic uncertainty and used it to increase their bank account. The Postal Inspection Service’s message and mission are clear: You commit fraud, exploit our financial systems, and do harm to our communities, we will find you and bring you to justice.”

According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the indictment, and other information presented in court: In 2020, Brown applied for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan by submitting false payroll information and fake IRS tax forms to a federally insured bank. As a result of the bogus application, Brown received a $162,500 PPP loan.

In 2022, Brown fraudulently claimed Employee Retention Credits (ERCs), a refundable tax credit designed to encourage employers to continue to pay employees during COVID-19, on behalf of his company. After filing fraudulent tax returns, Brown received seven United States Treasury checks totaling $644,452.98 in ERCs and other credits.

In addition, from at least February 2022 through February 2025, Brown obtained fraudulent bank and credit union loans worth nearly $450,000 by submitting fake documents, misrepresenting employment/income information, and providing fictitious vehicle details as loan collateral.

Today, U.S. District Judge Victoria M. Calvert sentenced Hugh A. Brown, Jr., 35, of Fayetteville, Georgia, to two years, nine months in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release. Brown also was ordered to pay $1,244,243.81 in restitution to the Small Business Administration, the Internal Revenue Service, and financial institutions. On June 3, 2026, Brown pleaded guilty to bank fraud conspiracy and bank fraud.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Internal Revenue Service, and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. Valuable assistance was provided by Homeland Security Investigations.

For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga .
title: Fayette County Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Car Loan Scheme and COVID-Related Fraud

CLEVELAND — Following a three-week trial, a federal jury in Cleveland convicted three members of the Fully Blooded Felons, a violent Cleveland street gang, of a number of crimes, including Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act murder, RICO conspiracy, RICO kidnapping, drug trafficking, and gun crimes.

“This extremely violent gang was a true blot on the city of Cleveland,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The Criminal Division’s work put a stop to the violence that this gang rained down on Ohio communities to protect law-abiding citizens from harm. Stopping violent crime in Cleveland and around the country remains a top priority for the Trump Administration.”

“These verdicts send a clear message: when gang members make it their business to hurt people and terrorize our communities, we make it our business to lock them in a cage far from home,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “FBI Cleveland and our local law enforcement partners conducted an outstanding investigation to take down this hostile gang. We hope today’s verdict brings the victims’ families a small sense of closure in knowing that justice has been served.”

“These verdicts send a clear message: when gang members make it their business to hurt people and terrorize our communities, we make it our business to lock them in a cage far from home,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “FBI Cleveland and our local law enforcement partners conducted an outstanding investigation to take down this hostile gang. We hope today’s verdict brings the victims’ families a small sense of closure in knowing that justice has been served.”

“The Fully Blooded Felons criminal network has been identified as Cleveland’s most significant gang threat,” said Special Agent in Charge Joshua DelManzo of FBI Cleveland. “Thanks to the tireless work and years-long commitment of the FBI Safe Streets Gang Task Force and our local, state, and federal partners, their reign of terror is over and justice will be served. Our work is not done. We will not waver in our mission nor lose sight of our promise to identify, investigate, disrupt, and dismantle gangs not only in the larger cities across America, but also right here in northern Ohio.”

"The convictions of these individuals bring closure to an extensive investigation into criminal activity that caused significant harm to our communities. This case is another example of the effectiveness of strong partnerships between local and federal law enforcement agencies—a proven approach to holding those responsible for criminal activity accountable," said Cleveland Division of Police Chief Dorothy A. Todd. "I commend our Third District detectives for their dedication, professionalism, and outstanding investigative work in leading this case. Our community is safer today because these individuals are being held accountable and are no longer on our streets."

According to evidence presented at trial, Raven Mullins, 37, Malik Brooks, 28, and Jayon Florence, 23, all of Cleveland, Ohio, were members and associates of the Fully Blooded Felons gang. The gang has existed in Ohio since approximately 2012, operating primarily out of the east side of Cleveland, as well as Akron, Youngstown, and elsewhere. It is also entrenched in the Ohio prison system.

Raven Mullins oversaw the “Commission,” the governing body of the Fully Blooded Felons, who maintain the structure and organization of the criminal enterprise through physical discipline and who determined which illicit means the organization would use to make money. The Commission had authority to determine if a member committed a “violation” and the appropriate punishment, which could range from a fine to death. The Commission was made up of a Head Commissioner and 10 subordinate Commissioners. Beneath the Commissioner were “Capos,” who led up to 25 Fully Blooded Felon members under their command.

The Fully Blooded Felons have rules that members are required to follow. For example, members are required to abide by “omerta,” or the code of silence. Members are also required to memorize and recite at meetings the “Fully Five,” a set of rules that require following all orders issued by the Commission, loyalty to fellow members, and being respectful to Capos. If a member does not know the “Fully Five,” they were punished. Members are also expected to know and abide by the “Fully Commandments,” a similar set of rules. The rules are disseminated to members by text message, and in face-to-face communications.

Evidence proved that the defendants, along with co-defendants who earlier pleaded guilty, kidnapped, and murdered a victim after the gang suspected that she was romantically involved with and sharing information with a rival gang member. On or about July 28, 2022, as punishment for the victim’s suspected disloyalty to the gang, Fully Blooded Felon members held her in an apartment where Mullins ordered gang members, including Brooks and Florence, to repeatedly punch and choke her.

Mullins, Brooks, and Florence, with other co-defendants, held her captive in that apartment while they talked about what to do with her. After taking and reviewing the contents of her phone, including text messages and contacts, gang members believed that she intended to provide a rival gang with Brooks’ location to facilitate Brooks’ assault or murder.

The next day, while still holding her captive and upon Mullins’ approval, Brooks and Florence along with other gang members drove her to an area on the west side of Cleveland where they fatally shot her 19 times, leaving her body in the front seat of a stolen Kia Optima.

From June 30 to July 5, 2022, Mullins and other Fully Blooded Felon members kidnapped and assaulted a 22-year-old woman. The victim, who was eventually released, had previously given a statement to police implicating a Fully Blooded Felon member in a robbery. Then, on Sept. 12, 2023, Mullins and two other Fully Blooded Felon members robbed and murdered a second victim on the west side of Cleveland. Evidence at trial included a knife sheath carrying Mullins’ DNA found at the scene.

The prosecution also introduced evidence showing that Brooks shot two rival gang members on the west side of Cleveland on July 18 and 20, 2022, and that Fully Blooded Felon members used two different stash houses at a local apartment complex. During the execution of two search warrants, law enforcement recovered over 300 grams of fentanyl, cocaine, and methamphetamine as well as seven firearms.

The defendants face maximum penalties of life in prison. Their sentencing date has not yet been set by the court.

As of today, 25 Fully Blooded Felon members have been charged and convicted of federal charges in relation to this indictment for crimes including RICO conspiracy, murder in aid of racketeering, kidnapping in aid of racketeering, and various firearms and drug-related offenses.

The case is the result of a yearslong investigation conducted by the FBI with assistance from the Cleveland Division of Police, ATF, and DEA. The Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Office, Ohio Adult Parole Authority (APA), Ohio Highway State Patrol, U.S. Marshals Service, and numerous other law enforcement agencies contributed to the investigation.

Trial Attorneys Brian W. Lynch and former Trial Attorney Alyssa Levey-Weinstein of the Justice Department’s Violent Crime & Racketeering Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Paul E. Hanna , Rachael E. Wood , Robert F. Corts , and Margaret A. Sweeney for the Northern District of Ohio are prosecuting the case.
title: Cleveland Gang Members Convicted of Racketeering, Murder, Kidnapping, Drug Trafficking, and Firearms Offenses

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. – A Guatemalan national was sentenced for illegally reentering the United States after being previously deported.

ALBUQUERQUE – Two men are facing federal charges after a series of violent assaults, one of which resulted in the death of a woman.

According to court records, on August 30, 2024, Eloy Perea , 39, and his brother, Harold Perea, Jr. , 34, both enrolled members of the Navajo Nation, struck Jane Doe 1 with a vehicle and at some point, Jane Doe 1 was shot by Eloy .

Harold then exited his vehicle with a shotgun and discharged several rounds in Jane Doe 2’s vicinity without hitting her.

Harold struck Jane Doe 2 with the butt of the firearm and yelled at her for speaking to law enforcement about the previous assault.

Eloy is charged with assault with two counts of using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence and one count each of second-degree murder, assault with a dangerous weapon and retaliation against a witness, victim or informant. He will remain in custody pending trial, which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Eloy faces no less than 17 years and up to life in prison.

Harold is charged with assault with three counts of using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence, two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon and one count each of second-degree murder and retaliation against a witness, victim or informant. He will remain in custody pending trial, which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Harold faces no less than 27 years and up to life in prison.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

text:
Fast Facts
Superfund sites—areas that have been contaminated by hazardous substances—have been linked to many health and environmental problems. And their cleanup can be expensive and lengthy.
EPA aims to have the parties responsible for contamination clean up sites themselves or reimburse EPA for doing so. However, we estimated that, from FYs 1996-2024, EPA recovered less than half of the $25.8 billion it spent on such cleanup.
We found that EPA isn't assessing the effectiveness of its efforts to recover costs. This would help the agency determine what kinds of efforts work best.
We recommended that EPA do so.
EPA Sign at the Hidden Lane Landfill Superfund Site in Virginia
Photograph of an EPA sign at the entrance of a Superfund site.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) uses the Hazardous Substance Superfund Trust Fund to finance cleanup costs at Superfund sites where responsible parties cannot be found or cannot pay. In fiscal years 2006 through 2024, the Trust Fund received about $34 billion in constant 2024 dollars, mostly from General Fund transfers. Congress appropriated about $32.8 billion from the Trust Fund for the Superfund program over this period. Revenue from the reinstated Superfund taxes provided substantial funds for the program in fiscal year 2024. In fiscal years 1996 through 2024, the time frame for which reliable data were available, EPA spent about $25.8 billion at nonfederal National Priorities List (NPL) sites. Remedial activities were the largest category, accounting for about half of EPA’s expenditures at these sites.
Through its efforts to hold potentially responsible parties accountable for cleanup, EPA has identified at least one such party for most nonfederal NPL sites, according to EPA data. However, EPA has faced challenges recovering costs. Challenges include having fewer experienced potentially responsible party search staff over the last 10 to 15 years and a limited ability to hold such parties liable. GAO estimates that in fiscal years 1996 through 2024, EPA recovered less than half of what it spent at nonfederal NPL sites.
EPA Expenditures and Amounts Recovered from Potentially Responsible Parties at Nonfederal NPL Sites, Fiscal Years 1996–2024
Note: Deleted sites are those where cleanup is complete. This analysis includes 1,622 National Priorities List (NPL) sites and expenditures from the Superfund Trust Fund. It is a point-in-time estimate since cost recovery efforts are ongoing, according to EPA officials.
EPA has established some Superfund performance goals and measures to ensure it takes timely cost recovery steps but does not have such tools to assess the effectiveness of its cost recovery across nonfederal NPL sites. EPA officials said they have not done this because cost recovery is a continuous process that may take years to complete. However, measuring the effectiveness of its cost recovery performance—such as by region—would allow EPA to determine how much of the billions of dollars in cleanup costs it is recovering and what kinds of efforts work best to successfully recover costs. This would help EPA determine resource needs and target enforcement efforts.
Why GAO Did This Study
The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended, established the Superfund program to address sites with hazardous substances. Hazardous substances found at Superfund sites have been linked to a variety of human health and environmental problems. The program is administered by EPA, which lists the most contaminated sites on the NPL.
Superfund site cleanups are often expensive and lengthy. EPA funds cleanups when it cannot identify parties responsible for the contamination, or when such parties fail to act. The Trust Fund was primarily financed by revenue from Superfund taxes until they expired in 1995. In 2021, Congress began reinstating some Superfund taxes.
GAO was asked to review EPA funding, expenditures, and cost recovery at nonfederal NPL sites. This report examines, among other things, (1) funding that the Trust Fund and Superfund program received; (2) amounts EPA spent at nonfederal NPL sites; and (3) the extent to which EPA has identified potentially responsible parties, recovered cleanup costs, and assessed the effectiveness of its cost recovery efforts.
GAO analyzed EPA and budget data, visited Superfund sites, and interviewed EPA officials.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that EPA (1) establish goals for cost recovery effectiveness, (2) collect performance information on cost recovery effectiveness, and (3) use the information to regularly assess progress towards goals and inform decision-making. EPA agreed with these recommendations.
title: Superfund: EPA Should Collect and Use Information on the Effectiveness of Its Recovery of Cleanup Costs

The Working Families Tax Cuts Created a Permanent Process for States to Direct More Capital to Overlooked Communities
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) today announced the Qualified Opportunity Zone (QOZ) designations for all 50 states, territories, and the District of Columbia.
Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the Opportunity Zone tax incentive was permanently renewed, enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities were added, and a process was established for redesignating zones every ten years. The new QOZ designations will become effective on January 1, 2027, and retain this designation for ten years.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, the Working Families Tax Cuts permanently renewed and strengthened Opportunity Zones, giving investors, entrepreneurs, and local leaders the long-term certainty they need to commit capital to communities that have been overlooked for too long,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Today’s announcement of the new designations will help direct private investment to communities that stand to benefit most, and expand economic opportunity, support job creation, and unlock long-term growth in these communities across the country.”
“Thanks to the leadership of President Trump, Qualified Opportunity Zones were permanently extended and expanded by the Working Families Tax Cuts giving states an opportunity to attract long-term investment into underserved, rural, and economically distressed areas,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano. “By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most.”
Background
Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the permanent renewal of the Opportunity Zone tax incentives, including enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities, will continue to drive private investment in some of America’s most distressed communities. This builds on more than $110 billion in private-sector investment made since these tax incentives were established by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.
The full list and map of designated Opportunity Zones are available here.
On April 6, Treasury and the IRS released a list of 25,332 eligible census tracts across the country for nomination, of which 8,334 are in rural areas eligible for increased benefits as part of the Working Families Tax Cuts. On July 1, Treasury and the IRS began accepting nominations from Governors and the Mayor of the District of Columbia for eligible census tracts. An additional 130 eligible census tracts, of which 28 were in rural areas, were nominated during the statutory window.
In total, 6,576 eligible census tracts were nominated by the end of the statutory window, of which 2,594 are in rural areas. All of the 6,576 eligible census tracts have been designated as QOZs effective January 1, 2027. Designation as a QOZ can help these 6,576 communities across the country attract new investment, create jobs, stimulate economic growth, and provide meaningful opportunities for residents.
Additional information on nomination procedures was sent directly to the Governors and Mayor of the District of Columbia. The list of eligible census tracts is available here. The poverty rate and median family income for each tract can be found here.

The Hatch Act is a federal law that regulates the partisan political activities of most executive-branch employees, excluding the President and Vice President. As amended in 1993, the Hatch Act exempts some high-level administration officials from some of its prohibitions, allowing them to engage in certain political activities while on duty. This exemption applies to certain officials appointed by the President with Senate confirmation (PAS), and some high-level political officials who are paid from an appropriation for the Executive Office of the President (EOP). Other Hatch Act provisions, however, continue to limit the political activities of these officials. This In Focus provides an overview of the law as it applies to certain high-level administration officials, including Cabinet Secretaries.
The Hatch Act, enacted in 1939, was designed to address concerns regarding political patronage in the civil service. The underlying rationale for the law is that "efficiency in Government service requires a lack of partisanship in administration." In its current form, the law regulates the partisan political activity of covered employees, which includes nearly all federal civilian executive-branch employees, but exempts from its coverage the President and Vice President. The U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) renders advisory opinions concerning the Hatch Act and is authorized to investigate and pursue sanctions for alleged violations of the law.
More information about the Hatch Act and its coverage is available in another In Focus. Two key provisions are relevant when discussing the Hatch Act's application to high-level administration officials. First, the Hatch Act prohibits a covered employee from engaging in political activity while the employee is on duty, in a federal building, wearing an official uniform, or using any government vehicle. Certain high-level officials, however, are exempt from this prohibition. Second, the Hatch Act prohibits all covered employees from using their "official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election."
Among other things, the Hatch Act prohibits covered employees from engaging in political activity while on duty, in the federal workplace, in uniform, or in a vehicle owned or leased by the federal government. Political activity is defined in regulation as "an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party, candidates for partisan political office, or partisan political group."
The Hatch Act, however, exempts from this prohibition certain employees who are deemed to be on duty at all times, and who are either paid from an EOP appropriation or are PAS employees. The exemption for PAS employees applies only to one "whose position is located within the United States and who determines policies to be pursued by the United States in relations with foreign powers or in the nationwide administration of Federal laws." Legislative history suggests that this exemption was intended to apply to "high-level political officials" who are continuously on duty and otherwise could never engage in political activity. OSC has referred to exemptions in the Annual and Sick Leave Act to help determine which employees are considered on duty at all times.
Employees exempted from the Hatch Act's on-duty prohibitions may engage in political activity, but costs associated with that activity may not be paid for with money derived from the Treasury. The Treasury must be reimbursed for costs associated with political activity "within a reasonable period of time," and Hatch Act regulations provide guidance on how officials must apportion costs of travel that includes both official and political events. OSC recommends that agencies seek reimbursement for political activity within 30 days of the event. Reimbursement may be sought from a campaign or from officials themselves.
High-level administration officials who are allowed to engage in political activity on duty must abide by another Hatch Act provision prohibiting all covered employees from using their "official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election." OSC has explained that this prohibition exists because "using an official title in connection with one's political activity . . . risks implying that the government itself has a preference for one political party or candidate over another."
Issues regarding the official-authority prohibition may arise when high-level administration officials mix political activities with official work, such as by using an official title when participating in political activity. OSC has indicated that it can be challenging to distinguish permissible official activity from prohibited political activity, as political activity may encompass more than just "express advocacy for the electoral success or failure of a candidate." OSC has offered some examples of comments that employees are "unquestionably" prohibited from making while engaged in official duties. These include
As one example of improper use of official authority, OSC found a high-level official violated the Hatch Act when he participated in an interview in his official capacity and suggested that one candidate's proposals would negatively affect the federal program the official oversaw.
The official-authority prohibition may also be implicated if a high-level administration official attends an event in his or her official authority while engaging in campaign-related activity. OSC has advised that when officials speak in a personal capacity for a political purpose, they must "avoid talking about the work of their agencies to ensure that they do not mix their official work with their personal political activity." For example, OSC concluded that a Cabinet Secretary violated the Hatch Act when she attended an event to speak about administration policies, but endorsed a candidate for partisan political office at the event. While the Secretary was permitted to attend the political event and engage in political activity, she was prohibited from doing so in her official capacity.
In the same vein, covered employees, including high-level administration officials, are prohibited from organizing official events for the purpose of promoting or supporting a candidate, a partisan political group, or a political party. In one instance, OSC determined that an Acting Secretary violated the Hatch Act when he presided over an official event that was held for the purpose of creating content for a political party convention.
The official-authority provision of the Hatch Act also prohibits all covered employees, including high-level officials, from taking official actions for the purpose of promoting a candidate's campaign for partisan political office. For example, OSC determined that a Cabinet Secretary violated the Hatch Act when he authorized a change to agency rules to allow himself to address a political convention to promote a candidate's reelection campaign. OSC also found a Hatch Act violation when a high-level administration official released nonpublic official information to help a candidate's campaign.
While some high-level officials may engage in on-duty political activity—such as attending political events—in their personal capacity, it is not always clear when an event is considered official versus political for purposes of determining Treasury reimbursement.
As a hypothetical example, a Cabinet Secretary may be invited to attend an event to promote agency work hosted by a sitting Member of Congress who is up for reelection. If the event is considered political or is part of a trip that involves both official and political events, the Hatch Act requires that the Cabinet Secretary reimburse the Treasury for any time spent on political activity. The Cabinet Secretary is also prohibited from using their official title while engaging in the activity.
OSC has identified multiple, non-exclusive factors to consider when determining whether an event is political for purposes of the Hatch Act. The factors outlined in an OSC advisory opinion include inquiries into
OSC advises that these factors "are intended to help determine whether the official aspect of an event is bona fide or merely a pretext for helping a candidate or political party."
Multiple agencies are responsible for interpreting, implementing, and imposing penalties under the Act. As mentioned, OSC renders advisory opinions concerning the law and is authorized to investigate and pursue sanctions for alleged violations before the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), a body that oversees disputes arising from the federal workforce. The MSPB then determines whether a violation has occurred and imposes available penalties, which, for federal employees, can include disciplinary action such as removal; a reduction in grade; debarment from federal employment for a period not to exceed five years; suspension; reprimand; or civil fines not exceeding $1,000.
Some unique challenges may arise when high-level administration officials violate the Hatch Act. For example, if an alleged violation involves an "employee in a confidential, policymaking, policy-determining, or policy-advocating position appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate," a complaint must be presented to the President for "appropriate action" in lieu of being presented to the MSPB. OSC also refers complaints involving White House commissioned officers to the President and has no role in disciplining PAS employees or White House commissioned officers beyond issuing a report. Thus, for example, if a high-level official participates in political activity on duty and fails to reimburse the Treasury, OSC lacks authority to pursue corrective action and cannot recover costs unless the employee voluntarily agrees to facilitate reimbursement.

WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities that support the business network of Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO) previously sanctioned by the United States for its role in cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking. Additionally, OFAC designated a Malaysian individual who defrauded U.S. victims by managing a network of Africa-based scammers.
“Cyber scam syndicates continue to steal billions of dollars from American victims while relying on sophisticated international business networks to launder their illicit proceeds,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Treasury remains committed to dismantling every layer of these organizations—from their leadership to the corporate structures and financial facilitators that enable them to operate with impunity.”
Today’s action builds on OFAC’s October 14, 2025 and June 23, 2026 designations targeting Prince Group leadership, affiliated companies, and financial facilitators. Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have generated billions of dollars in illicit proceeds through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online fraud that have victimized Americans and individuals around the world. Many of these operations have been linked to scam compounds in Southeast Asia that rely on trafficked and coerced workers, while criminal proceeds are laundered through complex networks of offshore companies and financial facilitators. The newly designated individuals and entities have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives. Individuals targeted today have participated in activities to evade previous sanctions targeting the Prince Group TCO, including the transfer of property and owning of companies with or on behalf of previously designated Prince Group TCO leaders. Today’s action further targets the corporate and financial infrastructure that has enabled Prince Group TCO leaders to conceal assets, evade prior sanctions, and maintain access to the international financial system.
These actions are in furtherance of President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14390 of March 6, 2026, “Combating Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens,” which orders the U.S. government to unleash every available tool to stop foreign-backed criminal networks that exploit vulnerable Americans through cybercrime, cyber-enabled fraud, and extortion. OFAC is designating 45 targets pursuant to E.O. 13581 (“Blocking Property of Transnational Criminal Organizations”), as amended by E.O. 13863 (“E.O. 13581, as amended”), and one target pursuant to E.O. 13694 (“Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities”), as further amended by E.O. 13757, E.O. 14144, and E.O. 14306 (“E.O. 13694, as further amended”).
These actions are in coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s New York and Honolulu Field Offices, Department of Justice’s Scam Center Strike Force, and the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Alaska. OFAC also appreciates the cooperation of the British Virgin Islands Financial Investigation Agency (BVI FIA) and the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), whose timely assistance and information sharing were instrumental in supporting this sanctions action.
TARGETING THOSE WHO EXPLOIT AMERICANS THROUGH FRAUD
Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have targeted victims in the United States and around the world through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online financial fraud. These schemes rely on deception and social engineering to persuade victims to transfer funds or digital assets to criminally controlled accounts, generating billions of dollars in illicit proceeds.
Many of these operations are carried out from large-scale scam compounds in Southeast Asia, where trafficked and coerced workers are forced to perpetrate online fraud against victims across the globe. Criminal proceeds are subsequently laundered through an international network of shell companies, offshore holding companies, financial facilitators, and digital asset transactions, allowing transnational criminal organizations to conceal the origin of illicit funds and integrate them into the legitimate financial system.
Today’s action builds on Treasury’s ongoing efforts to dismantle not only the leadership of these criminal enterprises, but also the overseas corporate infrastructure and professional facilitators that enable them to target American victims, move illicit proceeds across jurisdictions, and evade law enforcement. The Prince Group TCO has developed an extensive network of companies spanning multiple jurisdictions to support its commercial interests and conceal assets connected to its criminal enterprise. Rather than operating through a single corporate structure, senior Prince Group TCO executives have relied on layers of offshore holding companies, foreign entities, nominee directors, and corporate service providers to maintain control over assets while obscuring beneficial ownership. Today’s designations target key components of that network, including companies and individuals that have facilitated corporate administration, managed offshore entities, and provided business services to senior Prince Group TCO officials. These facilitators have played an important role in enabling the Prince Group TCO to access the international financial system and preserve the appearance of legitimate commercial activity.
DISMANTLING THE PRINCE GROUP’S CORPORATE INFRASTRUCTURE
Qiu Yong is a key Prince Group TCO member who controls multiple BVI and Hong Kong companies on behalf of Prince Group TCO, and who has served as an employee of a company controlled by Prince Group TCO’s leader, Chen Zhi. Chen Zhi was designated on October 14, 2025.
Qiu Yong holds passports from multiple jurisdictions, including Cambodia, St. Lucia, and Türkiye, and is the beneficial owner of multiple BVI-based companies that control a network of Hong Kong companies involved in money lending and other business ventures.
Hong Kong-based companies Premium Financial Limited (Premium Financial) and Solar Scape Financial Limited (Solar Scape Financial) are money lending companies ultimately owned by Qiu Yong through BVI-registered Sun Speed Holdings Limited (Sun Speed Holdings) and Solar Scape Limited (Solar Scape), respectively. Hong Kong-based Direct Astute HK Limited (Direct Astute HK) is ultimately owned by Qiu Yong via BVI-registered Direct Astute Limited (Direct Astute). Hong Kong-based Glad Vast Limited (Glad Vast), Glad Sparkle Limited (Glad Sparkle), and Glad Harvest Limited (Glad Harvest) are linked to the wine industry and are ultimately owned by Qiu Yong through BVI-registered Glad Glory Limited (Glad Glory). Per Hong Kong media reporting, Qiu was involved in the distribution and sale of wine across Hong Kong and Macao, illustrating Prince Group TCO’s reach into ostensibly legitimate businesses. Qiu is also the beneficial owner of BVI-registered shelf companies Victory Flora Limited (Victora Flora), Win Applause Limited (Win Applause), Celestial Drive Limited (Celestial Drive), and Sino Sagacious Limited (Sino Sagacious).
Hong Kong-based Zhao Mengyao, a.k.a. Amy Zhao, is Qiu Yong’s personal assistant and serves as company secretary and co-director of multiple Hong Kong-based companies ultimately controlled by Qiu Yong. Zhao Mengyao and Qiu Yong are both shareholders of Hong Kong-based Mighty Divine Trust Hong Kong Limited (Mighty Divine Trust), a company directed by Zhou Yun, an individual previously identified by OFAC as a financial assistant and wealth manager for Prince Group TCO leader Chen Zhi. Mighty Divine Trust and Zhou Yun were both designated on October 14, 2025.
Qiu Yong is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Prince Group TCO. Premium Financial, Solar Scape Financial, Sun Speed Holdings, Solar Scape, Direct Astute HK, Direct Astute, Glad Vast, Glad Sparkle, Glad Harvest, Glad Glory, Victora Flora, Win Applause, Celestial Drive, and Sino Sagacious are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Qiu Yong. Zhao Mengyao is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Qiu Yong.
OFAC is also targeting two individuals who are holding property for, or co-directing companies with, Prince Group TCO executive Chen Bo, who was designated on June 23, 2026. This includes Chen Bo’s wife, Cambodian national He Yujing, and Cambodian Prince Group TCO associate Visal Pang. Since OFAC’s action in October 2025, Chen Bo has transferred ownership of his Tokyo mansion to He Yujing, who also owns the Cambodian company Super Light Speed Kh Technology Co., Ltd. Cambodia-based Visal Pang controls eleven Cambodian companies, several of which he co-directs with Chen Bo: Cambodia First Unite Construction Group (CFU Group) Co., Ltd., First Unite International Logistics Co., Ltd., First Unite Networks Entertainment Co., Ltd., First Unite Property Co., Ltd., First Unite Decoration (Cambodia) Co., Ltd., Cambodian First Unite Construction Machinery Co., Ltd., Linkedus Technology Co., Ltd., Cambo Duty Free Merchandise Co., Ltd., Marco Polo Hotel Co., Ltd., U-Life Go Now Co., Ltd., and U-Life Kh Super App Co., Ltd. Visal Pang was also designated by the United Kingdom on March 26, 2026.
Chen Bo remains in control of eleven Cambodian companies: Asian Welfare Lotteries Co., Ltd., CB General Insurance PLC., Cambodian Resource Energy Development Co., Ltd., Cambodian Unite Wei Ye Investment Co., DT Zhi Zao, Co., Ltd., First Aquatic Industrial Co., Ltd., Mo Net Beauty Co., Ltd., Prince International Airlines Co., Ltd., Richeng Property Developer Co., Ltd., Tian Xu International Technology Plc., and ZHX Printing Equipment Cambodia Co., Ltd.
He Yujing is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of Prince Group TCO. Super Light Speed Kh Technology Co., Ltd is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, He Yujing.
Visal Pang is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of Prince Group TCO. Cambodia First Unite Construction Group (CFU Group) Co., Ltd., First Unite International Logistics Co., Ltd., First Unite Networks Entertainment Co., Ltd., First Unite Property Co., Ltd., First Unite Decoration (Cambodia) Co., Ltd., Cambodian First Unite Construction Machinery Co., Ltd., Linkedus Technology Co., Ltd., Cambo Duty Free Merchandise Co., Ltd., Marco Polo Hotel Co., Ltd., U-Life Go Now Co., Ltd., and U-Life Kh Super App Co., Ltd. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Visal Pang.
Asian Welfare Lotteries Co., Ltd., CB General Insurance PLC., Cambodian Resource Energy Development Co., Ltd., Cambodian Unite Wei Ye Investment Co., DT Zhi Zao, Co., Ltd., First Aquatic Industrial Co., Ltd., Mo Net Beauty Co., Ltd., Prince International Airlines Co., Ltd., Richeng Property Developer Co., Ltd., Tian Xu International Technology Plc., and ZHX Printing Equipment Cambodia Co., Ltd. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Chen Bo.
On June 23, 2026, OFAC designated Prince Group TCO associate Dai An, a high-level leader in the Prince Group TCO. Dai is the majority owner of Singapore-based Chen Hua Holdings Pte Ltd (Chen Hua Holdings) and serves as director for Mauritius-based Meritwise Group Public Ltd (Meritwise Group) and Malaysia-based Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd (Greenmeadows).
Chen Hua Holdings, Meritwise Group, and Greenmeadows are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to have acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Dai An.
Singapore-based Greenbay Multi Media Pte Ltd (Greenbay Multi Media) is 100 percent owned by OFAC-designated Prince Group TCO executive Thet Li. Thet Li was designated by OFAC on October 14, 2025.
Greenbay Multi Media is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to have acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Thet Li.
SANCTIONS AGAINST FACILITATOR OF MADAGASCAR-BASED SCAM NETWORK
Chui Kok Wa (Chui) led an extensive network of scammers located in Madagascar that targeted Americans with scams, including defrauding Americans of digital assets. The scammers led by Chui exploited cyber-enabled technologies, including cryptocurrencies and digital systems and technologies, to defraud numerous Americans of over $400,000 equivalent, thereby materially contributing to the cybercrime and scam center threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economic health of the United States. Chui’s network garnered sympathy from vulnerable victims in order to misappropriate their funds for the private financial gain of his network.
OFAC is designating Chui Kok Wa pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended, for being responsible for or complicit in, or having engaged in, directly or indirectly, cyber-enabled activities originating from, or directed by persons located, in whole or in substantial part, outside the United States that are reasonably likely to result in, or have materially contributed to, a threat to the national security, foreign policy, or economic health or financial stability of the United States, and that have the purpose of or involve causing a misappropriation of funds or economic resources, intellectual property, proprietary or business confidential information, personal identifiers, or financial information for commercial or competitive advantage or private financial gain.
SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS
As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC. In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked. Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons.
Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons. OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions. In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons. The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person. Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing or conspiring to cause U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades U.S. sanctions. Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.
The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law. The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior. For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on Filing a Petition for Removal from an OFAC List.
