Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program Final Rule (CMS-4215-F)
On Nov. 5, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that codifies policies established in guidance documents for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (“Negotiation Program”) for initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond (CMS-4215-F). For initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028 of the Negotiation Program, statute directed CMS to implement the Negotiation Program through program instruction and other forms of program guidance. With this authority expiring, CMS is codifying the Negotiation Program for 2029 and beyond. In addition to codifying these policies, we are establishing new policies to continue implementation of statutory provisions under the Negotiation Program as well as finalizing revisions or clarifications to certain policies previously established to incorporate lessons learned from ongoing experience.1
The Negotiation Program final rule is one of several activities that reflect a broader CMS-wide strategy to lower prescription drug costs for people with Medicare. CMS is approaching codification of the Negotiation Program consistent with the goals of achieving greater value for beneficiaries and taxpayers and continuing to foster innovation.
The final rule is effective Dec. 5, 2026.
Background on the Negotiation Program
Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (P.L. 117-169) establish the Negotiation Program to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. Specifically, in accordance with section 1191(c)(3) of the Social Security Act (the Act), MFP means, with respect to a year during a price applicability period and with respect to a selected drug (as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act) with respect to such period, the MFP negotiated in accordance with section 1194 of the Act, and updated to account for inflation in accordance with section 1195(b) of the Act, as applicable, for such drug and year.
Under the IRA, with respect to each initial price applicability year, CMS will: (1) publish a list of selected drugs for negotiation and renegotiation, if any; (2) enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs that choose to participate; (3) negotiate (or renegotiate) MFPs for such selected drugs; (4) publish any agreed-upon MFPs for selected drugs; (5) carry out administrative and compliance duties; and (6) impose civil monetary penalties (CMPs), when applicable.
CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Part D and/or payable under Part B for initial price applicability year 2029 and for each subsequent initial price applicability year. In addition to the drugs selected for negotiation, CMS may also select drugs for renegotiation if selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP meet certain eligibility and selection criteria.
Codification of the Negotiation Program
In codifying the requirements for the Negotiation Program, CMS builds upon policies established for the first three cycles of negotiations and establishes new requirements for the fourth and future cycles of negotiations with a particular focus on continuing to increase transparency in the Negotiation Program.
The final regulations include, but are not limited to:
- Identification of Selected Drugs. Section 1192 of the Act establishes the requirements governing the publication of the selected drug list for an initial price applicability year, the identification of selected drugs, ranking of negotiation-eligible drugs, and the identification of qualifying single source drugs. CMS codifies these policies consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028, with a new policy to clarify how CMS will identify qualifying single source drugs to address potential program integrity concerns posed by specific new formulations. Additionally, CMS clarifies the treatment of withdrawn approvals for indications when identifying whether a drug that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion meets eligibility criteria to be a qualifying single source drug, in accordance with amendments made by the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation (Pub. L. 119-21).
- Requirements for Manufacturers of Selected Drugs. Section 1193(a) of the Act establishes the Negotiation Program Agreement and the requirements for a willing primary manufacturer to enter into and sign the Negotiation Program Agreement no later than Feb. 28 following the selected drug publication date. The Negotiation Program Agreement will remain in effect, including through renegotiation, as applicable, until the selected drug is no longer considered a selected drug under section 1192(c) of the Act (due to a determination that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing) unless it is terminated sooner by the primary manufacturer under specified conditions. CMS finalizes additional details related to the primary manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to another entity. In addition, CMS codifies the timing and process for executing and terminating a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS and the requirements a willing primary manufacturer is subject to upon executing the Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS, including mandatory submission of data to CMS, consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028.
- Negotiation Factors. After entering into an Agreement with CMS and in accordance with section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, the primary manufacturer of each selected drug must submit the following information with respect to the selected drug: information on the non-Federal Average Manufacturer Price (non-FAMP) and any information that CMS requires to carry out the Negotiation Program, including but not limited to, information related to the manufacturer-specific factors listed in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act. Additionally, primary manufacturers and any interested party may voluntarily submit evidence about the selected drugs and potential therapeutic alternatives as described in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. In accordance with section 1194(e) of the Act, CMS uses manufacturer-specific data and available evidence about the selected drugs and their therapeutic alternatives as the basis for determining offers and considering counteroffers in the negotiation process. CMS codifies these policies, including submission requirements for primary manufacturers, requirements for primary manufacturers to update submitted data, and how CMS will consider evidence from comparative effectiveness studies. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028.
- Negotiation Process. CMS develops and uses a consistent methodology and process for negotiation with the aim of achieving agreement on “the lowest [MFP] for each selected drug” in accordance with section 1194(b)(1) of the Act. The negotiation process includes engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, including patients; the development and delivery of the written initial offer, including a concise justification, to the primary manufacturer of a selected drug; the ability for the primary manufacturer to accept an offer or provide a statutory written counteroffer; optional negotiation meetings between CMS and the primary manufacturer; additional price exchange opportunities; the conclusion of negotiation, including a final offer sent by CMS to the primary manufacturer, where applicable; and the publication of agreed-upon MFPs and explanations of such MFPs. CMS codifies these policies for the negotiation process, including engagement with primary manufacturers and interested parties, the offer and counteroffer process, and the publication and explanation of the MFP. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028.
- Ineligibility for Selection, or Deselection of a Selected Drug Before or During Negotiation, or Following the Negotiation Period. In accordance with sections 1192(c) and 1192(e) of the Act, a potential qualifying single source drug is not eligible for selection, a selected drug will no longer be subject to the negotiation process, and a selected drug will cease to be a selected drug, subject to certain timing and situations, if CMS determines: (1) the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a generic drug under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that identifies as its reference-listed drug a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable), or FDA has licensed a biosimilar under section 351(k) of the Public Health Service Act that identifies as its reference product a product that is included in the potential qualifying single source drug or selected drug (as applicable); and (2) the generic drug or biosimilar, as applicable, is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure. CMS codifies provisions regarding its identification of when such generic drug or biosimilar is marketed within the meaning of these statutory requirements (“Bona Fide Marketing”). Further, CMS codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to the determination of ineligibility of a potential qualifying single source drug that would otherwise be eligible for selection and to the determination of the deselection of a selected drug, with additional information provided on the points in time CMS reviews the information to determine if a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that the generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. CMS also codifies the criteria, process, and timing related to monitoring that the approved generic drug(s) or licensed biosimilar(s) continue to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing for any potential qualifying single source drug(s) that were previously considered ineligible for selection or for any selected drug(s) deselected because CMS determined that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and that generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. These policies are consistent with statute and build on CMS guidance regarding the timing of review of the information to evaluate whether a generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing.
- Renegotiation of an MFP. Section 1194(f) of the Act establishes the requirements governing the identification of renegotiation-eligible drugs, the selection of drugs for renegotiation, and the renegotiation process. CMS codifies the criteria CMS will use to determine renegotiation eligibility and selection, the types of information CMS will consider when determining renegotiation eligibility and selection, opportunities and requirements for data submission, and the process for renegotiation, which will remain consistent, to the extent practicable, with the process and methodology used for negotiation. These policies are consistent with statute and guidance for initial price applicability year 2028. For renegotiation with respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and beyond, CMS finalizes its policy to consider the agreed-upon MFP for a drug selected for renegotiation as part of the consideration of section 1194(e)(1) factors.
Strengthening Program Integrity to Address Fixed Combination Drug Loophole
Under policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, if a drug is a fixed combination drug with two or more active moieties, active ingredients, or, for a vaccine for infectious disease(s), antigen components, a potential qualifying single source drug is identified using the same distinct combination of active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components. Under this policy, CMS is aware of a program integrity risk in which a manufacturer may avoid selection of a product or, in the case that such product is a qualifying single source drug that becomes a selected drug, avoid the application of the MFP, by marketing a new formulation of the product that includes, in addition to the active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) in the product, an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). In this scenario, CMS is concerned that the fixed combination drug policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028 would be in tension with the statutory requirement to identify qualifying single source drugs by aggregating across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug, because CMS would not aggregate the original product and the new formulation containing the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables for an alternative route of administration, even though these may be appropriately understood as different formulations of the same qualifying single source drug for purposes of the Negotiation Program.
To address this program integrity risk and ensure CMS is adhering to the statutory requirement to identify qualifying single source drugs by aggregating across drug dosage forms and strengths, including new formulations, CMS is finalizing its proposed policy regarding treatment of specific fixed combination drugs in CMS’ determinations of qualifying single source drugs. Under this policy, if CMS determines that a fixed combination drug with two or more active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or, for a vaccine for infectious disease(s), antigen component(s) shares one or more active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) with another drug or biological product with the same New Drug Application (NDA)/Biologics License Application (BLA) holder, and such products differ in active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), CMS will identify a potential qualifying single source drug using all dosage forms and strengths of the drug or biological product with the shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) and the same NDA/BLA holder. For example, a product containing active ingredient X plus hyaluronidase will be identified as part of the same potential qualifying single source drug as a product offered by the same BLA holder that contains only active ingredient X, if the inclusion of hyaluronidase creates a new formulation and enables a new route of administration for active ingredient X.
Collection of Information to Inform Drug Selection and Drug Price Negotiation
In conjunction with publication of the final rule, CMS also submitted to OMB for approval revisions to two currently approved information collection packages (OMB 0938-1443 and OMB 0938-1452). These two packages collect information necessary for (1) a Biosimilar Manufacturer to submit a request, prior to the selected drug publication date for an initial price applicability year, for CMS’ consideration to delay the inclusion of a Reference Drug on the selected drug list for such given initial price applicability year; (2) a primary manufacturer to voluntarily submit information that CMS may consider in determining eligibility and selection of drugs for renegotiation; (3) a primary manufacturer to voluntarily submit information to enable CMS to determine if a selected drug is a Small Biotech Drug for purposes of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs; (4) primary manufacturers of selected drugs to submit information required for the negotiation and renegotiation of the MFP of the selected drug and for primary manufacturers and other interested parties to submit optional information about the selected drug and its potential therapeutic alternative(s) for use in negotiation and renegotiation of the MFP of the selected drug; and (5) instructions and a form for a primary manufacturer to submit a statutory written counteroffer for negotiation or a renegotiation written counteroffer for renegotiation in the case where the primary manufacturer does not accept CMS’ written initial offer of an MFP.
Implementing Certain Provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022
Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs
The exception for Small Biotech Drugs from being considered a negotiation-eligible drug under section 1192 of the Act applied to initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028. However, the definition of a “Small Biotech Drug” is applicable for the purpose of determining eligibility for the calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, which limits CMS from offering or agreeing to a counteroffer for an MFP below such floor for selected drugs that are qualifying Small Biotech Drugs. The Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs newly applies for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030 and is included in this final rule. After considering the public comments, CMS is finalizing a modification to the treatment of non-FAMP in the adjusted ceiling calculation for certain selected drugs that are qualifying Small Biotech Drugs.
Negotiated Price for Selected Drugs
Section 11001(b) of the IRA amended section 1860D-2(d)(1) of the Act by adding subparagraph (D), which provides that, for selected drugs with respect to a price applicability period, the negotiated price “used for payment (as described in this subsection) shall be no greater than the [MFP] for such drug…plus any dispensing fees for such drug.” CMS is codifying these policies consistent with prior guidance.
IRA Formulary Inclusion Requirement and Successor Regulation Exception
Section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act requires that for 2026 and each subsequent year, Part D plans must include each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug on Part D formularies if an MFP is in effect for that drug with respect to that year. Section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act states that nothing in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act shall be construed as prohibiting a Part D plan sponsor from removing a selected drug from a formulary if such removal would be permitted under § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) or any successor regulation. In the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, we identified § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2), (3), and (4) as the successor regulation for purposes of section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act. CMS is codifying these policies consistent with prior guidance.
Maximum Fair Price Effectuation for 2028
CMS intends to release final guidance in fall 2026 to implement policies related to manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2028 for the Negotiation Program, consistent with the program instruction directive in sections 11001(c) and 11002(c) of the IRA. This guidance will specify the requirements for effectuation of the MFP, including with respect to drugs payable under Part B. CMS intends to codify MFP effectuation policies for 2029 and future years through Negotiation Program rulemaking in calendar year 2027.
Additional Resources
- Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program – https://www.cms.gov/priorities/medicare-prescription-drug-affordability/overview/medicare-drug-price-negotiation-program
- Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program Initial Price Applicability Year 2029 Key Milestones and Timeline – https://www.cms.gov/files/document/negotiation-program-final-rule-timeline.pdf.

BOSTON – United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced today that, in Fiscal Year 2026, the District of Massachusetts entered into settlements with defendants for more than $133 million and collected more than $164 million in criminal and civil actions. Of the collections, the Office recovered $31 million in criminal actions and $132 million in civil actions. The Office also recovered more than $35 million in forfeited assets.

Additionally, the District of Massachusetts worked with other U.S. Attorney’s Offices and Department of Justice components to collect more than $162,849,201 in cases pursued jointly by these offices.

“The more than $164 million collected, $35 million forfeited and over $133 million secured through settlements this fiscal year represent far more than numbers. They reflect our Office’s relentless pursuit of those who exploit public taxpayer-funded programs, abuse positions of trust and seek to profit through fraud and criminal conduct. We will continue using every tool available to recover stolen funds, return money to victims and ensure that wrongdoing carries meaningful consequences.”

“The more than $164 million collected, $35 million forfeited and over $133 million secured through settlements this fiscal year represent far more than numbers. They reflect our Office’s relentless pursuit of those who exploit public taxpayer-funded programs, abuse positions of trust and seek to profit through fraud and criminal conduct. We will continue using every tool available to recover stolen funds, return money to victims and ensure that wrongdoing carries meaningful consequences.”

In Fiscal Year 2026, the Office’s Affirmative Civil Enforcement Unit (ACE) entered into 26 settlements with defendants totaling $133,198,525. These included a $46 million settlement with Veloxis to resolve criminal and civil allegations of kickbacks to healthcare professionals related to its marketing of its drug, Envarsus; a $15 million settlement with Dana-Farber Cancer Institute concerning fraud related to cancer research grants; and a $14.5 million settlement with Laboratory Corporation of America concerning medically unnecessary claims for urine drug testing to Medicare. The settlements also reflect the Office’s continued efforts to recover funds unlawfully obtained through the Paycheck Protection Program, which assisted businesses affected by the Covid-19 pandemic. Since the pandemic, the ACE Unit has entered into settlements totaling $166,434,620 with businesses concerning allegations of fraud in the Paycheck Protection Program.

In Fiscal Year 2026, the Asset Recovery Unit (ARU) was responsible for collecting more than $31,330,511 in restitution for victims, criminal fines and special assessments, as well as forfeiture of $35,315,258 in criminal proceeds or other property involved in crimes.

During Fiscal Year 2026, ARU filed six civil forfeiture complaints to recover cryptocurrency alleged to be traceable to financial fraud scams targeting Massachusetts victims, including romance and elder fraud, and other illicit activity. ARU obtained a final order of forfeiture for more than 100 wildlife parts including orangutan skulls, tiger skulls, jaguar skin and other parts from endangered, threatened and protected species. With the Department of Justice, ARU distributed more than $12.4 million in previously forfeited funds from Roger Knox and his co-conspirators to over 8,000 securities fraud victims.

The U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, along with the Department’s litigating divisions, are responsible for enforcing and collecting civil and criminal debts owed to the U.S. and criminal debts owed to federal crime victims. The law requires defendants to pay restitution to victims of certain federal crimes who have suffered a physical injury or financial loss. While restitution is paid to the victim, criminal fines and felony assessments are paid to the Department’s Crime Victims Fund, which distributes the funds collected to federal and state victim compensation and victim assistance programs. Forfeited assets deposited into the Department of Justice’s Assets Forfeiture Fund are used to restore funds to crime victims and for a variety of law enforcement purposes.

The District of Massachusetts’ Civil Division is led by Assistant United States Attorney Abraham R. George, Chief of Civil. Assistant United States Attorney Brian LaMacchia, Chief of the Affirmative Civil Enforcement Unit, leads the District’s efforts in affirmative civil enforcement and Assistant United States Attorney Carol Head, Chief of the Asset Recovery Unit, leads the District’s forfeiture and restitution efforts.
title: U.S. Attorney's Office Entered Settlements Exceeding $133 Million; Collected Over $164 Million in Civil and Criminal Actions in Fiscal Year 2026

The Department of the Air Force is accelerating its push to operationalize enterprise intelligence and deliver combat-ready artificial intelligence capabilities directly to the warfighter, unveiling a comprehensive modernization blueprint Oct. 27.
Speaking at the annual Institute for Defense and Government Advancement Military Flight Training USA Summit, Susan Davenport, chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the Department of the Air Force, outlined the DAF’s strategy to move super intelligence beyond experimental testing and into operational application across 15 mission domains.
The transition hinges on establishing these 15 operational domains — spanning core areas such as nuclear operations, intelligence and human resources — each spearheaded by a general officer or Senior Executive Service civilian to govern authoritative data and deliver mission-critical tools to the field." I always say SI is an organizational design decision and return on investment is measured by the outcomes we were able to achieve — in other words — did we shorten the kill chain, or return time back to the commander, or did we create decision advantage?” said Davenport. “In order to get the best outcome, we must redesign the process before we digitize it."
To prevent these strategies from becoming "shelfware," the DAF has established 15 distinct operational domains spanning critical areas from intelligence and nuclear operations to human resources. Each domain is overseen by a dedicated senior leader, a general officer or SES member, tasked with operationalizing the strategy and making trustworthy, authoritative data available immediately.
"To operationalize the strategies, we stood up 15 domains across air and space and placed a general officer or Senior Executive Service member on top of each domain, and they’re responsible for making trustworthy data available to the enterprise and accelerating SI in their domain," Davenport explained.
While Davenport’s team lays the technical groundwork for big Air Force systems, force development leaders stress that these technical advancements must align with human growth.
Dr. Wendy Walsh, Air Education and Training Command’s chief learning officer, also participated during the panel, alongside Davenport.
"We build a capability and a capacity, and those are the enabling structures of how people realize mission command, and that is perfect for SI as well," noted Walsh. "It's a new technology. How are we going to do this? How are we going to build the trust and work together?"
As the department systematically rolls out these capabilities domain by domain, leaders stress that human oversight remains the crucial element to success.
More information on SI literacy is expected to be delivered to Airmen and Guardians later this year.
title: DAF unveils enterprise blueprint to field operational SI across 15 mission domains

ALEXANDRIA, Va. – A former FBI agent from Ashburn pled guilty today to wire fraud and money laundering related to using his access to steal cryptocurrency.

According to court documents, from 2017 through early 2025, Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, worked at the FBI Boston Division on an investigative squad focused on an adversarial nation state. From February 2025 to July 31, 2026, Yaroch worked in the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, with access to FBI systems that contained cryptocurrency credentials that the FBI had collected as part of its investigations.

Beginning no later than December 2024, Yaroch used his position to steal cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by the subjects of various other investigations or by adversarial nation state actors, and from at least one wallet the FBI created to use in an operation. Throughout his wire fraud scheme, Yaroch conducted approximately 100 fraudulent transfers using credentials related to 35 separate FBI investigations. He illicitly gained approximately $2,474,380.66 in fraudulent proceeds.

Once Yaroch moved the stolen cryptocurrency, he would exchange it for a different type of cryptocurrency. Yaroch then laundered the cryptocurrency through additional financial transactions to obfuscate its source, nature, and ownership. Between Nov. 25, 2025, and Jan. 13, 2026, Yaroch transferred approximately $93,082 to one of his accounts, then transferred the funds between his other accounts from which he sent various payments to cover his debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

In addition to paying off his debts, Yaroch intended to use the fraudulent proceeds to make other purchases, including financing a new life abroad. Yaroch asked ChatGPT how to maximize profit from investments and where to live in the European Union. Following ChatGPT’s suggestion of buying a vineyard in Portugal, on June 15, 2026, Yaroch provided a power-of-attorney to lawyers in Portugal to represent him before the Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority, to register him and obtain his tax identification number in Portugal, and to collect the password to access his finance portal. Yaroch then made arrangements to travel to Portugal in September 2026.

As set forth in the agreed upon statement of facts, Yaroch’s actions compromised multiple FBI investigations related to both criminal groups and nation state adversaries. His actions deprived FBI employees of their ability to carry out their functions to protect public safety and national security. Yaroch’s actions also compromised FBI sources and methods used in foreign intelligence collection and criminal investigations.

Yaroch is scheduled to be sentenced on March 4, 2027. He faces up to 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Daniel S. Wierzbicki, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office’s Counterintelligence Division, made the announcement after U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted the plea.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kathleen Robeson and Russell Carlberg are prosecuting the case. The National Security Cyber Section (NatSec Cyber) of the Justice Department’s National Security Division and the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General Mid-Atlantic Region provided significant assistance.

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 1:26-CR-208.
title: Former FBI agent pleads guilty to Cryptocurrency theft

INDIANAPOLIS – Former Kokomo Police Department officer Sinmi Asomuyide, 33, has been sentenced to 40 years in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release. In June 2026, Asomuyide was convicted following a five-day jury trial of Deprivation of Rights Under Color of Law, Witness Tampering, and Destruction of Records.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Asomuyide, then 31 years old, first encountered Minor #1, a 14-year-old girl, on June 30, 2024, while serving as a Kokomo Police Department (KPD) patrol officer. Earlier that day, Minor #1's father called 911 to report her as a runaway. Asomuyide and another KPD officer responded to the call and located Minor #1 at the home of another underage girl.

After taking Minor #1 into custody, Asomuyide transported her to the Kinsey Youth Center. As he entered the facility’s sallyport garage, he turned off his body-worn camera in violation of KPD policy. He then took Minor #1’s cellphone and used it to call his personal TextNow phone number before questioning her about her sexual history. During a pat-down search, Asomuyide discovered a vape pen in Minor #1’s back pocket. After entering the Youth Center, he escorted Minor #1 to a side room and told her he would contact her later to return the vape pen.

Minor #1 was eventually picked up from the Youth Center by a family friend, at the direction of her father. As she left, she sent Asomuyide the username for one of her social media accounts, and he responded by requesting her TikTok username. The two continued communicating by text message throughout the evening while Asomuyide completed the remainder of his shift, and Minor #1 remained under the impression that Asomuyide intended to return her vape pen.

Later that evening, Asoyumide took several steps to see Minor #1 while simultaneously covering his tracks. He returned to the KPD police station and requested overtime, stating that he would be finishing his paperwork from 10:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m., but instead left the station to pick up Minor #1. He arrived at the family friend’s apartment in his KPD uniform and demanded to speak to Minor #1 privately to determine where she should stay. Instead, Asoyumide handcuffed Minor #1 in the back of his squad car and drove to an empty warehouse parking lot, as shown by his squad car’s GPS data. He uncuffed the girl, moved her to the front seat and sexually assaulted her. After, Asoyumide put the handcuffs back on and drove the minor back to the apartment complex.

Minor #1 reported the assault to family members and law enforcement, prompting the Indiana State Police (ISP) to open an investigation. During a forensic examination of Asomuyide's patrol vehicle, investigators located a dried semen stain matching Asomuyide’s DNA on the center console.

Approximately one week after the assault, ISP detectives interviewed Asomuyide. During the interview, he falsely claimed that he never provided Minor #1 with his phone number, suggesting instead that she may have overheard him reciting it to a Kinsey Youth Center employee. He also falsely asserted that Minor #1 had contacted him on a work phone, even though KPD officers are not issued work phones.

A forensic examination of Asomuyide’s cell phone revealed that, within hours of the assault, he searched phrases including "how to delete text me account" and "TextNow delete account."

This is not Asomuyide’s first instance of sexual misconduct with a minor. He was previously employed as a police officer at the Portsmouth (Virginia) Police Department (PPD) and was forced to resign after an allegation that he had sexual intercourse with a 15-year-old while he was off duty. When he later applied to the Kokomo Police Department, he misrepresented what he did, stating that he was forced to resign from PPD because he was “hanging out” with a 17-year-old girl who told him that she was 19.

“The Department of Justice takes civil rights abuses seriously, including those committed by the small minority of police officers that betray public trust,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon. “This defendant will be held accountable for the kidnapping and sexual abuse of a child. We hope the victim will be able to recover and prosper despite this horrific episode.”

“This defendant exploited the badge in one of the worst ways imaginable,” said Tom Wheeler, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Indiana. “What makes these crimes particularly disturbing is that he used the very tools, training, and authority entrusted to him as a police officer not only to assault a vulnerable child, but to try to conceal it. The evidence told a different story, and today's sentence sends a clear message that no one can use the authority of the badge as a shield from accountability.”

“The very people entrusted with protecting children must never become the ones who victimize them. This defendant preyed on a 14-year-old girl and then attempted to cover up his crimes,” said FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O’Malley. “That kind of calculated abuse is unconscionable. The FBI remains committed to protecting children and relentlessly pursuing those who prey on them.”

"The Indiana State Police aggressively investigates crimes committed against children, especially when perpetrated by individuals placed in positions of immense trust," said Captain Ron Galaviz, ISP Chief Public Information Officer. "It is unconscionable that someone in authority would abuse their power for personal gratification at the expense of an innocent child. We remain steadfast in our commitment to holding these abusers accountable and protecting the most vulnerable members of our communities."

Federal Bureau of Investigation, Indianapolis Division and Indiana State Police investigated this case. The sentence was imposed by Chief District Judge James R. Sweeney, II.

U.S. Attorney Wheeler thanked Assistant U.S. Attorney, Peter Blackett, Civil Rights Division Trial Attorney Anita Channapati, and former Senior Sex Crimes Counsel Tara Allison, as well as Victim Witness Coordinator, Stephanie Lloyd, for their work on this case.

text:
Fast Facts
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detains noncitizens in facilities across the U.S. Entities within the Department of Homeland Security inspect these facilities to ensure they meet standards for humane detention.
The numbers of facilities and detained noncitizens have increased since FY 2024. At the same time, the frequency of inspections has changed—decreasing in some cases—with more reliance on facility self-inspections.
ICE depends on inspections to find problems in areas like medical care and food service. But, ICE hasn't determined how changes to its inspections have affected its oversight.
Our recommendations address this issue.
ICE Detention Facility in Louisiana
The outside of a detention facility with three flag poles centered in front of the entrance and cars parked on both sides.
Highlights
What GAO Found
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) detention facility inspections have changed at the same time that the number of immigration detention facilities and the size of the detained population have increased. From April 2025 to April 2026, following a January 2025 Executive Order, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) added over 40 detention facilities that detain noncitizens for over 72 hours. The average daily population of detained noncitizens grew by over 50 percent, to 61,817 individuals, over the timeframe. From fiscal year 2024 to July 2026, three of the four DHS entities that conducted inspections changed the frequency (decreased or increased) or stopped conducting inspections.
Changes to Inspections Conducted by DHS Entities from Fiscal Year (FY) 2024 to July 2026
ICE relies on these inspections to identify deficiencies in its facilities and ensure compliance with its detention standards. However, the frequency of inspections has in some cases decreased, there is an increased reliance on self-inspections, and processes for these inspections have changed. ICE has not used evidence, such as data on deficiencies identified through inspections and performance information such as the extent to which facilities are in compliance with their contracts, to determine the effects of these recent changes on facility conditions. By using evidence to determine these effects and applying the results to improve oversight, ICE could ensure that facilities provide sound conditions and care for noncitizens, in accordance with its standards.
Why GAO Did This Study
ICE is authorized to detain noncitizens apprehended for violations of immigration law pending removal proceedings or execution of a removal order. ICE guidance states that ICE must detain noncitizens in the most humane manner possible. ICE has established detention standards that dictate how facilities should operate. ICE relies on various DHS entities within and outside of ICE to assess compliance. These inspections identify deficiencies related to medical care and food service, among other areas.
GAO was asked to review compliance with detention standards and related oversight. This report examines (1) changes to DHS inspections of detention facilities since GAO’s last report on this topic (GAO-25-107580) and (2) ICE's use of evidence to inform its oversight of detention facilities in light of the changes. GAO reviewed documentation on DHS’s various oversight mechanisms and how they changed between fiscal year 2024 and July 2026. GAO also analyzed ICE data on the number of facilities that detain noncitizens for over 72 hours and the average daily population from April 2025 to April 2026. GAO interviewed officials responsible for conducting oversight from various offices within DHS.
Recommendations
GAO is making two recommendations for ICE to (1) use evidence to determine the effects of changes to inspections by DHS entities and whether they are collectively sufficient for identifying deficiencies, and (2) use the findings to modify ICE inspections, as appropriate. DHS concurred with the recommendations.
title: Immigration Detention: Changes In Inspections of ICE Facilities Raise Questions About Oversight

HOUSTON – Three fugitive leaders of the foreign terrorist organization Tren de Aragua (TdA), designated by the Trump Administration last year, are charged in the Southern District of Texas and now have rewards totaling up to $50 million for information leading to their arrests and/or convictions.

Yohan José Romero a/k/a Yohan Petrica, 48; Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano a/k/a El Viejo, 37; and Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez a/k/a Juancho, 44, were previously charged in a six-count second superseding indictment returned in 2025. A nine-count third superseding indictment followed in July 2026.

According to the allegations, all three face charges of conspiring to provide and providing material support to Tren de Aragua (TdA). Serrano is on the FBI’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List and also faces charges of conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine and international cocaine distribution.

“Since President Trump returned to office, the Department of Justice has charged more than 350 members and associates of Tren de Aragua, including Yohan Petrica, El Viejo, and Juancho,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Their criminal enterprise has spread fear, violence, and lawlessness, and we will not stop until those responsible are brought to justice. Anyone with information regarding the location of the three individuals listed in today’s superseding indictment should help save lives by notifying the FBI.”

“These gang members are monsters, and we’ve indicted them as such,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz. “I’m confident the enhanced bounties will incentivize these terrorists’ return to my district, where we will bring them to justice.”

“These gang members are monsters, and we’ve indicted them as such,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz. “I’m confident the enhanced bounties will incentivize these terrorists’ return to my district, where we will bring them to justice.”

“By leveraging DEA's investigative expertise alongside our partners through the Homeland Security Task Force, we are bringing the full force of the U.S. government to bear against narco-terrorists that threaten our communities. Today's announcement demonstrates what can be achieved through unprecedented coordination and intelligence sharing across federal law enforcement,” said Administrator Terrance Cole of the Drug Enforcement Administration. “Yohan José Romero, Mosquera Serrano, and Rivas Núñez have played key roles in directing and expanding Tren de Aragua's operations throughout the Western Hemisphere. TdA spreads violence, fear, and instability wherever it operates. Make no mistake - DEA will stop at nothing to identify, disrupt, and dismantle this criminal network.”

“There’s a reason Giovanni Mosquera Serrano is one of the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted fugitives. He, along with “Petrica,” “Juancho,” and their foreign terror organization, are accused of a long list of crimes that include murders, kidnappings, drug and sex trafficking, and illegal gold mining operations that help finance TdA’s terrorist activities,” said Special Agent in Charge Jason Hudson of the FBI Houston Field Office. “TdA’s criminal activity spills into streets and communities across the U.S., including Houston. We hope today’s multimillion-dollar rewards motivate someone, anywhere, to say ‘enough is enough’ and lead us to one or all three fugitives. The arm of the law is long, and no border will shield them from American justice.”

“As Secretary Rubio has repeatedly stated, transnational criminal and terrorist organizations such as Tren de Aragua are the most urgent security threat in our hemisphere,” said Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Thomas G. DiNanno. “Today, we are offering rewards totaling up to $50 million under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions of the top three leaders of Tren de Aragua. The Trump Administration remains fully committed to eliminating narcoterrorist organizations in the region that traffic illicit drugs, commit violent acts, and cause harm to American communities.”

The Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs is offering the rewards through its Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program for information leading to arrests or convictions of the three fugitives in any country.

The reward for information leading to Romero’s arrest or conviction increased from $4 million to $20 million, while the reward for Serrano has increased to $15 million from $5 million. A new reward of up to $15 million is also being offered for information regarding Núñez.

According to court documents, TdA originated as a Venezuelan prison gang in the mid-2000s and has since expanded its criminal network throughout the Western Hemisphere, including the United States. The organization engages in drug and firearms trafficking, commercial sex trafficking, kidnapping, robbery, theft, fraud, and extortion. Members also commit murder, assault, and other violent acts to further its criminal activities, according to the charges.

TdA also allegedly generated revenue through financial crimes targeting financial institutions, including ATM jackpotting schemes used to steal millions of dollars. The investigation revealed the conspiracy targeted or carried out ATM jackpotting attacks in 47 states, the District of Columbia, and several foreign countries, according to the allegations.

If you have any information concerning these individuals, please contact the FBI via WhatsApp or Telegram at +1-281-787-9939. Those with information may also contact their local FBI office, nearest U.S. Embassy or Consulate or can submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov .

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Casey N. MacDonald and Anibal J. Alaniz of the SDTX are prosecuting the case along with Deputy Director David C. Smith and Trial Attorneys James Keller and Kelly McGann of Joint Task Force Vulcan.

text:
Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Mexican Federal Judge’s Arrest on U.S. Charges of Accepting $2 Million Bribe to Free Canadian Drug Trafficker Charged with Ryan Wedding
Note: Please see the second superseding indictment here.
A Mexican judge has been arrested on a nine-count federal indictment charging him with accepting a $2 million bribe in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of a Canadian drug trafficker who was the second-in-command to a former Olympic snowboarder charged with leading a transnational cocaine trafficking operation and with murder and attempted murder.
Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia.
He is charged in a second superseding indictment with nine counts of being an accessory after the fact. The United States will request Benítez’s extradition from Colombia.
“Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home, will face justice in the United States,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the work of the Homeland Security Task Force and our international law enforcement partners, Mr. Benítez will be held accountable. The Department of Justice will continue identifying and dismantling transnational criminal organizations that threaten the safety of the American people.”
“The FBI and our partners have arrested Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexican judge who allegedly accepted bribes and used his position to aid former FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitive Ryan Wedding and his associates,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Benítez Alcántara was a district judge in Mexico City who allegedly accepted $2 million in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of Wedding’s second in command, while Wedding was orchestrating a billion-dollar transnational criminal organization and the largest supplier of cocaine to Canada with connections in Colombia, Mexico, and the U.S. Benítez Alcántara is charged with nine counts of accessory after the fact for assisting the individual in order to hinder or prevent his apprehension, trial or punishment. Thanks to FBI Los Angeles, our Bogatá Law Enforcement Attaché, our local partners, and our Department of Justice who made the success of this operation possible.”
“This case underscores my office’s commitment to dismantling criminal organizations at every level, including by holding accountable those who abuse positions of public trust,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California.
According to the superseding indictment returned on Sept. 4, Benítez used his official position to unlawfully secure Clark’s release, enabling a major figure in an international drug organization to evade lawful detention. In return for the $2 million bribe payment, Benítez issued rulings that directly facilitated the release from custody of Andrew Clark, 36, a Canadian drug trafficker and second-in-command to Ryan James Wedding, 44, a former Olympic snowboarder for Canada who led one of the biggest, most notorious, and violent transnational criminal organizations.
In October 2024, Clark was arrested in Mexico on U.S. drug trafficking, murder, and attempted murder charges in which Wedding also was named. Following his arrest, Clark appeared before Benítez, then serving as the district judge in Mexico City responsible for overseeing Clark’s extradition proceedings.
Photos of Luis Benítez Alcántara in custody.
In November 2024, the United States formally requested Clark’s extradition to face prosecution in the United States. From November 2024 through February 2025, Clark transferred approximately $2.75 million, through intermediaries and in small increments, for the purpose of securing his release from Mexican custody. During this period, Clark also negotiated an agreement to pay Benítez approximately $2 million in exchange for ordering his release.
On Feb. 24, 2025, the same day Benítez received the full $2 million bribe payment, he granted Clark bond and ordered him released. Days later, Clark was re‑arrested and removed to the United States, where the criminal case against him remains pending.
Wedding, who, at the time, was one of the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted Fugitives, was apprehended in Mexico in January 2026 and subsequently, removed to the United States, where he remains in federal custody. He faces drug‑trafficking, murder, and attempted murder charges and is currently scheduled for two separate trials on March 31, 2027, and Oct. 26, 2027.
If convicted, Benítez would face a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison on each count.
The FBI investigated this matter with the Los Angeles Police Department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police – Federal Policing. In addition, significant assistance was provided by U.S. law enforcement partners, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection Buffalo, New York, and Colombian law enforcement partners, including Colombian National Police – Directorate of Criminal Investigation and Interpol, Special Interagency Investigation Group (Policía Nacional de Colombia – Dirección de Investigación Criminal e Interpol, Grupo Especial de Investigación Interagenciales).
The Justice Department’s Judicial Attaché Office in Bogotá and Office of International Affairs worked with the Government of Colombia to secure the arrest.
This investigation, arrest, and prosecution are part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Los Angeles comprises agents and officers from the FBI and LAPD with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California.
Assistant U.S. Attorneys Lyndsi Allsop and Joshua J. Lee for the Central District of California are prosecuting this case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided substantial assistance.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

text:
Reward Offers Up to $50M for Information Leading to Arrests and/or Convictions of Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) Leaders Following Homeland Security Task Force Investigation
Note: Read the Superseding Indictment here.
Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) leaders Yohan José Romero, also known as “Yohan Petrica,” 48; Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano, also known as “El Viejo,” 37; and Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez, also known as “Juancho,” 44, were previously charged in a 2025 six-count second superseding indictment in the Southern District of Texas, for conspiring to provide and providing material support to TdA. A nine-count third superseding indictment was later returned in July 2026 and unsealed this week. In those indictments, Mosquera Serrano is also charged with conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine and international cocaine distribution.
“Since President Trump returned to office, the Department of Justice has charged more than 350 members and associates of Tren de Aragua, including Yohan Petrica, El Viejo, and Juancho,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Their criminal enterprise has spread fear, violence, and lawlessness, and we will not stop until those responsible are brought to justice. Anyone with information regarding the location of the three individuals listed in today’s superseding indictment should help save lives by notifying the FBI.”
“These gang members are monsters, and we’ve indicted them as such,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas. “I’m confident the enhanced bounties will incentivize these terrorists’ return to my district, where we will bring them to justice.”
Mosquera Serrano is on the FBI’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List. Jose Romero and Rivas Núñez are also fugitives. The Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL) is offering rewards under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program (TOCRP) of up to $50 million total for information leading to their arrests and/or convictions in any country.
Yohan José Romero, also known as “Yohan Petrica” increased from up to $4 million to up to $20 million Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano, also known as “Giovanni” and “El Viejo” increased from up to $5 million to up to $15 million Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez , also known as “Juancho”: new offer of up to $15 million
“By leveraging DEA's investigative expertise alongside our partners through the Homeland Security Task Force, we are bringing the full force of the U.S. government to bear against narco-terrorists that threaten our communities,” said Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Administrator Terrance Cole. “Today's announcement demonstrates what can be achieved through unprecedented coordination and intelligence sharing across federal law enforcement. Yohan José Romero, Mosquera Serrano, and Rivas Núñez have played key roles in directing and expanding Tren de Aragua's operations throughout the Western Hemisphere. TdA spreads violence, fear, and instability wherever it operates. Make no mistake - DEA will stop at nothing to identify, disrupt, and dismantle this criminal network.”
“As Secretary Rubio has repeatedly stated, transnational criminal and terrorist organizations such as Tren de Aragua are the most urgent security threat in our hemisphere,” said Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Thomas G. DiNanno. “Today, we are offering rewards totaling up to $50 million under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions of the top three leaders of Tren de Aragua. The Trump Administration remains fully committed to eliminating narcoterrorist organizations in the region that traffic illicit drugs, commit violent acts, and cause harm to American communities.”
If you have any information concerning these individuals, please contact the FBI via WhatsApp or Telegram at 281-787-9939. Those with information may also contact their local FBI office, nearest American Embassy or Consulate or can submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov.
The FBI and the DEA are jointly conducting the investigation with the assistance of the Houston Police Department, Harris County Sheriff’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), Colombian National Police and the Colombian Attorney General’s Office (Fiscalía General de la Nación), with significant assistance from the Justice Department’s Office of Judicial Attaché in Bogota and Office of International Affairs.

TdA is a violent transnational criminal organization that originated as a prison gang in Venezuela in the mid-2000s. Since that time, TdA has expanded its criminal network throughout the Western Hemisphere and established a presence in the United States. TdA’s criminal activities range from drug trafficking and firearms trafficking to sex trafficking, kidnapping, robbery, theft, fraud, and extortion. TdA members also commit murder, assault, and other violent acts to advance the organization’s criminal activities. TdA has also developed an additional source of revenue stream by committing financial crimes that target financial institutions throughout the United States, including using ATM jackpotting to steal millions of dollars in cash. Additionally, the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), USMS, and the Federal Bureau of Prisons are essential law enforcement partners with JTFV.
This prosecution is also part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. MONROE – The United States Attorney’s Office announced that a federal jury has found Jason P. Peacock , 41, of Tallulah, guilty of Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon and Illegal Possession of a Machinegun after a two‑day trial before United States Chief District Judge Terry A. Doughty. Peacock faces up to 25 years in prison. His sentencing is scheduled for December 2, 2026, before Judge Doughty.

According to evidence presented at trial, the case arose from a report of shots fired in Tallulah on May 31, 2025. Victims reported that Peacock, a previously convicted felon prohibited from possessing firearms, had brandished a black handgun at them before firing several rounds into the air and then fleeing. Police pursued Peacock to the home of another Tallulah resident who reported that Peacock had entered her home with a gun and then retreated to the back of the house. Officers proceeded to clear the residence and Peacock then emerged from the house and surrendered.

After Peacock was in custody, the homeowner consented to a search of the residence for the firearm she had seen him carrying. Officers recovered a black Glock equipped with a machinegun conversion device hidden inside a pot in the kitchen. The homeowner confirmed that no one in the home owned a firearm of that type. At trial, prosecutors presented evidence of Peacock’s recorded jail calls which established a clear timeline of events and proved Peacock’s possession of the weapon beyond a reasonable doubt.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Louisiana State Police, and the Tallulah Police Department investigated the case. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Allison Foster and J. Aaron Crawford, with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan and Paralegal Specialist Emily Favrot.

This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities . Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) at the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla .

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer. The case number for this matter is 3:26‑cr‑00184.

PORTLAND, Ore. — A federal jury has found a Tigard man guilty of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion after he attempted to profit from the commercial sexual exploitation of his girlfriend and later fled to Thailand to avoid prosecution, U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today.

Selva Delano Mudaliar , 40, was found guilty of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion following a federal jury trial.

According to evidence presented at trial, in December 2021, Mudaliar transported the victim from Portland, Oregon, to a hotel in Vancouver, Washington, where he attempted to arrange for her to engage in commercial sex acts with a customer in exchange for money. Prosecutors proved that Mudaliar fraudulently induced the victim to accompany him and used force, threats, and coercion in connection with the sex trafficking scheme.

Trial evidence showed that after meeting a customer at a Portland nightclub, Mudaliar became interested in the customer after observing that he had substantial funds available in his bank account. Mudaliar directed the victim to introduce herself to the customer and later drove both individuals to a hotel in Vancouver, Washington. Once there, Mudaliar negotiated a deal under which the customer would pay $1,500 in exchange for sexual access to the victim.

When the arrangement failed, Mudaliar became enraged and assaulted the victim. Evidence at trial established that Mudaliar repeatedly struck the victim in the face and head and strangled her until she lost consciousness. The victim suffered severe injuries that required emergency medical treatment and transfer to a Level 1 trauma center.

Following the assault, the Washington County District Attorney's Office charged Mudaliar with multiple state offenses. Shortly before his scheduled state court trial in February 2024, Mudaliar fled the United States and traveled to Thailand. The FBI assisted in locating Mudaliar overseas, and he was arrested by Thai authorities. Mudaliar later consented to extradition and was returned to the United States to face the Washington County charges and additional federal charges. The charges in state court remain pending.

“Sex trafficking is a violent crime that exploits vulnerable victims for financial gain,” said Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon . “The defendant attempted to sell a woman for sex and then brutally assaulted her when his scheme failed. Today's verdict holds him accountable for that conduct and demonstrates our commitment to prosecuting those who use force, fraud, and coercion to exploit others.”

Mudaliar faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years in federal prison and a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 2, 2027.

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Tigard Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mira R. Chernick and William M. McLaren prosecuted the case.
title: Tigard Man Found Guilty of Federal Sex Trafficking Offense After Fleeing to Thailand

Reps. Chu, Moore Reintroduce EITC Age Parity Act to Expand Tax Credit to Younger and Older Workers
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Reps. Judy Chu (CA-28) and Gwen Moore (WI-04) reintroduced the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) Age Parity Act, which would eliminate age restrictions that currently prevent millions of young and older workers without children from claiming the EITC.
The EITC is one of our nation’s most effective anti-poverty tools. In 2024, it lifted 4.4 million people above the poverty line, including over two million children, and reduced the severity of poverty for more than 16 million Americans. But the credit excludes a crucial segment of the workforce. Unless you have a qualifying child, the EITC is only available to those between ages 25 and 64, leaving millions of younger and older works ineligible solely because of their age. The EITC Age Parity Act would solve this issue by eliminating the EITC’s upper age limit and expanding eligibility to workers as young as 18.
“The EITC is one of the most impactful and transformative anti-poverty tools we have at our disposal. Unfortunately, arbitrary age limits exclude millions of hardworking Americans who could benefit from it greatly,” said Rep. Chu. “Right now, a 23-year-old stocking shelves and a 66-year-old still working to make ends meet, neither with children at home, are shut out of the EITC for no reason other than their age. I’m proud to reintroduce the EITC Age Parity Act with Rep. Moore to lift more families out of poverty and put more money back in the pockets of millions of workers.”
“At a time when American families and workers are struggling with higher costs for just about everything, our tax laws should not be taxing workers into poverty. That is why I have long championed updates to the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), one of our nation’s largest anti-poverty tools. While the American Rescue Plan Act made important changes to the EITC, including allowing younger and older adults without children to benefit from this refundable credit, those temporary changes expired, depriving some of our most vulnerable workers of critical assistance. The EITC Age Parity Act would permanently allow younger and older workers to benefit from the EITC, a crucial first step in ensuring that our tax code can better serve all our workers,” said Rep. Moore.
“We applaud the leadership of Rep. Chu and Rep. Moore on behalf of the EITC Age Parity Act to permanently eliminate age restrictions that prevent young and older workers from claiming the EITC,” said Amy Everitt, President of Golden State Opportunity. “This invaluable tax credit boosts workforce participation and sparks local economic growth. Yet, we need to make sure our policies better serve the workers who have been left behind by our best policies. With the cost of living rising, every worker needs every dollar they have already earned.”
The bill is cosponsored by Reps. Gwen Moore (WI-04), Dwight Evans (PA-03), Jimmy Gomez (CA-34), Terri Sewell (AL-07), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), Jill Tokuda (HI-02), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-At Large), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), and Valerie Foushee (NC-04).
The bill is endorsed by Golden State Opportunity (GSO)
Read the full bill text HERE.

text:
BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
A PROCLAMATION
The Oval Office stands as one of the most recognizable and historically significant spaces in the United States. Since its establishment in its present location and form during the administration of President Franklin D. Roosevelt, it has served as the principal working office of the President of the United States. Decisions of profound national and international consequence have been made within its walls. It has hosted heads of state, shaped the daily conduct of the executive branch, and become a symbol of the American Presidency itself.
The room’s distinctive oval design, first introduced in the West Wing under President William Howard Taft and refined in the early 1930s, reflects both practical and ceremonial purposes. Its architecture, finishes of lasting character, and continuous association with the Presidency give the Oval Office exceptional and unique value in illustrating the history of the United States. The Oval Office possesses an unmatched and unique combination of location, design, setting, materials, workmanship, and an association with historical events that are embedded in our national consciousness.
The White House and its grounds are Federal property administered as part of the President’s Park by the National Park Service and are already recognized as a National Historic Landmark. Nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance.
WHEREAS, section 320301 of title 54, United States Code (the “Antiquities Act”), authorizes the President, in the President’s discretion, to declare by public proclamation historic landmarks, historic and prehistoric structures, and other objects of historic or scientific interest that are situated upon the lands owned or controlled by the Federal Government to be national monuments, and to reserve as a part thereof parcels of land, the limits of which shall be confined to the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected;
WHEREAS, it is in the public interest to preserve the Oval Office as a national monument; and
WHEREAS, I find that the boundaries of the Oval Office represent the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects of historic and scientific interest identified above;
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by the authority vested in me by section 320301 of title 54, United States Code, hereby proclaim the Oval Office as the Oval Office National Monument (monument).
The monument shall consist of the Oval Office itself (Room 110) together with the Outer Oval Office (Rooms 106 and 108) and the Cabinet Room (Room 105). The boundaries of the monument are the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects of historic interest to be protected.
The Secretary of the Interior (Secretary), through the National Park Service, shall manage the monument in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency. The Secretary shall:
(1) develop and implement a management plan, in consultation with the White House Office of Administration and other relevant executive departments, agencies, and offices, that prioritizes the preservation of the monument’s structural and significant architectural features;
(2) require documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument or its essential architectural elements;
(3) ensure that any proposed changes affecting the monument’s historic character are evaluated for consistency with its national significance; and
(4) coordinate with the Committee for the Preservation of the White House and other appropriate advisory bodies.
The Secretary is directed to take all necessary steps to implement this proclamation.
Nothing in this proclamation shall be construed to restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.
Nothing in this proclamation alters existing statutory exemptions applicable to the White House under the National Historic Preservation Act or diminishes the Congress’s authority over Federal property.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this fifth day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.
DONALD J. TRUMP
title: ESTABLISHMENT OF THE OVAL OFFICE NATIONAL MONUMENT
