United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, and Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), Terrance Cole, announced today the unsealing of charges against, and the arrests of, five Ecuadorian nationals who conspired to import vast quantities of cocaine into the United States for more than a decade. The defendants include a former member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, a former Ecuadorian mayor and current mayoral candidate, the son of the former president of Ecuador, and other powerful narcotraffickers.

“The charges announced today represent a coordinated effort to dismantle political corruption and narcotics trafficking that had wreaked havoc in Ecuador and plagued the country with increasing violence in recent years,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “As alleged in the Indictment, the defendants played a critical role in transforming the country into a major transit hub for 70 percent of the cocaine reaching the United States and Europe. These prosecutions hold accountable powerful politicians and narcotraffickers alike who profited from and facilitated the international narcotics trade and who degraded Ecuador’s internal security.”

“The charges announced today represent a coordinated effort to dismantle political corruption and narcotics trafficking that had wreaked havoc in Ecuador and plagued the country with increasing violence in recent years,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “As alleged in the Indictment, the defendants played a critical role in transforming the country into a major transit hub for 70 percent of the cocaine reaching the United States and Europe. These prosecutions hold accountable powerful politicians and narcotraffickers alike who profited from and facilitated the international narcotics trade and who degraded Ecuador’s internal security.”

“Political influence, financial resources, and powerful connections do not place anyone beyond the reach of American justice,” said DEA Administrator Terrance Cole. “Those who exploit legitimate businesses to move cocaine toward our communities should understand that DEA will follow the evidence, expose their networks, and work with our international partners to bring them before the courts. No title, fortune, or family connection changes that commitment.”

As reflected in the Indictment:(1)

Ecuador sits at the heart of the global cocaine trade. Situated between two of the world’s largest cocaine-producing countries, hundreds of tons of cocaine are exported each year out of Ecuador’s main seaports, including from the coastal cities of Manta, in Manabi Province, and Guayaquil, in Guayas Province. Cocaine traffickers operating in Ecuador and the broader region exploit legal commercial maritime routes to conceal their narcotics, using container ships and other commercial vessels transporting legitimate commodities, including seafood, bananas, timber, and minerals, as well as an extensive network of fishing vessels and “go-fast” boats, to smuggle cocaine to the United States and other international markets. The image below depicts the movement of cocaine from Colombia and Peru, through Ecuador, and on to international destinations, including the United States:

Like other countries in the region, Ecuador is beset by rampant corruption and partnerships between politicians and large-scale narcotics traffickers. As alleged, two such politicians are JAIME ESTRADA MEDRANDA and JAIME ESTRADA BONILLA. MEDRANDA and BONILLA have long partnered with some of the region’s largest and most violent drug traffickers to ship massive quantities of cocaine out of Ecuador to the United States and elsewhere, contributing to the deteriorating internal security of Ecuador and the corruption of its political systems.

In Ecuador’s National Assembly, MEDRANDA represented a district within the province of Manabi that includes the coastal city of Manta—the center of Ecuador’s tuna-processing industry and home to one of Ecuador’s largest ports, which serves as a major transit point for the global cocaine supply. BONILLA, who is MEDRANDA’s father, was the former mayor of Manta, is currently running for the same office, and was the former President of the Port Authority of Manta. MEDRANDA and BONILLA are also owners and executives of a major Manta-based seafood company and an Ecuadorian professional soccer club. For years, as alleged, MEDRANDA and BONILLA have smuggled vast quantities of cocaine disguised within their seafood company’s shipments out of Ecuador in partnership with large-scale drug traffickers, including the leaders of violent drug trafficking and designated foreign terrorist organizations such as Los Choneros and Los Lobos . Many of the cocaine loads they have conspired to export were sourced from paramilitary groups operating in the jungles of Colombia.

To minimize the risk to themselves, MEDRANDA and BONILLA allegedly have relied on trusted intermediaries to meet with drug traffickers, receive payments, and coordinate the logistics of receiving, packing, and smuggling cocaine out of Ecuador using containers packed with legitimate goods, such as tuna. For example, in or about 2026, MEDRANDA and BONILLA sent their representatives GEOVANNY FERNANDEZ MENENDEZ and WILLIAM JOSE BRIONES LOPEZ to meet with JACOBO ABDALA BUCARAM-PULLEY—an alleged Ecuadorian drug and firearms trafficker and the son of the former President of Ecuador—to negotiate the export of a purported two-ton load of cocaine from Ecuador to Mexico, for further shipment to the United States.

In another example, in or about 2023, the seafood exporting company of MEDRANDA and BONILLA was used to ship ton-quantity loads of cocaine out of Ecuadorian seaports. From one such shipment, on or about May 27, 2023, the Ecuadorian National Police seized approximately 1,444 kilograms of cocaine inside of the company’s shipping container at the Port of Guayaquil. The image below depicts the cocaine seized from the company’s shipping container.

WASHINGTON – Dijon Williams, 27, and Daivion Williams, 28, both from Georgia, were found guilty today for charges related to the murder of 30-year-old Nurudeen Thomas, in July 2020, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

"These brothers, Dijon and Daivion Williams, traveled from Georgia to Washington, D.C., intending to rob their drug supplier, and the robbery ended in murder," said U.S. Attorney Pirro. "Although they fled back to Georgia after the killing, they could not evade justice. Today's guilty verdict demonstrates our commitment to holding violent offenders accountable, no matter where they run."

"These brothers, Dijon and Daivion Williams, traveled from Georgia to Washington, D.C., intending to rob their drug supplier, and the robbery ended in murder," said U.S. Attorney Pirro. "Although they fled back to Georgia after the killing, they could not evade justice. Today's guilty verdict demonstrates our commitment to holding violent offenders accountable, no matter where they run."

A jury in D.C. Superior Court found both Dijon Williams and Daivion Williams guilty of one count each of first-degree murder while armed, conspiracy and attempted robbery. The Honorable Jason Park scheduled sentencing for January 22, 2027.

According to the government’s evidence, Dijon Williams, a former Georgetown University football player, and his brother, Daivion Williams, conspired to rob their drug supplier, Nurudeen Thomas, of a large quantity of drugs. They drove from Georgia to Washington, D.C. to effectuate their plan. Shortly after arriving in D.C., on July 21, 2020, they drove to the 4100 block of 14th Street, Northwest, where they met Mr. Thomas, ostensibly to engage in a drug sale. Once there, they put their plan to rob him into action, during which Mr. Thomas was shot and killed. They then fled the District of Columbia for Georgia.

Joining the announcement was Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department.

This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department and was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Yasmin Emrani and Daniel Bromwich. AUSA Rachel Forman investigated and indicted the cases.

text:
FORT LEONARD WOOD, Mo. — With their lungs burning and sweat pouring, Fort Leonard Wood trainees traded the calm precision of static qualification for the chaos of high-stress shooting to hone lethal accuracy under physical duress during Week 6 of U.S. Army Basic Combat Training.
More than 100 recruits with Company A, 3rd Battalion, 10th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Chemical Brigade, spent hours on Fort Leonard Wood ranges Oct. 26 to 28, 2026, to qualify with their M4A1 carbines, proving they are disciplined combat-ready shooters who can dominate targets.
“Earning a marksmanship badge is special — it is the first badge that they are able to receive in the Army,” said Capt. Brittany Aikin, Company A commander. “Qualifying is a BCT milestone because it is a direct reflection of their individual performance outside of the Army Fitness Test.
“During White Phase, there is a shift in focus to individual performance, while teamwork is still important and applicable during this phase, no one is going to shoot for them, they must earn their marksmanship badge on their own.”
To Aikin, Week 6 is the most rewarding as it allows her to measure the lethal precision of the next generation of warfighters.
“Week 6 is my favorite week because we get to see how far along the trainees have come in their rifle marksmanship progression,” Aikin said. “I enjoy seeing how much the coaching and mentorship of the drill sergeants have paid off.”
On the range, every minute counts. She said her unit maximizes trainees’ time with drill sergeants — especially those requiring tailored coaching — with a focus on elevating every individual’s capability so the entire company achieves combat readiness.
“I want everyone to qualify because it is a graduation requirement, and I also believe that everyone is capable so long as they invest themselves,” Aikin said. “I want them to believe in themselves and be confident in their abilities so that when it comes time to perform, they know that they can execute.”
Company A delivered a clean sweep, with every trainee qualifying.
“I am proud of my trainees because they demonstrated grit, teamwork and a commitment to their individual Soldier tasks and skills with all of them qualifying as marksman or higher,” Aikin said.
Exhibiting superior discipline on the line, 39 trainees exceeded the marksman standard to qualify as sharpshooters and experts.
Pvt. Isaac Marble, with 2nd Platoon, secured the company’s Top Shot title by scoring 38 out of 40.
“He qualified expert on his first opportunity at the qualification range,” Aikin said.
Aikin presented Marble with a company coin during formation and plans to recognize him with a Top Shot Coin on family day later this month, allowing his visiting loved ones to share in the achievement.
Although experienced with firearms, Marble said he had never fired an M4A1 and credited his drill sergeants’ coaching with improving his marksmanship.
“They ran us through the drill so many times it became muscle memory. Their critiques helped me better my stance and steady my aim,” Marble said. “I never expected to be the top shot. I was just shooting for expert.”
Daily physical readiness training in Week 6 focused on military movement, shoulder stability and recovery drills.
Aikin noted how PRT is systematically tailored to prepare trainees for the physical demands of that day's mission.
“Prior to conducting Battle March and Shoot they conducted hip stability drills to prepare them for the 4-mile movement into a stress shoot,” Aikin said.
During BMS training Oct. 27, 2026, FLW 30 and Range 2 became the site for the company’s latest trial by fire. Drill sergeants systematically stripped away their physical reserves with a rapid tactical ruck and high-intensity physical drills, immediately thrusting them onto the firing line.
With elevated heart rates and zero recovery time, exhausted recruits emptied two, 20-round magazines in under 60 seconds to prove their lethality under pressure.
Pvt. Alexander Suta, in BCT with Company A on his way to becoming a 15Y AH-64 Apache helicopter armament, electrical and avionic systems repairer, said he “learned a lot” from the BMS exercise.
“It is a totally different feeling than calmy grouping, zeroing and qualifying with my weapon. I shot 37 out of 40 yesterday while qualifying,” Suta said. “Today, my heart rate was up. I had to make sure I controlled my breathing and didn’t panic. It is all about being composed.”
Company A trainee, Pvt. Adam Stephen Malasits, in BCT to be an 88M motor transport operator, said his drill sergeants were “very descriptive” during marksmanship training, and he is thankful for their expertise before having to conduct the fast-paced BMS training.
“Our drill sergeants prepared us for what to expect,” Malasits said. “We didn’t have time to build up our sandbags, so my prone position was unsupported. My grouping wasn’t as tight under pressure. I learned that in combat I won’t have time to prepare, so I need to always be ready no matter the conditions.”
Week 6 took Company A's discipline beyond the range as they supported installation clean-up by executing a precision policing action along Colorado Avenue, contended for superiority through precision drill and ceremonial execution, and forged unit cohesion during a company run.
“The Drill and Ceremony Competition is another streamer event where we grade the platoons on how well they can execute basic facing movements and marching in formation,” Aikin said. “We conducted a company run followed by awarding streamers and coins for outstanding performance.”
She awarded 1st Platoon with the Land Navigation Streamer for their performance on Oct. 14, 2026; 2nd Platoon received the Rifle Marksmanship Streamer for the highest overall rifle marksmanship scores in the company; and 3rd Platoon received the Battle March and Shoot Streamer for having the highest overall hits.
Week 6 marked the second official benchmark for trainees to validate their physical readiness via the Army Fitness Test.
“I am seeing a definite improvement in their AFT scores and their overall endurance in our formation movements. I think that they are getting stronger, and I’m excited for their families to see the change in them,” Aikin said.
More Week 6 photos are available to view on Fort Leonard Wood's Flickr.
title: Send Me: The making of a Soldier | Week 6

text:
National Park Service Grant will Fund an Exhibit on African American Naval Service - Institute of Museum of Library Services Grant Supports a Virtual Wall of Honor
BUFFALO, N.Y. - Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) today announced two federal grants totaling nearly $150,000 for the Buffalo and Erie County Naval & Military Park. The National Park Service  (NPS) awarded $97,176 through its African American Civil Rights Preservation and History Grants program for an African American Naval Service exhibit, which will interpret the history of racial segregation aboard the park’s historic naval vessels and the experiences of the African American sailors who served during that era. The Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) awarded a $51,591 matching grant through its Inspire! Grants for Small Museums program to create a Virtual Wall of Honor that preserves and shares the stories and service records of Western New York veterans.
“The Buffalo Naval Park is where Western New York comes to remember those who served, and these grants will help it tell even more of that story,” said Congressman Kennedy. “African American sailors served our country with honor and distinction while facing segregation aboard the very ships that visitors tour today, and an honest account of their experiences belongs in our understanding of that complex history. The Virtual Wall of Honor will make it easier for families to find and learn about the veterans they love. I congratulate everyone at the Naval Park on earning these highly sought after awards and I’m glad to see this support coming to Buffalo’s waterfront.”
“These federal investments will help us preserve more than history,” said Brian Luallen, President & CEO, Buffalo Naval Park. “They will help us tell the stories of the men and women who lived it. From the experiences of African American sailors aboard our historic ships to the legacies of Western New York veterans honored on our Wall of Honor, every name represents a life and every story deserves to be told. We're grateful to Congressman Kennedy, the National Park Service, and the Institute of Museum and Library Services for helping us carry these stories forward for generations to come.”
The NPS grant is one of 54 projects in 18 states funded this year through the African American Civil Rights Preservation and History program, which draws on the Historic Preservation Fund. The IMLS grant was highly competitive. The agency received 299 applications requesting more than $11 million and made 88 awards totaling $3.3 million. In 2025, Kennedy fought back against efforts to dismantle the IMLS. The Virtual Wall of Honor will give visitors a multisensory way to explore veterans’ stories and learn about family members, hometown neighbors, and others connected to them, and the project includes staff training. Located at Canalside, the park is home to the USS The Sullivans, USS Little Rock, USS Croaker, and PTF 17. The park first opened to the public in 1979.
 
###
title: Kennedy Announces Nearly $150,000 in Federal Grants for Buffalo Naval Park to Tell the Stories of African American Sailors and Honor Western New York Veterans

PORTLAND, Ore.— A Salem man associated with the Varrio Catorce Norteño street gang was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison today for trafficking firearms and controlled substances, United States Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced.

Christopher Hermens , 29, was sentenced to 120 months in federal prison and three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to transferring firearms to another person while having reasonable cause to believe the recipient intended to use, carry, or possess the firearms in connection with felony offenses.

According to court documents, in July 2023, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) began investigating members of the Varrio Catorce Norteño gang in the Salem area. During the investigation, an undercover ATF agent conducted a series of controlled purchases of firearms and controlled substances from Hermens and his associates.

Between January and February 2025, Hermens participated in multiple transactions involving firearms, cocaine, marijuana, and fentanyl. During these meetings, Hermens coordinated firearm sales, supplied controlled substances, connected undercover agents with fentanyl suppliers, and discussed obtaining additional firearms, including unserialized “ghost guns.”

On Jan. 23, 2025, Hermens and a co-conspirator sold five firearms and approximately one ounce of cocaine to an undercover agent. During the transaction, Hermens discussed future firearm sales and his ability to obtain additional weapons.

On Feb. 6, 2025, Hermens facilitated the sale of two firearms, approximately two pounds of marijuana, and approximately 32 grams of fentanyl. During the same transaction, Hermens arranged for an additional fentanyl sale through a drug supplier.

Later that month, on Feb. 27, 2025, Hermens coordinated a transaction in which an undercover agent purchased approximately 122 grams of fentanyl from one of Hermens’s associates.

On July 22, 2025, law enforcement executed a search warrant at Hermens’s residence and recovered 19 firearms, including a rifle found beneath his bed and a pistol located in a neighboring bedroom. Investigators also recovered additional firearms and firearm components from a safe in the residence.

“The defendant repeatedly trafficked firearms and dangerous controlled substances, including fentanyl, while leveraging gang ties and criminal associates to expand his illegal activities,” said Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon . “Individuals who profit from the distribution of illegal firearms and deadly narcotics pose a serious threat to public safety. This sentence holds the defendant accountable for his conduct and reflects our commitment to disrupting the criminal networks that endanger Oregon communities.”

As part of his plea agreement, Hermens agreed to forfeit firearms and other property connected to his criminal conduct.

The case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicole M. Bockelman prosecuted the case.
title: Salem Gang Member Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison for Trafficking Firearms and Controlled Substances

The Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) announced today a $250 million conditional loan commitment with 6K, Inc., to scale the company's domestic production of Nickel-Manganese-Cobalt (NMC) cathode active material (CAM) in Jackson, TN.
6K is a leading advanced materials company focused on critical energy and aerospace technologies. OSC's investment, which would catalyze an additional $250 million in private capital, is intended to expand 6K's domestic manufacturing, which would help secure American advanced battery supply chains.
OSC's conditional loan commitment to 6K directly advances President Donald J. Trump's national security priorities to revitalize the American defense industrial base, counter malign foreign trade practices, and ensure critical technologies are made domestically. In accordance with President Trump's Executive Order 14154, Unleashing American Energy, this commitment delivers on the President's direction to onshore critical battery materials to strengthen American national security.
6K specializes in using its proprietary UniMelt microwave plasma technology to synthesize finished, single-crystal NMC cathode powders in a single step. This novel direct-to-CAM approach fundamentally disrupts legacy multi-day chemical processes by bypassing the foreign-dominated precursor (pCAM) processing stage entirely, reducing production cycle times by up to tenfold, and driving down capital intensity and environmental impact.
The company's U.S. manufacturing operations at its PlusCAM facility in Jackson, Tennessee would help onshore production of these essential battery components, which are vital for next-gen defense platforms, uncrewed aerial systems (UAS), tactical communications, and critical energy infrastructure. Leveraging the company's proprietary advanced microwave plasma technology, invented in the U.S., 6K provides a differentiated, U.S.-focused approach to producing critical battery materials that is not reliant on vulnerable foreign sources.
"OSC champions the domestic production of critical battery materials. 6K's microwave plasma technology represents a ground-breaking approach to establish a cost-effective domestic supply chain and break our reliance on foreign adversaries. We're pleased to support 6K's domestic expansion, which would represent an important step in strengthening the advanced battery industrial base in the United States," said David A. Lorch, Director of the Office of Strategic Capital and Senior Advisor to Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg.
Due to price flooding from foreign countries, the U.S. produces less than 1% of its NMC cathode needs domestically. OSC's conditional financing would enable 6K to expand its U.S. manufacturing operations, achieve cost-parity with foreign competitors, and ultimately deliver a secure, NDAA-compliant supply chain for the Department of War and commercial markets.
"OSC is focused on investments that can bridge the commercialization gap for homegrown technology," said James R. Shanahan, Senior Managing Director (Investments) with OSC. "By providing long-term, patient capital, OSC helps innovative companies like 6K achieve scale and compete globally, ensuring the U.S. defense industrial base remains at the forefront of critical technology."
The conditional loan commitment between OSC and 6K specifies customary additional steps the company must take to proceed toward financial close, including satisfying financial, investment, legal, technical, diligence, and other requirements.
"I applaud the Office of Strategic Capital on this important investment. We cannot dominate the modern battlefield if we rely on foreign supply chains. Securing advanced materials is critical, and this OSC financing secures the trusted, domestic battery supply needed to protect our national security," said Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering.
title: Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital Signs $250 Million Conditional Loan Commitment With 6K Inc.

Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control as Part of Ongoing Modernization Effort
Deployment of Brand New Air Traffic Control continues at record pace
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system.
The Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) replaces four systems dating back to the 1980s that are in more than 400 FAA facilities. E-IDS provides a single, secure system that gives air traffic controllers faster access to information they need. It also will reduce costly repairs and workarounds while enhancing safety for the American flying public.
The first five facilities to receive these upgrades include:
- Atlantic City International Airport
- Nashville International Airport
- Greater Rochester International Airport
- Data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City
The FAA plans to install E-IDS in 435 sites by the end of 2028.
“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system, and under President Trump, we’re delivering just that. The installation of E-IDS is just the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
“E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System.”
You can track the progress of the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) by state and airport on our Modern Skies website.
Additional Information:
E-IDS is a digital display board that puts important operational information in one place so controllers can quickly see updates, status information, and alerts they need to keep air traffic moving safely and efficiently. This information includes notices about equipment issues and disruptions, air traffic conditions, weather impacts, and important advisories.
E-IDS will also improve how Pilot Reports (PIREPS) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. PIREPs are first-hand reports on weather conditions from pilots to air traffic controllers. Both provide vital information on real-time pilot conditions and improve situational awareness for controllers.
Reminder:
Under Secretary Duffy’s leadership, the FAA is rapidly moving to make upgrades to our air traffic control system nationwide. We have already:
- Replaced 69% of copper wires
- Installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers
- Transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips
- Installed 226 IP Voice Switches

title: Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control as Part of Ongoing Modernization Effort

LAS VEGAS – A federal grand jury in Las Vegas returned an indictment charging a Henderson, Nevada, resident with allegedly making threats to kill President Donald J. Trump.

“Let me be unmistakably clear: anyone who targets the Commander in Chief of the United States with threats of violence is painting a target on their own back,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “Threatening the life of the President is not free speech—it is an act of cowardice and a direct assault on the stability of our nation. Our office and our federal law enforcement partners do not tolerate, do not negotiate with, and do not overlook those who weaponize fear against our public institutions. We will deploy every single resource at our disposal, hunt you down, and prosecute you to the absolute fullest extent of federal law. If you threaten the leader of this country, expect to face the unyielding weight of the federal justice system, and expect to spend a very long time behind a federal prison bar.”

“Threats of political violence and mass murder have no place in our society,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Office. “Mr. Utlaut allegedly threatened the life of President Trump, promoted a mass shooting, and expressed a willingness to carry out horrific acts of violence. Such threats undermine public safety and will be treated with the utmost seriousness. This arrest sends a clear message: anyone who threatens violence against our nation's leaders or our communities will face the full weight of federal law. You cannot hide behind a screen, and you cannot escape accountability. Justice will find you!”

"Stopping violence before it starts requires a coordinated effort across all levels of law enforcement,” said Henderson Police Chief Reggie Rader. “Through strong regional partnerships and collaboration with our federal counterparts, we can share information, identify potential threats and work together to keep our communities safe."

According to court documents, on October 16, 2026, the FBI National Threat Operations Section received an emergency notification regarding five threatening posts uploaded to a YouTube channel. The posts included threats to kill the President of the United States, to carry out a mass shooting, and other threats of violence. Subsequent investigation attributed those posts to Jason Randall Utlaut.

On October 16, 2026, the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department executed a search warrant at Utlaut’s residence and vehicle in Henderson, Nevada. During the search, 15 firearms, together with multiple firearm magazines and ammunition, were seized.

Utlaut is charged with one count of threat against the President. If convicted, the maximum statutory penalty is five years in prison. Arraignment has been scheduled before United States Magistrate Judge Maximiliano D. Couvillier III on November 18, 2026.

The FBI, Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, and Henderson Police Department investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Dan Cowhig is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an accusation. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

title: Nevada Man Indicted for Making Threats to Kill the President of the United States

The federal government incurs a budget deficit when its total outgoing payments (outlays) exceed the total money it collects (revenues). If instead federal revenues are greater than outlays, then the federal government generates a surplus. Deficits are measured over the course of a defined period of time—in the case of the federal government, a fiscal year.
Debt measurements may be taken at any point in time, and represent the accumulation of all previous government borrowing activity from private citizens, institutions, foreign governments, and other parts of the federal government. Federal debt increases when there are net budget deficits and outflows made for federal credit programs, which combine to represent debt held by the public—the debt measure of primary interest to budget and financial observers. Federal debt also rises through increases in intragovernmental debt, which is generated by trust fund surpluses that are used to finance other government activity. Federal debt declines when there are budget surpluses, a reduction in the federal credit portfolio, or decreases in intragovernmental borrowing.
Federal deficit and debt outcomes are interdependent: budget deficits increase federal debt levels, which in turn increase future net deficits. The nature of the relationship between deficits and debt varies depending on the type of debt considered. Budget deficits are the principal contributor to debt held by the public. The effect of deficits on intragovernmental debt is less certain than their contribution to debt held by the public. All else equal, increases in net trust fund deficits will lead to increases in total budget deficits but decreases in intragovernmental debt.
Interest payments made on publicly held debt instruments contribute directly to federal deficits. Holders of federal debt are compensated by receiving interest payments from Treasury. Intragovernmental debt does not contribute to future deficits.
Persistent budget deficits and a large and increasing federal debt have generated discussions over the long-term sustainability of current budget projections. The historic economic shocks of the Great Recession and COVID-19 pandemic and ensuing federal responses generated the five largest real federal deficits (measured as a share of total output) since World War II. Publicly held debt is projected to be 101% of GDP at the end of FY2026, more than triple the value recorded at the end of FY2001 (32% of GDP). Budget forecasts project rising deficits and accelerated increases in publicly held debt in ensuing decades.
Over time, persistent budget deficits can hamper economic growth. Deficits represent an intertemporal transfer from later generations to the current one, as money borrowed now will eventually require repayment with interest. The effect of deficit financing on economic output depends on the nature of the government activity being financed and the private activity that would have otherwise taken place.
Federal debt is constrained by the willingness of investors to finance borrowing. While the amount of federal borrowing investors will finance may be affected by economic growth and other factors, real federal debt cannot increase indefinitely. There are no signs that federal borrowing capacity will be exhausted in the short term. However, the consequences of exhausted fiscal space may be worth considering when examining the medium- and long-term trajectory of the federal budget.
Persistent annual budget deficits and a large and increasing federal debt have generated discussions over the long-term sustainability of current budget projections. The Great Recession and COVID-19 pandemic and ensuing federal responses generated the five largest real federal deficits (measured as a share of gross domestic product, or GDP) since World War II. Publicly held debt is projected to be 101% of GDP at the end of FY2026, more than triple the value recorded at the end of FY2001 (32% of GDP). Budget forecasts project rising deficits and accelerated increases in publicly held debt in ensuing decades. This report explores distinctions in the concept and composition of deficits and debt and explains how they interact with economic conditions and other aspects of fiscal policy.
A deficit describes one of the three possible outcomes for the federal budget.1 The federal government incurs a deficit (also known as a net deficit) when its total outgoing payments (outlays) exceed the total money it collects (revenues). If instead federal revenues are greater than outlays, then the federal government generates a surplus. A balanced budget describes the case where federal receipts equal federal expenditures.2 The size of a deficit or surplus is equal to the difference between the levels of spending and receipts. Deficits are measured over the course of a defined period of time—in the case of the federal government, a fiscal year.3
Federal budget outcomes incorporate both "on-budget" activities, which represent the majority of federal taxes and spending, and "off-budget" government activities, which include revenues and outlays from Social Security trust funds and the Postal Service. For federal credit programs, the subsidy cost of government activities is included in deficit and surplus calculations.4 The federal budget is constructed in a manner that provides for lower net deficits in more robust economic conditions, attributable to higher revenues (from taxes on increased output) and, to a smaller degree, lower spending levels (from reduced demand for programs like unemployment insurance).
The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that the federal government will record a deficit of $1.85 trillion in FY2026, equivalent to 5.8% of GDP. From FY1976 to FY2025, the average net deficit equaled 3.6% of annual GDP ($1.22 trillion in FY2026 dollars). Over the FY1976-FY2025 period, the government generated a surplus on four occasions—in each year from FY1998 through FY2001. In all other years, the federal government incurred a net deficit.5
The federal debt is the money that the government owes to its creditors, which include private citizens, institutions, foreign governments, and other parts of the federal government. Debt measurements may be taken at any time and represent the accumulation of all previous government borrowing activity. Federal debt increases when there are net budget deficits, outflows made for federal credit programs (net of the subsidy costs already included in deficit calculations), and increases in intragovernmental borrowing. Federal credit programs include loans issued for college tuition payments, small business programs, and other activities the government may seek to support.6 In those cases, debt levels increase as additional loans are granted and decrease as money for such programs is repaid.
Intragovernmental debt is generated when trust funds, revolving funds, and special funds receive money from tax payments, fees, or other revenue sources that is not immediately needed to make payments. In those cases the surpluses are used to finance other government activities, and Government Account Series (GAS) securities are issued to the trust fund. GAS securities may then be redeemed when trust fund expenditures exceed revenue levels. Intragovernmental debt may be thought of as money that one part of the government owes another part.
The Department of the Treasury is responsible for managing federal debt. The primary objective of Treasury's debt management strategy is to fulfill the government's borrowing needs at the lowest cost over time.7 Treasury finances federal borrowing activities by issuing government-backed securities that generate interest payments for their owners. Treasury securities are typically sold to the public through an auction process, and have maturity periods (the length of time that they are held before repayment) of anywhere from several weeks to 30 years.8
Federal debt may be divided into two major categories: (1) debt held by the public, which is the sum of accrued net deficits and outstanding money from federal credit programs; and (2) intragovernmental debt. As of August 31, 2026, the amount of federal debt outstanding was $40.2 trillion, with 80.7% of that debt held by the public and 19.3% held as intragovernmental debt.9 Table 1 summarizes the composition of debt held by the public and intragovernmental debt.
Source: U.S. Treasury, Monthly Statement of the Public Debt, August 31, 2026, https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/monthly-statement-public-debt/summary-of-treasury-securities-outstanding.
Note: Debt values as of August 31, 2026.
Individuals, firms, the Federal Reserve, state and local governments, and foreign governments are all eligible to purchase publicly held debt. Debt may be acquired directly through the auction process, from which most publicly held debt is initially sold, or on the secondary market if the debt is deemed "marketable" or eligible for resale.10 The total amount of publicly held debt outstanding was $32.4 trillion as of August 31, 2026.
The majority of publicly held debt is marketable, and includes all Treasury Notes, Bonds, Bills, Treasury Inflation Protected Securities (TIPS), and Floating Rate Notes (FRNs) issued by Treasury. Nonmarketable debt held by the public is composed of U.S. Savings Bonds, State and Local Government Securities (SLGS), and other, smaller issues. As of August 31, 2026, 98% of publicly held issues, or $31.8 trillion, was marketable.
Intragovernmental debt is debt where the federal government is both the creditor and the borrower. Intragovernmental debt issuances are almost exclusively nonmarketable, as marketable debt comprised only $0.02 trillion (0.3%) of the $7.8 trillion in total intragovernmental debt on August 31, 2026. The majority of nonmarketable intragovernmental debt was held by trust funds devoted to Social Security and military and federal worker retirement. Marketable intragovernmental debt is composed primarily of debt held by the Federal Financing Bank, which is a government corporation created to reduce the cost of federal borrowing.
Since intragovernmental debt is held only in government accounts, such debt cannot be accessed by institutions outside the federal government. Conversely, the bonds that finance publicly held debt activity may compete for assets in private and financial markets. Public debt issues may be a particularly attractive collateral option on the secondary market if the federal government is perceived as a safe credit risk.
Federal deficit and debt outcomes are interdependent; budget deficits increase federal debt levels, which in turn increase future net deficits because of the need to service higher interest payments on the nation's debt. The nature of the relationship between deficits and debt varies depending on the type of debt considered. This section describes the relationship between federal deficits and debt.
Budget deficits are the principal contributor to debt held by the public. To finance budget deficits, Treasury sells debt instruments. The value of those debt holdings (which include interest payments) represents the vast majority of publicly held debt. From FY1976 to FY2025, annual nominal budget deficits and surpluses of the federal government summed to $27.2 trillion; over the same period, total debt held by the public increased by $29.8 trillion.11 Publicly held debt has been the biggest determinant of historical changes in the total stock of federal debt. Figure 1 shows changes in federal debt levels from FY1976 through FY2025 as a percent of GDP. Though there have been gradual changes in the level of intragovernmental debt in recent decades, the decline in real debt following World War II and subsequent increase in debt levels beginning in the late 1970s were each caused primarily by similar changes in the stock of publicly held debt over those time periods.
Present borrowing outcomes affect future budgeting outcomes. Publicly held debt contributes directly to federal deficits through interest payments on debt issuances. Interest payments are made to both debt held by the public and intragovernmental debt. As the government serves as buyer and seller of intragovernmental debt, interest payments on those holdings do not affect the federal budget deficit.12 However, interest payments made on publicly held debt represent new federal spending, and are recorded in the budget as outlays when payments are made. The government incurs interest costs when it opts to finance spending through borrowing rather than through increased revenues. Net interest payments represent the amount paid from the government to debt holders in a given time period, less interest payments received for federal loan programs.13
For investors, purchasing a debt issuance represents both a loss of liquidity relative to currency holdings (money paid for the debt holding can be used immediately, while the debt issuance may only be resold on the secondary market or held until the date of maturity) and an opportunity cost (the money used for the purchase could have been spent on other items, invested elsewhere, or saved). Debt holders are compensated for those costs by receiving interest payments from Treasury on their issuances.
From FY1976 to FY2025, net interest payments averaged 2.1% of annual GDP, equivalent to about $678 billion annually in 2026 dollars. High interest rates and increasing debt levels caused the net interest burden to peak in the 1980s and 1990s. Until recently, net interest payments had been lower than their long-term averages; however, in FY2026, net interest payments are projected to be $1.039 trillion, or 3.3% of GDP. Recent net interest payments were the product of sustained low interest rates and relatively high levels of real debt. Unless the federal debt is reduced, net interest payments will increase if the recent shift away from a low interest rate environment persists. In its most recent forecast, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that real net interest payments will increase to 4.6% of GDP by FY2036.14
One way to measure the effect of debt on future deficits is to examine the relationship between total federal deficits and the primary deficit, which measures the balance of revenues and expenditures with net interest payments excluded. Figure 2 shows total and primary budget outcomes from FY1976 through FY2025. The gap between the total and primary outcomes in a given year is explained by net interest payments. The primary deficit averaged 1.7% of GDP from FY1976 to FY2025, as compared to the average total budget deficit of 3.8% of GDP recorded over the same time period. While the federal government recorded a budget surplus four times from FY1976 to FY2025, in seven other years it registered a primary surplus, most recently in 2007.
This section provides a primer of how government deficits and debt are integrated into the larger economy in both the short and long run. It also provides some ways to measure such interactions. Interactions between fiscal outcomes and economic performance may have ramifications for how Congress wishes to distribute its activity both within a recession or expansion, and for what fiscal targets it wishes to set in the long run.
In the short run, when economic output is assumed to be fixed, output is a function of both private and public activity. Equation (1), also known as the national accounting identity, shows the different choices that can be made with all economic output in a given time period. It states that output (Y) in a given economy is equal to the sum of private consumption (C), private investment (I), government investment (G), and net exports (X). Put another way, equation (1) asserts that output is the sum of private consumption, private saving, and net government activity. The net government deficit, or G, is shown in equation (2) as spending (S) less revenues (R). Absent a monetary policy intervention by the Federal Reserve (which makes monetary decisions independently), G must be obtained through government borrowing, or debt.15
(1) Y = C + I + G + X
(2) G = S - R
Since the levels of output (Y) and consumption (C) in a given time period are fixed, increases in government investment (G) will reduce private investment (I), net exports (X), or some combination thereof. Government borrowing increases that reduce private investment are commonly categorized as "crowding out," and represent a shift from private investment to public investment.
Increased government borrowing that reduces net exports (generated by borrowing from foreign sources) represents an expansion of the short-term money supply, as money is being brought into the economy now at the expense of the future stock of money (as foreign borrowing is repaid). Such a fiscal expansion increases the quantity of money demanded, which drives up interest rates (or cost of borrowing).16
The federal government may choose to generate short-run budget deficits for a few reasons. Deficit financing, or payment for federal government activity at least partly through debt increases, increases the total level of spending in the economy. Most economists believe that the implementation of deficit financing can generate a short-term stimulus effect, either for a particular industry or for the entire economy. In this view, increases in expenditures and tax reductions can generate employment opportunities and consumer spending, reducing the intensity of stagnant economic periods.
Deficit financing is a less effective countercyclical strategy when it leads to "crowding out," or when government financing merely replaces private-sector funding instead of inducing new economic activity, and is more likely to occur in periods of robust economic growth. Deficit reduction when the economy is operating near or at full potential can help prevent the economy from overheating and avoid "crowding out" of private investment, which could have positive implications for intergenerational equity and long-term growth.
Deficit financing may also be used as part of a structurally balanced budget strategy, which alters government tax and spending levels to smooth the effect of business cycles. Smoothing budgetary changes may reduce the economic shocks that sudden changes in deficits induce among businesses and households. Governments may also use federal deficits or surpluses to spread the payment burden of long-term projects across generations. This sort of intergenerational redistribution is one justification for the creation of long-run trust funds, such as those devoted to Social Security.
In the long run, when economic output is affected by supply-side choices, the effect of government borrowing on economic growth depends on how amounts borrowed are used relative to what would have otherwise been done with those savings (i.e., an increase in private investment or net exports) if such borrowing had not taken place. As shown in equation (3), economic growth, or the change (Δ) in output (Y), is a function (f) of the stock of labor (L, or the number of people working and hours that they work), the stock of capital (K, which includes equipment, machines, and all other nonlabor factors), and the knowledge and technological capability (A) that determines the productivity of labor and capital.
(3) ΔY= f(ΔL, ΔK, ΔA)
Assuming that the stock of labor is insensitive to fiscal policy choices, the effect of federal debt on economic growth depends on how the additional government activity affects the capital stock and productivity of labor and capital relative to what would have happened had amounts borrowed been invested privately or increased net exports. If that government activity (debt-financed spending) contributes to those factors more than the economic activity it replaced, then that debt financing will have had a positive effect on future economic growth (or potential). Alternatively, if such activity contributes less to those factors than the replaced private investment and net exports, it will reduce long-term economic potential.
Changes in federal debt levels shift economic resources across time periods, a process sometimes described as an intertemporal transfer. Federal debt issuances represent an increase in the current level of federal resources and a decrease in future federal resources. Net interest payments, or the total interest payments made by the federal government (to creditors) on borrowed money less interest payments received (from individuals and institutions borrowing from the federal government or debtors), may be thought of as the total expense associated with past federal borrowing. Those resources cannot be allocated to other government services.
Total borrowing is constrained by the money available for investment (savings in dollars) at a given point in time. This limit means that the amount of federal debt relative to output cannot increase indefinitely. The trajectory of federal debt is therefore thought to be unsustainable if debt taken as a share of output (measured in this report with gross domestic product, or GDP) rises continuously in long-term projections. This happens when growth in the stock of debt outpaces total economic growth, which can cause a variety of adverse outcomes, including reduced output, increased unemployment, higher inflation, higher private interest rates, and currency devaluation.17
Recent international experiences speak to the complexity of borrowing capacity. Both Greece and Japan experienced rapid growth in government debt in the early 21st century. International Monetary Fund data on general government debt (including municipal government debt) indicate that Greek debt rose from 101% of GDP in 1998 to 175% of GDP in 2011, while Japanese debt rose from 102% of GDP to 191% of GDP over the same time period.18 A loss in market confidence in Greek debt led to a severe recession in the middle of that period, with GDP contracting by 9 percentage points in 2011 and long-term interest rates reaching 22% in 2012. Japanese borrowing was viewed to be more sustainable despite being higher, with relatively flat GDP levels and long-term interest rates close to zero in many years. Among the 37 countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) with observable data, the United States had the fourth-largest level of gross general government debt (121% of GDP, including debt from state and local governments) in 2024.
The deficit's cyclical pattern can be attributed in part to "automatic stabilizers," or spending programs and tax provisions that cause the budget deficit to move in tandem with the business cycle without any change in law. More robust economic periods generally produce lower net deficits (or higher net surpluses), due to increases in receipts (from greater tax revenues) and reduced expenditures (from decreased demand for public assistance). The opposite effect occurs during recessions: as incomes and employment fall, the existing structure of the federal tax system automatically collects less revenue, and spending on mandatory income security programs, such as unemployment insurance, automatically rises. CBO estimated that automatic stabilizers increased deficits in FY2020 and FY2021 by 1.6% of GDP and 1.3% of GDP, respectively, shifts that were attributable to the economic effects of the COVID-19 crisis.19 CBO estimated that automatic stabilizers will decrease the deficit in FY2026 by 0.1% of GDP.
Figure 3 shows the real economic growth (as a percentage on the horizontal axis) and the federal budget outcome (as a percentage of GDP, on the vertical axis) in each fiscal year from FY1976 through FY2025. The positive correlation between economic outcomes and budget outcomes shown through the general direction of the trend line from the lower left part of the graph to the upper right area.
All else equal, higher levels of nominal GDP make a given amount of debt easier to repay by eroding its real value. For example, the highest measurement of debt since 1940 occurred in 1946, when the federal debt level was 119% of GDP, or $271 billion in (nominal) FY1946 dollars. In contrast, $271 billion projects to equal 0.8% of GDP in FY2026.20 Increases in nominal GDP may be caused by productivity increases, economic inflation—which measures the purchasing power of currency—or a combination of each factor.21
Though changes in economic growth rates typically have a relatively small effect on real debt levels in the short run, long-run changes in economic productivity can have a significant effect on the trajectory and sustainability of the debt burden. For instance, from FY2009 through FY2018, federal deficits averaged 5.3% of GDP, and real economic growth averaged 1.76% per year over the same period; those factors combined to increase federal publicly held debt from 39% of GDP at the beginning of FY2008 to 78% of GDP at the end of FY2018.22 Though real deficits were actually larger from FY1943 to FY1952 (averaging 7.3% of GDP), robust real economic growth over that period (3.6% per year) meant that the change in publicly held debt in that decade was smaller (45% of GDP to 60% to GDP) than in the FY2009-FY2018 period.
The FY2026 deficit is projected to equal 5.8% of GDP, which would be higher than the average federal deficit from FY1976 to FY2025 (3.8% of GDP). Both real deficits and real debt are projected to increase over the course of the 10-year budget window, which runs through FY2036. In its latest economic forecast, CBO projected that the total burden of U.S. debt held by the public would steadily increase over the course of the budget window, from 101% of GDP in FY2026 to 120% of GDP in FY2036.23
Table 2. Recent CBO Forecasts of Federal Debt Held by the Public
(all figures expressed as a percentage of GDP)
Source: CBO, The Budget and Economic Outlook: 2026 to 2036, February 2026; and CBO, The 2026 Long-Term Budget Outlook, February 2026. CRS calculations.
Notes: All baselines operate largely on a current law basis unless otherwise noted. Accelerated discretionary spending assumes discretionary spending growth that matches that of nominal GDP; frozen nominal discretionary spending assumption holds nominal discretionary spending constant (leading to declining real discretionary spending with positive inflation).
The CBO baseline assumes that current law continues as scheduled. CBO also provides alternative projections where such assumptions are revised. If all discretionary spending from the February 2026 baseline is assumed to grow with nominal GDP, CBO projects that federal debt held by the public would increase to 124% of GDP by FY2036, which would easily exceed the highest stock of federal debt experienced in the FY1940-FY2025 period (106% of GDP in FY1946). Actions since the 2026 CBO baseline was published, such as the U.S. military conflict with Iran, will also affect federal deficit and debt outcomes.
CBO also produces a long-term baseline that uses additional assumptions to extend its standard baseline an additional 20 years (so the 2026 long-term baseline runs through FY2056). The current long-term forecast projects that publicly held federal debt will equal 172% of GDP in FY2056. Addressing the potential consequences of long-term federal debt projections will likely involve policy adjustments that reduce future budget deficits, through either tax increases, reductions in spending, or a combination of the two.
CBO projects increases in both net interest payments and publicly held federal debt over the next 10 years, leading to a significant rise in U.S. net interest payments. CBO projects federal net interest payments of 4.6% of GDP in FY2036, which would eclipse the highest real amount devoted to net interest since FY1940 (3.2% of GDP in FY1991).
It may be useful to compare the recent U.S. federal borrowing trajectory with the practices of international governments, as future interest rate and fiscal space considerations will both be affected by the behavior of other major actors. Table 3 includes the general government debt for Group of Seven (G7) countries from 2004 to 2024.24
Table 3. IMF General Gross Debt for G7 Countries, 2004-2024
(as a percentage of GDP; change from preceding column in parentheses)
Source: International Monetary Fund, World Economic Outlook, July 2026.
Notes: General gross debt includes debt held by municipal governments and includes only publicly held debt. Increases from preceding period colored red; decreases from preceding period colored green. Changes represent percentage points of GDP. Debt from all G7 countries represents combined borrowing amounts for all governments.
Table 3 highlights the effect of economic recessions on general government debt, with large G7 debt increases following the Great Recession (a 32 percentage point increase in debt's share of GDP from 2004 to 2014) and the COVID-19 pandemic (a 7 percentage point increase from 2019 to 2024). Over the 2004 to 2024 period, the United States saw a higher percentage-point increase in its national debt as a share of its GDP than did the group of G7 countries as a whole: the U.S.'s share grew by 55 percentage points, while the share for all G7 countries grew by 40 percentage points.
title: Deficits, Debt, and the Economy: An Introduction

text:
FORT LEONARD WOOD, Mo. — Under joint celebration by Fort Leonard Wood and its neighboring communities, the Waynesville-St. Robert Regional Airport officially unveiled its new 9,000-square-foot terminal Nov. 4, 2026. Featuring a 50-passenger capacity, the expanded facility stands as a testament to regional partnership and modernized travel, according to officials.
Brig. Gen. Alexander Lovasz, Maneuver Support Center of Excellence and Fort Leonard Wood commanding general, said the Waynesville-St. Robert Regional Airport at Forney Army Airfield is one of 21 joint-use airfields throughout the Department of War.
“The Army appreciates the long-standing partnership we have between the installation and our respective communities,” Lovasz said. “Last year alone this airfield serviced almost 11,000 people. So this ceremony is truly a celebration of not only a facility but of a capability that will ultimately improve access to Fort Leonard Wood.”
Waynesville Mayor Sean Wilson said the new terminal represents growth, transformation and evolution for the community.
“Our community has people working together to transform this community and to continue to evolve and adapt,” Wilson said.
St. Robert Mayor James Breckinridge said with the volume of passengers the airport has seen this year, the new terminal “couldn’t come at a better time.”
“Today we celebrate much more than the completion of a new building, we celebrate an investment in our community, our regional transportation infrastructure and our future,” Breckinridge said. “This airport will serve our residents, our businesses, our visitors and perhaps most importantly, our military community.
“Fort Leonard Wood brings in thousands of service members, families and visitors to our region each year and having a quality regional airport is an important part of that mission.”
According to a Waynesville-St. Robert Joint Airport Board official, the new terminal is expected to open to passengers Dec. 8, 2026.
Contour Airlines provides commercial air service for the Waynesville-St. Robert Regional Airport to and from Dallas, Texas and Nashville, Tennessee.
More information about the Waynesville-St. Robert Regional Airport can be found here.
More photos from the ribbon-cutting ceremony may be viewed on Fort Leonard Wood’s Flickr.
title: Fort Leonard Wood community celebrates Waynesville-St. Robert Regional Airport expansion

Mexican National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Charged with Laundering Drug Proceeds and Unlawfully Possessing a Firearm
EUGENE, Ore.— A Mexican national unlawfully residing in the United States has been charged with laundering purported drug proceeds and being an alien in possession of a firearm.
According to court documents, Esteban Peralta Fragozo, 50, of Springfield, Oregon, owned and operated El Kaiman Western Wear, a Springfield business that sold clothing and provided international money transfer services. Investigators with Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) allege that Fragozo used the business to launder drug trafficking proceeds through wire transfers sent to Mexico and Honduras.
Court documents allege that between January 2018 and July 2026, El Kaiman processed approximately 179,874 wire transfers totaling more than $93 million. Investigators further allege that more than $34 million in suspected drug proceeds were transmitted from Springfield to drug-trafficking corridors in Mexico and Honduras during that period.
As part of the investigation, law enforcement conducted a series of undercover operations using a confidential informant. According to the complaint, Fragozo processed multiple wire transfers after being told the funds were derived from drug trafficking and used false sender information and identification documents to complete the transactions.
The complaint further alleges that drug traffickers used El Kaiman to transmit proceeds derived from narcotics trafficking. In one instance detailed in court records, investigators recovered wire transfer receipts from El Kaiman during a traffic stop that resulted in the seizure of approximately 72 pounds of methamphetamine.
On Nov. 4, 2026, federal agents executed search warrants at Fragozo's residence, business, vehicle, and on his person. During a search of the business, agents recovered a Ruger 9mm pistol, ammunition, and bulk currency. According to court documents, Fragozo admitted possessing the firearm and acknowledged that he did not have lawful immigration status in the United States.
“As alleged, the defendant was illegally present in the United States while using his business to launder millions of dollars in drug trafficking proceeds and unlawfully possessing a firearm,” said Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon. “Drug trafficking organizations depend on financial facilitators to move and hide their criminal profits. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to identify, dismantle, and prosecute the financial infrastructure that supports transnational drug trafficking organizations and fuels the flow of fentanyl and other dangerous drugs into our communities.”
According to the complaint, investigators have observed a dramatic increase in drug trafficking activity involving Honduran nationals in Oregon. Court documents allege that Mexican drug trafficking organizations increasingly use Honduran nationals to distribute fentanyl and other dangerous narcotics in major metropolitan areas, including the Portland metropolitan area.
Fragozo made his initial appearance in federal court on Nov. 4, 2026, before a U.S. magistrate judge and was ordered detained pending further proceedings.
A criminal complaint is only an accusation of a crime, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.
The case is being investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

title: Mexican National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Charged with Laundering Drug Proceeds and Unlawfully Possessing a Firearm

text:
Biological threats are rapidly evolving in modern warfare. Recent advances in synthetic and artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies make it easier for adversaries to engineer pathogens that can go undetected by traditional methods and potentially harm countless people. To better understand the evolving threat and maintain force protection, warfighters need to know what threats they are dealing with and whether they have the means to protect and defend themselves at the ready.
The Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Layered Protection and Integration (PAE LP&I) is working toward fielding advanced sequencing technologies under the Far-Forward Biological Sequencing (FFBS) and Non-targeted Sequencing Identification System (NSIS) programs to detect and identify biological agents as far forward, or as close to the site of exposure, as possible. FFBS program, led by Joint Project Manager for CBRN Special Operations Forces (JPM CBRN SOF), is a system that allows users to rapidly identify more than 30,000 biological organisms from samples using a small, ruggedized integrated console that requires minimal materials and expertise to operate. The NSIS program led by Joint Project Manager for CBRN Integrated Early Warning (JPM CBRN IEW) is a laboratory-based system that utilizes a laptop with an even larger database (over 129,000 organisms). The NSIS is designed for more advanced users with prior microbiological training to provide robust biological sequencing capability on site.
Both systems use untargeted DNA and RNA sequencing technology, which determines the genomic make-up of the sample. The sequencing data is mapped against a large database to determine the species present in the sample on site. Even if a biothreat has never been encountered before, the sequencing data can potentially be quickly assessed and characterized based on information in the database.
Currently, warfighters identify biothreats in the field using targeted handheld and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays that are limited to identifying a small number of known biological threats. Genetically engineered pathogens or novel biological threats may not be detected using these technologies, but they can be identified using sequencing technology.
For the sequencing method to work effectively, specific reagents must be used during sample preparation. Current reagents used in sequencing require cold storage as low as -20°C. This presents an issue requiring cold shipping and storage in resource limited, far-forward settings, which restricts a unit’s ability to effectively use these biological identification systems.
To reduce logistical burden and expand access to tools provided under the FFBS and NSIS programs, PAE LP&I is collaborating with commercial and government partners to develop shelf-stabilized reagents using methods such as vitrification and lyophilization. Vitrification is a process that transforms a substance into a glass-like, non-crystalline structure through rapid cooling or melting. Lyophilization is the process of freeze-drying material. Both techniques allow reagents to be stored at room temperature, potentially eliminating the need for cold storage and expanding the number of operational units that can successfully operate sequencing equipment in the field.
“If we are able to equip more units with sequencing technology, we could greatly enhance our biosurveillance capabilities in the field,” said Cory Bernhards, Ph.D., FFBS/NSIS subject matter expert and research biologist from the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Chemical Biological Center. “Sequencing has the power to identify any biological threat. Eliminating the need for cold storage removes a barrier and will enable broader use.”
Army Maj. Ashley Sperry, assistant program manager, JPM CBRN SOF, added, “Reagent vitrification solves a critical operational bottleneck. Eliminating cold-chain logistics ensures reagents remain stable in austere environments, broadens far-forward deployment and significantly lowers program lifecycle sustainment costs across the force.”
Unlocking ways to make the sequencing capability more accessible is a game changer. The in-field sequencing capability allows the War Department to transform and move faster.
“Cold-chain shipping and storage has long been a challenge in the biodefense and medical fields,” said Shanmuga Sozhamannan, Ph.D., subject matter expert and technical coordinator for the Joint Project Lead (JPL) for CBRN Enabling Technologies. “Our hope is that we can quickly field this capability and apply what we’re learning in this effort toward other warfighter capabilities that are constrained by cold-chain shipping and storage and short shelf-lives.”
Sozhamannan said the team is about halfway through developing the proof-of-concept for the shelf stabilization effort and is looking forward to deploying the finished product to support far-forward sequencing technology by the warfighter and other USG customers in austere environments.
Bernhards added, “Achieving shelf stabilization in the field is more than solving a logistical challenge, it’s giving our warfighters an enhanced biological identification capability that increases survivability, decision advantage and the ability to remain active in the face of biological threats on the battlefield.”
title: Out with the Cold: expanding biosurveillance capability through shelf stable products

text:
LOS ANGELES – A Mexican judge has been arrested on a nine-count federal indictment charging him with accepting a $2 million bribe in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of a Canadian drug trafficker who was the second-in-command to a former Olympic snowboarder charged with leading a transnational cocaine trafficking operation and with murder and attempted murder, the Justice Department announced today.

Luis Benítez Alcántara, 49, of Mexico City, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia.

He is charged in a second superseding indictment with nine counts of being an accessory after the fact. The United States will request Benítez’s extradition from Colombia.

“Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the work of the Homeland Security Task Force and our international law enforcement partners, Mr. Benítez will be held accountable. The Department of Justice will continue identifying and dismantling transnational criminal organizations that threaten the safety of the American people.”

“This case underscores my office’s commitment to dismantling criminal organizations at every level, including by holding accountable those who abuse positions of public trust,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli.

“The FBI and our partners have arrested Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexican judge who allegedly accepted bribes and used his position to aid former FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitive Ryan Wedding and his associates,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Benítez Alcántara was a district judge in Mexico City who allegedly accepted $2 million in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of Wedding’s second in command, while Wedding was orchestrating a billion-dollar transnational criminal organization and the largest supplier of cocaine to Canada with connections in Colombia, Mexico, and the U.S. Benítez Alcántara is charged with nine counts of accessory after the fact for assisting the individual in order to hinder or prevent his apprehension, trial or punishment. Thanks to FBI Los Angeles, our Bogatá Law Enforcement Attaché, our local partners, and our Department of Justice who made the success of this operation possible.”

According to the superseding indictment returned on September 4, Benítez used his official position to unlawfully secure Clark’s release, enabling a major figure in an international drug organization to evade lawful detention. In return for the $2 million bribe payment, Benítez issued rulings that directly facilitated the release from custody of Andrew Clark, 36, a Canadian drug trafficker and second-in-command to Ryan James Wedding, 44, a former Olympic snowboarder for Canada who led one of the biggest, most notorious, and violent transnational criminal organizations.

In October 2024, Clark was arrested in Mexico on U.S. drug trafficking, murder, and attempted murder charges in which Wedding also was named. Following his arrest, Clark appeared before Benítez, then serving as the district judge in Mexico City responsible for overseeing Clark’s extradition proceedings.

In November 2024, the United States formally requested Clark’s extradition to face prosecution in the United States. From November 2024 through February 2025, Clark transferred approximately $2.75 million, through intermediaries and in small increments, for the purpose of securing his release from Mexican custody. During this period, Clark also negotiated an agreement to pay Benítez approximately $2 million in exchange for ordering his release.

On February 24, 2025, the same day Benítez received the full $2 million bribe payment, he granted Clark bond and ordered him released. Days later, Clark was re‑arrested and removed to the United States, where the criminal case against him remains pending.

Wedding, who, at the time, was one of the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted Fugitives, was apprehended in Mexico in January 2026 and subsequently, removed to the United States, where he remains in federal custody. He faces drug‑trafficking, murder, and attempted murder charges and is currently scheduled for two separate trials on March 31, 2027, and October 26, 2027.

An indictment contains allegations that a defendant has committed a crime. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court.

If convicted, Benítez would face a statutory maximum sentence of 15 years in federal prison on each count.

The FBI investigated this matter with the Los Angeles Police Department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police – Federal Policing. In addition, significant assistance was provided by U.S. law enforcement partners, including U.S. Customs and Border Protection Buffalo, New York, and Colombian law enforcement partners, including Colombian National Police – Directorate of Criminal Investigation and Interpol, Special Interagency Investigation Group ( Policía Nacional de Colombia – Dirección de Investigación Criminal e Interpol, Grupo Especial de Investigación Interagenciales ).

The Justice Department’s Judicial Attaché Office in Bogotá and Office of International Affairs worked with the Government of Colombia to secure the arrest.

This investigation, arrest, and prosecution are part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Los Angeles comprises agents and officers from the FBI and LAPD with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California.

Assistant United States Attorneys Lyndsi Allsop and Joshua J. Lee of the Transnational Organized Crime Section are prosecuting this case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided substantial assistance.
title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Mexican Federal Judge’s Arrest on U.S. Charges of Accepting $2 Million Bribe to Free Canadian Drug Trafficker
