Justice Department Says Federal Education Aid Cannot Be Tied to Unconstitutional Race-Based Criteria
Today, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion clarifying the limits on the Department of Education’s authority to consider race when administering the Magnet Schools Assistance Program (MSAP). MSAP is a federal grant program designed to promote voluntary school desegregation and expand educational opportunities for students through competitive grants to school districts. The opinion reaffirms the federal government’s longstanding support for magnet schools while ensuring that federal assistance is not conditioned on unconstitutional race‑based criteria.
“Today’s opinion reaffirms a foundational principle of our constitutional order: government programs must treat individuals as individuals, not as members of racial groups,” said Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel. “Although Congress has long recognized the value of magnet schools, the Equal Protection Clause limits how the federal government may lend them support. Only in exceptionally rare circumstances may funding decisions turn on a school’s racial composition.”
“The Magnet School Assistance Program can continue to serve students across the country—but only if it is administered constitutionally,” said Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock, who signed the opinion. “Federal dollars must never be used to engineer unconstitutional racial balancing. Our Constitution is colorblind, and federal programs must reflect that.”
The opinion explains that MSAP’s statutory and regulatory framework ties federal funding to race‑based concepts such as “minority‑group isolation” and the use of racial data to shape funding decisions. Because these criteria condition federal support on racial considerations, the opinion concludes that the program must be evaluated under the Constitution’s most rigorous standard: strict scrutiny.
Under that standard, the Department of Education may approve MSAP grants only when an applicant demonstrates that its use of race is narrowly tailored to remedy a specific and identified instance of illegal discrimination. The opinion makes clear that grants based solely on goals such as increasing racial diversity, reducing racial isolation, or altering racial balance—untethered from the remediation of unlawful discrimination—cannot be approved.
The Department of Justice will work closely with the Department of Education to ensure that MSAP awards fully comply with these constitutional requirements while continuing to support the mission of magnet schools: fostering academic excellence, innovation, and meaningful educational opportunities for students across the country.
Read the full opinion here.
Press Release Number: 26-1326
title: Justice Department Says Federal Education Aid Cannot Be Tied to Unconstitutional Race-Based Criteria

Gainesville, Florida – Terry Lee, 43, of Gainesville, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to one count of Conspiracy to Violate the Animal Welfare Act. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This case was built upon the outstanding collaborative work of our state and federal law enforcement partners, each of which is committed to putting an end to animal fighting ventures like this one. These crimes are heinous, cruel, and depraved, and deserve severe punishment and condemnation.”

Court documents reflect that the defendant conspired with others to possess, sell, and receive dogs for purposes of having the dogs participate in animal fighting ventures. For instance, on May 23, 2024, the defendant used a social media platform to send a video of two dogs fighting to another individual. The defendant attempted to sell one of the dogs in that video on behalf of a co-defendant. On September 30, 2024, the defendant posted an advertisement for the sale of another dog, stating that the dog was a “1xw,” which stands for one-time winner. Further, on or before June 6, 2024, the defendant attended a dog fight that occurred inside a property under the control of another co-defendant. One of the dogs, which the defendant sponsored and forced to participate in the June 2024 fight, was later recovered on his property.

Lee faces a maximum of five years’ imprisonment and up to three years of supervised release.

The case was jointly investigated by the United States Department of Agriculture – Office of Inspector General, the Gainesville Police Department, Alachua County Sheriff’s Office, and Alachua County Animal Resources. Assistant United States Attorney Adam Hapner is prosecuting the case.

Lee’s sentencing is scheduled for January 26, 2027, at 1:30 p.m., at the United States Courthouse in Gainesville before United States Chief District Judge Allen C. Winsor.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .

The Department of Justice Files Complaint Against the Pennsylvania State University Challenging Its Policy that Provide In-State Tuition to Illegal Aliens
Today, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania State University for violating federal law by prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands. The Department is challenging the Pennsylvania State University’s policy which grants in-state tuition to illegal aliens while denying reduced tuition to U.S. citizens. This policy unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate, in direct conflict with federal law.
“The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. “Congress long ago made clear that states, through their public universities, cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans.”
“Congress made a deliberate policy choice that states and their public institutions may not grant tuition benefits to illegal aliens unless those same benefits are made to all U.S. citizens,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “This university has ignored that mandate. The Department will continue to challenge policies that unlawfully disadvantage American citizens.”
In the complaint, the United States seeks to enjoin the Pennsylvania State University from enforcing its policy that provides undocumented students, including illegal aliens who reside in Pennsylvania, with in-state tuition rates, regardless of whether those undocumented students are lawfully present in the United States. Additionally, the complaint seeks to enjoin the Pennsylvania State University from enacting any new tuition policies that favor undocumented students over U.S. citizens.
Today’s lawsuit brings the Department’s total to 27 lawsuits challenging in-state tuition for illegal aliens. Under the leadership of Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Department’s efforts have delivered numerous wins for the American people, as six lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois and Kansas have resulted in favorable orders permanently enjoining and declaring unconstitutional similar laws which gave reduced tuition to illegal aliens, including an order from the Fifth Circuit.
For more information about the Enforcement & Affirmative Litigation Branch and its enforcement efforts visit https://www.justice.gov/civil/enforcement-affirmative-litigation-branch.
Press Release Number: 26-1321
title: The Department of Justice Files Complaint Against the Pennsylvania State University Challenging Its Policy that Provide In-State Tuition to Illegal Aliens

The Joint Trauma System validated the 121st Field Hospital “Legends,” part of the 549th Hospital Center and the 65th Medical Brigade “Pacific Medics,” on its battle drill for activating a walking blood bank here during exercise Pacific Medic Forge 26-2 in August 2026.
Serving as the 121st Field Hospital’s external evaluation, the brigade exercise marked the first time the Joint Trauma System validated a Role 3 field hospital under its walking blood bank program, according to the hospital’s after-action review.
Because a hospital in a large-scale conflict can lose both its blood resupply and its network connection at the same time, the 121st Field Hospital trained to overcome both challenges simultaneously.
A walking blood bank allows a hospital to collect, screen and transfuse fresh whole blood from pre-screened volunteer donors when stored blood runs short. The hospital’s training roster included laboratory specialists, physicians, physician assistants, nurses and combat medics, along with volunteer donors ranging in rank from private first class to lieutenant colonel.
According to the unit’s after-action review, the validation confirmed the hospital’s ability to safely source, screen and test whole blood from pre-registered volunteer donors during mass casualty surges while establishing a pre-screened donor pool.
“When you volunteer as a donor, you realize the blood supply is standing right next to you in formation,” said Lt. Col. A. Nicole Gonzalez, commander of the 121st Field Hospital, who volunteered as a donor during the training. “Every Soldier we pre-screen is blood we may not be able to get any other way.”
Pacific Medic Forge 26-2 was also the first time a field hospital employed the Joint Operational Medicine Information Systems, or JOMIS, suite in a simulated combat environment, according to the JOMIS program office.
Preparation began weeks before the first simulated patient arrived. Beginning July 20, the hospital’s signal Soldiers and the JOMIS program team spent three weeks connecting the system to a tactical network, setting up user accounts, loading exercise patients onto handheld devices and working through challenges ranging from software configuration to severe weather. Training covered five applications, equipping the hospital’s signal Soldiers to administer the systems independently.
The exercise also evaluated how clinical teams operate when connectivity is disrupted. At one point during the evaluation, the team intentionally took the network offline. Clinical staff continued documenting patient care offline, and the digital records automatically transmitted once the connection was restored.
“An after-action review only helps the people who read it,” said Maj. Joshua Okoemu, executive officer of the 121st Field Hospital. “Sharing these lessons means the next field hospital does not have to learn them the hard way.”
Blood and data are both lifelines for a modern field hospital. Through Pacific Medic Forge 26-2, the Soldiers of the 121st Field Hospital advanced both capabilities and are sharing those lessons across Army Medicine.
title: 121st Field Hospital Earns Walking Blood Bank Validation, Employs Digital Health Records in the Field

ROCHESTER, N.Y. - U.S. Attorney Michael DiGiacomo announced today that Paul Paredes, 54, of Buffalo, NY, who was convicted of wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, was sentenced to serve 87 months in prison by Chief U.S. District Judge Elizabeth A. Wolford. Paredes was also ordered to pay restitution totaling $8,754,446.64 to 57 victims.

Since 2013, Paredes has owned J&E Business Consulting LLC, which provides services to client businesses, including acting as a broker between the credit card processing companies and smaller retail businesses. Small businesses provide J&E with their financial information, such as the owner’s identifying information, including driver’s license, social security number, and email, as well as bank account information.

Between April 2019, and August 2023, Paredes submitted hundreds of fraudulent financing applications to dozens of lenders under the identities of his business customers (victims), for goods and services allegedly provided by Paredes, with the funds payable to bank accounts controlled by Paredes. These financing agreements were prepared in the names if victims, using their personal information, and without their knowledge, consent, or authorization. After a financing agreement was approved, money from the victim lender was deposited into one of numerous bank accounts controlled by Paredes, who used the money he obtained from the scheme to fund his personal expenses, pay salaries and operating expenses, or to make payments to victim lenders to avoid detection of the fraudulent loans. By making those payments to the victim lenders, Paredes was able to continue making similar fraudulent financing agreements with multiple victim lenders without discovery. To further avoid detection, on occasions when victims received communications from victim lenders about the fraudulent financing agreements, Paredes misled them about the purpose of the communications and told them he would handle it.

Paredes used the identity of at least 63 individuals to defraud at least 23 victim lenders, utilizing at least 12 different bank accounts and moving the money he obtained from the scheme throughout different accounts. Paredes submitted false loan applications from Rochester, NY, to the out-of-state lenders located throughout the country, including in New Jersey, Virginia, Illinois, Texas, North Carolina, Florida, Washington, Pennsylvania, Iowa, Colorado, and Minnesota. The total loss amount is at least $3,500,000.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Katelyn M. Hartford. The sentencing is the result of an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Allen D. Davis, II, the Internal Revenue Service, Criminal Investigation Division, under the direction of Special Agent-in-Charge Harry Chavis, and the New York State Department of Financial Services-Criminal Investigation Bureau, under the direction of Acting Superintendent Kaitlin Asrow.

Ecuadorian Politicians, Business Executives, and Narcotraffickers Arrested for Narcotics Importation and Weapons Offenses
NEW YORK — The Justice Department announced today the unsealing of charges against, and the arrests of, five Ecuadorian nationals who conspired to import vast quantities of cocaine into the United States for more than a decade. The defendants include a former member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, a former Ecuadorian mayor and current mayoral candidate, the son of the former president of Ecuador, and other powerful narcotraffickers.
“The charges announced today represent a coordinated effort to dismantle political corruption and narcotics trafficking that had wreaked havoc in Ecuador and plagued the country with increasing violence in recent years,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “As alleged in the Indictment, the defendants played a critical role in transforming the country into a major transit hub for 70 percent of the cocaine reaching the United States and Europe. These prosecutions hold accountable powerful politicians and narcotraffickers alike who profited from and facilitated the international narcotics trade and who degraded Ecuador’s internal security.”
“Political influence, financial resources, and powerful connections do not place anyone beyond the reach of American justice,” said DEA Administrator Terrance Cole. “Those who exploit legitimate businesses to move cocaine toward our communities should understand that DEA will follow the evidence, expose their networks, and work with our international partners to bring them before the courts. No title, fortune, or family connection changes that commitment.”
Ecuador sits at the heart of the global cocaine trade. Situated between two of the world’s largest cocaine-producing countries, hundreds of tons of cocaine are exported each year out of Ecuador’s main seaports, including from the coastal cities of Manta, in Manabi Province, and Guayaquil, in Guayas Province. Cocaine traffickers operating in Ecuador and the broader region exploit legal commercial maritime routes to conceal their narcotics, using container ships and other commercial vessels transporting legitimate commodities, including seafood, bananas, timber, and minerals, as well as an extensive network of fishing vessels and “go-fast” boats, to smuggle cocaine to the United States and other international markets. Image 1 depicts the movement of cocaine from Colombia and Peru, through Ecuador, and on to international destinations, including the United States:
Like other countries in the region, Ecuador is beset by rampant corruption and partnerships between politicians and large-scale narcotics traffickers. As alleged, two such politicians are Jaime Estrada Medranda and Jaime Estrada Bonilla. Medranda and Bonilla have long partnered with some of the region’s largest and most violent drug traffickers to ship massive quantities of cocaine out of Ecuador to the United States and elsewhere, contributing to the deteriorating internal security of Ecuador and the corruption of its political systems.
In Ecuador’s National Assembly, Medranda represented a district within the province of Manabi that includes the coastal city of Manta — the center of Ecuador’s tuna-processing industry and home to one of Ecuador’s largest ports, which serves as a major transit point for the global cocaine supply. Bonilla, who is Medranda’s father, was the former mayor of Manta, is currently running for the same office, and was former President of the Port Authority of Manta. Medranda and Bonilla are also owners and executives of a major Manta-based seafood company and an Ecuadorian professional soccer club. For years, as alleged, Medranda and Bonilla have smuggled vast quantities of cocaine disguised within their seafood company’s shipments out of Ecuador in partnership with large-scale drug traffickers, including the leaders of violent drug trafficking and designated foreign terrorist organizations such as Los Choneros and Los Lobos. Many of the cocaine loads they have conspired to export were sourced from paramilitary groups operating in the jungles of Colombia.
To minimize the risk to themselves, Medranda and Bonilla allegedly have relied on trusted intermediaries to meet with drug traffickers, receive payments, and coordinate the logistics of receiving, packing, and smuggling cocaine out of Ecuador using containers packed with legitimate goods, such as tuna. For example, in or about 2026, Medranda and Bonilla sent their representatives Geovanny Fernandez Menendez and William Jose Briones Lopez to meet with Jacobo Abdala Bucaram-Pulley — an alleged Ecuadorian drug and firearms trafficker and the son of the former President of Ecuador — to negotiate the export of a purported two-ton load of cocaine from Ecuador to Mexico, for further shipment to the United States.
In another example, in or about 2023, the seafood exporting company of Medranda and Bonilla was used to ship ton-quantity loads of cocaine out of Ecuadorian seaports. From one such shipment, on or about May 27, 2023, the Ecuadorian National Police seized approximately 1,444 kilograms of cocaine inside of the company’s shipping container at the Port of Guayaquil. Image 2 depicts the cocaine seized from the company’s shipping container.
Jaime Estrada Medranda, 41, Jaime Estrada Bonilla, 71, Jacobo Abdala Bucaram-Pulley, 48, Geovanny Fernandez Menendez, 53, and William Jose Briones Lopez, 47, all of Ecuador, are charged with participating in a conspiracy to import cocaine into the United States, which carries a mandatory minimum penalty of 10 years in prison and a maximum penalty of life; possession of machineguns, which carries a mandatory minimum sentence of 30 years in prison and a maximum penalty of life; and conspiracy to possess machineguns, which carries a maximum penalty of life.
The mandatory minimum and maximum potential sentences in this case are prescribed by Congress and provided here for informational purposes only, as any sentencing of the defendants will be determined by a judge.
Jaime Estrada Medranda and Jaime Estrada Bonilla were arrested on or about Nov. 2, while traveling in Panama.
Jacobo Abdala Bucaram-Pulley, Geovanny Fernandez Menendez, and William Jose Briones Lopez were arrested on or about Nov. 4, in Ecuador.
Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding efforts of the DEA’s Special Operations Division Bilateral Investigations Unit. Mr. McDonald also thanked the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, which provided significant assistance in securing the arrests of the defendants, the DEA Country Offices in Quito and Panama City, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Embassy in Quito. Mr. McDonald also praised the significant assistance provided by the Government of Ecuador and the Government of Panama.
This prosecution is being handled by the Office’s National Security and International Narcotics Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jonathan L. Bodansky, Jane Y. Chong, Jeffrey W. Coyle, and Varun A. Gumaste for the Southern District of New York are in charge of the prosecution.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

WASHINGTON – A 10-count Indictment, unsealed today in U.S. District Court, charges two executives of a District-based healthcare provider and one of their Community Support Workers in connection with a scheme to bill D.C. Medicaid for mental health services for juveniles that were never provided or were invoiced at grossly inflated rates, causing a loss to the District of Columbia’s Medicaid program that exceeded millions of dollars, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“No one stealing from taxpayer-funded programs is safe. As alleged, these defendants treated Medicaid as a personal piggy bank in a scheme that caused millions in losses, billing for services never provided while funding luxury vehicles and other extravagant purchases,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “We will continue to uncover and prosecute fraud until these schemes are dismantled and taxpayer dollars are protected from abuse.”

“No one stealing from taxpayer-funded programs is safe. As alleged, these defendants treated Medicaid as a personal piggy bank in a scheme that caused millions in losses, billing for services never provided while funding luxury vehicles and other extravagant purchases,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “We will continue to uncover and prosecute fraud until these schemes are dismantled and taxpayer dollars are protected from abuse.”

According to the Indictment, from January 2022 through February 2025, Quality Healthcare Services billed D.C. Medicaid approximately $14 million for Mental Health Rehabilitation Services.

Two of the defendants are executives of Quality Healthcare Services, LLC, a Washington D.C.-based provider of mental health rehabilitative services to youth and adolescent beneficiaries from low-income families. A third defendant is a community support worker at Quality Healthcare Services.

Mwasi Songambele, 52, is a citizen of Tanzania who resides in Laurel, Maryland, and has a pending final order of removal from the United States. She is charged in the Indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud, four counts of health care fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. She is the controlling executive of Quality Healthcare Services, LLC, and runs the day-to-day operations of the company.

Maya Cheyo, 31, of Brambleton, Virginia, is charged in the Indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and two counts of health care fraud. Cheyo, aka “Mwaya Songambele,” is Mwasi Songambele’s daughter and the Chief Operating Officer and Human Resources Director of Quality Healthcare Services, LLC.

Vanessa Kuh, 29, of Lanham, Maryland, is charged in the Indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and two counts of health care fraud. Kuh is a community support worker at Quality Healthcare Services, LLC.

According to the Indictment, beginning at least as early as January 2022 and continuing through February 2025, Songambele instructed employees at Quality Healthcare on how to document and bill Medicaid for Mental Health Rehabilitative Services (MHRS). Specifically, Songambele, along Cheyo, Kuh, and at least three other unnamed co-conspirators, allegedly inflated the amount of time spent conducting MHRS or documented MHRS encounters that never occurred.

Songambele allegedly instructed the co-conspirators to bill four units, or about one-hour, for all MHRS telehealth encounters even if the call only lasted a few minutes. To avoid scrutiny from D.C. Department of Behavioral Health, the co-conspirators were instructed by Quality Healthcare management to pick a random time for the length of service, between 53 and 67 minutes, to make the length of the telehealth call appear more realistic. Songambele additionally instructed the co-conspirators to “make sure to use” all 600 units for a telehealth consumer—the total amount of units authorized by Medicaid for a consumer during a 180-day period—without regard to medical necessity and without regard to whether the services actually had been performed.

Cheyo and Kuh are charged in the Indictment with submitting and causing to be submitted, false and fraudulent claims for payment to D.C. Medicaid for MHRS that were not provided as claimed.

The Indictment also seeks the forfeiture of a fleet of luxury vehicles. Those include a 2024 Mercedes-Benz G550W4, a 2023 Mercedes-Benz G550W4, a 2022 Mercedes-Benz 2500 Cargo Van, a 2020 Mercedes-Benz C300W4, and a 2023 Rover Defender. It also seeks the forfeiture of a house on the 7000 block of Tranquility Road in Laurel, Maryland, and a Panthere De Cartier Watch, Medium Model.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office, the D.C. Office of the Inspector General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, and the Department of Health and Human Services – Office of the Inspector General. The matter was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jason Facci of the Fraud, Public Corruption, and Civil Rights Section.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

title: Executives of Healthcare Provider Charged by Indictment in Fraud that Caused Millions in Losses to D.C. Medicaid

WICHITA, KAN. – A Kansas man was sentenced to 77 months in prison for maliciously setting a fire that damaged an apartment building where families lived.

According to court documents, Skyler D. Imel, 31, of Wichita, pleaded guilty to one count of arson.

In March 2023, Imel intentionally damaged an apartment complex on West Central Avenue in Wichita by setting a fire inside the bedroom of a vacant unit. Before starting the fire, Imel used a red Sharpie to write, “Sam apparment 2502 is geting killed” on the bedroom wall, and he disabled a smoke alarm. Imel attempted to set a second fire at apartment No. 2502 by throwing a Molotov Cocktail at the front entryway. That apartment was occupied at the time.

“There were families living in the apartment complex so this incident could have easily turned into a horrific tragedy,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “The fact that the defendant disabled the smoke detector indicates he wanted the fire to have time to spread before it was likely to be noticed, increasing the danger to the building’s residents.”

The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) and the Wichita Fire Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Ola Odeyemi prosecuted the case.

DENVER – Law enforcement officials from across Colorado gathered this week for the annual Colorado Law Enforcement Coordination Conference hosted by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado. The event brings together agencies across local, state, and federal levels of government with the purpose of partnership development, collaboration, and preparedness.

Over the two-day session, law enforcement officials spent time hearing from experts from across the justice system who spoke about topics including human trafficking, online radicalization of juveniles, violent crime, transnational criminal organizations, tracing illicit proceeds, and emerging tools and techniques.

Another critical area of conversation involved state and federal collaboration during crisis response. The event’s keynote panel included U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly, Denver District Attorney John Walsh, and Boulder District Attorney Michael Dougherty – each of whom have unique professional experiences responding to and managing serious situations in the state.

“It is both an honor and a critical opportunity for law enforcement officials from across Colorado to gather with the goal of developing partnerships, collaboration, and preparedness,” said United States Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “Law enforcement is complex and critical work, and I am proud to stand with our partners at the local, state, and federal levels to advance justice and protect the people of Colorado.”

“Colorado has a long history of cooperation between local, state and federal law enforcement," said Denver District Attorney John Walsh. "That cooperation, which continues today, has played a major role in significantly reducing crime in the state over the past few years. This conference is a great opportunity for law enforcement agencies from across the state to make our partnership even stronger, and Colorado even safer.”

“Collaboration and preparedness are critical to enhancing public safety which is a role we take very seriously,” said Boulder District Attorney Michael Dougherty. “When federal, state, and local partners come together with shared purpose, we strengthen our ability to protect communities and respond to emerging challenges. These discussions and partnerships reflect our collective commitment to working together to delivering meaningful results to the people we serve.”

The Colorado Association of Chiefs of Police, the County Sheriffs of Colorado, the Colorado District Attorney’s Council, and the Colorado Fraternal Order of Police helped to make the event possible.
title: Law Enforcement Officials Gather To Discuss Partnerships, Collaboration, Preparedness

CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Justin Dale Graves, 44, of St. Albans, was sentenced today to nine years in prison, to be followed by five years of supervised release, for possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine, and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug-trafficking crime.

According to court documents and statements made in court, on October 30, 2024, law enforcement officers executed a search warrant at Graves’ residence in St. Albans and seized over 3.3 kilograms of methamphetamine, a loaded Hi-Point model C-9 9mm pistol, a loaded Glock model 19 9mm pistol, 37.69 grams of fentanyl, 17.17 grams of cocaine, 2.29 grams of heroin, two digital scales, various rounds of live ammunition, a drug ledger, and $1,190.

As part of his guilty plea, Graves admitted that he possessed the seized methamphetamine and intended to distribute it, and possessed the seized firearms to protect himself, his drugs, and his drug proceeds. Graves further admitted that he sold approximately 27.21 grams of methamphetamine to a confidential informant in exchange for $225 in St. Albans on October 29, 2024, the day before the execution of the search warrant.

United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the St. Albans Police Department.

United States District Judge Irene C. Berger imposed the sentence. Assistant United States Attorney JC MacCallum prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

This case is also part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

CEO and VA Employee Sentenced for Paying and Receiving Illegal Health Care Kickbacks and Bribes
Two Florida men were sentenced today for their roles in a conspiracy to pay and receive illegal health care kickbacks. Laurent Cassagnol was sentenced to 6 months in prison, and Heriberto Rivera was sentenced to 13 months in prison. In addition to the prison terms, Cassagnol was ordered to forfeit $175,172, and Rivera was ordered to forfeit $515,542, which represented the proceeds that the defendants obtained from the offense.
According to court documents, Cassagnol, 43, and Rivera, 43, both of Orlando, Florida, conspired to pay and receive illegal kickbacks and bribes to direct veterans and their families, who were patients of the VA Community Care Program (VACCP), to Rivera’s clinic, Family Integrative Medicine of Orlando, LLC (FIMO), for acupuncture, chiropractic adjustments, and other holistic medical services. Rivera, the CEO of FIMO, paid illegal kickbacks and bribes to Cassagnol, an Advanced Medical Support Assistant for VACCP, in exchange for Cassagnol using his position with the VA to steer VA patients to FIMO for medical services. Cassagnol was a vital point of contact between veterans and the VA health care system; his abuse of that role took advantage of veterans and their families who rely on the VA to obtain medical care. The actions of both defendants put profit before the needs of VA patients.
As a result of the illegal kickbacks, over $14 million in fraudulent claims were submitted to the VA and VACCP, of which over $11 million was paid. The investigation was the result of a complaint made to the VA Office of the Inspector General (VA-OIG) fraud hotline.
Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; Special Agent in Charge Rodney E. Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office; and Acting Special Agent in Charge Josh Lollar of the VA-OIG Southeast Field Office made the announcement.
FBI and VA-OIG investigated the case.
Trial Attorneys Jody King and Angela Benoit of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section are prosecuting the case.
On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at https://www.justice.gov/fraud/health-care-fraud-section.
title: CEO and VA Employee Sentenced for Paying and Receiving Illegal Health Care Kickbacks and Bribes

SEATTLE — ICE Seattle arrested an illegal alien from Kenya claiming to work for the Washington State Department of Children, Youth and Families during a targeted enforcement operation Oct. 26. Stanley Robert Kengu Muthee, first entered the U.S. on Feb. 6, 2019, and was required to depart no later than Aug. 5 that year. Instead, he remained in the country unlawfully, applying for and receiving work authorization three times under the Biden administration.
“Illegal aliens should not be working for state governments — Americans should expect better from the offices meant to serve them — but nonetheless, a job with the state of Washington doesn’t come with a free pass to ignore federal immigration law,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock.
When ICE officials questioned Muthee, the Nairobi native also claimed to have worked previously in Washington state corrections. Officers served him with a warrant of arrest and he will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Emily Custodio, 52, a citizen of the Philippines, entered a plea of guilty this afternoon before United States District Judge Joel H. Slomsky to voting by an alien. Under both federal and state law, only U.S. citizens may vote in Pennsylvania.

The defendant was charged by indictment in September of last year.

As detailed in court filings and statements, on July 18, 2020, Custodio applied online to the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania’s Department of State to register to vote in Pennsylvania, falsely answering “Yes” to the question about whether she was a United States citizen.

On July 21, 2020, based on the information provided by Custodio, including her false answer to the citizenship question, her application to register to vote was accepted and she was successfully registered to vote in Pennsylvania.

On November 3, 2020, Custodio appeared in person at her assigned Philadelphia County polling place to cast a vote in the 2020 general election. She signed her name in the poll book next to the statement “I hereby certify that I am qualified to vote at this election…” and cast a vote in the 2020 general election, which included the election for the offices of President and Vice President of the United States.

The defendant is scheduled to be sentenced on February 16 and faces a maximum possible sentence of one year in prison, one year of supervised release, and a $100,000 fine.
title: Non-Citizen Pleads Guilty to Illegally Voting

BOWLING GREEN, KY – A Taylor County, Kentucky man was sentenced to 15 years in prison for methamphetamine trafficking and firearm offenses.

U.S. Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, Special Agent in Charge John Nokes of the ATF Louisville Field Division, and Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. of the Kentucky State Police, made the announcement.

Brad L. Smith, 63, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, for trafficking in over 2 kilograms of methamphetamine and possessing a handgun as a convicted felon. Smith was prohibited from possessing a firearm because he had previously been convicted of the following felony offenses.

On May 19, 2020, in Taylor Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance, second offense, involving less than 2 grams of methamphetamine. On September 5, 2009, in Perry Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance.

On September 8, 2009, in Perry Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance (two counts), and second-degree trafficking in a controlled substance.

In total, Smith had previously been convicted of 11 prior felony offenses and was considered an “armed career criminal” by statute.

United States Attorney Kyle Bumgarner stated, “Brad Smith’s career as a drug trafficker is over. He will be in prison until his 80’s. Smith wasted his life committing felony offenses and harming his community as a drug dealer. I sincerely hope that others see Smith’s sentence 15-year sentence and decide to stop their destructive behavior.”

ATF Special Agent in Charge John Nokes stated, “This sentence underscores the serious threat posed by repeat drug traffickers who combine the distribution of dangerous narcotics with illegal firearm possession. ATF will continue working alongside our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners to hold violent offenders accountable, disrupt drug trafficking operations, and protect our communities.”

“Through strong partnerships and shared resources, the commonwealth was able to bring this individual to justice,” KSP Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. said. “These partnerships send a clear message that those who bring illegal drugs into our communities will be held accountable.”

There is no parole in the federal system.

This case was investigated by the ATF Bowling Green Field Office and the Kentucky State Police.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark J. Yurchisin II of the U.S. Attorney’s Bowling Green Branch Office prosecuted the case.

Interior_Press@ios.doi.gov

WASHINGTON – The Department of the Interior is proposing updates to decades-old land use planning regulations to cut unnecessary red tape, improve coordination with state and local governments, and speed up decision-making for public lands across the country. The proposed changes are intended to make the Bureau of Land Management’s planning process more efficient, easier to understand and better aligned with current law and agency priorities.

"Public lands are set aside for the benefit and use of the American people," said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum . "They should be managed by the people closest to the land, not held back by outdated bureaucracy in D.C. By empowering state and local leaders and cutting decades-old red tape, we’re making it easier to conserve our natural resources, boost production and create a more affordable and abundant supply of food and energy for American families."

The BLM first adopted its land use planning regulations in 1979. The rules have only been updated twice since then, largely to clarify the role of cooperating agencies and remove outdated provisions. The proposed revisions would modernize the regulations to better align with the Federal Land Policy and Management Act . These changes would update planning terminology, eliminate duplicate requirements and simplify parts of the planning process that have become unnecessarily burdensome over time.

“The current planning process is too slow, too complicated and weighed down by outdated requirements,” said BLM Director Steve Pearce. “These proposed changes would help the BLM make decisions more efficiently, reduce costs for taxpayers and improve coordination with the people and communities that rely on public lands.”

Additionally, the proposal would also give the BLM more flexibility when designating Areas of Critical Environmental Concern , which are public lands that require special management to protect important values and resources from irreparable damage. Specifically, the regulations would right-size Areas of Critical Environmental Concern designations so the BLM can focus on protect these important and valuable resources, rather than on oversized buffer zones when those lands are supposed to be managed for multiple use. In addition, the revisions would remove program-specific procedures that are more appropriately addressed elsewhere in agency regulations and ensure public input occurs at the most meaningful stages of the planning process.

The proposed rule will publish in the Federal Register next week and includes a 60-day public comment period. Written comments may be submitted through regulations.gov by searching “RIN 1004-AF53” and following the instructions. Comments may also be mailed to: Bureau of Land Management, Director (630), Attn: RIN 1004-AF53, 1849 C St. NW, Room 5646, Washington, DC 20240.

The BLM will host a virtual public information session, providing the public with an opportunity to learn more about the proposed regulations. The session is planned for Dec. 3, beginning at 5 p.m. MT, using Microsoft Teams video conferencing. Registration is required at Webinar: Revision of Regulations for Planning, Programming, Budgeting . Registrants will receive information on how to participate. The session will be recorded and posted to BLM.gov for those unable to attend. Please contact BLM_HQ_PlanningRule@blm.gov or call 208-373-3818, if you need reasonable accommodations to participate.

text:
Justice Department Awards East Baton Rouge Parish More Than $63.5M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
Yesterday, the Justice Department awarded East Baton Rouge Parish $63,532,285 million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.
“The Model Cities Initiative reflects the Trump Administration’s commitment to reducing crime across the country and ensuring the safety of every American,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “These cities are setting an example of proactive law enforcement that will strengthen the rule of law and improve public safety in their jurisdictions. As violent crime rates continue to fall to historic lows, the Department of Justice is redoubling our efforts to invest in local communities and keep American families safe.”
East Baton Rouge Parish was selected from nearly 50 cities for its strong interagency partnerships and comprehensive public safety strategy, which brings together law enforcement, local government, and community organizations to combat violent crime. The city also stood out for its ambitious plans to expand crime‑fighting, investigative, and prosecution capacity; modernize crime data, intelligence, and analytics; and enhance law enforcement readiness and frontline support.
The city’s persistent and worsening violent crime problem demanded sustained investment of law enforcement. Over the past two decades, the homicide rate in Baton Rouge has averaged roughly three times that of large U.S. cities. From 2021 through 2025, police responded to over 1,300 non-fatal shootings, over 12,000 shots-fired calls, and over 1,200-armed robberies.
“When I was elected as Governor, I promised to put an end to the crime plaguing cities like Baton Rouge. With the help of the Trump Administration, AG Blanche, and our incredible law enforcement officials, we are making good on that promise,” said Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry. “Today’s announcement will help us take more criminals off our streets and put them where they belong: behind bars. Louisiana is committed to public safety — for our children, for our families, and for those who wear the badge.”
“Anytime a city receives tens of millions to make it a safer, better place to be, that is fantastic news. I look forward to this money helping Baton Rouge but also serving as a model to other communities as well,” said Louisiana Senator Dr. Bill Cassidy. “Compliments to the mayor, the district attorney, and others for entering a winning application. I am proud to have supported their effort.”
“President Trump and the Department of Justice have proven their commitment to Louisiana and the people of this country,” said Attorney General Liz Murrill of Louisiana. “Together, Louisiana and our federal partners are fighting back against violent crime and ensuring that our men and women in blue have the support and resources they need to be successful.”
“From day one, we have made public safety our top priority. This grant is one of the most historic and significant public safety investments in Baton Rouge’s history,” said East Baton Rouge Mayor-President Sid Edwards. “We plan to turn this three-year grant into a 30-year return on investment that transforms Baton Rouge for decades to come.”
Image of Attorney General Todd Blanche Image of Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. Image of $63.5M check to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
The MCI takes a whole-of-city approach to public safety, bringing together law enforcement agencies, local government officials, and community partners to develop comprehensive strategies that address the unique public safety challenges facing their communities. The applications submitted by the four selected jurisdictions exemplified the innovative, forward-thinking approaches the Department sought through the initiative.
While each jurisdiction faces unique public safety challenges and brings different priorities, resources, and starting points to the initiative, the Department is confident in the strength of their proposals and their commitment to achieving meaningful results. Despite differing approaches, all four jurisdictions demonstrated a shared determination to reduce violent crime and make their communities safer.
Through the initiative, the Justice Department will work with each jurisdiction to finalize and implement its public safety plan. Funding will support a range of priorities, including hiring sworn and non-sworn law enforcement officers and other personnel to support enforcement, prosecution, and related public safety activities; adopting new and improved technology; purchasing or leasing equipment; enhancing forensic capabilities and capacity; and providing services to address mental health and substance use issues and reduce recidivism.
The Justice Department announced the Model Cities Initiative in June 2026 to build on early successes in jurisdictions such as Memphis, Tennessee, and Washington, D.C., in reducing violence, crime, and disorder. The initiative directs nearly $300 million in federal resources toward comprehensive public safety strategies that strengthen law enforcement, improve coordination among public safety partners, and address the factors contributing to crime and recidivism.
Through these investments, the Justice Department will work alongside local partners to implement sustainable public safety solutions and deliver measurable results. The four Model Cities will help advance the Administration’s efforts to reject the status quo of allowing crime and disorder to go unchecked and restore law, order, and safety to communities across the nation.
Jacksonville, Florida; Jackson, Mississippi; and St. Louis, Missouri, have additionally been selected to receive federal investments supporting innovative, comprehensive, locally driven strategies to combat crime and enhance coordination among federal, state, and local law enforcement partners.
The specific departments funded are:
- Baton Rouge - East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana;
- Jackson - City of Jackson, Mississippi;
- Jacksonville - City of Jacksonville Sheriff’s Office; and
- St. Louis - City of St. Louis Police Department.

LOS ANGELES – A former Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD) deputy was sentenced today to 67 months in federal prison for possessing more than one pound of heroin – hidden inside Pringles potato chips cans – that he admitted to attempting to smuggle inside a county jail in the Santa Clarita Valley.

Michael Meiser, 40, of Lancaster, was sentenced by United States District Judge Fernando M. Olguin.

Meiser pleaded guilty in July 2025 to one count of possession with intent to distribute heroin.

According to his plea agreement, in April 2024, Meiser was working as an LASD deputy at the North County Correctional Facility in Castaic. He had agreed with inmates to smuggle narcotics into the jail in exchange for cash and payments via the Cash App digital wallet that inmates would arrange for Meiser and one of his relatives to receive.

As part of that arrangement, on April 24, 2024, one of Meiser’s relatives received $1,500 via Cash App from an individual connected to an inmate and later informed Meiser about it.

Six days later, Meiser drove his BMW to a Chevron gasoline station in Valencia, parked it next to a Chevrolet SUV, exited his car and opened its trunk. Inside the Chevrolet were two women, one of whom was associated with a jail inmate.

Meiser walked to the Chevrolet’s driver’s side, where one of the two women handed him a plastic grocery bag containing two Pringles cans loaded with approximately 511 grams (1.1 pounds) of heroin. The bag also contained two white envelopes that contained a total of $15,000 in cash, which represented Meiser’s payment from the inmates for smuggling heroin into the jail.

Later that day, Meiser took the grocery bag and put it into his green backpack, which also contained his loaded handgun, before driving to a fellow LASD deputy’s apartment complex. Once there, Meiser – with his green backpack in tow – got into that deputy’s truck and headed to the jail in Castaic. The other deputy drove his truck into the jail with Meiser in the passenger seat and parked the vehicle in the jail’s parking lot, which was past the jail’s initial security checkpoint.

Meiser then exited the deputy’s truck and took the green backpack – containing the heroin and the cash – and placed it inside the trunk of an LASD radio car. Eventually, Meiser placed the two heroin-containing Pringles cans, which were hidden in a grocery bag, under computer towers inside the radio car’s trunk.

By that time, he had removed the $15,000 in cash from the grocery bag and placed it in his green backpack. Meiser then closed the trunk, carried the green backpack to the other deputy’s truck, placed it inside that vehicle, and went to the jail’s gym with the other deputy. Later that day, Meiser met with an inmate participating in the smuggling scheme and spoke to him for several minutes.

At the end of that day, Meiser got in the passenger seat of the other deputy’s truck. LASD investigators stopped them as the other deputy began driving the truck outside the jail.

LASD investigators arrested Meiser and searched the other deputy’s truck, where they found the green backpack containing $15,000 in cash, Meiser’s loaded handgun, and his badge and LASD identification.

Investigators also searched the radio car’s trunk and found the two heroin-containing Pringles cans.

The FBI investigated this matter with assistance from LASD’s Internal Criminal Investigations Bureau.

Assistant United States Attorney Kathy Yu prosecuted this case.
title: Former LASD Deputy Sentenced to More Than 5½ Years in Prison for Possessing Pringles Cans of Heroin Intended for Smuggling into Jail

text:
ANNISTON, Ala. – A multi-convicted felon has been sentenced for his role in a drug trafficking conspiracy involving hundreds of grams of methamphetamine, announced U.S. Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr.

U.S. District Court Judge Corey L. Maze sentenced Logan Chase Turner, 28, to 15 years in prison. In June, Turner pleaded guilty to conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and felon in possession of a firearm.

“This defendant’s criminal history did not deter him from continuing to engage in serious criminal activity,” said U.S. Attorney Williams. “This 15-year sentence holds him accountable and reinforces our commitment to working with our law enforcement partners to target repeat offenders and dismantle drug-trafficking operations.”

“ATF prioritizes public safety and is committed to bringing individuals who unlawfully possess firearms to justice,” said ATF Special Agent in Charge James VanVliet. “Mr. Turner, a three-time convicted felon, demonstrated a pattern of criminal behavior by distributing dangerous drugs, illegally possessing a firearm in the furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, and ultimately rendering our community vulnerable to harm. ATF will continue to work with our state and local law enforcement partners to disrupt offenders like these.”

According to the plea agreement, agents with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) had been investigating Turner and his drug trafficking operations since December 2025. In January 2026, the 7 th Judicial Major Crimes Unit obtained a search for Turner’s residence. During the search of the residence, officers seized drug paraphernalia, a Llama 1911 .45 caliber handgun, and more than 300 grams of methamphetamine.

Turner is prohibited from possessing a firearm because of his three prior felony convictions in 2023 and 2024, in the Circuit Court of Calhoun County. In March 2023, Turner was convicted of Trafficking Fentanyl and Attempted Assault; and in July 2024, he was convicted of Promoting Prison Contraband.

In April, he was charged as part of a Homeland Security Task Force investigation targeting a drug-trafficking organization in east Alabama.

This operation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. The Alabama HSTF is comprised of agents and officers from the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF), the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the United States Marshals Service (USMS), and the Internal Revenue Service, with prosecutions being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama.

ATF investigated the case, along with the 7th Judicial Major Crimes Unit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Allison J. Garnett prosecuted the case.
title: - Multi-Convicted Felon Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison for Methamphetamine Trafficking Conspiracy and Firearms Offenses

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. – A Springfield, Mo., man was sentenced to 12 months and one day imprisonment and three years’ supervised release, for his conviction of tax evasion.

Burton Cummings, 43, was sentenced before U.S. District Judge Douglas Harpool, for one count of tax evasion.

Cummings, a business owner, intentionally evaded paying his federal and state income taxes. Between 2013 and 2024, except for tax years 2015 and 2016, Cummings failed and willfully evaded his financial responsibility to pay his yearly income taxes to both the United States and the State of Missouri. Cummings was ordered to pay $326,290.56 to the United States Government, and an additional $50,171.00 to the State of Missouri, for a total restitution amount of $376,411.56.

This case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Patrick Carney. It was investigated by the Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation and the Missouri Department of Revenue.

Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Spokesman Office of the Spokesman

November 5, 2026

Today, the Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, in coordination with the FBI, DEA, and Department of Justice, is announcing new and increased reward offers totaling up to $50 million under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program (TOCRP) for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions of the top three leaders of Tren de Aragua (TdA), a violent Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) designated by the Trump Administration last year.

Yohan José Romero , a.k.a. “Yohan Petrica”: reward offer increase from up to $4 million to up to $20 million;

Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano , a.k.a. “Giovanni” and “El Viejo”: reward offer increase from up to $5 million to up to $15 million; and

Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez , a.k.a. “Juancho”: new reward offer of up to $15 million.

According to court documents, Romero is the current leader of TdA and directs the group’s operations, including narcotrafficking, illegal gold mining in Venezuela, and murders. PORTLAND, Maine: An Indian national was sentenced yesterday in U.S. District Court in Portland for conspiring to commit wire fraud.

Chief U.S. District Judge Lance E. Walker sentenced Prakashkumar Prajapati, 47, to nine years in prison and ordered him to pay $1,897,386 in restitution. Prajapati pleaded guilty on January 15, 2026.

According to court records Prajapati conspired with others in a multi-state scheme to defraud at least eight victims in five states, including Maine. As part of the scheme, victims received telephone calls from individuals posing as government officials. These imposters instructed victims to withdraw cash and purchase gold to turn over to the government for safekeeping. The callers then arranged for victims to meet fake government agents to hand over the cash and gold. As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati directed his co-defendant Bharat Awasarmol to collect gold and cash from victims. Awasarmol was intercepted when FBI agents caught him accepting a package from a victim in Maine. The Maine victim had been instructed by an individual posing as an employee of the Federal Trade Commission to meet Awasarmol and provide him with gold bars.

As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati and his coconspirators collected cash and gold from seven additional victims in New Hampshire, New York, New Jersey, and Virginia, all of whom had been deceived by individuals posing as government officials. As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati caused $1,897,386 in losses to the victims.

Awasarmol pleaded guilty on December 9, 2025, and faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 on the wire fraud conspiracy charge and up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 on a false statement charge. Awasarmol is scheduled to be sentenced in January 2027.

The FBI investigated the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice is committed to aggressively combating elder abuse, neglect, financial exploitation and fraud. Between July of 2025 and July of 2026, the Department pursued nearly 350 criminal and civil enforcement actions against 712 defendants either charged with stealing, or alleged to have stolen, over $4.8 billion from over 700,000 victims. The Department also returned millions of dollars to older victims and helped to prevent tens of millions of dollars in losses from older Americans. But enforcement alone is not enough. Preventing fraud and abuse in the first place is always the best outcome. For more information on elder fraud and abuse, visit the Department of Justice’s Elder Justice Initiative website at justice.gov/elderjustice. If you or someone you know has been the victim of elder fraud, please call the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 833-FRAUD-11.

RESEARCH TRIANGLE PARK, N.C. – The Army Research Office released “ARO Year in Review Fiscal Year 2025,” commemorating 75 years of creating, directing and protecting scientific discovery for the Army and highlighting fiscal 2025 extramural research achievements.
Founded in 1951 and based in Research Triangle Park, North Carolina, ARO is the Army's extramural basic research arm operating under U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command. For 75 years, ARO’s team of scientists, engineers and staff has shaped scientific discovery by bringing together the Army, universities, industry and research organizations to pursue high-risk, high-payoff research that can enable future Army capabilities.
“ARO Year in Review Fiscal Year 2025” highlights ARO’s continued focus on scientific breakthroughs that keep the Army at the forefront of technological innovation.
“As ARO celebrates 75 years of discovery, the scientific big bets in our FY25 portfolio prove we are actively setting the tempo for the future of warfare,” said Dr. Purush Iyer, ARO acting director. “Our purpose remains absolute: deliver transformational science to the American Soldier and ensure the U.S. Army remains the most advanced fighting force in the world.”
During fiscal 2025, ARO awarded 309 new funding agreements across its extramural research portfolio. The annual reportprovides an overview of ARO’s investment strategy and program funding and features 45 success stories spanning biotechnology, energy, autonomy, quantum science, advanced materials and electromagnetic sciences. Each success story describes the basic research challenge, key breakthroughs and potential Army applications.
ARO serves as the Army’s front door to universities, building relationships with more than 7,000 researchers at approximately 300 institutions of higher learning. Through these partnerships, ARO program managers guide long-range scientific investments, connect emerging research opportunities to Army priorities and help create pathways for discoveries to transition into future capabilities.
In addition to advancing science, ARO is investing in the people who will sustain the Army’s future technological edge. During fiscal 2025, ARO engaged nearly 3,500 high school, undergraduate and graduate students through education, outreach and research programs designed to help build the future science and engineering workforce and strengthen the U.S. industrial base.
Together, these investments reflect ARO’s long-term approach to anticipating future operational challenges through foundational research, strategic partnerships and talent development.
“To survive and dominate in this contested environment, we must push technological boundaries across the entire scientific spectrum,” Iyer said. “As ARO marks its 75th anniversary, we continue our approach of proactively seeking disruptive scientific breakthroughs and innovation, placing calculated, high-impact scientific big bets for the future Army.”
###
About DEVCOM Army Research Office
Leveraging its 75-year history, the DEVCOM Army Research Office is the Army’s principal office for university research and partnerships, shaping scientific discovery worldwide for the Army of the future. As part of the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, known as DEVCOM, ARO designs and directs bold science, builds partnerships, and cultivates talent to initiate the future operational superiority of our Soldiers, Army and nation.
For more information, visit the DEVCOM Army Research Office webpage on the DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory website at, arl.army.mil/who-we-are/aro/.
title: ARO Year in Review 2025 honors 75 years of shaping scientific discovery

ALBUQUERQUE – A Pinehill man pleaded guilty to federal charges for sexually abusing two minors over a seven-year period.

According to court documents, between February 2017 and April 2022, TJ James , 42, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, sexually abused Jane Doe 1, a minor, and placed her in fear. Additionally, between October 2019, and January 2023, James sexually abused another victim, Jane Doe 2, a minor, and also placed her in fear.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

Pelosi Statement on the Sentencing of Joshua Wong
San Francisco — Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi issued this statement on the Hong Kong court’s decision to sentence pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison.
“A Hong Kong court’s decision to sentence Joshua Wong to a new 10-year prison term under Beijing’s so-called national security law is an appalling abuse of power. After nearly six years behind bars, Joshua was just two months from going home. Now he faces imprisonment until 2036.
“Joshua has stood with the people of Hong Kong in their struggle for freedom since he was a teenager. While the judge said the sentence was meant to deter others, it’s clear the example Joshua has set will outlast any prison sentence.
“The United States and the international community must demand Joshua’s immediate and unconditional release. Beijing is counting on Joshua and others imprisoned for defending Hong Kong’s freedoms to believe no one cares enough to speak out for them. We will never forget Joshua Wong, Jimmy Lai or their fellow political prisoners, and we will keep speaking out until they are free.”
title: Pelosi Statement on the Sentencing of Joshua Wong

Memphis, TN – U.S. Attorney D. Michael Dunavant and 25th Judicial District Attorney General Mark E. Davidson announced today a joint federal, state, and local law enforcement investigation, “Operation Tiger Punch” which resulted in the federal indictments of 10 defendants and state indictments of 6 defendants from Lauderdale and Shelby counties.

As alleged in the federal indictment, between February 2024 and April 2026, law enforcement engaged in operations identifying and targeting methamphetamine trafficking in rural West Tennessee. This resulted in a federal indictment of 10 defendants and state indictments of 6 defendants, as well as the seizure of several thousand suspected alprazolam pills sent through the U.S. Mail, approximately 2 pounds of suspected methamphetamine from the Ripley Terrace Apartments in April 2026, a total of 6 firearms, and $23,345 in U.S. Currency.

Specifically, the indictment alleges the following individuals conspired to possess with intent to distribute controlled substances, including methamphetamine and alprazolam:

TONY ARNEZ SINGLETON-COOK , aka “Tony Cook” aka “Woadee” 26, of Ripley

ALFRED HILL , 39, of Memphis, Tennessee

DEZMON WHITELOW , 23, of Ripley, Tennessee

BOBBY LESTER BROWN , aka “Big Bob", 64, of Covington, Tennessee

TRISTAN BUCKNER , aka “T Baby”, 28, of Ripley, Tennessee

RICHARD LEE DALE , 49, of Gates, Tennessee

TYREECE MACKEY , aka “Big TY”, 51, of Ripley, Tennessee

ROBERT STEVEN MIMS , aka “Steven”, 49, of Lauderdale County, Tennessee

ROSE WILSON , aka “Momma Rose”, 62, of Ripley, Tennessee

SHELIA JEAN COKER , 57, of Ripley, Tennessee

The federal indictment alleges that defendant Tony Arnez Singleton-Cook obtained and distributed methamphetamine to others. During this timeframe, Mr. Cook was on state probation for felony narcotics convictions.

The state indictments returned by the Lauderdale County Grand Jury charged the following individuals with possession of methamphetamine with the intent to deliver or sell, in violation of T.C.A. § 39-17-434:

ASHLEY VANCE

ROBERT BREWER

GEORGE HOFFMAN

JOY AMMONS

CHARLIE JONES, SR.

CRYSTAL PICKARD

U.S. Attorney D. Michael Dunavant said, "We are pleased to join with our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners to focus on the priority areas of narcotics distribution cases that impact public safety in our rural communities, and we are glad to support this successful joint operation by adopting these cases for aggressive federal prosecution. We are tired of drug traffickers that endanger Lauderdale County and West Tennessee, and we will continue our laser focus on punishing and deterring those who distribute poison for profit."

District Attorney General Mark E. Davidson stated, “The seizure of several pounds of methamphetamine, several thousand suspected alprazolam pills, six firearms, and more than $20,000 in cash underscores the scope of this investigation and its importance to our communities. Operation Tiger Punch reflects the persistence of our law enforcement and the strength of our local, state, and federal partnerships. Our office is committed to pursuing these cases and protecting families throughout the 25th Judicial District.”

Lauderdale County Sheriff Brian Kelley said, “Operation Tiger Punch sends a clear and unmistakable message: Those who bring dangerous drugs into our communities will face a united and determined law enforcement response. I want to personally thank our federal and state law enforcement partners for their dedication, relentless efforts, and commitment to this operation. These results represent a significant victory for public safety, with a direct and lasting impact on Lauderdale County and the communities we serve. The Lauderdale County Sheriff’s Office is proud to stand shoulder to shoulder with our law enforcement partners. Our commitment to protecting our citizens and aggressively pursuing those who threaten their safety is unwavering. Our mission is clear, our resolve is stronger than ever, and we will not relent!”

Officials from the following participating agencies announced the results of Operation "Tiger Punch" at a joint press conference on November 5, 2026, in Ripley, Tennessee:

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Tennessee, the District Attorney General’s Office for the 25th Judicial District, 25 th Judicial District Drug Task Force, Lauderdale County Sheriff’s Office, West Tennessee Drug Task Force, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI), Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Jackson Police Department, United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), United States Marshals Service (USMS), Shelby County Sheriff’s Office (SCSO), and the Memphis Police Department (MPD).

Assistant United States Attorneys Gregory D. Allen and Raven Icaza are prosecuting the federal case on behalf of the United States.

Assistant District Attorney General Julie K. Pillow and Harrison Hight are prosecuting the state cases on behalf of the State of Tennessee.

The charges and allegations contained in the indictments are merely accusations, and the defendants are considered innocent unless and until proven guilty.
