First Lady Melania Trump Unites Russia and Ukraine at The White House Following Historic Ceasefire
First Lady Melania Trump gathered leaders from Russia and Ukraine at the White House today. The occasion is believed to mark the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations actively at war together to the White House for diplomacy.
The unprecedented gathering united key officials from both nations who played instrumental roles in establishing the ceasefire in Oleshky.
“Now, we must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people. Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire. Let us see Oleshky as a spark in a world of darkness, capable of illuminating the best in humanity. Build a powerful flame of peace, visible to the world. Ignite hope, foster cooperation, and brighten a path toward lasting peace,” said First Lady Melania Trump.
Mrs. Trump detailed her role as Exclusive Intermediary in securing the ceasefire, facilitating the delivery of humanitarian aid to the region, and organizing the safe evacuation of nearly 800 people.
“My role as Exclusive Intermediary was memorialized in written agreements drafted and signed by both Russia and Ukraine,” the First Lady shared. “I was involved in every stage of the planning. I reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources. I was made aware of the preferred dates and timing of the operation.”
First Lady Melania Trump acknowledged, “The ceasefire in Oleshky would not be possible without President Putin and President Zelensky. Their cooperation establishes a meaningful precedent for advancing peace throughout the region.”
Ukrainian representatives presented First Lady Melania Trump with President Zelensky’s award, Ukraine’s Order of Princess Olga, First Class, the highest degree of this prestigious state honor. The award recognizes Mrs. Trump’s leadership in securing the ceasefire in Oleshky, which enabled the evacuation of 800 individuals.
Mrs. Trump concluded her historic speech by presenting the highest-ranking leaders in attendance with letters she had written to President Putin and President Zelensky.
Following her remarks, Mrs. Trump invited the distinguished guests to view two historic artifacts from the White House collection, which she personally selected as powerful symbols of peace.
The first, a late 18th-century medicine chest, was removed from the White House after British forces set the building on fire during the War of 1812. Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance
The First Lady also presented an 1899 Presentation Cup, gifted to French Ambassador M. Jules Cambon in recognition of France’s diplomatic efforts to negotiate peace and bring the Spanish-American War to an end.
Mrs. Trump’s remarks, as prepared for delivery, are below.
Oleshky, a Spark in a World of Darkness that Can Illuminate the Best in Humanity
Oleshky will forever unite the brave individuals gathered at the White House today.
We have chosen humanity over war.
Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the divisions of war.
I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark.
What matters is not the modesty of this beginning, but the determination to turn it into something extraordinary.
Now, we must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people. Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire.
Let us see Oleshky as a spark in a world of darkness, capable of illuminating the best in humanity. Build a powerful flame of peace, visible to the world. Ignite hope, foster cooperation, and brighten a path toward lasting peace.
I became aware of the severity of the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky in September. Recognizing the urgency, I acted immediately and directed my representative, Marc Beckman, to engage with Russia and Ukraine on my behalf, to pursue peace in Oleshky.
Both nations welcomed my participation, acknowledging that previous efforts to establish a ceasefire in the region had not succeeded.
Russia and Ukraine honored our relationship and agreed to work with me in the capacity of Exclusive Intermediary to establish a ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region.
Our shared objective was to deliver critical humanitarian aid to Oleshky residents and establish a safe evacuation route for civilians.
My role as Exclusive Intermediary was memorialized in written agreements drafted and signed by both Russia and Ukraine.
Marc and I began our work using the communication channels we had previously established to reunite children with their families in Russia and Ukraine. Humanitarian, military, and government officials from Russia and Ukraine worked diligently to coordinate every aspect of the operation.
I was involved in every stage of the planning. I reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources. I was made aware of the preferred dates and timing of the operation.
My communication with Russia and Ukraine was extensive, professional, detailed, and highly cooperative. Marc and I did everything possible to support both nations in advancing their shared commitment to reach a ceasefire in Oleshky.
We fulfilled our responsibilities at every stage, collaborating with Russian and Ukrainian teams through completion. Russia and Ukraine signed the agreements in both languages on Friday, October 23rd, 2026.
I commend both sides for your good-faith efforts to define and implement all components of this sophisticated ceasefire.
I would like to welcome Mr. Kirill Dmitriev, Special Envoy to President Putin of the Russian Federation, to the podium to say a few words. Thank you for your cooperation and professionalism.
My deepest appreciation to Ms. Yana Lantratova, Commissioner for Human Rights in the Russian Federation. Your dedication brings hope and dignity to those devastated by the war.
Freedom exists only when the mind is without fear. It is both an ethical and intellectual condition.
A free world is one where people can live with dignity, truth, and knowledge, without fear. To soar freely beneath the sun, we must have the promise of life without oppression.
For a brief period, Oleshky residents enjoyed relief from the psychological horrors of war. For innocent people living in the shadow of war, freedom is more personal than we can fully understand. It is found in the simplest moments of life.
Last week in Oleshky and neighboring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022. They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions.
Four brave American journalists entered the war-torn region to document the wishes of Oleshky’s residents. Working in the true spirit of journalism, Newsmax provided transparency, accountability, and protection to safeguard the truth. Thanks to these journalists, who are with us here today.
The leaders of Russia and Ukraine worked to establish calm. Food, clean water, and medicine entered the area, and nearly 800 people left their homes in search of safety, loved ones, and a renewed sense of being.
Mr. David Arakhamina, faction leader of the Servant of the People party of Ukraine, is also with us today. Please join me and share a few words.
Thank you President Zelensky and the nation of Ukraine for this highest honor – the Order of Princess Olga, First Class.
My tremendous gratitude to Mr. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, for the incredible bravery and heart you show in serving your people every day.
Imagine a young child confined to her home, unable to dream of her future because she lives in constant fear. We were not born to spend our lives hiding in terror, watching the sky for drones and missiles, or scanning the ground for mines.
What benefit is there when the lives of innocents are lost forever?
We are alive to laugh, create, explore, and love.
Let Oleshky be the modest spark that grows into a lasting flame of peace.
The ceasefire in Oleshky would not be possible without President Putin and President Zelensky. Their cooperation establishes a meaningful precedent for advancing peace throughout the region
As this historic moment concluded, I wrote personal letters to President Putin and to President Zelensky.
David and Kirill, please deliver these letters to your presidents on my behalf. I trust you will ensure their safe delivery.
title: First Lady Melania Trump Unites Russia and Ukraine at The White House Following Historic Ceasefire

text:
Fast Facts
The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's patent application backlog reached 838,000 in January 2025. In September 2025, the agency announced a goal to reduce this backlog to under 599,000.
We found that patent examiner attrition may prevent the agency from meeting this goal within the next 5 years—even if examiners review more applications.
The agency has had a high examiner attrition rate since 2025. According to examiners and others we spoke to, agency efforts like requiring examiners to review more applications and decreasing training could keep attrition high and reduce examination quality.
Our recommendation addresses this issue.
One hand holds a stamp over a document that has been stamped with the word PATENTED in red ink, and another hand holds the document still.
Highlights
What GAO Found
The backlog of unexamined patent applications awaiting an initial decision from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) rose to about 838,000 applications in January 2025. In September 2025, the USPTO announced a goal to reduce the backlog to under 599,000 applications but did not specify a time frame for reaching it. The backlog was last at that level in 2020. To reduce the backlog, the USPTO is requiring patent examiners to review more applications, has decreased examiner training, and has expanded the use of AI patent search tools. As of August 2026, the USPTO reduced the backlog to about 756,000 applications, but average applicant wait times for a final patentability decision had increased by 11 percent since January 2025.
GAO’s analysis found that, even with examiners doing more work, the USPTO is unlikely to reduce the backlog to under 599,000 patent applications before 2031 without lowering examiner attrition (see figure). The examiner attrition rate increased from 2.9 percent in fiscal year 2020 to 7.6 percent in fiscal year 2025. The agency is seeking to hire more examiners, but if high examiner attrition continues, it will affect the USPTO’s ability to reduce the backlog. As of August 2026, the 12-month examiner attrition rate was 7.6 percent.
The USPTO May Not Reach Its Backlog Goal Without Lowering Examiner Attrition
According to the stakeholders GAO interviewed, including the patent examiners’ union and former agency officials, the USPTO’s efforts to reduce the backlog may not be sustainable and could contribute to high attrition. Requiring examiners to review more applications and eliminating time for subject-matter training pose risks to the quality of examination. While the USPTO has expanded the use of AI tools, stakeholders told GAO these tools are not yet effective, because they do not reliably return useful patent search results. In addition, the USPTO paused a survey that provided the agency with stakeholder views on agency responsiveness and overall examination quality. Assessing and addressing risks to retention and examination quality could better position the USPTO to balance its efforts to reduce the backlog.
Why GAO Did This Study
The U.S. patent system encourages innovation by generally allowing a patent owner to exclude others from making, using, or selling patented inventions for up to 20 years. Patent examiners at the USPTO review applications to determine if the inventions meet legal patentability requirements.
The USPTO has long had a patent application backlog, and GAO reported in 2007 that the agency’s examiner hiring efforts were insufficient to address it. In recent years, the increase in the backlog has resulted in applicants waiting more than 20 months for an initial USPTO decision.
GAO was asked to review factors related to the patent application backlog at the USPTO. This report examines (1) the USPTO’s current goals and efforts to reduce the backlog and (2) what available data predict about the agency’s ability to achieve those goals, stakeholder views on these efforts, and the extent to which the USPTO assessed related risks.
GAO analyzed USPTO fiscal year 2020–2025 patent application and examiner data to estimate the future size of the backlog. GAO also analyzed federal workforce data on recent patent examiner attrition at the USPTO. GAO interviewed the patent examiners’ union, former USPTO officials, patent attorneys, trade associations, and researchers. GAO also sought information from the agency. The USPTO did not provide GAO with requested information.
Recommendations
GAO recommends that the USPTO assess and address the risks that the agency’s backlog reduction efforts pose to patent examiner retention and examination quality. The USPTO did not provide comments.
title: U.S. Patent and Trademark Office: Patent Backlog Reduction Efforts Pose Risks to Examiner Retention and Examination Quality

text:
Lone Star in the Capital: Doggett, Daughters of the Republic of Texas Unveil Base of Republic of Texas Legation Memorial
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Representative Lloyd Doggett (D-TX), Assistant Secretary of the Interior for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Kevin Lilly, a fellow Texan, and the Elisabet Ney Chapter of the Daughters of the Republic of Texas unveiled the Lone Star base of the Republic of Texas Legation Memorial at 630 Indiana Avenue NW, adjacent to its intersection with Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. The memorial was approved by Congress in legislation authored by Doggett, the Republic of Texas Legation Memorial Act. It memorializes the Texans who worked for almost a decade to negotiate the admission of Texas into the United States as the 28th state.
Congressman Lloyd Doggett (fourth from right) with Assistant Secretary of the Interior Kevin Lilly, Priscilla Roberts, Kitty Hoeck, Grace Boatright, members of the Elisabet Ney Chapter of the Daughters of the Republic of Texas and National Park Service staff at the ceremony marking the start of construction of the Republic of Texas Legation Memorial on Indiana Avenue NW, November 5, 2026.
The Lone Star base, a five-pointed star of white Mount Airy granite, sits in an existing granite planter on the 600 block of Indiana Avenue NW, steps from the U.S. Navy Memorial. Today’s unveiling marks the start of construction of the memorial. The site sits among five of the eight places where, according to research by the Daughters of the Republic of Texas, the Legation’s diplomats lived and worked out of boarding houses and hotels, including the site of today’s Navy Memorial, where Texas Minister Memucan Hunt resided in 1837 and 1838.
“As a native Texan with more pride in our State after the recent election than ever before, I am pleased that this new monument recognizes an important part of our Texas heritage," said Congressman Doggett. “For almost a decade, eight different Texans conducted negotiations for the admission of Texas into the United States as the 28th state. This will likely become another point of interest especially for Texas visitors to our capital.”
“When tourists come to our Nation’s capital, they are likely unaware of an important piece of Texas lore that hides in plain sight: the lost landmarks of the Republic of Texas Legation in Washington,” he continued. “Its diplomats were sent on the very long and difficult journey from Texas to Washington, and Americans traveling in Europe can find plaques in both London and Paris that commemorate the Texas Legation. Washington had not followed suit. Most appropriately, this work has been spearheaded by the Daughters of the Republic of Texas, our State’s oldest patriotic women’s organization, and Kitty Hoeck has led the way, proving that one person can make a difference with their tenacity and determination.”
“The history of the Texas Legation did not end with the annexation of Texas in 1845. Today, it lives on through the strength of the multicultural and multilingual communities that make our Lone Star State so dynamic,” shared the Congressman. “With this memorial, all those who visit our Nation’s Capital will have the opportunity to learn about this turning point in our Nation’s history and reflect on the sacrifices made by the brave diplomats who made it possible. Because Texas history is America’s history.”
About the memorial
Modest in scale, the memorial will rise from the Lone Star base unveiled today: a five-sided plinth of white granite topped by the Daughters of the Republic of Texas medallion and engraved with the story of the Texas Legation, a map of the Republic of Texas and the names of the eight diplomats the Republic sent to Washington. Plantings native to Texas and the Mid-Atlantic will surround a single sweetbay magnolia, representing the Lone Star State. The site is federal land under the National Park Service.
Background
From 1836 to 1845, the Republic of Texas kept a diplomatic legation in Washington, working first for U.S. recognition and then for annexation; Texas became the 28th state on December 29, 1845. Doggett introduced the Republic of Texas Legation Memorial Act (H.R. 3349) in June 2019. It passed the House and Senate with bipartisan support and was signed into law on December 22, 2020. The Daughters then won final approval of the site and design from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission in 2025 and raised the full cost privately; the law bars federal funds to build the memorial.
###
title: Lone Star in the Capital: Doggett, Daughters of the Republic of Texas Unveil Base of Republic of Texas Legation Memorial

Rep. Sykes Announces Nearly $5,000 Federal Grant to Preserve Hudson’s 1845 Herbarium
HUDSON, OH — Today, U.S. Representative Emilia Sykes (OH-13) announced that the Hudson Library & Historical Society has been awarded $4,999 in federal Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) Library Services and Technology Act funds by the State Library of Ohio. The funds will be used to conserve an herbarium created in 1845 by Mary Strong, founder of the Hudson Female Seminary.
Strong’s herbarium is a single leather volume containing a wide variety of dried and pressed plant specimens mounted on paper, including leaves, plants, flowers, fungi, and moss. The collection offers insight into Ohio’s natural history and a window into the role female education played in Hudson’s early history.
“Our libraries and historical societies are where our community’s story is kept, and Mary Strong’s herbarium is a remarkable piece of that story,” said Rep. Sykes. “It captures Ohio’s natural history and honors the role of women’s education in Hudson’s early days. I’m proud that federal dollars are helping preserve it, and I commend the Hudson Library & Historical Society for its work to protect this treasure for future generations.”
The grant is one of 10 awarded statewide, totaling $48,627 in federal IMLS Library Services and Technology Act funds. Conservation and Preservation Grants enable libraries to conserve a single item or preserve a small, discrete group of items within their collections. Funds are used primarily to contract a professional conservator or conservation lab to ensure the materials are preserved according to best practices.
title: Rep. Sykes Announces Nearly $5,000 Federal Grant to Preserve Hudson’s 1845 Herbarium

BOWLING GREEN, KY – On November 3, 2026, Robert Scott Froberg, 61, was sentenced to life in prison for the 1996 abduction and murder of 7-year-old Morgan Violi.

United States Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, FBI Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson, Chief Michael Delaney of the Bowling Green Police Department and Commonwealth’s Attorney for the 8th Judicial Circuit Kori Beck Bumgarner, made the announcement.

Morgan Violi was abducted on July 24, 1996, while playing with her sisters and friends at the Colony Apartments in Bowling Green, Kentucky. Witnesses saw a white man grab Morgan, put her in a maroon Chevrolet van and drive away. Two days later, the van suspected to be involved in the abduction was found in Franklin, Tennessee, and searched for evidence. Morgan’s body was found discarded in woods near White House, Tennessee. on October 20, 1996. For years, Morgan’s kidnapping and murder went unsolved despite significant national media attention and ongoing efforts by law enforcement.

Relying on advances in forensic science, the FBI tested evidence found in the abandoned maroon Chevrolet van. A hair found in the abandoned van was tested by the FBI laboratory and returned an association with Robert Scott Froberg, who was serving a lengthy sentence in the Alabama Department of Corrections.

Acting on this forensic lead, law enforcement began investigating whether Froberg may have committed the kidnapping and murder. Investigators determined that Froberg had escaped from the Alabama Department of Corrections during the timeframe Morgan was abducted and murdered.

Law enforcement learned that after escaping from the Alabama Department of Corrections, Froberg traveled to Mount Carmel, Pennsylvania. While in Mount Carmel, Froberg attempted to abduct a seven-year-old little boy. Froberg was arrested and taken to the Northumberland County Jail. Subsequently, Froberg escaped from the Northumberland County Jail. He traveled to Dayton, Ohio, where he stole a maroon Chevrolet van approximately half a mile from his parent’s house. Froberg traveled south, exiting I-65 in Bowling Green, Kentucky, where he spotted Morgan playing in her apartment complex, snatched her and drove south.

Froberg admitted to investigators that he drove Morgan to White House, Tennessee and parked near a barn. Morgan was screaming and crying. Froberg acknowledged strangling Morgan to death and throwing her in a ditch. He fled to Franklin, Tennessee where he left the stolen van on his way to Huntsville, Alabama. Eventually, Froberg made his way back to Pennsylvania where he was arrested and returned to the Alabama Department of Corrections. For decades, Froberg’s horrific crime remained unsolved. Froberg was scheduled to be released from custody by the Alabama Department of Corrections in the near future but will now spend the rest of his life in federal prison.

On November 3, 2026, United States District Court Judge Greg Stivers accepted the plea agreement and sentenced Froberg to life. A life sentence in federal court means that Froberg will never be released from prison as there is no parole in the federal system.

United States Attorney Kyle Bumgarner and First Assistant United States Attorney Brian Butler stated, “Morgan Violi’s kidnapping and murder forever changed the lives of her family and, indeed, the entire Bowling Green community. The terror of an unknown stranger lurking to steal and murder an innocent child hung over Bowling Green for three decades. Not a day has gone by that her family did not grieve Morgan and work for answers. Morgan’s family and law enforcement’s tenacity finally led to answers, the culprit’s arrest, and ultimately, to his life sentence. Fortunately, the man that committed this monstrous crime will never see a day outside of the custody of the Bureau of Prisons.”

Special Agent in Charge Olivia Olson of the FBI Louisville Field Office stated, “While Mr. Froberg’s life sentence will never fill the void left in the hearts of Morgan Violi’s loved ones, the FBI hopes it closes a dark chapter for her family and for the Bowling Green community. Even though thirty years has passed since the abduction and murder of Morgan, this FBI, alongside our law enforcement partners, never stopped tracking down every lead and exhausting all available resources. Through diligent, persistent investigative work, Mr. Froberg has finally received the punishment he deserves.”

This case was investigated by the FBI, the Bowling Green Police Department and the Robertson County, Tennessee Sheriff’s Office.

United States Attorney Kyle Bumgarner and First Assistant United States Attorney Brian Butler prosecuted the case.

###
title: Robert Scott Froberg Sentenced to Life for Kidnapping and Murdering of 7-Year-Old Morgan Violi

MOAB , Utah – An Aneth man, with a criminal history of possessing child pornography, was sentenced to 16 years’ imprisonment. In April 2026, Johnston Blackhorse, 43, of Aneth, Utah, was convicted by a jury after he received and possessed child pornography, also known as child sex abuse material (CSAM). At the time of the offense, Blackhorse was already on supervised release for a 2015 conviction of possession of child pornography.

In addition to his term of imprisonment, U.S. District Court Judge Ann Marie McIff Allen sentenced Blackhorse to a lifetime of supervised release.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, in February 2025, while serving a lifetime of supervised release for prior child sex crimes, two probation officers conducted a home visit where Blackhorse lived alone. Pursuant to Blackhorse’s supervised release conditions, the officers conducted an examination of Blackhorse’s computer. Officers discovered that a forensic wiping program had been installed and used on the computer the day of the probation visit. Officers conducted a more thorough examination of the computer and located several files depicting child sexual abuse material in a deleted space. As a result, a search warrant was secured, and the computer was examined by a forensic examiner with Homeland Security Investigations. The examination revealed six images of CSAM all in a deleted space on the computer. An original file path also showed the file originally existed under Blackhorse’s username, in his Mozilla Firefox folders, and came from child pornography websites. Additional evidence also showed Blackhorse used the computer to access other child pornography files located on a separate electronic storage device that was not recovered during the search of his residence.

“My office is committed to protecting our communities, particularly our most vulnerable,” said U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak of the District of Utah. “Blackhorse’s pattern of criminal behavior makes clear that he remains a dangerous offender with a significant likelihood of recidivism. This result reflects our trial team’s exceptional diligence, skill, and dedication to keeping children safe.”

“My office is committed to protecting our communities, particularly our most vulnerable,” said U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak of the District of Utah. “Blackhorse’s pattern of criminal behavior makes clear that he remains a dangerous offender with a significant likelihood of recidivism. This result reflects our trial team’s exceptional diligence, skill, and dedication to keeping children safe.”

“Let me be absolutely clear: Those who possess child sexual abuse material are not passive observers of a horrific crime. They are fueling an industry built on the exploitation, abuse, and suffering of innocent children,” said Homeland Security Investigations Denver Special Agent in Charge Charles Engle. “Every image represents a child whose innocence was stolen, and every person who seeks out this material perpetuates that victimization.”

The case was investigated by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Investigations.

Assistant United States Attorneys Christopher Burton and Joseph M. Hood of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Utah prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
Thursday, November 5, 2026
Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
Evidence continues to grow on how environmental factors affect women’s health.
Women with higher blood levels of two common per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also familiarly known as PFAS, were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer, according to a new study by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in common consumer products. Often referred to as “forever chemicals,” PFAS do not break down easily in the environment and can remain in the body for years.
The study found that women with higher blood plasma levels of two of these substances, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), were associated with a higher incidence of ER-negative breast cancer. No clear association was observed between the two chemicals and breast cancer risk overall.
“Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.”
ER-negative tumors lack receptors that allow hormone estrogen to help cancer cells grow. Compared with breast cancers that respond to hormone estrogen, ER-negative breast cancers tend to be more aggressive and have worse outcomes. Scientists know less about what raises the risk of this type of breast cancer.
“Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors,” explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study. The findings are reported in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.
NIH researchers and their collaborators measured 17 PFAS in blood, collected years before women were diagnosed with cancer. Women in the group with the highest PFOA levels had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than those in the lowest group. For PFOS, the rate was 93% higher, or nearly twice as high. These numbers describe relative differences between groups, not an individual woman’s chance of getting breast cancer.
The research drew on the Sister Study, led by NIH’s National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). The larger study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35–74 in the United States and Puerto Rico from 2003 to 2009. None had breast cancer when they joined the Sister Study, but each had a full or half-sister who had been previously diagnosed with breast cancer. For the PFAS study, researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women.
“These findings matter for women’s health broadly,” said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., a former research fellow at NIH and a current researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. “Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.”
Because the strongest associations involved tumors without hormone receptors, the authors suggest that PFAS may affect cancer risk through other non-hormonal biologic pathways. Possible pathways include changes in gene activity or immune system. However, this study did not test those explanations. The authors say future studies should evaluate people with higher PFAS exposure and in groups more affected by ER-negative breast cancer.
Although most individuals have measurable levels of PFOA and PFOS in their bodies, these compounds have been largely phased out and replaced with new PFAS compounds. “More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals,” White said.
This research was supported by NIEHS grants: Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.
About the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS): NIEHS conducts and supports research to understand how the environment affects human health. It is part of the National Institutes of Health. For more information, visit www.niehs.nih.gov.
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®
Reference
Chang CJ, Pullella K, Keil AP, et al. Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Exposure and Breast Cancer Incidence in the Sister Study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO-26-00318.
title: Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis

This report provides an overview of federal statutes in their various forms, as well as basic guidance for Members and congressional staff interested in researching statutes. When a bill becomes a law, the newly enacted statute may amend or repeal earlier statutes or it may create a new or "freestanding" law. Either way, these new statutes are first printed individually as "slip laws" and numbered by order of passage as either public laws or, less frequently, private laws. Slip laws are later aggregated and published chronologically in volumes known as the United States Statutes at Large (Statutes at Large). Statutes of a general and permanent nature are incorporated into the United States Code (U.S. Code), which arranges the statutes by subject matter into 54 titles and five appendices.
As these statutes are revised, superseded, or repealed, the provisions of the U.S. Code are updated to reflect these changes. The authoritative language of a statute is the statute itself. A statute may be enacted as a title of the U.S. Code, in which case this statute is a "positive law" title of the U.S. Code and therefore the title itself is legal evidence of the law (the authoritative language). Statutes not enacted as a title of, or an amendment to, a title of the U.S. Code are classified to the U.S. Code as a non-positive provision of the U.S. Code and are prima facie evidence of Federal Law, which is rebuttable by showing a difference to the underlying statute.
A notable difference between the U.S. Code and the Statutes at Large is that the laws codified or classified in the U.S. Code exist "as amended," which reflects changes made by later laws.
Consequently, the U.S. Code is more convenient to search than the Statutes at Large. Moreover, the Office of the Law Revision Counsel publishes tools known as "Tables," to assist researchers in locating statutes, as well as identifying statutes that may have been amended, omitted, transferred, or repealed. Nevertheless, certain laws are not added to the U.S. Code, such as laws appropriating funds, and thus researchers will often need to search laws in the other forms discussed herein.
When a bill is enacted into law, it may amend or repeal earlier laws, or it may create an entirely new or "freestanding" law. Recently enacted laws are first printed individually as separate statutes known as "slip laws." At the end of a Congress, the slip laws are sequentially compiled in the annual federal session law volumes known as the United States Statutes at Large. Most statutes are then broken down by subject matter and incorporated into the 54 volumes and five appendices of the United States Code. This report provides an overview of federal statutes in each of these forms, as well as basic guidance for congressional offices researching statutes.
When an individual piece of legislation is enacted under the procedures set forth in Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution,1 it is characterized as a "public law" or a "private law" depending on its intended audience. The overwhelming majority of laws passed by Congress are public laws because they have general applicability to the whole of society and are continuing and permanent in nature.2 Private laws are enacted for the benefit of a named individual or entity (for example, private laws can be enacted to assist a citizen injured by a government program).3
Each newly passed law—public or private—is assigned a number according to the order of its enactment within a particular Congress.4 This system began in 1957 with the 85th Congress. Laws enacted before 1957 are cited by the date of enactment and the chapter number assigned to them in the Statutes at Large, discussed further below.5
When researchers want to obtain a copy of a newly enacted law, they will most likely be looking for the "slip law." A slip law is the first official publication of a public or private law, prepared by the Office of the Federal Register (OFR), and published by the Government Publishing Office (GPO).
Slip laws are available from non-commercial, public sources in various forms.
Slip laws in printable pamphlet form can be obtained online from GPO. GPO provides free electronic access to official federal government publications, including public and private laws from the 104th Congress (1995-1996) forward.6 Additionally, Federal Depository Libraries, which are libraries designated to receive free government documents, provide no-cost access to certain classes of government documents, including slip laws.7
Public and private laws can also be found through the Library of Congress at Congress.gov, the official website for U.S. federal legislative information.8 Information on public and private laws, including the full text of the laws, may be searched from the 82nd Congress (1951-1952) forward.
In addition to the publicly available resources described above, many commercial, subscription-based sources provide access to slip laws as well. Subscriptions to these sources vary from House to Senate and within individual offices.
Lexis makes public laws available in the USCS – Public Laws database from 1988 to the present.9
ProQuest Congressional makes public laws available in slip law format from 1988 to the present.10
Westlaw makes public laws available from 1973 to the previous legislative session in the U.S. Public Laws – Historical database, and public laws from the current legislative session in its U.S. Public Laws database.11
Public laws, from 1973 to the present are reprinted in the United States Code Congressional and Administrative News (USCCAN), published by Thomson Reuters. Laws are compiled in slip law format chronologically, along with selected Senate, House, and conference reports associated with the laws, as well as presidential signing statements, proclamations, and executive orders. USCCAN is published both as a bound volume and electronically through a Westlaw subscription.
Every two years at the end of a congressional session, slip laws (both public and private laws) are accumulated and published chronologically in a series of volumes entitled the United States Statutes at Large (Statutes at Large). The Statutes at Large also contain concurrent resolutions, reorganization plans, proposed and ratified amendments to the Constitution, and proclamations by the President. Until 1948, treaties and international agreements approved by the Senate were also published in the Statutes at Large.12 Laws are cited by the Statutes at Large volume and page number (e.g., 125 Stat. 753 refers to page 753 of volume 125 of the Statutes at Large). The printed edition of the Statutes at Large is "legal evidence of the laws ... in all the courts of the United States" and thus researchers may likely refer to this publication when citing a law before a court.13
GPO provides free, electronic access to the Statutes at Large, 1951-2016.14
Earlier volumes of the Statutes at Large, from 1789 to 1951, can be found and searched through the Library of Congress's Digitized Collection.15
In addition to the publicly available resources described above, many commercial, subscription-based sources provide access to the Statutes at Large. Subscriptions to these sources vary from House to Senate and within individual offices as well.
HeinOnline makes available the Statutes at Large from 1789 to the present, and can also be searched by chapter or public law number.
Lexis makes available a Statutes at Large database which contains all public and private laws from 1789 to the present, as well as treaties with foreign nations and Indian tribes beginning in 1776.
ProQuest Congressional makes available the Statutes at Large from 1789 to the present.
Westlaw makes available the Statutes at Large from 1789 to 1972.
The United States Code (U.S. Code or U.S.C.) is the official government codification of all general and permanent laws of the United States. The U.S. Code has its roots in an 1866 law that initiated a project to "revise, simplify, arrange, and consolidate all statutes of the United States, general and permanent in their nature.... "16 This endeavor was not fully realized until 1874 when the Revised Statutes of 1874 became the first official codification of U.S. laws.17 A second edition making corrections and updates followed in 1878.18 However, despite numerous efforts to supplement and revise inaccuracies in the Revised Statutes, the publication contained errors.19 The Revised Statutes were also not updated regularly, making it difficult to know if a particular law had been amended. In 1919, work on a new codification project began, but it was not until 1926 that what is today known as the United States Code came to exist.20
The U.S. Code has been published by the GPO every six years since its initial publication in 1926.21 The current edition of the U.S. Code was printed in 2018 and is updated annually with cumulative print supplements. In the U.S. Code, statutes are grouped by subject matter into 54 titles and five appendices. Each title is organized into chapters and then sections, which is how a particular provision is cited (e.g., 27 U.S.C. §124 refers to Section 124 of Title 27). Source credits and historical notes at the end of each section provide additional information, including the statutory origin of the provision, its effective date, a brief citation, a discussion of any amendments, and cross-references to related provisions.
As a general rule, the U.S. Code is an unofficial restatement of the Statutes at Large organized by topic for ease of access. As discussed further below, the exception to this general rule is when a particular title of the U.S. Code has been enacted into positive law.
The Office of the Law Revision Counsel (OLRC) of the U.S. House of Representatives is responsible for maintaining and publishing the U.S. Code.22 The OLRC oversees the organization of statutes by subject matter, assigning a statute to a U.S. Code section if the law has general applicability and permanence. If a provision is not intended to be permanent or does not have relevance to a wide audience, the OLRC may not include that language in the U.S. Code, or the OLRC may classify the provision as a statutory note or appendix to an existing U.S. Code section. Language enacted as part of government appropriations measures is a common instance of this; for example, provisions appropriating funds to the Office of Highway Administration each fiscal year are not likely to be codified because, by their own terms, they govern for only one year.23 Nevertheless, it is important to remember that whether a provision is codified or classified as a note or appendix in no way diminishes the statute's significance or authority. Provisions that are not codified in the U.S. Code are still acts of Congress.24
The language of a law as set forth in the U.S. Code is not necessarily a literal duplication of the law as it was enacted. Because the U.S. Code is arranged by subject, a slip law is often divided up among titles, with different sections of a slip law being assigned to different volumes, chapters, and sections of the U.S. Code. There may also be slight changes from the original statute, particularly with regard to section numbers and cross-references, corresponding to U.S. Code sections, not statute sections.
The most notable difference between the U.S. Code and the Statutes at Large is that language in the U.S. Code exists as amended to reflect subsequent changes made by later laws.
When a bill becomes a law, the OLRC will examine whether the law has any non-amendatory or "freestanding" provisions to introduce to the Code, or any language that revises, repeals, or adds to already existing statutes.25 Consider the following sequence of enactments.
As the above sequence illustrates, the canvas upon which Congress typically works is the existing realm of federal statutes and not a blank slate. To that end, it is usually more effective to consult the U.S. Code for the current language of a statute than it is to consult either the slip law or the Statutes at Large, both of which are essentially frozen in their respective times.
It can be difficult for a researcher to find amended public laws with up-to-date language, but there are resources available. The House of Representatives Office of the Legislative Counsel assembles compilations of statutes that are not codified in the U.S. Code or are found in a title that has not been enacted into positive law.29 Congressional committees and federal agencies may periodically issue similar compilations of amended public laws, especially for statutes significant to their respective jurisdictions. For example, the Civil Rights Division of the Department of Justice provides access to the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, As Amended, which includes changes made by the ADA Amendments Act of 2008 to the 1990 law.30 Additionally, commercial publishers may track changes to existing law by recently enacted legislation. For instance, the commercial database CQ LawTrack notes and lists changes made by each new law to prior laws, though it does not aggregate the text of the amended law itself.31
In 1947, Congress began enacting whole titles of the U.S. Code into law, generally repealing the underlying statutes. When Congress does this, the authoritative legal language is no longer the slip law that enacted it, but the language as presented in a U.S. Code title. This process is known as "positive law codification" and the titles that have been enacted are "positive law titles."
Why would Congress go through the effort of reenacting laws already in force? According to the OLRC, the U.S. Code is an effective and valuable tool for researching and verifying general and permanent laws, and "positive law codification improves the usefulness of the Code in several significant ways."32 These include
The process of positive law codification is a meticulous and time-consuming endeavor; consequently, not all titles have undergone the process.36 At present, there are 27 positive law titles, which are identified with an asterisk on the OLRC's U.S. Code "Search & Browse" page.37
For a researcher, one of the most important differences between positive and non-positive law titles is the difference in the history of the enacting laws. In non-positive law titles, the first act listed in the history source credits is what the OLRC terms the "base law," or the act that originated that particular U.S. Code section. For example, 2 U.S.C. §1 reads,
Time for election of Senators.
At the regular election held in any State next preceding the expiration of the term for which any Senator was elected to represent such State in Congress, at which election a Representative to Congress is regularly by law to be chosen, a United States Senator from said State shall be elected by the people thereof for the term commencing on the 3d day of January next thereafter.
(June 4, 1914, ch. 103, §1, 38 Stat. 384; June 5, 1934, ch. 390, §3, 48 Stat. 879.)
The base law for 2 U.S.C. §1 is the Act of June 4, 1914, ch. 103, 38 Stat. 384. In other words, the Act of June 4, 1914, created the language that currently occupies 2 U.S.C. §1. The opening clause of the Act of June 4, 1914, reads, "An act Providing a temporary method of conducting the nomination and election of United States Senators."
In positive law titles, the history source credits convey different information. For example, 3 U.S.C. §7 reads:
Meeting and vote of electors.
The electors of President and Vice President of each State shall meet and give their votes on the first Monday after the second Wednesday in December next following their appointment at such place in each State as the legislature of such State shall direct.
(June 25, 1948, ch. 644, 62 Stat. 673.)
Here, the Act of June 25, 1948, ch. 644, 62 Stat. 673 is not the base law for 3 U.S.C. §7, because this Act did not create the language of Section 7. Rather, this Act codified and enacted the entirety of Title 3 into positive law. The opening clause of this Act reads, "An Act To codify and enact into law Title 3 of the United States Code, entitled 'The President.'" In other words, every section contained in Title 3 has "Act of June 25, 1948, ch. 644" as the enacting law in the source credits because the underlying statutes that individually created the whole of Title 3 have been repealed. Accordingly, for a researcher who needs to cite the authoritative language of a section, the words of the section itself will be sufficient. However, a researcher who is looking for the history of the language itself and is perhaps interested in the intent behind its enactment must take additional steps to locate such information.
A researcher seeking information on the history or intent of the language in positive law titles of the U.S. Code should examine the "Front Matter" located at the very beginning of the title, preceding the legal language. This preface includes a table showing the disposition of all sections of the former title, including where the new sections were previously located, and the original source credits. In the previous example, before positive law codification, the language of 3 U.S.C. §7 was located at 3 U.S.C. §5, and the original base law was the Act of February 3, 1887, ch. 90, 24 Stat. 373.38
As discussed in the previous section, one reason for positive law codification is to improve the organization of existing titles. Another way the OLRC improves the organization of existing titles is through a process known as "Editorial Reclassification." In this process, the OLRC reorganizes portions of the law without altering or eliminating any statutory text.39
The OLRC recently conducted ten editorial reclassification projects. Each one is explained in detail on the OLRC's website, with reasons for the change, major actions, current status, and resources for the transition. As an example, the OLRC transferred Title IV, Part C of the Higher Education Act of 1965 from its previous location in the Public Health and Welfare Title, 42 U.S.C. §§2751, et seq., to the Education Title, 20 U.S.C. §§1087-51, et seq. In addition, portions of Title 20 were reordered to conform to the transfer.40
In addition to the official U.S. Code, researchers may be familiar with such resources as the United States Code Annotated (U.S.C.A.), published by Thomson Reuters, and the United States Code Service (U.S.C.S.), published by LexisNexis. These are privately published editions of the U.S. Code. In addition to the text and historical source credits, such editions include annotations with further historical commentary, cross-references to the Code of Federal Regulations (C.F.R.), judicial decisions or attorney general opinions interpreting the sections, and citations to secondary sources, such as law reviews and practice guides. Although these supplements can offer benefits to the researcher, it is important to remember that these versions are unofficial and should be cross-referenced to an official publication, be it the slip law, Statutes at Large, or, in the case of a positive law title, the U.S. Code.
As previously noted, statutes are incorporated into U.S. Code to facilitate retrieval and access, because searching by subject may be easier than searching by date in some cases. However, there are several resources that further simplify locating information in the U.S. Code. The tools listed below are available in both print and electronically via the OLRC unless otherwise noted.
The General Index is a comprehensive directory organized alphabetically by subject with the corresponding title and section listed. The General Index is only available in print format.41
The Popular Names Table lists statutes alphabetically by their colloquial names. This can reflect the substance of the law, the sponsor(s) of the law, or any creative acronym for the law. For example, there are entries for the "Energy Policy Act," the "Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act," and the "USA PATRIOT Act." The electronic version of the Popular Names Table provides the enacting public law number, Statutes at Large cite, and the U.S. Code citation.42 The Popular Names Table's print version published by Thomson West with the U.S.C.A. also lists all the amending laws under the enacting law.
The Classification Tables aid researchers by indicating where enacted laws appear in the U.S. Code and which sections of the U.S. Code those laws amended. The tables will also indicate which sections of the U.S. Code were repealed, omitted, or transferred.43
Table I conveys where sections of titles enacted as positive law were incorporated into the revised title.44 If a section is not listed in Table I, then it was either repealed or omitted in the process of becoming positive law.
Table II shows where sections of the Revised Statutes of 1878 were classified into the U.S. Code.45
If a researcher has a Statutes at Large citation and would like to know where it has been codified, Table III provides the corresponding U.S. Code section.46
Similarly, Tables IV and V indicate where a particular executive order or presidential proclamation is set out in the U.S. Code.47
Likewise, Table VI lists the codification and status of reorganization plans promulgated since 1939.48 A reorganization plan is a proposal offered by the President to restructure or modify existing federal agencies to improve efficiency by consolidating, transferring, or eliminating certain functions.49
For additional information or specific questions on federal statutes, congressional clients may contact CRS. For programs offering training on statutory research, congressional clients please consult "Federal Legal Research" under the "Events" section of CRS.gov.
title: From Slip Law to United States Code: A Guide to Federal Statutes for Congressional Offices

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Bryan Jackson, 42, of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, entered a plea of guilty before United States District Judge Joel H. Slomsky yesterday afternoon to conspiracy to manufacture child pornography, manufacture and attempted manufacture of child pornography, and receipt of child pornography, charges arising from his and a co-conspirator’s sexual exploitation of an underage boy.

The defendant was arrested on a criminal complaint and warrant in June of this year and charged by information in September. With today’s plea, he has waived prosecution by indictment.

As detailed in court filings and statements, Jackson and the co-conspirator enticed and directed Minor 1, who was under the age of 18, to photograph and video record himself engaging in sexually explicit conduct.

As further detailed, the defendant and his co-conspirator deceived Minor 1 into believing that he was communicating with an older girl, in order to induce Minor 1 into producing child sexual abuse material (“CSAM”), which the conspirators then shared with each other.

In addition, from about November 22, 2025, through about May 28, 2026, Jackson knowingly received visual depictions whose production involved the use of a second minor, Minor 2, engaging in sexually explicit conduct.

The defendant is scheduled to be sentenced on February 19 and faces a maximum possible term of 80 years in prison.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit projectsafechildhood.gov .

The case was investigated by the Philadelphia Police Department Special Victims Unit and Homeland Security Investigations and is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Branwen McNabb O’Donnell.
title: Philadelphia Pastor Pleads Guilty to Child Sexual Exploitation Charges

ICE Los Angeles leads operation targeting trafficking of illicit tobacco products
LOS ANGELES — On Oct. 22, ICE Homeland Security Investigations Los Angeles agents led a National Trade Fraud Task Force operation to target the trafficking of illicit tobacco products and prohibited items. HSI joined with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department and the LAPD to seize over 6,200 illicit items from 12 locations across L.A. County and arrested 22 individuals for violations of California state law.
The National Trade Fraud Task Force is a U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security initiative launched in August 2025 to investigate and prosecute customs and trade fraud across the entire supply chain. Its formation marked a strategic shift from administrative penalties toward aggressive civil and criminal enforcement. The campaign surpassed $1 billion in recoveries by July 2026.
“HSI’s core mission is to protect the homeland from transnational crime and threats,” said HSI Los Angeles acting Special Agent in Charge Erin Burke. “Protecting legitimate trade by shutting down illegal operations is one of the primary mechanisms for discouraging criminals from considering these types of activities. This was a huge effort by HSI and our partners to put a serious dent in the illegal tobacco trade in L.A. County."
title: ICE Los Angeles leads operation targeting trafficking of illicit tobacco products

A man who had a stolen firearm in his waistband and resisted arrest was sentenced on November 3, 2026, to more than five years in federal prison.

Da’Tellyon Dawon Nix, age 19, from Waterloo, Iowa, received the prison term after a June 24, 2026, guilty plea to possession of a firearm by a felon.

Information from the plea and sentencing hearings showed that Nix was previously convicted of a felony crime of violence, intimidation with a dangerous weapon, which involved him firing a gun at multiple people. On January 28, 2026, law enforcement officers had information that Nix was in possession of a gun. There was also a valid warrant for Nix’s arrest for probation violations. Officers followed Nix as he left a Chuck E. Cheese in Cedar Falls and subsequently pulled over the car he was in. Nix attempted to flee and was ultimately tased by an officer at which time he admitted that there was a firearm in his waistband. The firearm had previously been stolen from a federal firearms licensee.

Nix was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand. Nix was sentenced to 70 months’ imprisonment. He must also serve a three-year term of supervised release after the prison term. There is no parole in the federal system.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Nix is being held in the United States Marshal’s custody until he can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Kyndra Lundquist and investigated by Federal Task Force composed of the Waterloo Police Department, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms assisted by the Black Hawk County Sheriff’s Office and Cedar Falls Police Department.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is 26-CR-2009.

WASHINGTON— U.S. Customs and Border Protection has issued an Interim Final Rule (IFR) to establish new requirements for foreign Importers of Record (IORs) when bringing goods into the United States. Consistent with Executive Order 14411, “Strengthening Customs Enforcement,” the IFR is designed to strengthen importer accountability, improve CBP’s ability to address noncompliance, and help ensure that all importers operate under clear and enforceable requirements.
“The executive order levels the playing field by holding foreign IORs to the same standards as U.S.-based IORs and requiring them – or their customs brokers – to be CTPAT-validated,” said Diane J. Sabatino, Executive Assistant Commissioner, Office of Field Operations. “This increases transparency, prevents the importation of unlawful and dangerous goods, and ensures fair competition for U.S. businesses and importers.”
These heightened requirements support CBP’s mission to protect the American public and ensure the collection of revenue owed to the United States. By requiring CTPAT validation, CBP is leveraging its trusted trader program to prevent foreign parties from evading U.S. customs and trade laws and leveling the playing field for U.S. businesses.
“Licensed customs brokers are now responsible for verifying that their clients meet the qualifications of a U.S. IOR before filing entries on their behalf,” said CBP Office of Trade Executive Assistant Commissioner Susan S. Thomas. “This requirement ensures that foreign importers are held accountable to U.S. laws which helps mitigate risks to revenue, U.S. industries, American consumers, and national security.”
The IFR becomes effective on January 5, 2027. The public may submit comments through the Federal Rulemaking Portal at www.regulations.gov under docket number USCBP-2026-1387. Comments must be received on or before January 5, 2027, and comments will be considered in determining whether to amend, confirm, or withdraw the rule following its interim implementation.
These efforts support CBP’s broader work to protect the economy of the United States, ensure the health and safety of the American people, and strengthen the security and resilience of international supply chains.
For additional information on the IFR, Executive Order 14411, and related CBP actions, visit CBP's Strengthening Customs Enforcement website. Follow the CBP Office of Trade on LinkedIn and Instagram, and CBP Office of Field Operations on Instagram.
-CBP-
title: CBP announces heightened requirements for Foreign Importers of Record

text:
WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) announced the new Intelligent Capital Access Platform (iCAP), a modern origination, processing, and management platform designed to make SBA lending faster, simpler and more secure. The new platform marks a historic technology overhaul for the agency as it moves away from fragmented, decades-old software including ETRAN and the Capital Access Financial System (CAFS). By bringing the efficiency, usability, and risk controls of modern banking together, iCAP simplifies loan application preparation, accelerates review, and strengthens fraud prevention. Following consultation with SBA lenders, the agency is empowering its lenders with the tools they need — especially community banks and rural lenders — to deliver more loans, faster, for small businesses.
“As an agency entrusted with backing billions of dollars in small business loans, we’re offering our thousands of banking partners the technology and risk management tools consistent with the demands of a modern financial institution to better serve their small business clients by clearing out decades of bureaucratic inefficiency,” said SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler. “The same discipline my team and I brought to building financial services and technology businesses now guides SBA’s modernization: equipping lenders with dynamic, integrated systems that accelerate transactions, provide visibility, and strengthen risk controls instead of PDFs, piles of paperwork, and uncertainty. With iCAP, we are putting private-sector standards into practice — replacing manual workflows with modern technology that accelerates loan review and stops fraud. SBA is transforming into a faster, more accountable partner, giving our lenders greater capacity to serve small businesses while strengthening protections for taxpayer dollars.”
For two decades, SBA’s legacy ETRAN origination systems went without a single major upgrade, leaving lenders to navigate cumbersome manual workflows. Over the next few months, iCAP will replace those outdated processes with the connected workflows, automated controls, and intuitive interface lenders expect from a modern banking partner. These upgrades simplify the origination process, in part to empower community and regional banks to join SBA’s lender network and deliver more financing to rural America.
iCAP is available through lender.sba.gov and includes the following key capabilities:
- Real-time application validation. Automated checks flag missing or inconsistent information as lenders prepare applications, reducing submission errors, avoidable rework, and review delays.
- Single-entry data capture. Information automatically populates related application sections, eliminating duplicate entry and redundant document submissions while improving data consistency.
- Dynamic application requirements. Data fields and documentation requirements adjust to the loan type, processing method, and transaction details, streamlining application preparation.
- Integrated review and communication. Lenders and SBA reviewers work from shared screens, with in-app messaging and notifications that keep requests, responses, and supporting information within the loan workflow.
- Transaction visibility. Application status tracking and a consolidated activity record give lenders and SBA reviewers visibility into loan progress and a traceable history of actions and communications.
- Embedded fraud screening. Up-front fraud and eligibility reviews, combined with visibility into prior SBA debt, help lenders and SBA identify potential risks earlier in origination.
The launch follows a six-month pilot program that helped refine iCAP through lender participation and feedback. To date, more than 250 lenders have joined the platform, processing 2,000 loans totaling millions of dollars. The feedback during the pilot was used to refine application flows, simplify document requirements, and expand functionality to support both delegated and non-delegated lending. This approach has allowed the SBA to develop a bespoke platform cost-effectively in well under two years, without waiting for a single, years-long system replacement.
The SBA will deliver its lender experience transformation in phases. ETRAN continues to support certain functions during the transition, including post-submission changes and modification requests through ETRAN Servicing, as well as access to approved loans’ Terms & Conditions documents. The new 7(a) origination application programming interface (API), which enables lenders’ software systems to exchange information with SBA, is scheduled to become available in production in December 2026, with migration from the ETRAN origination interface required by June 2027; information on the phases will be provided in the coming weeks.
Although iCAP’s origination capabilities currently extend only to 7(a) lending, the platform does support modernized secondary-market transactions through its Guaranty Sale application, with prepopulated documents, in-app signatures, and real-time transaction tracking. SBA’s roadmap for future capabilities includes adding 504 origination, servicing, and liquidation to iCAP, bringing the same commercial-grade tools for streamlined processing, earlier risk detection, and greater transaction visibility to the 504 lending community.
The iCAP rollout anchors the agency’s broader lending agenda for fiscal 2027: building an efficient, integrated lender experience to expand the agency’s lending network, simplifying the 504 loan process, and surging financing to small businesses in the defense industrial base in support of initiatives such as the new Smaller War Plants Commission. By pairing modern banking tools and stronger fraud controls with simpler loan processes, the SBA is positioning itself to work with more lenders and deliver more capital to the small businesses essential to the nation’s economic strength and security.
The SBA will be communicating directly with lenders to begin using the iCAP platform. All lenders will have access to loan origination in iCAP by January 1, 2027. For users originating loans in ETRAN today, no additional enrollment is needed. You will receive login instructions, live training, system guides and self-service resources. Secondary market investors may access the modernized Guaranty Sale process through the new investor.sba.gov.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of entrepreneurship. As the leading voice for small businesses within the federal government, the SBA empowers job creators with the resources and support they need to start, grow, and expand their businesses or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Launches iCAP to Modernize 7(a) Loan Origination, Streamline Workflows, and Accelerate Small Business Lending

The U.S. Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced a $1.5 million investment to help states improve vehicle recall rates and keep American roads safe.
 
Dollars will be delivered to states prioritizing:
- The development and execution of a reliable process to inform vehicle owners of any open safety recalls when registering their vehicles
- Data-driven methods to measure recall completions
- Comprehensive reports outlining the methodologies and processes used so best practices can be shared.
“A vehicle with an open recall creates an avoidable hazard on our roads,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison. “By giving states the resources to flag open recalls when drivers register or renew their vehicles, we can keep dangerous cars off our roads and American families safe.”
Administrator Morrison announced the investment at today’s public meeting on the future of vehicle safety recalls. The event, Recalls Next: Technological Innovations and Safety Recalls, convened government, industry, and research leaders to discuss how to boost recall completion rates.
Additional Information:
NHTSA encourages applicants to include assessments of driver attitudes toward specific notification methods, as well as strategies to track which vehicles receive remedies following state notification.
The Notice of Funding Opportunity outlines additional criteria here. Applicants are encouraged to apply as soon as possible but must do so by Feb. 4, 2027.
title: Trump’s Transportation Department to Invest $1.5 Million to Help States Alert Drivers About Vehicle Recalls

An illegal alien from Honduras who returned to the United States after being deported was sentenced today to eight months in federal prison.

Fidel Antonio Cruz Cruz, age 32, a citizen of Honduras illegally present in the United States and residing in the Cedar Rapids, Iowa, area received the prison term after a June 8, 2026, guilty plea to one count of illegal reentry into the United States after having been convicted of a felony offense.

At the guilty plea, Cruz Cruz admitted he had previously been deported from the United States and illegally reentered the United States without the permission of the United States government. Cruz Cruz was previously deported five times between 2017 and 2019. In 2020, Cruz Cruz was convicted of illegally reentering the United States and sentenced to 76 days in prison. He was then deported for the sixth time. Cruz Cruz returned to the United States at an unknown time. He was convicted in Johnson County, Iowa, in 2023 for an OWI offense.

On April 28, 2026, local law enforcement stopped Cruz Cruz for committing traffic violations while he was driving. ICE officers responded to the scene of the stop. They verified that Cruz Cruz had been ordered removed from the country. ICE then took him into custody.

Cruz Cruz was sentenced in Cedar Rapids by United States District Court Chief Judge C.J. Williams. He was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment. He must also serve a three-year term of supervised release after the prison term. There is no parole in the federal system.

Cruz Cruz remains in the custody of the United States Marshal’s Service.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Anthony Morfitt and investigated by the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Enforcement and Removal Operations.
