text:
Former Kokomo Police Department Officer Sentenced to 40 Years in Prison for Sexually Assaulting Minor, Lying to Investigators, and Destruction of Records
Sinmi Asomuyide, a former Kokomo, Indiana, police officer, was sentenced on Wednesday to 40 years in prison and three years supervised release for charges related to his on-duty sexual assault of a 14-year-old, and related obstruction. Asomuyide was previously convicted by a federal jury after a five-day trial in the Southern District of Indiana.
“The Department of Justice takes civil rights abuses seriously, including those committed by the small minority of police officers that betray public trust,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This defendant will be held accountable for the kidnapping and sexual abuse of a child. We hope the victim will be able to recover and prosper despite this horrific episode.”
“This defendant exploited the badge in one of the worst ways imaginable,” said U.S. Attorney Tom Wheeler for the Southern District of Indiana. “What makes these crimes particularly disturbing is that he used the very tools, training, and authority entrusted to him as a police officer not only to assault a vulnerable child, but to try to conceal it. The evidence told a different story, and today's sentence sends a clear message that no one can use the authority of the badge as a shield from accountability.”
“The very people entrusted with protecting children must never become the ones who victimize them. This defendant preyed on a 14-year-old girl and then attempted to cover up his crimes,” said Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O’Malley of the FBI Indianapolis Field Office. “That kind of calculated abuse is unconscionable. The FBI remains committed to protecting children and relentlessly pursuing those who prey on them.”
In particular, jurors found Sinmi Asomuyide, 33, guilty of willfully depriving the victim, who was then 14 years old, of her constitutional rights by sexually assaulting her. The jury found that the defendant’s conduct included kidnapping and abusive sexual contact of a child under the age of 16.
Jurors also found Asomuyide guilty of lying to the Indiana State Police in an attempt to cover up the assault by denying having sexual contact with the victim, and lying about the presence of other corroborating evidence. Additionally, jurors found Asomuyide guilty of deleting a messaging application he had been using to communicate with the minor victim prior to the sexual assault in attempt to cover up the assault.
The case was investigated by the FBI. Assistant U.S. Attorney Peter Blackett for the Southern District of Indiana, Civil Rights Division Trial Attorney Anita Channapati, and former Senior Sex Crimes Counsel Tara Allison prosecuted the case.
title: Former Kokomo Police Department Officer Sentenced to 40 Years in Prison for Sexually Assaulting Minor, Lying to Investigators, and Destruction of Records

text:
CAMP SMITH TRAINING SITE, N.Y. — Army Maj. Gen. Ray Shields, the adjutant general of New York, opened a $3.5 million housing facility at Camp Smith Training Site in Cortlandt Manor, New York, Oct. 29.
The facility replaces aging quarters for senior enlisted leaders and officers training at the post. The 3,000-square-foot building is designed to be environmentally friendly and meet modern hotel standards. "This facility offers single rooms with private latrines, a lounge, laundry, break area — meeting modern Army standards similar to a typical hotel room you might find," said Army Lt. Col. Chad Clark, the base operations manager.
Shields said improving facilities demonstrates support for the state's more than 12,000 Army National Guard soldiers.
"We need to focus on things that soldiers see and the facilities that they use," he said, adding that prioritizing modern workspaces and housing directly impacts how troops view their service.
Plans are also underway to build a federally funded 24-unit housing complex behind the new senior leader facility.
Shields noted that New York covered 25% of the cost of the new facility, and he highlighted the state’s support for the Army National Guard during an Oct. 28 meeting in Washington, with Army Lt. Gen. Jonathan Stubbs, director of the Army National Guard.
"Most National Guard units in the country do not get the level of fiscal support and support from their governor's office that we get," he said.
New York has invested $493 million in military facilities over the past two years, with $165 million funded directly by the state. New York also plans to fund a new firing range at Camp Smith.
Sharon Buck, executive deputy commissioner for the Office of General Services, said her agency is proud to support the New York National Guard.
Buck said her office is committed to ensuring that the National Guard members have the modern facilities they need to serve and respond when called upon.
title: New York National Guard unveils $3.5 million housing facility

AUSTIN, Texas – An Austin man was sentenced in federal court to 292 months in prison for sexually exploiting numerous male minors, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, Tre Von Lamount Harris, 21, used several social media platforms as well as Cash App to entice and extort minor male victims to engage in sexually explicit conduct for the purpose of producing and transmitting visual depictions. Harris, who began his sexual exploitation scheme at the age of 16, falsely posed as a teenaged female named “Michelle” on platforms including Facebook, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok.

Communicating with his victims as “Michelle,” Harris used graphic and explicit language to describe the nature of the visual depictions he wanted them to produce and send him. Victims would self-produce the child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and send it to Harris through their social media accounts. Harris would then send the victims extortionate threats to coerce them to pay him or else he would post the CSAM online or send it to their family and friends, which Harris did, in fact, follow through on.

Harris was arrested by the Travis County Sheriff’s Office on May 31, 2022, on two counts of sexual assault and one count of publishing or threatening to publish invasive visual recordings related to the employment of the same scheme under the fictitious name, “Karla”. A Travis County judge released him on a $5,000 cash bond and removed a GPS monitoring condition originally imposed. Harris was also allowed to attend high school.

Beginning in December 2022, the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) received several CyberTip reports from social media providers and private citizens regarding CSAM activity involving one or more of Harris’s online usernames. The FBI learned of the NCMEC complaints in May 2023 and conducted an extensive investigation which included interviews with multiple victims. Harris was arrested on federal charges on May 21, 2024, at his high school.

“Tre Von Harris will spend more than a decade of his young adult life behind bars because he hid behind a fake profile to humiliate and sexually exploit teenage boys for profit, continuing to do so even after he was caught the first time,” said U.S. Attorney Simmons. “American children are active all across social media and, as this case proves, they do not always know who is on the other end. As parents, we must be educated and stay involved with our children’s online activities. This case was possible because parents did just that. Together, we can stop predators and protect our children.”

Gainesville, Florida – Gurpinder Singh, 20, Yashdeep Singh, 20, Kuljeet Singh, 22, Navjeet Singh, 25, Akashdeep Singh, 25, Harshdeep Kaur, 24, and Manpreet Singh, 26, all of California; Sierra Stites, 35, and Carissa Snow, 37, both of Deland, Florida; and Reese Lightner, 39, of Pennsylvania have been indicted in federal court for one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and mail fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the charges.

All defendants have appeared in federal court for their arraignment before United States Magistrate Judge Midori A. Lowry in Gainesville, Florida. Jury trial is scheduled for December 30, 2026, at 8:30 am before Chief United States District Court Judge Allen C. Winsor in Gainesville, Florida.

If convicted, each defendant faces up to 20 years’ imprisonment on the conspiracy to commit wire fraud and mail fraud count and up to 20 years’ imprisonment on the conspiracy to commit money laundering count.

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, and the Gainesville Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Adam Hapner.

An indictment is merely an allegation by a grand jury that a defendant has committed a violation of federal criminal law and is not evidence of guilt. All defendants are presumed innocent and entitled to a fair trial, during which it will be the government’s burden to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt at trial.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF comprises agents and officers from multiple agencies with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. For more information about the United States Attorney’s Office, Northern District of Florida, visit https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndfl .
title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Multi-Defendant Indictment for Gold Bar Scheme to Defraud Elderly Victims

EUGENE, Ore.— A Mexican national unlawfully residing in the United States has been charged with laundering purported drug proceeds and being an alien in possession of a firearm, U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today.

According to court documents, Esteban Peralta Fragozo , 50, of Springfield, Oregon, owned and operated El Kaiman Western Wear, a Springfield business that sold clothing and provided international money transfer services. Investigators with Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) allege that Fragozo used the business to launder drug trafficking proceeds through wire transfers sent to Mexico and Honduras.

Court documents allege that between January 2018 and July 2026, El Kaiman processed approximately 179,874 wire transfers totaling more than $93 million . Investigators further allege that more than $34 million in suspected drug proceeds were transmitted from Springfield to drug-trafficking corridors in Mexico and Honduras during that period.

As part of the investigation, law enforcement conducted a series of undercover operations using a confidential informant. According to the complaint, Fragozo processed multiple wire transfers after being told the funds were derived from drug trafficking and used false sender information and identification documents to complete the transactions.

The complaint further alleges that drug traffickers used El Kaiman to transmit proceeds derived from narcotics trafficking. In one instance detailed in court records, investigators recovered wire transfer receipts from El Kaiman during a traffic stop that resulted in the seizure of approximately 72 pounds of methamphetamine .

On Nov. 4, 2026, federal agents executed search warrants at Fragozo's residence, business, vehicle, and on his person. During a search of the business, agents recovered a Ruger 9mm pistol, ammunition, and bulk currency. According to court documents, Fragozo admitted possessing the firearm and acknowledged that he did not have lawful immigration status in the United States.

“As alleged, the defendant was illegally present in the United States while using his business to launder millions of dollars in drug trafficking proceeds and unlawfully possessing a firearm,” said Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon . “Drug trafficking organizations depend on financial facilitators to move and hide their criminal profits. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to identify, dismantle, and prosecute the financial infrastructure that supports transnational drug trafficking organizations and fuels the flow of fentanyl and other dangerous drugs into our communities.”

According to the complaint, investigators have observed a dramatic increase in drug trafficking activity involving Honduran nationals in Oregon. Court documents allege that Mexican drug trafficking organizations increasingly use Honduran nationals to distribute fentanyl and other dangerous narcotics in major metropolitan areas, including the Portland metropolitan area.

Fragozo made his initial appearance in federal court on Nov. 4, 2026, before a U.S. magistrate judge and was ordered detained pending further proceedings.

A criminal complaint is only an accusation of a crime, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

The case is being investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Julia Jarrett and Christopher Cardani are prosecuting the case.
title: Mexican National Unlawfully Residing in the United States Charged with Laundering Drug Proceeds and Unlawfully Possessing a Firearm

WASHINGTON – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, in partnership with the United States Marshals Service, reports a second year of city‑wide operations to verify that sex offenders residing in the District remain compliant with the law, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro and United States Marshals Service (USMS) Director Gadyaces S. Serralta.

The initiative , originally launched in October of last year, resulted in compliance checks on 883 sex offenders in 2025, with federal agents determining that 25 had failed to register. Nine of those individuals were classified as “Class A” offenders, meaning they had been convicted of extremely serious sexual assaults or had victimized multiple individuals.

Between August and September of this year, federal agents conducted compliance checks on 694 sex offenders. Based on those compliance checks, arrest warrants have been issued for 40 sex offenders for failing to register. 13 of the 40 are “Class A” offenders.

“My job as United States Attorney is to protect this community, especially our children, from repeat offenders who prey on the vulnerable,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Over two years, we’ve conducted more than 1,500 compliance checks, including 694 in just the last two months. If you ignore the law, we will find you, arrest you, and prosecute you.”

“My job as United States Attorney is to protect this community, especially our children, from repeat offenders who prey on the vulnerable,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Over two years, we’ve conducted more than 1,500 compliance checks, including 694 in just the last two months. If you ignore the law, we will find you, arrest you, and prosecute you.”

“Sex offender registration is a legal obligation, not a choice,” said U.S. Marshals Service Director Gadyaces S. Serralta. “Those who disregard the law should not expect to escape accountability. Working alongside the U.S. Attorney’s Office and our law enforcement partners, we will continue to investigate violations, locate noncompliant offenders, and execute arrest warrants. This is not a one-time crackdown. It is a sustained commitment to protecting our communities and ensuring that those who violate the law cannot evade its consequences”.

The Supreme Court recognized decades ago that the “risk of recidivism posed by sex offenders is frightening and high.” Smith v. Doe , 538 U.S. 84, 103 (2003).

The United States Marshals Service and The Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA) have been aggressively pursuing non-compliant offenders since August 24, 2025. The offenders are now being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Sex Offense and Domestic Violence and the Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Sections.

The operation identifies the sex offenders in the District who are required to register with CSOSA, uncovers and investigates offenders who are out of compliance, and arrests and aggressively prosecutes absconders.

The operation is a high-priority project. The U.S. Attorney’s Office has devoted substantial prosecutorial resources to these two operations; USMS has committed 28 Deputy U.S. Marshals from across the country, and CSOSA has likewise participated fully.

As of November 2, 2026, the Second operation has resulted in the following:

Obtained 40 Superior Court Sex Offender Registration Act (SORA) arrest warrants (34 misdemeanor warrants and 6 felony warrants) 13 of these arrest warrants are for Class A offenders 1 of these arrest warrants is for an offender with 11 prior sex convictions

13 of these arrest warrants are for Class A offenders

1 of these arrest warrants is for an offender with 11 prior sex convictions

Arrested and charged 17 sex offenders for SORA violations (12 on misdemeanor charges and 5 on felony charges)

One offender was also referred to the Major Crimes Section for prosecution for possible ID Theft charges

Indicted one sex offender for a felony violation of Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA)

Two sex offenders were also charged and convicted of Misdemeanor Failure to Register during the 2025 operation and are now charged again in the 2026 operation with Felony Failure to Register because they continued to be non-compliant (Tre Risper and Karl Gaddy, active Superior Court Cases pending for Felony FTR)

The U.S. Army Marksmanship Unit (USAMU) claimed the overall individual and team championships during the 66th Annual Interservice Pistol Championships, held Nov. 1-4, 2026, at Fort Benning, Georgia.
The annual competition brought together military marksmen from across the armed forces, including active-duty Soldiers, National Guard members, reservists and competitors from the U.S. Coast Guard, Air Force, and Space Force. Throughout the event, competitors tested their skills in individual and team pistol matches while sharing knowledge and experience with fellow service members.
USAMU's Service Pistol Team secured the top three positions in the overall individual standings. Sgt. 1st Class Ryan Adams earned first place with a score of 3,495-163, followed by Sgt. 1st Class Greg Markowski in second and Staff Sgt. Walker Buckman in third.
For Adams, the victory came during his first official Interservice Pistol Championships as a member of the USAMU team.
"A lot of good shooters out here. Just happy to be among and shoot with some of the best shooters in the country," Adams said.
Adams credited his teammates for helping him improve his performance, explaining that he does his best shooting alongside the team. His advice to other competitive shooters was straightforward.
"Train, train, train. Relax," Adams said. "Align the sights, pull the trigger."
The USAMU Blue Team also earned first place in the overall team championship, along with victories in the .22-caliber, centerfire, .45-caliber and service pistol team matches.
Sgt. 1st Class Walter Johnson, USAMU Service Pistol assistant Team chief, praised the team's preparation and performance, noting that several competitors achieved personal records during the event.
"The entire team worked very hard to prepare for it," Johnson said. "I'm very proud of all the hard work that they did."
Beyond the competition, Johnson emphasized the importance of bringing service members together to exchange marksmanship knowledge and strengthen relationships across the military.
The championships provided competitors from different service branches an opportunity to test their abilities against some of the military's top pistol marksmen while promoting marksmanship excellence across the armed forces.

The Working Families Tax Cuts Created a Permanent Process for States to Direct More Capital to Overlooked Communities
IR-2026-132, Nov. 5, 2026
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) today announced the Qualified Opportunity Zone (QOZ) designations for all 50 states, territories, and the District of Columbia.
Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the Opportunity Zone tax incentive was permanently renewed, enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities were added, and a process was established for redesignating zones every ten years. The new QOZ designations will become effective on January 1, 2027, and retain this designation for ten years.
“Under President Trump’s leadership, the Working Families Tax Cuts permanently renewed and strengthened Opportunity Zones, giving investors, entrepreneurs, and local leaders the long-term certainty they need to commit capital to communities that have been overlooked for too long,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “Today’s announcement of the new designations will help direct private investment to communities that stand to benefit most, and expand economic opportunity, support job creation, and unlock long-term growth in these communities across the country.”
“Thanks to the leadership of President Trump, Qualified Opportunity Zones were permanently extended and expanded by the Working Families Tax Cuts giving states an opportunity to attract long-term investment into underserved, rural, and economically distressed areas,” said IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano. "By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most."
Background
Under President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts, the permanent renewal of the Opportunity Zone tax incentives, including enhanced incentives for investment in eligible rural communities, will continue to drive private investment in some of America’s most distressed communities. This builds on more than $110 billion in private-sector investment made since these tax incentives were established by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017.
The full list and map of designated Opportunity Zones are available here.
On April 6, Treasury and the IRS released a list of 25,332 eligible census tracts across the country for nomination, of which 8,334 are in rural areas eligible for increased benefits as part of the Working Families Tax Cuts. On July 1, Treasury and the IRS began accepting nominations from Governors and the Mayor of the District of Columbia for eligible census tracts. An additional 130 eligible census tracts, of which 28 were in rural areas, were nominated during the statutory window.
In total, 6,576 eligible census tracts were nominated by the end of the statutory window, of which 2,594 are in rural areas. All of the 6,576 eligible census tracts have been designated as QOZs effective January 1, 2027. Designation as a QOZ can help these 6,576 communities across the country attract new investment, create jobs, stimulate economic growth, and provide meaningful opportunities for residents.
Additional information on nomination procedures was sent directly to the Governors and Mayor of the District of Columbia. The list of eligible census tracts is available here. The poverty rate and median family income for each tract can be found here.
title: Treasury, IRS Announce Opportunity Zones Designations for Over 6,500 Communities Across America

WILMINGTON, Del. – United States Attorney Benjamin L. Wallace announced the creation of the District of Delaware’s Program Fraud Task Force. The Task Force brings together the U.S. Attorney’s Office, the Department of Justice’s National Fraud Enforcement Division, more than a dozen federal law enforcement agencies, and multiple state law enforcement agencies, all focused on identifying, investigating, and prosecuting fraud against federal government programs and American taxpayers.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office hosted the Task Force’s first meeting on Thursday, October 29, 2026. U.S. Attorney Wallace, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Paul Kaufman, Civil Chief Dylan Steinberg, and District Fraud Counsel Bryan Williamson all addressed the Task Force, thanking the partner agencies for their commitment to fighting fraud and leading a discussion on how to further strengthen the federal government’s collective effort to ensure that every taxpayer dollar goes to good and proper use.

“Americans work hard for their paychecks, and they rightfully expect that every cent taken out of those paychecks in federal taxes is used as Congress intended,” said U.S. Attorney Wallace. “For too long, though, fraudsters have exploited the various benefit programs that Congress has erected. In doing so, those fraudsters steal not only from the vulnerable populations that the programs are meant to benefit, but also from every American taxpayer whose hard-earned money funds the programs. My Office and our law enforcement partners have always been dedicated to fighting fraud on the American taxpayer. But through our Program Fraud Task Force, we can—and will—improve our fraud-fighting efforts by banding together and reaping the benefits of increased collaboration.”

Delaware receives approximately $4.1 billion in direct federal funding each year for public health, housing, agriculture, transportation, infrastructure, education, and other programs. Even before the formation of the Task Force, the U.S. Attorney’s Office and its law enforcement partners have been vigilant about detecting—and recovering—any portion of that $4.1 billion that is diverted by fraud. Over the past three fiscal years, the Civil Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office’s has resolved more than 20 fraud-on-the-government matters under the False Claims Act, obtaining judgments and settlements in excess of $76 million. Over the same period, meanwhile, the Office’s Criminal Division has prosecuted approximately 14 defendants for defrauding the government, with those defendants being ordered to repay the government approximately $22 million dollars in restitution.

The District of Delaware’s Program Fraud Task Force is part of a nationwide initiative to combat fraud on government programs. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs .

WATERVLIET ARSENAL, N.Y. — Watervliet Arsenal is expanding its manufacturing capabilities through lights-out machining, using automation to increase available production capacity and strengthen its ability to respond to the Army’s evolving cannon requirements.
In one application, arsenal machinists have validated a 12.5-hour manufacturing process that requires approximately 2.5 hours of operator involvement, primarily for setup and other essential activities. Once underway, the machine completes the remaining 10 hours unattended, allowing skilled personnel to perform other tasks while equipment continues operating.
“Modernization at Watervliet Arsenal is not an abstract future goal—it is work being applied on the production floor today,” said Rob Cavanaugh, Watervliet Arsenal production manager. “By combining industry-proven automation with the expertise of our workforce, we are improving capacity, repeatability and responsiveness for the capabilities our soldiers depend on.”
Lights-out machining uses automated equipment and validated processes to perform manufacturing operations without continuous operator attendance. Arsenal teams have developed and tested these processes on production material for key components of the M109 Paladin 155-mm howitzer, clearing them for production use while maintaining established tooling, process and quality controls.
The effort builds on the expertise of the arsenal’s workforce. Production leaders have developed component-specific work instructions and completed preliminary personnel training, with additional instruction planned to expand advanced machining, monitoring and quality assurance capabilities.
The initiative is part of a broader modernization strategy that integrates technology, equipment, manufacturing processes and workforce development. By applying automation where it delivers operational value, the arsenal is improving its ability to use existing production resources and to adapt to changing requirements.
“Our responsibility is to deliver trusted manufacturing capability to the Army, today and in the future,” said Col. Danilo Green, Watervliet Arsenal commander. “Lights-out machining is one example of how our workforce is improving the way we produce critical components. We are building on the progress to create a more capable, flexible and responsive arsenal.”
These advancements strengthen the Army’s organic manufacturing capability and support a more responsive and resilient domestic industrial base.
Watervliet Arsenal is a U.S. Army-owned and operated manufacturing center specializing in the production of critical cannon, howitzer and mortar components. As part of the Army’s Organic Industrial Base, the arsenal combines precision manufacturing, specialized workforce expertise and advanced production technologies to deliver trusted capability in support of U.S. and allied military requirements.
title: Watervliet Arsenal expands manufacturing capability through lights-out machining

EL PASO, Texas – A federal grand jury in El Paso returned an indictment on Wednesday charging an illegal alien from Mexico with five counts related to his alleged transportation of a minor for the purpose of engaging in illicit sexual conduct and production, possession and transportation of child sexual abuse materials, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, Clemente Fernando Vazquez Serna, 34, was encountered on Oct. 11 aboard a Transborde bus that was selected for an outbound inspection at the Bridge of the Americas Port of Entry. A criminal complaint affidavit alleges that Vazquez Serna and a 14-year-old female both presented Mexican birth certificates. The two passengers were escorted off the bus for further inspection. It was then discovered that Vasquez Serna was engaged in a romantic relationship with the minor and that he was taking her to Mexico to live with him.

Court documents further allege that an inspection of cell phones belonging to Vazquez Serna and the minor revealed multiple files of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) depicting the 14-year-old. Vazquez Serna was arrested and, on Oct. 16, he was ordered detained by U.S. Magistrate Judge Anne Berton.

Vazquez Serna is now charged with transportation of a minor; production of visual depictions of minors engaging in sexually explicit conduct; transportation of a visual depiction involving the use of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct; attempt to transport a visual depiction involving the use of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct; and possession of a visual depiction involving the sexual exploitation of a minor. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Customs and Border Protection are investigating the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Scott Wisniewski is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

title: Illegal Alien from Mexico Indicted for Attempting to Transport Minor from Colorado to Mexico, Producing Child Pornography

FORT LEE, Va. – The U.S. Army Quartermaster School’s Joint Culinary Training Department held a ceremony Oct. 30 at the Tactical Field Readiness Training Center on Fort Lee signifying the renaming of the 92G military occupational specialty from culinary specialist to tactical field feeding specialist.
The name change comes as the Army transitions to planning and conducting large-scale combat operations in contested environments.
“When we change an MOS title in the Army, we do it not for superficial rebranding or administrative convenience; we do it because the character of war has changed,” said Col. Stacy Moore-Callaway, Quartermaster commandant. “Our operational imperatives have shifted, and the battlefield demands that our doctrines, our titles, and our soldier minds instead reflect the brutal reality of large-scale combat operations.
“We formally redesignate our culinary specialists, stepping forward under the title that truly captures the 92G's operational weight, and that is to turn them into tactical field feeding specialists,” said Moore-Callaway. “When we look at modern battle spaces that are taking shape around the globe, we know that we must shift the mindset of every single soldier in our formation towards survivability and true lethality.”
Army cooks were given specific positions during World War II before that it was an additional duty in a unit. In the 1960s, the Army formalized military occupational specialties, and the 94B Food Service Specialist was born. On Oct. 1, 1995, 94B became 92G Culinary Specialist.
“As the Army prepares for large-scale combat operations, we must evolve with the mission,” said Sgt. Maj. Paul Denson, Installation Operations Directorate, Army G-4, Washington, D.C., and the guest speaker for the ceremony. “Our tactical field feeding warfighters deliver endurance to the force.
“I submit to you that a well-fed warfighter is a lethal, agile, and adapted soldier that will win in a prolonged close fight,” said the sergeant major. “We're not simply producing food; we're sustaining warfighters; a tactical field feeding specialist has to understand food production, nutrition, and food safety.”
The sergeant major, who started his career in 1999 as a 92G, went on to say that 92Gs must understand tactical operations, logistics, and operating in a contested environment.
The mission of the 92G tactical field feeding specialist is responsible for ordering supplies, managing inventory, and preparing nutritious meals field environments. In challenging terrains, they utilize the Army Field Feeding System and Mobile Kitchen Trailers to deliver hot meals, significantly boosting morale and energy levels among troops.
title: 92G MOS renamed as Tactical Field Feeding Specialist

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (Nov. 5, 2026) – The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Nashville District announces that day-use fees at its USACE-operated recreation areas in the Cumberland River Basin are waived Nov. 11, 2026, in observance of Veterans Day.
The national fee waiver covers fees for boat launch ramps and swimming beaches at USACE-operated sites nationwide. Camping and camping-related services, as well as fees for specialized facilities such as group picnic shelters and special events, are not included in the waiver. Other agencies managing recreation areas on USACE lands are encouraged, but not required, to offer the waiver.
“Veterans Day is an opportunity for us to recognize and honor the men and women whose courage, sacrifice, and dedication have helped protect our nation and preserve the freedoms we enjoy,” said Trey Church, Nashville District’s Operations Section chief. “Waiving day use fees at our recreation areas is a meaningful way to show our appreciation for their service while inviting veterans, their families, and the public to enjoy the natural resources and recreational opportunities entrusted to our care. As stewards of these important public lands and waters, we are proud to join in this national observance and honor those who have served.”
While there are 25 USACE-managed recreation areas within the Nashville District that typically charge a day-use fee, several are already fee-free during the off-season. The waiver applies to all 25 sites, including those that remain open and active in charging fees during November:
Center Hill Lake: Floating Mill, Hurricane Bridge, Ragland Bottom
Dale Hollow Lake: Lillydale, Obey River, Pleasant Grove
USACE first introduced the Veterans Day fee waiver in 2006 to honor service members across all branches of the armed forces. In addition to Veterans Day, USACE offers fee-free days throughout the year to mark other key occasions, including the USACE birthday, Independence Day (July 4th), and National Public Lands Day.
As one of the nation's leading federal providers of outdoor and water-based recreation, USACE hosts millions of visitors annually across more than 400 lake and river projects. With an estimated 90% of USACE recreation areas located within 50 miles of major metropolitan areas, visitors can easily access diverse outdoor activities close to home.
Visitors are encouraged to contact USACE lake and river projects before visiting to ensure recreation areas are open. More information can be found at www.corpslakes.us.
To discover a USACE recreation site near you, please visit www.corpslakes.us or www.recreation.gov.
The public can obtain news, updates and information from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Nashville District on the district’s website athttps://www.lrd.usace.army.mil/About/Districts/Nashville-District/, on Facebook atwww.facebook.com/nashvillecorpsand on X (formerly Twitter) atwww.x.com/nashvillecorps. Follow us on LinkedIn for the latest Nashville District employment and contracting opportunities athttps://www.linkedin.com/company/u-s-army-corps-of-engineers-nashville-district.
title: Corps of Engineers waives day-use fees at recreation areas in observance of Veterans Day

Biofuels—fuels made from biomass—have been used in the United States as a transportation fuel for decades. Ethanol produced from corn starch and biodiesel produced from soybean oil are two examples of biofuels used in vehicles. In most cases, these biofuels when used as transportation fuel in vehicles are blended with their petroleum fuel counterpart at a low level. In general, low-blend fuel (LB fuel) includes ethanol blended at a rate of 10% or lower (e.g., E10) and biodiesel blended at a rate of 5% or lower (e.g., B5). High-blend fuel (HB fuel) includes biofuel blended at a higher rate, such as ethanol blended at a rate greater than 10% (e.g., E15, a fuel blend of gasoline blended with 10.5-15% ethanol).
The Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program (HBIIP) is an initiative created by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) in 2020 to increase the sales and use of higher blends of ethanol and biodiesel. HBIIP funding has mostly come from the USDA Commodity Credit Corporation. However, under the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169), Congress provided $500 million to HBIIP for "installing, retrofitting, or otherwise upgrading fuel dispensers or pumps," among other investments.
One HB fuel that HBIIP supports, E15, receives considerable attention in the 119th Congress:
The second Trump Administration has taken several actions related to HBIIP, including the freezing of funds for HBIIP and releasing obligated funding for HBIIP for projects. Regarding E15, in the June 2026 supplemental funding request to Congress, the Trump Administration requested "an urgent and needed fix that codifies the permanent, year-round sale of E-15."
Congress may have questions about HBIIP and choose to conduct oversight of the program. For example, Congress may want to know more about the value received from HBIIP, program funding and implementation going forward, if there are environmental impacts associated with the use of HB fuel, monitoring nationwide HB fuel use, transportation fuel projections that could impact biofuel markets, and more. Alternatively, Congress may choose to take no action.
Congress has discussed high-blend fuel (HB fuel) and has provided support for HB fueling infrastructure.1 In short, a biofuel is a fuel (e.g., ethanol, biodiesel, biogas) produced from a biomass feedstock (e.g., crops, tree residue, animal waste, food waste) that can be used for transportation (e.g., cars, aviation). Typically, for most applications, biofuel has been blended at a low level with its petroleum counterpart for use in vehicles as a transportation fuel. For this report, low-blend fuel (LB fuel) includes ethanol blended at a rate of 10% or lower (e.g., E10) and biodiesel blended at a rate of 5% or lower (e.g., B5).2 The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reports that the "most common blend of ethanol is E10 (10% ethanol, 90% gasoline)."3 And, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that "almost all gasoline are E10 blends."4 In general, an HB fuel is a biofuel-petroleum fuel mixture with biofuel blended at a higher rate, such as ethanol blended at a rate greater than 10% (e.g., E15, a fuel blend of gasoline blended with 10.5-15% ethanol).
One type of HB fuel that has received attention from Congress is E15, gasoline blended with 10.5-15% ethanol.5 In January 2026, the House established the E-15 Rural Domestic Energy Council (Council) to investigate the sale of E15, among other actions.6 In May 2026, the House passed H.R. 1346, the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025, which would, in part, allow for the year-round sale of E15.7 In a supplemental funding request sent to Congress in June 2026, the Trump Administration requested "an urgent and needed fix that codifies the permanent, year-round sale of E-15."8 In September 2026, the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry reported out of committee S. 5526, the Agricultural Act of 2026, which would also allow for the year-round sale of E15.9
Congress has considered the year-round sale of E15 previously. Congress included a provision for the permanent year-round sale of E15 in a short-term FY2025 spending bill introduced in the House in December 2024 (H.R. 10445; 118th Congress), but it was removed from the FY2025 continuing resolution package that became law (P.L. 118-158).
Congress has taken action to both revoke and issue federal funding for HB fueling infrastructure (e.g., blender pumps).10 For example, the Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 farm bill; P.L. 113-79) precludes the use of Rural Energy for America Program (REAP) funding for any mechanism for dispensing energy at the retail level (e.g., ethanol-gasoline blender pumps).11 Conversely, the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (P.L. 117-169) provided $500 million to the Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program (HBIIP) for "installing, retrofitting, or otherwise upgrading fuel dispensers or pumps," among other investments.
HBIIP is an initiative led by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to "increase significantly the sales and use of higher blends of ethanol and biodiesel."12 In 2025, the Trump Administration froze funding for HBIIP and then announced it would release obligated funding under the program.13 In 2026, the Trump Administration announced that "[f]unds for the program have now been exhausted, and USDA will not be making further obligations absent future appropriation."14
This report provides an overview of HBIIP and HB fuel usage and infrastructure costs and contains questions Congress may consider in its oversight of HBIIP.
Biofuels are liquid fuels and blending components produced from biomass feedstocks, used primarily for transportation.15 The two leading biofuels produced and used for transportation in the United States are ethanol and biomass-based diesel.16 LB fuel is approved for use in light-duty vehicles by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and vehicle manufacturers.17 HB fuels include higher blends of "ethanol (i.e., greater than 10 percent ethanol) and biodiesel (greater than 5 percent biodiesel)."18 The approval to use HB fuels in light-duty vehicles can vary by fuel type, vehicle model year, and vehicle manufacturer.19
In general, infrastructure required for HB fuel is the same type of infrastructure required for LB fuel (e.g., fuel dispenser, underground storage tank), but the HB fueling infrastructure is constructed specifically to endure the composition of HB fuel.20 In short, not all vehicles on the road are certified by their vehicle manufacturer to use HB fuel, and not all fueling stations have the required infrastructure to sell HB fuel.
Both corn-starch ethanol and biomass-based diesel are established biofuels that can be blended into conventional fuel (i.e., petroleum fuel). For several years, production, consumption, and logistics for these fuels have been traditionally centered on low percentage levels (i.e., 10% ethanol and 5% biodiesel). In current LB fuel markets, industry knows how to produce the biofuel, the infrastructure exists to get the LB fuel to market, and consumers know that their vehicle manufacturer has approved the use of the LB fuel. Corn-starch ethanol and biomass-based diesel may be blended into conventional fuel at a higher rate. Using these biofuels at higher-blend rates could require different infrastructure and may raise some questions by lawmakers, consumers, and others.21
The predicament, mainly for biofuel supporters, is adapting the existing infrastructure—potentially nationwide—to use HB fuel.22 This might require, at a minimum, legislative and regulatory changes (depending on the HB fuel), funding (e.g., private funding, federal appropriations), administrative support (e.g., program staff to issue federal funding, technical expertise to install the infrastructure), and a willingness by industry and consumers to do so (e.g., a station owner who will upgrade their equipment, a consumer who will purchase an HB fuel). It remains unclear whether federal involvement and investment would encourage fueling station owners and others to upgrade their infrastructure to handle HB fuel and motivate consumers to purchase HB fuel.
HB fuel brings opportunities and challenges. Increased production of biomass feedstocks and biofuels could stimulate certain rural economies and segments of the agricultural sector. Conversely, if consumers were to purchase additional amounts of HB fuels, the increased demand could cause competition for feedstocks, interrupt feedstock pricing, and raise environmental concerns, among other issues.
Some HB fuels face circumstances unique to the biofuel blend type. For example, for ethanol, consumers may consider the energy content and engine performance of the HB fuel (e.g., E15). Ethanol has a lower energy content than gasoline yet a higher octane rating than gasoline.23 Consumers choosing to use HB fuel may consider fuel economy and performance, among other factors.
It is not clear how much HB fuel is consumed in the United States annually.24 Due to variations in fuel mixtures (e.g., E15, E20, E85, B20), infrastructure capacity, vehicle manufacturer requirements, and state regulations—and for other reasons—it is difficult to ascertain nationwide consumption trends for HB fuel using publicly available data.25
Some states and stakeholders monitor HB fuel consumption, but their observations are generally focused on specific HB fuel(s) and/or a particular region. For example, the Iowa state government prepares an annual report of fuel gallons sold or dispensed in Iowa.26 The report contains a table that provides Iowa gasoline, diesel, and biofuel sales for 2025, as reported by retailers, including 870.7 million gallons of E10, 410.1 million gallons of E15, 0.9 million gallons of E20, and 24.0 million gallons of E85.27 The annual report also states that "ethanol blends of E15 or higher constituted 27 percent of all gasoline sold or dispensed in 2025."28
It is also not clear how many fueling stations sell HB fuel. This is partly due to the variety of HB fuels that can be sold. Some data are available for certain HB fuels, but comprehensive data are not available. For example, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) reports that more than 3,000 fueling stations sell E15, and more than 4,200 fueling stations sell E85.29 DOE also provides the number of public and private biodiesel fueling station locations by state that offer HB fuel of B20 or higher.30 For example, DOE reports Illinois has 490 such public biodiesel fueling stations.31 The fueling stations that sell HB fuel are a small fraction of the total number of fueling stations located in the United States. For example, the Oak Ridge National Laboratory reports there were 142,000 conventional refueling stations in 2020.32
The cost of equipping a fueling station to sell HB fuel varies.33 Infrastructure costs are facility-specific depending on what HB fuel will be sold and what equipment the station may need to upgrade to sell HB fuel. DOE reports there are approximately 60 pieces of equipment at a fueling station that handle fuel and vapor, some of which are below ground.34 Station owners interested in selling an HB fuel might inspect their fueling station equipment to determine what equipment may be compatible and what equipment would need to be upgraded, and may also take into consideration the design life of the existing equipment and consumer demand, among other things, before making a decision to upgrade or not upgrade their equipment to sell an HB fuel.
Using ethanol as an example, USDA reports that "[w]hile virtually all stations have equipment necessary for storing and dispensing E10, it is difficult to discern how many have fueling equipment compatible with ethanol blends above E10."35 USDA reports the costs, as calculated by researchers with the U.S. DRIVE Partnership, under various conversion scenarios for a station to sell different ethanol-gasoline fuel blends.36 As of 2019, the individual equipment station upgrade costs for E11-E25 fuel ranged from approximately $21,000 for a light conversion scenario to $379,000 for an extensive conversion scenario.37
EPA has taken actions pertaining to HB fueling infrastructure. In 2021, EPA released a proposed rule to, in part, make "changes to E15 fuel dispenser labeling requirements" and "to modify underground storage tank (UST) regulations to accommodate the safe storage of E15 and higher gasoline-ethanol blends at retail stations' existing tank systems."38 EPA reports that "the chemical and physical properties of biobased fuels, such as ethanol and biodiesel, can be more degrading to certain UST system materials than petroleum alone."39 EPA also acknowledges the growth in biofuels over time and the fuel waivers EPA issued allowing for the sale of E15 in the summer, and EPA thus proposed "a requirement that UST systems installed, or UST equipment and components replaced, must be constructed with equipment and components compatible with ethanol blends up to 100 percent."40 EPA has not yet issued the final rule.41
HBIIP, a USDA initiative created in 2020, aims to "increase significantly the sales and use of higher blends of ethanol and biodiesel" and "is intended to encourage a more comprehensive approach to marketing higher blends by sharing the costs related to building out biofuel-related infrastructure."42 HBIIP awards cost-share grants that assist transportation fueling and biodiesel distribution facilities with upgrading or installing new infrastructure to be compatible with high-blend ethanol and biodiesel (e.g., E15 fuel dispensers, B20 fuel dispensers, ethanol storage tanks, and biodiesel storage tanks).43 USDA reports that consideration will also be given to biodiesel terminal operations and home heating oil distribution centers.44
HBIIP has been mentioned in the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions (unified agenda).45 According to the Fall 2023 unified agenda, HBIIP is "intended to encourage a more comprehensive approach to market higher blends by sharing the costs related to building out biofuel-related infrastructure."46 The Fall 2023 unified agenda also states that the USDA Rural Business-Cooperative Service (RBCS) implements the program and that the "underlying statutes authorizing RBCS to create these regulations are 5 U.S.C. 301 and 7 U.S.C. 1989."47 According to a 2026 unified agenda entry for HBIIP, RCBS intends on "proposing a rule to codify the policies and procedures for the program in the Code of Federal Regulations" and "intends to conduct public engagement to hear from stakeholders and potential applicants about what they would like to see in the regulation."48
HBIIP funding comes from the USDA Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC).49 The program received $500 million in supplemental funding from the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA; P.L. 117-169).50 The funding is statutorily authorized in 7 U.S.C. §8103(i).51 Congress has not authorized or directly appropriated additional funding for the program since the IRA. USDA last issued a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) for HBIIP in June 2023, establishing five consecutive quarterly application windows that accepted submissions starting July 1, 2023, through September 30, 2024, with the option for a sixth application window if funding was not exhausted.52 As of October 2026, USDA reports that "[f]unds for the program have now been exhausted, and the Department will not be making further obligations absent future appropriation."53
USDA has released some award data for HBIIP (see Table 1). CRS estimates of HBIIP awards provided in Table 1 are not comprehensive, were derived from publicly available information, and may not reflect all HBIIP awards granted by USDA. The publicly released HBIIP award data announced in 2026 are less granular than the award data announced in prior years. In January 2025, USDA reported that "[t]o date, USDA has invested … more than $287 million in 345 projects through HBIIP that increase the availability of domestic biofuels across the country" and "[s]ince the start of the Biden-Harris Administration, USDA has invested … more than $323 million in 399 awards through HBIIP."54 CRS estimates in Table 1 for HBIIP awards that USDA announced in 2020 through 2025 derived from publicly available information differ from what USDA reported on January 10, 2025.
The HBIIP awards announced in January 2025 give financial support for infrastructure (e.g., fuel pumps, dispensers, and storage tanks) that supports ethanol and biodiesel fuel mixtures, mostly in the forms of E15, E85, and B20.55 The program also supports B100.56 For example, there is a project focused on the infrastructure for a home heating oil distribution facility company (i.e., modify a storage tank to store B100 and blend B20) and a fleet facility company (i.e., install two B100 fuel dispensers and one B100 storage tank).57
Table 1. Announced Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program (HBIIP) Awards Identified by a Public Search
Sources: Adapted by CRS from award tables provided by U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program, October 8, 2020, https://www.rd.usda.gov/sites/default/files/NR_HBIIP_CHART10082020.pdf; USDA, Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program, August 19, 2021, https://www.rd.usda.gov/sites/default/files/usda_rd_nr_hbiip_chart.pdf; USDA, Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program, June 26, 2023, https://www.rd.usda.gov/media/file/download/usda-rd-nr-hbiip-chart-06262023pdf; USDA, Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program, October 29, 2024, https://www.rd.usda.gov/media/file/download/final-hbiip-102924.pdf; USDA, Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program, January 10, 2025, https://www.rd.usda.gov/media/file/download/reap-hbiip-final-01102025.pdf; and USDA, "USDA Rural Development Invests $11.5 Million in 13 Projects to Advance Economic Development and Expand the Sale of Renewable Fuels in Iowa," press release, April 7, 2026.
Notes: Data in this table should not be considered comprehensive. Data are based on a search of publicly available information using certain keywords. For example, USDA reports $570.6 million in investment dollars for 646 investments for HBIIP. See USDA, Rural Investments by State/County Dashboard – Grants and Loans by Program, accessed November 3, 2026, https://www.rd.usda.gov/rural-data-gateway/rural-investments/by-county. Additional information for the HBIIP awards—including the recipients, project grant amounts, project descriptions, and congressional representatives—are provided in the USDA sources referenced above. The combination of two or more states, separated by forward slashes, indicates that entities operating in multiple states may receive infrastructure improvements under the project award.
a. The year the awards were announced by USDA.
b. Some projects were funded under HBIIP and some under funding provided for HBIIP by the law commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA; P.L. 117-169).
In the first three months of the second Trump Administration, the White House froze funding for HBIIP, implemented USDA staffing changes, and reported that it had released obligated funding under HBIIP for projects. On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14154, which paused the disbursement of funds appropriated through the IRA and required a review of the processes for issuing grants for programs funded by the IRA, among other things.59 Also on January 20, 2025, President Trump ordered a hiring freeze for the executive branch and requested the creation of a federal hiring plan, among other things.60 On March 31, 2025, the Trump Administration announced it would release approximately $537 million in obligated funding for HBIIP for 543 projects, including "new projects approved within the first 100 days of the Trump Administration".61
The second Trump Administration continues to take actions where the outcome to HBIIP is unclear. For example, it is not clear if the staffing changes at USDA will impact USDA's implementation of HBIIP.62 On June 17, 2026, USDA announced the reorganization of the Rural Development (RD) mission area, including for the RBCS, which administers HBIIP. USDA reported, "Select functions and positions with the Rural Business-Cooperative Service will relocate from the [National Capital Region] to Dallas-Fort Worth, Texas, which will serve as the primary national hub for the agency's RBCS and RUS [Rural Utilities Service] loan and grant functions."63 On July 24, 2025, USDA Secretary Rollins announced the reorganization of USDA.64 Finally, on July 29, 2026, Secretary Rollins announced a USDA "100 Hires in 100 Days" initiative that will "recruit veterans, transitioning service members, and military spouses."65
The Supreme Court has established that Congress has the power to conduct oversight of federal programs.66 As such, Congress may or may not choose to assess past, current, and potentially future HBIIP administration by USDA. And Congress may or may not choose to consider HB fuel consumption rates, infrastructure costs, potential environmental impacts, and other issues related to HBIIP. Congress could choose to take no action. Alternatively, Congress could decide to explore the above-mentioned areas, and may consider the following questions and data requests, which are presented in no order of priority.67
title: The Higher Blends Infrastructure Incentive Program (HBIIP): An Overview

Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Supercharges American Dominance in Commercial Space
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced four key regulatory actions by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to streamline commercial space launch and reentry licensing along with plans for a major regulatory overhaul in 2027. The Department also announced a hiring initiative to supercharge the agency’s Office of Commercial Space Transportation.
The actions cut regulatory burdens and enhance operational flexibility without compromising FAA safety standards:
- Proposed Rule: Defines when a flight abort isn’t mandatory and allows operators to toggle abort capability during flight.
- Proposed Rule: Clarifies requirements and thresholds for when an abort must occur.
- Proposed Rule: Lets operators account for vehicle breakup to rule out high-consequence multi-casualty events during random reentry.
- Final Rule: Applies minor technical corrections across commercial space rules.
“President Trump is supercharging America’s booming commercial space industry making it more innovative and safer than ever before,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “That includes getting rid of the outdated rules that hold innovators back, recruiting the best and brightest aerospace engineers, and unleashing American space dominance while never compromising on safety.”
Looking ahead, the FAA will initiate a comprehensive overhaul of its licensing framework in 2027 to keep pace with rapid commercial space innovation and support an anticipated cadence of 1,000 launches per year by 2030.
To support this mission, the agency is expanding its Office of Commercial Space Transportation workforce with its first Associate Administrator and a new team of aerospace engineers. These engineers will conduct safety analysis, evaluations, and mission authorizations to accelerate application turnaround while keeping the public safe during space operations. Applications must be received by December 4.
“The SPACE Task Force is moving at warp speed to support President Trump’s goal of continuing America’s dominance in space,” said U.S. Under Secretary for Transportation Ryan McCormack. “We’re leaving no stone unturned to safely reform licensing and environmental regulations, identify new spaceport locations, create priority airspace for space launches, and hire the workforce to make it all a reality."
“We are clearing the regulatory runway for an unprecedented golden age of commercial spaceflight,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “And we have great job opportunities on our licensing team to play a direct and integral role in shaping the future of American space innovation.”
The U.S. was responsible for 217 of the 329 commercial space launches worldwide in 2025 and we expect to see that number will soar to 10,000 FAA-licensed launches and reentries a year by 2035.
Additional Information:
These actions build on the five proposed rules that Secretary Duffy announced last month, which were developed in concert with the recently launched USDOT Space Policy Administration, Coordination, and Execution (SPACE) Task Force, as well as President Trump’s space policy goals in his Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry Executive Order and National Space Transportation Policy.
The FAA also issued a proposed rule that would allow the agency to waive unnecessary environmental laws and regulations that are impeding American space innovation. In addition, the FAA is asking the public and industry for ideas on two big issues: where to build new spaceports and creating “priority airspace” for space-launch routes.
title: Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Supercharges American Dominance in Commercial Space

Two ‘forever chemicals’ associated with higher risk of aggressive breast cancer in NIH analysis
WASHINGTON, D.C.—NOVEMBER 5, 2026—Women with higher blood levels of two common per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also familiarly known as PFAS, were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer, according to a new study by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). PFAS are a large group of chemicals used in common consumer products. Often referred to as “forever chemicals,” PFAS do not break down easily in the environment and can remain in the body for years.
The study found that women with higher blood plasma levels of two of these substances, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), were associated with a higher incidence of ER-negative breast cancer. No clear association was observed between the two chemicals and breast cancer risk overall.
“Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump’s leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.”
ER-negative tumors lack receptors that allow hormone estrogen to help cancer cells grow. Compared with breast cancers that respond to hormone estrogen, ER-negative breast cancers tend to be more aggressive and have worse outcomes. Scientists know less about what raises the risk of this type of breast cancer.
“Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors,” explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study. The findings are reported in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.
NIH researchers and their collaborators measured 17 PFAS in blood, collected years before women were diagnosed with cancer. Women in the group with the highest PFOA levels had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than those in the lowest group. For PFOS, the rate was 93% higher, or nearly twice as high. These numbers describe relative differences between groups, not an individual woman’s chance of getting breast cancer.
The research drew on the Sister Study, led by NIH’s National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). The larger study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35–74 in the United States and Puerto Rico from 2003 to 2009. None had breast cancer when they joined the Sister Study, but each had a full or half-sister who had been previously diagnosed with breast cancer. For the PFAS study, researchers included 1,609 women who developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women.
“These findings matter for women’s health broadly,” said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., a former research fellow at NIH and a current researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. “Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention.”
Because the strongest associations involved tumors without hormone receptors, the authors suggest that PFAS may affect cancer risk through other non-hormonal biologic pathways. Possible pathways include changes in gene activity or immune system. However, this study did not test those explanations. The authors say future studies should evaluate people with higher PFAS exposure and in groups more affected by ER-negative breast cancer.
Although most individuals have measurable levels of PFOA and PFOS in their bodies, these compounds have been largely phased out and replaced with new PFAS compounds. “More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals,” White said.
This research was supported by NIEHS grants: Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.
Reference: Chang CJ, Pullella K, Keil AP, et al. Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Exposure and Breast Cancer Incidence in the Sister Study. Journal of Clinical Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO-26-00318.

HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael D. Nammar, Assistant U.S. Attorney Aislinn K. Affinito, Victim Assistance Specialist Leilani Uganiza, Supervisory IT Specialist Cheryl Tagaca, and Supervisory Paralegal Specialist Kari Sherman, all of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Hawaii, as well as Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Murray Acosta, IRS Criminal Investigation Special Agent Shaun Morita, Environmental Protection Agency Special Agent Jan Yukumoto, FBI Special Agent Thomas Palmer, and FBI Special Agent Joshua Parker were among 183 Department of Justice employees recognized by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director Francey Hakes at the 2026 Director’s Awards Ceremony held October 28, 2026, in the Great Hall of the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building in Washington, D.C. The awards recognize outstanding achievements by employees of the U.S. Attorney’s Offices.

The team received the Director’s Award for Superior Performance by a Litigation Team for their role in the investigation and prosecution of the Miske Enterprise, led by Michael J. Miske, which was a violent criminal organization operating in Hawaii for decades. Although not eligible for the Director’s Award, having since left the Department of Justice, the team also included former Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Inciong and KeAupuni Akina. Inciong was the lead prosecutor who directed the investigation and prosecution of the Miske Enterprise and served as lead counsel at the trial of Michael J. Miske. Inciong retired in March 2025 after nearly 27 years of service as a federal prosecutor.

“I could not be prouder of the tireless work of the outstanding Assistant U.S. Attorneys, staff, and agents who dismantled the Miske Enterprise and brought Michael Miske’s reign of murder, felony assaults, kidnappings, intimidation, chemical attacks, drug trafficking, and fraud to an end,” said U.S. Attorney Ken Sorenson. “Miske and his henchmen were a scourge upon the State of Hawaii, terrorizing our communities and openly profiting from violence, drug trafficking, and fraud. In addition to those who received the Director’s Award, this achievement belongs to the many additional agents, staff members, and other prosecutors who assisted our team in this extraordinary prosecution, including those like lead Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Inciong, who have since left the Department of Justice or law enforcement.”

Following an investigation lasting more than 10 years, the team presented a seven-month federal trial involving thousands of exhibits and hundreds of witnesses. Its work addressed racketeering activities involving murder, kidnapping, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking, fraud, obstruction, and chemical weapons attacks. The investigation and prosecutions resulted in the federal convictions of 20 members and associates, including Michael J. Miske, who was convicted at trial. The team’s sustained preparation and coordination dismantled the enterprise and strengthened public safety in communities throughout Hawaii.

The convictions were the result of an investigation conducted by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, the Criminal Investigation Division of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, with assistance from the Honolulu Police Department, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Coast Guard Investigative Service, the United States Marshals Service Fugitive Task Force, the Cybercrime Lab of the Department of Justice Criminal Division Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center, the Honolulu Fire Department, the Hawaii National Guard, 93rd Civil Support Team, the Office of Investigations-Office of the Inspector General for the Social Security Administration, and the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General.

EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 94 United States Attorneys’ offices around the country. For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao.
title: Attorney General Todd Blanche Honors 10 District of Hawaii Assistant U.S. Attorneys, Staff, and Agents at 2026 Director’s Awards

Press Statement

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

November 5, 2026

Cuba’s ruling elite is hoarding the island’s energy, shipping, and technology resources for its own enrichment, leaving the Cuban people to contend with blackouts, shortages, and a stagnant economy. The Marxist regime in Havana relies on a web of state-owned enterprises, joint ventures, and offshore intermediaries to keep this system running; its foreign backers supply the military equipment that helps sustain the regime’s military forces and enable its brutal repression, while propping up its persistent efforts to threaten, infiltrate and subvert the American homeland.

Today, pursuant to President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14404, “Imposing Sanctions on Those Responsible for Repression in Cuba and for Threats to United States National Security and Foreign Policy,” I am designating ten targets including additional Cuban elites, a crude oil shipping network, state-owned import and technical-support entities, and China-based suppliers of the regime’s military forces. I am also identifying five associated vessels as blocked property.

Among today’s targets is GUILLERMO FAUSTINO RODRIGUEZ LOPEZ CALLEJA, who is part of an extensive web of offshore shipping companies that move Cuban crude oil shipments to and from the island. I am also designating ANY RODRIGUEZ LASTRES, daughter of the previously designated Grupo de Administración Empresarial (GAESA) President Ania Guillermina Lastres Morera.

Additionally, the Department of the Treasury issued a determination pursuant to E.O. 14404 that authorizes the imposition of economic sanctions on any foreign person operating or having operated in the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

The Trump Administration will not stand by while the Cuban regime funnels the island’s resources to its military elite, while regime insiders and their family members profit from opaque offshore networks, and while Cuba continues to serve as a staging ground for a global coalition of hostile anti-American actors to threaten, spy on, and plot against the United States and its interests.

The Department’s actions are being taken pursuant to E.O. 14404, which authorizes sweeping sanctions on Cuba, including against persons who support the Cuban regime’s security apparatus and those responsible for repression in Cuba and other threats to U.S. national security. These actions also further both E.O. 14380, Addressing Threats to the United States by the Government of Cuba and National Security Presidential Memorandum 5 , which directs the Executive Branch to improve human rights, encourage the rule of law, foster free markets and free enterprise, and promote democracy in Cuba. For more information on today’s action, see the Department of State’s Fact Sheet .

WASHINGTON, D.C./November 5, 2026 – Today, Federal News Network published an op-ed by Special Counsel Charles Baldis on the U.S. Office of Special Counsel’s (OSC’s) work in fiscal year (FY) 2026. The Special Counsel applauds OSC’s career employees for the impressive results they achieved, even with the 43-day government shutdown. Those results include a record 363 prohibited personnel practice cases resolved with at least one favorable outcome. OSC also referred 47 whistleblower disclosures for agency investigation, the most since FY 2021.
The article also highlighted several of OSC’s whistleblower disclosure cases that closed in FY 2026, including understaffing at the Federal Aviation Administration, overstaffing at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, reimbursement backlogs at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and systemic failures in opioid prescribing practices at the VA.
"These cases show why the disclosure process matters: an employee can identify a problem, an investigation establishes the facts, and the agency has an opportunity to correct it," Special Counsel Baldis wrote.
Read the full op-ed here.
The U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) is a federal investigative and prosecutorial agency. OSC’s statutory authority comes from four federal laws: the Civil Service Reform Act, the Whistleblower Protection Act, the Hatch Act, and the Uniformed Services Employment & Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA).
title: Special Counsel Baldis Highlights OSC's Fiscal Year 2026 Results in Federal News Network Op-Ed
