KANSAS CITY, KAN. – An illegal alien from Nicaragua pleaded guilty to using forged immigration documents to unlawfully gain employment in the United States.

According to court documents, Rolando Ariel Gonzalez-Gonzalez, 33, pleaded guilty to one count of fraud of misuse of a Visa (Permanent Resident Card).

In July 2026, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrested Gonzalez-Gonzalez who was being held at the Washington County Jail on an ICE detainer. While the agents were looking through the personal belongings Gonzalez-Gonzalez had on him when Washington County deputies arrested him, they found a lawful permanent resident card (also known as a green card) with his name, date of birth, and an alien registration number. A check of the database revealed Gonzalez-Gonzalez was not in the country legally and that the registration number on the green card was invalid.

Gonzalez-Gonzalez admitted paying someone $250 for the fraudulent green card. He unlawfully gained employment by filling out a Form I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification form and presenting the fraudulent card. He also used a Social Security number that was not issued to him.

On August 3, 2026, an immigration judge in Kansas City, Missouri, granted Gonzalez-Gonzalez the option of voluntary departure from the United States with the safeguards of being returned to Nicaragua.

"Illegal aliens often must commit fraud or identity theft to illegally work in the United States," said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. "Policies that lure people into entering the United States illegally are fundamentally unfair to the rule of law, the communities harmed by these crimes, and the individuals who must continually violate the law to remain and work here."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is investigating the case.

###
title: Illegal alien pleads guilty to using forged immigration documents

NEWPORT NEWS, Va. – Nicolas Antonio Lainez, 19, was sentenced today to 20 years in prison for sexual exploitation of a child.

According to court documents, Lainez was living with a family on Fort Eustis on Feb. 7 when he recorded himself sexually exploiting a six-year-old victim. The video was uploaded to Lainez’s Google account via his cellphone, resulting in a CyberTipline Report notification from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) to the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division (Army CID) on March 11. The same day, Army CID agents arrived at the residence, seized the cellphone, and arrested Lainez.

Lainez was the subject of six NCMEC CyberTipline Reports and is attributed with a total of four video files and 14 image files of CSAM, including additional CSAM depicting the victim in this case.

Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Jake Cameron, Special Agent in Charge of the Washington Field Office, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division, made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge Mark S. Davis.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Peter G. Osyf prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc .

Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 4:26-cr-28.
title: Man who sexually exploited child at Fort Eustis sentenced to 20 years in prison

KANSAS CITY, Mo. – A Kansas City, Mo., woman has pleaded guilty to a firearms violation.

Courtney L. Jones, 48, pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm before U.S. District Judge Stephen R. Bough.

On July 5, 2025, Kansas City, Missouri Police officers were dispatched to the 3600 block of Agnes Avenue on a report of a disturbance involving a firearm. Upon arrival, an officer observed Jones moving around the driveway near her car. The officer approached Jones’s car and looked inside, observing in plain view a Romarm, Model Mini Draco, 7.62 x 39 mm pistol on the passenger seat. Jones, a convicted felon, was arrested.

Under federal statutes, Jones is subject to a sentence of up to 15 years in federal prison without parole. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rudolph R. Rhodes IV. It was investigated by Kansas City, Mo. Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .

Veteran-led events nationwide, new site making outdoor opportunities easier to find

Interior_Press@ios.doi.gov

WASHINGTON — The Department of the Interior today announced a slate of veteran-led outdoor recreation events on public lands and waters in the week surrounding Veterans Day, developed with partner agencies of the Federal Interagency Council on Outdoor Recreation (FICOR). Alongside the events, Interior and partners published a new repository on Rec.gov — a single location where veterans, service members and military families can find information about many outdoor recreation opportunities across participating federal agencies.

“Every American owes an enormous debt of gratitude to the brave men and women who have worn our nation’s uniform and defended the freedoms we cherish. Those freedoms include the opportunity to explore and enjoy the incredible beauty of our great country,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “This Veterans Day, I’m especially grateful for the members of our Interior team who served in uniform and are continuing their service by helping military families and fellow veterans experience the public lands that belong to all Americans.”

"This new article highlights opportunities for veterans that already existed, but were scattered across a dozen agency websites,” said FICOR Chair and Bureau of Land Management Director Stevan Pearce . “The FICOR is committed to continuing to make opportunities easier for veterans and military families to find.”

Events include:

In our nation’s capital area of Washington, DC, the National Park Service is offering both a walking tour of the war memorials around the National Mall and a guided birding walk through the Kenilworth Park and Aquatic Gardens in Anacostia.

Just outside Denver, Colorado, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is offering an accessible wildlife loop walk and visitor center program on a former Army arsenal at the Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge.

At Grandstaff Canyon in Moab, Utah, the Bureau of Land Management is hosting a veteran-led canyon hike.

In California, the Bureau of Reclamation is offering a fish hatchery tour, paired with a short riverside hike at the Nimbus Fish Hatchery in Cordova.

Additional events are planned at Interior sites, including the Grand Canyon in Arizona, Pompeys Pillar National Monument in Montana, Steamtown National Historic Site in Pennsylvania and even a Veterans Family Fishing Classic in Wyoming, just to name a few.

Accessibility features served as a leading criteria for event sites, not an afterthought. Featured locations include accessible boardwalks and paved routes, indoor and visitor-center alternatives and facility tours that do not depend on weather or terrain.

To find the event nearest you, email: DOI_Veteran_Outdoor_Engagement_Initiative_Team@ios.doi.gov

The Department of the Air Force is accelerating its push to operationalize enterprise intelligence and deliver combat-ready artificial intelligence capabilities directly to the warfighter, unveiling a comprehensive modernization blueprint Oct. 27.
Speaking at the annual Institute for Defense and Government Advancement Military Flight Training USA Summit, Susan Davenport, chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the Department of the Air Force, outlined the DAF’s strategy to move super intelligence beyond experimental testing and into operational application across 15 mission domains.
The transition hinges on establishing these 15 operational domains — spanning core areas such as nuclear operations, intelligence and human resources — each spearheaded by a general officer or Senior Executive Service civilian to govern authoritative data and deliver mission-critical tools to the field." I always say SI is an organizational design decision and return on investment is measured by the outcomes we were able to achieve — in other words — did we shorten the kill chain, or return time back to the commander, or did we create decision advantage?” said Davenport. “In order to get the best outcome, we must redesign the process before we digitize it."
To prevent these strategies from becoming "shelfware," the DAF has established 15 distinct operational domains spanning critical areas from intelligence and nuclear operations to human resources. Each domain is overseen by a dedicated senior leader, a general officer or SES member, tasked with operationalizing the strategy and making trustworthy, authoritative data available immediately.
"To operationalize the strategies, we stood up 15 domains across air and space and placed a general officer or Senior Executive Service member on top of each domain, and they’re responsible for making trustworthy data available to the enterprise and accelerating SI in their domain," Davenport explained.
While Davenport’s team lays the technical groundwork for big Air Force systems, force development leaders stress that these technical advancements must align with human growth.
Dr. Wendy Walsh, Air Education and Training Command’s chief learning officer, also participated during the panel, alongside Davenport.
"We build a capability and a capacity, and those are the enabling structures of how people realize mission command, and that is perfect for SI as well," noted Walsh. "It's a new technology. How are we going to do this? How are we going to build the trust and work together?"
As the department systematically rolls out these capabilities domain by domain, leaders stress that human oversight remains the crucial element to success.
More information on SI literacy is expected to be delivered to Airmen and Guardians later this year.
title: DAF unveils enterprise blueprint to field operational SI across 15 mission domains

USAG BAVARIA – HOHENFELS, Germany – Children of Hohenfels can immerse themselves in sight, sound, touch, scent and play now at the Child Development Center’s new sensory garden, the result of a garrison community member’s Eagle Scout project.
Ryder Fletcher, a scout with Hohenfels Troop 303, conceived the project from his experience with similar sensory trails in the woods of Germany, and, with the help of more than 20 volunteers, he built up the garden over the course of two weekends.
“I wanted to make something that would last and have a lasting impact,” said Fletcher. “The most important thing that we emphasize in scouts is giving back to the community, and that’s what the Eagle project’s main goal is.”
While the CDC already has play areas outside, the sensory garden has many features that distinguish it. The children can play tic-tac-toe with a set of rocks painted to resemble bees and ladybugs. There is a rock garden with painted stones featuring words from the Boy Scout Law, hedged by plants that thrive outdoors in Germany. In warmer months and sunnier weather, children may go unshod on a path with different textures – wood, grass, pebbles, stone, and woodchips. And when the sun shines, transparent colored panels provide colorful umbrage from a wooden structure, from which are also suspended chimes of different notes in chromatic sequence. And, as the sensory garden is indeed a garden, there are many plants, including a few redolent species such as lavender and southernwood.
Volunteers accomplished most of the garden construction during the first weekend. They brought a wheelbarrow to haul dirt and other materials. Concrete was poured to anchor the wood structure. Volunteers heaved pickaxes to dig up the sensory walk and remove fist-size stones. Despite the difficulties the volunteers faced this one weekend, most of the volunteer time was not accounted for then.
“You always think the execution’s going to be more difficult and take longer,” Fletcher said. “I had a good more 50 hours of planning time than I did as execution.”
Fletcher coordinated with many organizations to accomplish a weekend of building including with the 15th Engineer Battalion, who helped Fletcher procure lumber and other material. He had help from the Directorate of Public Works, who provided gravel, soil and sand. The local Cub Scout pack also aided in the construction. The USO also helped Ryder with his coordination.
Alongside the plants, the children have small plastic watering cans with which to care for the plants. Ryder also ensured the staff of the CDC have a plan to care for the garden and its equipment.
“Right now I have my maintenance guy every morning make sure that – in the summer – the plants are watered,” said Corey Coon, facility director for the CDC. “We want to extend this project, not just for this year but for years to come.”
“This brings a different element to our playgrounds,” said Beth Payne, Child and Youth Services coordinator. “We’re very fortunate here at Hohenfels CDC to have been the recipient.”
“I’m so happy it turned out the way it did,” said Coon. “He went over and beyond. I was amazed by how he did it.”
Fletcher lives in Grafenwoehr, but every Wednesday he makes the trip down to USAG Bavaria – Hohenfels. While his father was a service member, the Family called Hohenfels their home. His father retired and found work as a civilian at Tower Barracks, and so Fletcher makes a weekly commute to remain part of the troop he had been with before moving an hour north.
“I just had that connection with my troop,” said Fletcher of his decision to stay with Troop 303.
While Fletcher is still years out from leaving the Army community, he foresees a career in education or in music for himself.
title: Hohenfels children feel good about sensory garden eagle scout project

Administrator Zeldin Completes 4-Day Swing Across Florida, Meeting with Ranchers, Scientists, Energy Producers, and Manufacturers
WASHINGTON — Last weekend, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin traveled across Midwestern and Southeastern Florida where he met with Florida ranchers, manufacturers, storm recovery professionals, and scientists. The visit to the Sunshine State highlighted the importance of protecting water infrastructure and resources needed to adequately treat wastewater against natural disasters, erosion, outdated pesticides, and inadequate wastewater treatment procedures.
On Friday, October 30, Administrator Zeldin visited Duke Energy’s Storm Recovery Command Center in St. Petersburg, Florida. While there, he discussed the importance of coordination between electric utilities, EPA, and state and local emergency responders to protect communities, prevent environmental emergencies, and accelerate recovery efforts following hurricanes.
Later that day, Administrator Zeldin visited the M&B Bottling and Processing Facility in Tampa, Florida. They discussed how farming, wastewater management, hay fields, and milk production connect with an operation that has lasted for nearly 40 years.
On Saturday, October 31, Administrator Zeldin toured Soilcea Citrus Field in Seffner, Florida. Administrator Zeldin witnessed CarriCea T1, Soilcea’s precision-bred citrus rootstock that helps trees defend themselves against citrus greening. This technology was approved by the Trump EPA in April, 2026, after the agency completed its safety review. The visit highlighted the Trump EPA’s commitment to using gold-standard science to provide solutions to environmental issues impacting communities.
The next day, Administrator Zeldin visited the Doc Partin Ranch in St. Cloud, Florida. He toured the working cattle ranch with the Osceola County Commissioner, Ricky Booth, and Florida State Representative, Erika Booth, and met with the Partin family to learn about their nearly two-century family history of farming in Florida. The Administrator also discussed the ranch’s partnership with the South Florida Water Management District and highlighted how private landowners and agricultural producers can play a role in protecting water resources and supporting the restoration of the Everglades.
On Monday, November 2, Administrator Zeldin met with Sox Erosion Solutions in Boca Raton, Florida. They discussed their erosion-control technology designed to stabilize shorelines, prevent soil erosion, and protect waterways. Companies such as Sox Erosion Solutions advance the Trump EPA’s commitment to gold-standard science and environmental problem solvers to strengthen and protect water resources.
Administrator Zeldin wrapped his four-day swing touring the FPL West County Energy Center in Loxahatchee, Florida, and witnessing their emissions-control technology and facility. The Trump EPA’s commitment to protecting water infrastructure, water resources, and promoting gold-standard science used by environmental problem solvers were major topics throughout the visit. The visit focused on the Trump EPA’s commitment to unleashing American energy and promoting gold-standard science to protect and power communities across the state.
title: Administrator Zeldin Completes 4-Day Swing Across Florida, Meeting with Ranchers, Scientists, Energy Producers, and Manufacturers

LAS VEGAS – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Nevada announced that five individuals were indicted, and two more individuals made their initial appearances in court, all for crimes involving firearms.

“The indictments handed down today represent a decisive strike against illegal gun violence,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “This office will not stand by while violent actors abuse firearms to terrorize our neighborhoods. If you unlawfully possess a firearm, if you traffic weapons, or if you use a gun to commit crimes in this district, federal law enforcement is coming for you. There will be no leniency. There will be no safe harbor.”

A federal grand jury has indicted the following individuals.

Lil Jarmarr Baker-Reed , of North Las Vegas, allegedly fired multiple rounds from a 9mm Ruger pistol at another individual. Some of those rounds hit a nearby restaurant. Baker-Reed has three prior felony convictions for burglary, grand larceny, and possession or transfer of a stolen vehicle. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. He is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. If convicted, Baker-Reed faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Kyle Fuller is prosecuting the case.

Michael Kirk Brooks , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a 9mm P365 and possessed with intent to distribute methamphetamine. He has prior felony convictions for ownership or possession of a firearm by a prohibited person; battery resulting in substantial bodily harm constituting domestic violence; attempt of grand larceny; felon in possession of a firearm; and conspiracy to commit robbery, all in Clark County, Nevada. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. Brooks is charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, one count of possession of a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, and one count of felon in possession of a firearm. If convicted, Brooks faces a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case.

Jimmy Dean McFarland , of Las Vegas, allegedly robbed a store at gunpoint. McFarland has a prior felony conviction for robbery with the use of firearms. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. McFarland is charged with one count of interference with commerce by robbery, one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, and one count of brandishing a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison. The FBI investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Melinda Brewer is prosecuting the case.

A Las Vegas woman allegedly purchased a firearm for a Las Vegas man who is a prohibited person. Both are charged with one count of conspiracy to straw purchase firearms, false statement in acquisition of a firearm, aiding and abetting, and the woman is also charged with straw purchasing of firearms. If convicted, they each face a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Tina Snellings is prosecuting the case.

Additionally, two men made their initial appearances in court on Wednesday for alleged violations of federal firearms laws.

Dominic Flanagan , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a 9mm caliber pistol. He has prior felony convictions for battery by strangulation, attempted battery with a deadly weapon with substantial bodily harm, and armed robbery, all in Clark County, Nevada. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. Flanagan is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. Jury trial is scheduled for January 4, 2027, before United States District Judge Cristina D. Silva. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The FBI investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Melinda Brewer is prosecuting the case.

Christiano Decarlo , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a .38 caliber firearm; a 12-gauge shotgun; a 410 bore firearm; and a 12-gauge shotgun. He has prior felony convictions for interfering with commerce by threat of violence and felon in possession of a firearm, both in Nevada. Decarlo is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. Jury trial is scheduled for January 4, 2027, before United States District Judge Gloria M. Navarro. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The FBI investigated the case.

The public may submit anonymous tips about gun crimes to ATF by calling 1-888-ATF-TIPS (1-888-283-8477) or by submitting a tip online at www.atf.gov/contact/atf-tips .

An indictment merely contains accusations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Reps. Salinas, Mackenzie Introduce Bill to Protect Patients When Insurance Companies Drop Their Providers
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman Andrea Salinas (OR-06) and Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (PA-07) introduced the Right to Re-Enroll Act. The bipartisan bill would protect patients from unexpected changes to their health insurance coverage. It would allow Americans enrolled in Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace plans to switch insurance plans outside of the annual open enrollment period if their provider or health system is dropped from their insurance network.
When providers and insurance companies fail to reach agreements on contracts, patients can suddenly lose access to the clinicians and hospitals they rely on. These disputes are becoming increasingly common. Between 2021 and 2025, nearly one in five non-federal hospitals experienced a public contract dispute with an insurance company, and nearly 10 percent temporarily fell out of network with an insurer.
“Families are already paying too much for health care. They shouldn't have to worry about losing their provider on top of it,” said Rep. Salinas. “Right now, patients can find themselves stuck paying for a plan that no longer covers their provider or hospital. That's especially concerning for people living in rural areas who are far from other providers, or for people undergoing treatment who can't afford an interruption in care. No one should lose access to their provider because their insurance company and health system can't agree on a contract. This bill gives patients the freedom to find a plan that meets their needs and protects them from unexpectedly losing access to care.”
“Patients and families across the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos should not have to worry about losing access to their trusted doctors or facing unexpected disruptions in care because of changes to their insurance network,” said Congressman Ryan Mackenzie. “The bipartisan Right to Re-Enroll Act would give patients more options when unexpected changes to their insurance coverage disrupt their access to care. By working across the aisle, we can put patients first and help ensure greater access to quality, affordable health care.”
Currently, Medicare Advantage enrollees have the ability to change plans when significant changes are made to their provider networks. However, Americans who purchase health insurance through ACA marketplaces do not have the same protections when their insurance company drops a provider from its network.
The Right to Re-Enroll Act would:
- Give patients the right to switch plans: Create a 60-day special enrollment period for individuals enrolled in ACA marketplace plans when a provider leaves their insurance network, outside of the annual enrollment period.
- Protect patients from unexpected costs: Require insurers to maintain existing coverage terms and in-network cost-sharing for qualifying patients who continue receiving care from an affected provider for 90 days.
- Require insurers to notify patients: Ensure patients receive notice within seven days of a network change, including information about their right to switch plans and how changing plans could affect their deductible and out-of-pocket costs.
The legislation would apply to ACA marketplace plans beginning in 2027.
“When changes happen in insurance networks or coverage, continuity of care keeps treatment for patients safe and consistent,” said Becky Hultberg, president and CEO of the Hospital Association of Oregon. “Reducing avoidable disruption is the right thing to do for patients, safeguarding their care and easing their burden during treatment. Rep. Salinas’ Right to Re-Enroll Act puts patients first, giving them the peace of mind of knowing they can choose a different health plan during a special re-enrollment period so they can continue getting the care they need without interruption.”
This legislation is endorsed by Families USA, American Psychological Association, Young Invincibles, and the Hospital Association of Oregon.
title: Reps. Salinas, Mackenzie Introduce Bill to Protect Patients When Insurance Companies Drop Their Providers

U.S. Trustee Program Prevails at Trial to Revoke $3.9M Discharge from Seattle Man Who Concealed Inheritance Rights and Business Interest
A Seattle man who concealed an inheritance and his interest in a business lost his bankruptcy discharge of more than $3.9 million after a trial victory by the Justice Department’s U.S. Trustee Program (USTP).
On October 20, the Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Washington entered a judgment revoking Nevin Middleton’s chapter 7 bankruptcy discharge. As a result, Middleton remains liable for his debts, and creditors are free to pursue payment from him after the case is closed.
“The bankruptcy discharge is the key to a fresh start, but debtors must be transparent about their financial affairs to receive it,” said USTP Director Stephen V. Falanga. “The USTP remains steadfast in its commitment to protect the integrity of the bankruptcy system from dishonest debtors.”
Middleton originally filed an individual chapter 11 reorganization case to resolve debts stemming from a failed custom home construction business, but the case was eventually converted to a chapter 7 liquidation. In April 2024, Middleton received his chapter 7 discharge of $3,967,997 in unsecured debt—most of it involving claims from creditors who had invested in his projects.
Several months later, the court held an evidentiary hearing to resolve a dispute over Middleton’s claim to a homestead exemption on some of his real estate. There, Middleton disclosed for the first time that after filing for bankruptcy but before receiving his discharge, he had received two deposits totaling about $39,600 in distributions from his late father’s probate estate to a business bank account that Middleton controlled. But Middleton had failed to list his inheritance rights and his interest in the business in his bankruptcy schedules and statements.
An investigation by the USTP’s Seattle office found that Middleton had instructed his sister, the executor of the probate estate, to direct the funds to a business account that the private trustee administering his bankruptcy case was unaware of. But at trial on the USTP’s complaint to revoke his discharge, Middleton changed his story and testified that the funds were loans from his sister. After weighing the evidence, however, the bankruptcy court entered judgment in the USTP’s favor, concluding that Middleton had obtained his discharge by fraud and that he had knowingly and fraudulently failed to report the funds to the chapter 7 trustee.
The USTP’s mission is to promote the integrity and efficiency of the bankruptcy system for the benefit of all stakeholders — debtors, creditors and the public. The USTP consists of 21 regions with 82 field offices nationwide and an Executive Office in Washington, D.C. Learn more about the USTP at www.justice.gov/ust. To report suspected bankruptcy fraud or abuse, please visit www.justice.gov/ust/report-suspected-bankruptcy-fraud.
title: U.S. Trustee Program Prevails at Trial to Revoke $3.9M Discharge from Seattle Man Who Concealed Inheritance Rights and Business Interest

DALLAS — United States Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced in a press conference today that a one of the Deep Ellum Halloween shooters has been federally charged for allegedly opening fire into a crowded Deep Ellum street wounding seven people.

David Dashaun Yancy, 27, was charged by criminal complaint with being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition. Yancy surrendered to the Dallas Police Department on Nov. 4 and remains in custody.

The federal charge follows the launch of Operation Deep Cover on Monday—a coordinated federal, state, and local law enforcement surge targeting violent crime and illegal firearms in high-density entertainment and commercial corridors across Dallas. In addition to a defendant charged on Monday during the operation’s initial rollout, federal authorities have now charged one of the alleged shooters responsible for the holiday weekend violence in Deep Ellum.

“When we launched Operation Deep Cover, we made an unequivocal promise: anyone who terrorizes our neighborhoods will face the full weight of the federal government,” said the U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “In less than one week, our task forces have already produced multiple federal charges—including holding accountable an alleged gunman whose reckless actions wrought violence and terror to Deep Ellum. To the criminals out there, we are just getting started.”

“When we launched Operation Deep Cover, we made an unequivocal promise: anyone who terrorizes our neighborhoods will face the full weight of the federal government,” said the U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “In less than one week, our task forces have already produced multiple federal charges—including holding accountable an alleged gunman whose reckless actions wrought violence and terror to Deep Ellum. To the criminals out there, we are just getting started.”

“Let me be clear: Dallas will not be a safe haven for violent criminals. We are done allowing a small number of individuals to threaten the safety of our residents, businesses, and visitors,” said Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux. “Operation Deep Cover sends an unmistakable message: If you choose to commit violent crimes in Deep Ellum, we will use every available resource, every investigative tool, and every law enforcement partnership to identify you, find you, and hold you accountable. We are not backing down, and we are not going anywhere.”

“ATF is committed to working alongside our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners to remove illegal firearms from our communities and hold violent offenders accountable. The alleged shooting in Deep Ellum, which left seven innocent people injured, is a stark reminder of the devastating impact gun violence has on our neighborhoods. Through Operation Deep Cover, we will continue to leverage our investigative resources and expertise to identify those responsible for violent crimes and ensure they face justice.”

According to court documents, at approximately 1:00 a.m. on Nov. 1, Dallas Police officers responded to reports of gunfire at 2626 Main Street in the historic Deep Ellum entertainment district, which was crowded with patrons celebrating Halloween. Upon arrival, officers found seven individuals suffering from gunshot wounds. All seven victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries. Crime scene investigators recovered eleven 9mm fired cartridge casings and projectiles from the area.

Surveillance footage obtained from CCTV cameras in the vicinity captured Yancy prior to the shooting pulling a handgun from his waistband, racking the slide, and concealing it again. Moments later, additional footage captured Yancy pulling the firearm out and firing directly into the crowd in multiple directions, striking seven bystanders.

Following witness interviews, anonymous tips, and surveillance analysis, detectives positively identified Yancy as the shooter. On Nov. 4, Yancy contacted the Dallas Police Department to turn himself in and was taken into custody by the Dallas Police Fugitive Unit.

A review of Yancy’s criminal history revealed a prior felony conviction in Dallas County. At the time of the shooting, Yancy was on felony deferred adjudication probation for child endangerment and had an active warrant for a probation violation. An interstate nexus analysis conducted by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives confirmed that the ammunition recovered from the scene had traveled in interstate commerce.

If convicted, Yancy faces up to 15 years in federal prison.

The ATF and the Dallas Police Department conducted the investigation under the umbrella of Operation Deep Cover. Assistant U.S. Attorney Marissa Aulbaugh from the Violent Crimes section is prosecuting the case.

A criminal complaint is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

title: Alleged Deep Ellum Halloween Shooter Charged Federally as Law Enforcement Ramps Up “Operation Deep Cover”

NORWICH, CT — Today, Congressman Joe Courtney (CT-02) issued the following statement celebrating the completion of the Revolution Wind offshore wind energy project.
“At a time when Americans are facing skyrocketing energy costs and New England households are being hit with over 70% price hikes on home heating oil due to President Trump’s war in Iran, Revolution Wind will deliver much needed cheaper energy to Connecticut’s grid,” Courtney said. “The cost of Revolution Wind’s power at nine cents per kWh is far less than the average of 30 cents per kWh in our region, and crucially, because this power is generated and transmitted from right off the coast of New England, its price will not be at the mercy of global energy markets. Congratulations to the talented Connecticut building trades workers who completed this massive project through the Trump Administration’s illegal halt work orders that were flatly rejected by every court. Your hard work and perseverance will bring lower costs to Connecticut households.” 
On September 10th, 2025, Congressman Courtney successfully led a bipartisan rejection of a measure in the U.S. House of Representatives which would have shut down the Revolution Wind project.

Cleveland Gang Members Convicted of Racketeering, Murder, Kidnapping, Drug Trafficking, and Firearms Offenses
Following a three-week trial, a federal jury in Cleveland convicted three members of the Fully Blooded Felons, a violent Cleveland street gang, of a number of crimes, including Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act murder, RICO conspiracy, RICO kidnapping, drug trafficking, and gun crimes.
“This extremely violent gang was a true blot on the city of Cleveland,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “The Criminal Division’s work put a stop to the violence that this gang rained down on Ohio communities to protect law-abiding citizens from harm. Stopping violent crime in Cleveland and around the country remains a top priority for the Trump Administration.”
“These verdicts send a clear message: when gang members make it their business to hurt people and terrorize our communities, we make it our business to lock them in a cage far from home,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “FBI Cleveland and our local law enforcement partners conducted an outstanding investigation to take down this hostile gang. We hope today’s verdict brings the victims’ families a small sense of closure in knowing that justice has been served.”
“The Fully Blooded Felons criminal network has been identified as Cleveland’s most significant gang threat,” said Special Agent in Charge Joshua DelManzo of FBI Cleveland. “Thanks to the tireless work and years-long commitment of the FBI Safe Streets Gang Task Force and our local, state, and federal partners, their reign of terror is over and justice will be served. Our work is not done. We will not waver in our mission nor lose sight of our promise to identify, investigate, disrupt, and dismantle gangs not only in the larger cities across America, but also right here in northern Ohio.”
According to evidence presented at trial, Raven Mullins, 37, Malik Brooks, 28, and Jayon Florence, 23, all of Cleveland, Ohio, were members and associates of the Fully Blooded Felons gang. The gang has existed in Ohio since approximately 2012, operating primarily out of the east side of Cleveland, as well as Akron, Youngstown, and elsewhere. It is also entrenched in the Ohio prison system.
Raven Mullins oversaw the “Commission,” the governing body of the Fully Blooded Felons, who maintain the structure and organization of the criminal enterprise through physical discipline and who determined which illicit means the organization would use to make money. The Commission had authority to determine if a member committed a “violation” and the appropriate punishment, which could range from a fine to death. The Commission was made up of a Head Commissioner and 10 subordinate Commissioners. Beneath the Commissioner were “Capos,” who led up to 25 Fully Blooded Felon members under their command.
The Fully Blooded Felons have rules that members are required to follow. For example, members are required to abide by “omerta,” or the code of silence. Members are also required to memorize and recite at meetings the “Fully Five,” a set of rules that require following all orders issued by the Commission, loyalty to fellow members, and being respectful to Capos. If a member does not know the “Fully Five,” they were punished. Members are also expected to know and abide by the “Fully Commandments,” a similar set of rules. The rules are disseminated to members by text message, and in face-to-face communications.
Evidence proved that the defendants, along with co-defendants who earlier pleaded guilty, kidnapped and murdered a victim after the gang suspected that she was romantically involved with and sharing information with a rival gang member. On or about July 28, 2022, as punishment for the victim’s suspected disloyalty to the gang, Fully Blooded Felon members held her in an apartment where Mullins ordered gang members, including Brooks and Florence, to repeatedly punch and choke her.
Mullins, Brooks, and Florence, with other co-defendants, held her captive in that apartment while they talked about what to do with her. After taking and reviewing the contents of her phone, including text messages and contacts, gang members believed that she intended to provide a rival gang with Brooks’ location to facilitate Brooks’ assault or murder.
The next day, while still holding her captive and upon Mullins’ approval, Brooks and Florence along with other gang members drove her to an area on the west side of Cleveland where they fatally shot her 19 times, leaving her body in the front seat of a stolen Kia Optima.
From June 30 to July 5, 2022, Mullins and other Fully Blooded Felon members kidnapped and assaulted a 22-year-old woman. The victim, who was eventually released, had previously given a statement to police implicating a Fully Blooded Felon member in a robbery.
Then, on Sept. 12, 2023, Mullins and two other Fully Blooded Felon members robbed and murdered a second victim on the west side of Cleveland. Evidence at trial included a knife sheath carrying Mullins’ DNA found at the scene.
The prosecution also introduced evidence showing that Brooks shot two rival gang members on the west side of Cleveland on July 18 and 20, 2022, and that Fully Blooded Felon members used two different stash houses at a local apartment complex. During the execution of two search warrants, law enforcement recovered over 300 grams of fentanyl, cocaine, and methamphetamine as well as seven firearms.
The defendants face maximum penalties of life in prison. Their sentencing date has not yet been set by the court.
As of today, 25 Fully Blooded Felon members have been charged and convicted of federal charges in relation to this indictment for crimes including RICO conspiracy, murder in aid of racketeering, kidnapping in aid of racketeering, and various firearms and drug-related offenses.
The case is the result of a yearslong investigation conducted by the FBI with assistance from the Cleveland Division of Police, ATF, and DEA. The Cuyahoga County Sheriff’s Office, Ohio Adult Parole Authority (APA), Ohio Highway State Patrol, U.S. Marshals Service, and numerous other law enforcement agencies contributed to the investigation.
Trial Attorneys Brian W. Lynch and former Trial Attorney Alyssa Levey-Weinstein of the Justice Department’s Violent Crime & Racketeering Section and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Paul E. Hanna, Rachael E. Wood, Robert F. Corts, and Margaret A. Sweeney for the Northern District of Ohio are prosecuting the case.
title: Cleveland Gang Members Convicted of Racketeering, Murder, Kidnapping, Drug Trafficking, and Firearms Offenses

FDIC Issues List of Banks Examined for CRA Compliance
WASHINGTON—The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) today issued its list of state nonmember banks recently evaluated for compliance with the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA). The list covers evaluation ratings that the FDIC assigned to institutions in August 2026.
The CRA is a 1977 law that requires the FDIC to assess a bank’s record of meeting the credit needs of its entire community, including those of low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. As part of the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989 (FIRREA), Congress mandated the public disclosure of an evaluation and rating for each bank or thrift that undergoes a CRA examination on or after July 1, 1990.
You may obtain a consolidated list of all state nonmember banks whose evaluations have been made publicly available since July 1, 1990, including the rating for each bank, or obtain a hard copy from FDIC's Public Information Center, 3501 Fairfax Drive, Room E-1002, Arlington, VA 22226 (877-275-3342 or 703-562-2200).
A copy of an individual bank's CRA evaluation is available directly from the bank, which is required by law to make the material available upon request, or from the FDIC's Public Information Center.
title: FDIC Issues List of Banks Examined for CRA Compliance

CALDERON has been a Sergeant with the New York State Police since in or about 2022. On or about October 25, 2026, he was arrested and charged in the Town of Crawford with assault in the second degree and third degree.

CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Eddie Daivon Morgan, also known as “Gutta,” 45, of Mount Hope, was sentenced today to 10 years in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release, for being a felon in possession of a firearm.

According to court documents and statements made in court, on November 30, 2022, law enforcement officers had an active warrant for Morgan’s arrest on a malicious wounding charge when they observed him enter a vehicle in Fayette County. Officers conducted a traffic stop of the vehicle and found Morgan laying in the back seat of the vehicle. Officers seized a loaded Glock model 42 .380-caliber pistol and a loaded SCCY 9mm pistol from Morgan’s person.

Federal law prohibits a person with a prior felony conviction from possessing a firearm or ammunition. Morgan knew he was prohibited from possessing a firearm because of his prior felony conviction for use of a communication facility to facilitate a drug trafficking offense in United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia on January 24, 2013.

The warrant for Morgan’s arrest was issued after a November 18, 2022, confrontation between Morgan and another individual at a Fayette County residence. During the confrontation, a verbal altercation between Morgan and the other individual escalated when Morgan threatened to “shoot the place up.” Morgan later fired two rounds from a .380-caliber pistol, wounding the other individual in the arm. Morgan pleaded guilty to attempted second-degree murder, malicious assault, wanton endangerment involving a firearm, and use or presentation of a firearm during the commission of a felony in Fayette County Circuit Court on March 28, 2024.

Morgan’s criminal history also includes prior convictions for second-degree manslaughter, second-degree assault, felony escape, wanton endangerment with a firearm, possession with intent to deliver a controlled substance within 1,000 feet of a school, battery, and domestic battery.

United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Oak Hill Police Department.

United States District Judge Irene C. Berger imposed the sentence. Assistant United States Attorney JC MacCallum prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

This case is also part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

A copy of this press release is located on the website of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of West Virginia. Related court documents and information can be found on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:23-cr-92.

title: Fayette County Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Federal Gun Crime

PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - Government, industry and technical experts convened here and online on Tuesday, Sept. 15 to confront one of the most urgent challenges in unmanned systems development: bringing true plug‑and‑play lethality to the drone ecosystem.
Hosted by the National Armaments Consortium (NAC) and led by the Project Manager Close Combat Systems (PM CCS) team, the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center, the webinar served as a gateway for more than 500 industry partners to learn what resources are available to pair conventional payloads to drone platforms. Also contributing to making it a success were the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS) team and those at Drone Dominance.
This initiative, called Conventional Munitions for UxS, aims to pair conventional payloads with unmanned systems through modular interfaces. Plug‑and‑play modularity and collaborative development stood front and center as major topics, with much of the discussion focused on using standard interfaces and protocols at the junctures between components, known in industry as the Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA).
According to PM CCS Col. Isaac Cuthbertson, the webinar was influenced by a clear gap in acquisition landscape, as while the commercial sector leads the way in drone flight controls, battery life and materials, the Army and industry must develop a true partnership to catch up on integrating state-of-the-art drone with state-of-the-art lethal payloads for military missions.
Cuthbertson noted the importance of maintaining common interfaces and protocols so payloads and platforms can evolve modularly without forcing redesigns across the entire system. The intent is to prevent changes in one component, like a sensor, platform or munition, from cascading into unneeded redesigns elsewhere. MOSA supports this by allowing individual parts to be upgraded swiftly while keeping the system’s broader capabilities stable.
He also emphasized the importance of incorporating safety into design early and often. “The traditional approach of bolting safety on at the end of the engineering process simply does not work for the speed at which we are trying to achieve today,” said Cuthbertson.
Cuthbertson showed great confidence that the webinar would close gaps by giving companies technical insights and guidance to integrate lethal payloads swiftly, responsibly and in a modular manner.
The Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM UxS) is a newly established office reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary of War. Established in July, the office enforces joint technical standards, interoperability baselines and MOSA requirements.
By shifting away from fragmented and service-specific acquisitions, DRPM UxS rapidly accelerates the development, procurement and fielding of autonomous systems specifically tailored to the operational demands of Geographic Combatant Commands. Notably, this unified approach aggregates joint requirements into a clear and sustained demand signal, giving industry the confidence and scale necessary to rapidly accelerate domestic production.
Experts from the Armaments Center highlighted the various intricacies of drone lethality, covering fuze safety, energetics, the Picatinny Common Lethality Interface Kit (CLIK) and fire control, alongside other topics.
All maintained throughout how accelerating drone lethality requires collaboration, rather than competition, as evidenced by active projects under the Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) between the Armaments Center and the NAC member companies. Interfaces such as CLIK follow the MOSA standard, which provides its followers with shared resources and interoperability between platform and payloads.
The NAC is a coalition of leading engineers, designers and technologists which acts as a bridge between parties to advance armaments technologies. Director of Customer Affairs Don Palathinkal encouraged companies to join the NAC and partner with the Army through the NAC-Armaments Center CRADA. This collaboration pathway will help prepare the strongest possible lethal drone designs for production.
PM CCS Chief Systems Engineer Snehali Patel explained that questions mostly regarded efforts to homogenize safety review criteria and the timeframe for selecting a standardized interface. Attendees expressed a desire for consistent safety review rules, processes and expectations. Organizers received 72 questions during the open forum.
The webinar painted a picture of how unmanned systems are gradually shifting toward standardized interfaces and the importance of consolidated oversight and early collaboration. Rapid advances, the speakers noted, will come from shared frameworks and partnerships, not isolated development, and for unmanned systems to thrive going forward, plug-and-play will remain at the forefront.
title: DEVCOM Armaments Center push continues to enable industry to develop and deliver lethality via plug-and-play drone payloads

text:
Seattle – A 46-year-old Seattle man was sentenced late yesterday in U.S. District Court in Seattle to two years in prison for his role in a drug trafficking organization that sold cocaine and fentanyl in Seattle homeless encampments and in the International District, announced Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd. Sang Su has been in custody since his arrest in August 2025. Su was heard on a wiretap investigation discussing cocaine distribution and obtaining ‘samples’ of fentanyl powder. At the sentencing hearing U.S. District Judge Tana Lin said, “It is aggravating that you were selling significant amounts of cocaine and fentanyl to some of the most marginalized members of our community.”

“Our goal with the Homeland Security Task Force is to remove dangerous criminals from our community – especially in neighborhoods that have been disproportionately victimized like the Chinatown International District.” said Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd. “Whether you are a low-level distributor or a high-volume dealer, we will prosecute you. Mr. Su was a repeat offender selling drugs while armed and preying on the vulnerable population in the international district. He has earned his time in prison which will hopefully break his cycle of crime.”

“As a redistributor, Mr. Su contributed to the high volumes of deadly and addictive drugs this drug trafficking organization poured into our most vulnerable communities,” said W. Mike Herrington, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Seattle field office. “He directly interacted with the group leader and further endangered the public by possessing a loaded firearm to protect the proceeds of the trafficking. The FBI and our partners will continue to hold each of these conspirators, and others like them, responsible for the damage they do to our communities.”

“Drug traffickers who distribute fentanyl and cocaine to vulnerable communities put lives at risk and fuel addiction, violence, and instability,” said Robert A. Saccone, Special Agent in Charge, DEA Seattle Field Division. “Sang Su’s role in this organization helped extend the reach of these dangerous drugs and threatened public safety. DEA remains committed to working alongside our federal partners through the Homeland Security Task Force to dismantle drug trafficking organizations, hold those responsible accountable, and protect our communities as we work toward a Fentanyl Free America.”

According to records filed in the case, in 2023, after incidents of drug trafficking-related violence in and around homeless encampments in Seattle’s Chinatown-International District and the greenbelt adjacent to Interstate-5, commonly known as the “Jungle,” the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”) and the Seattle Police Department (“SPD”) began a narcotics trafficking investigation into individuals distributing controlled substances in these areas.

On May 29, 2025, law enforcement executed 16 search warrants in Federal Way, Vancouver, Everett, Pacific, Tukwila, Kent, Issaquah, Seattle, Woodlake California and Beaverton, Oregon. Investigators seized more than seven kilograms of cocaine, 18 kilograms of methamphetamine, more than 57,000 fentanyl pills, and 17 firearms. They also seized more than $353,000 in cash.

Sang Su was not arrested during the execution of the May 2025 warrants and was sought by law enforcement until his arrest on August 18, 2025.

Sang Su was initially contacted by law enforcement as part of the investigation in October 2024. Su had just made a drug purchase from the organization leader at a market on Beacon Hill in Seattle when he was stopped by law enforcement and the drugs and a firearm were seized from his car.

Su pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance on July 2, 2026.

In asking for a 30-month sentence, prosecutors noted that Su had ignored police interventions that could have put him on a better path writing, “However, between 2002 and 2025, Su had multiple contacts with law enforcement, which include multiple arrests for assault, controlled substances violations, and carrying loaded firearms. While these arrests were either later dismissed or charges were never filed, it is concerning the number of contacts that Su has had with the criminal justice system. Despite benefiting from charges never being filed or later being dismissed, these law enforcement interventions failed to curtail Su’s criminal acts.”

Judge Lin ordered Su to be on three years of supervised release following prison.

The investigation was led by the FBI, Seattle Police Department and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) with significant assistance from the Internal Revenue Service - Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program (HIDTA), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and Washington National Guard Counterdrug Program. Investigators also worked with the Oregon State Police and Clark County, Washington Sheriff’s Office.

This investigation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. title: Homeland Security Task Force investigation leads to two-year sentence for distributor of cocaine and fentanyl

text:
ATLANTA – A federal jury convicted Roderick Battle, the leader of a nationwide drug trafficking organization, of multiple drug trafficking, money laundering, and firearms-related charges.

“Despite a prior conviction for trafficking narcotics, Battle was undeterred, operating a prolific drug trafficking network that supplied large quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other narcotics throughout the country,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “This conviction reaffirms the steadfast dedication of my office and our federal and state law enforcement partners in the Homeland Security Task Force to protect the public from individuals who poison our communities with deadly drugs.”

“Roderick Battle led a sophisticated, multi-state drug trafficking operation that flooded communities across the country with dangerous narcotics, including fentanyl and methamphetamine,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “This conviction is a testament to the strong partnerships and coordinated efforts of law enforcement to dismantle these criminal networks and hold those responsible accountable.”

“Cases of this magnitude are not solved by one agency alone,” said Michael J. Connolly, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Atlanta Field Division. “This investigation demonstrates what can be accomplished when federal, state, and local law enforcement partners work together with a shared mission. As part of the Homeland Security Task Force, our collective efforts exposed a sophisticated drug trafficking and money laundering network, disrupted its operations, and secured a conviction against the individual responsible for leading it.”

According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the charges, and other information presented in court: Between at least January 2021 and December 2024, Battle and his conspirators concealed drugs and drug proceeds in guitar amplifiers and transported the drugs nationwide using a stolen FedEx account that belonged to a sports memorabilia company. Additionally, Battle and his conspirators transported drugs hidden beneath vehicles on tow trucks.

On May 6, 2023, the Pennsylvania State Police intercepted a package that contained six kilograms of cocaine shipped from Battle’s residence in southeast Atlanta. Four days later, federal and state law enforcement executed a search warrant at Battle’s home and seized large quantities of narcotics, including fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin, all packaged for distribution. Agents also located two firearms under Battle’s bed and approximately $76,000 in cash.

Federal agents arrested Battle on a criminal complaint that day. While Battle was detained in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending trial, he continued to facilitate the distribution of narcotics using a contraband cellular telephone.

On November 3, 2026, a federal jury convicted Roderick Battle, 49, of Atlanta, Georgia, of conspiracy and possession with the intent to distribute fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin, as well as money laundering and firearms-related charges. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for March 2, 2027, before U.S. District Judge J.P. Boulee.

Battle faces a mandatory minimum 20 years in prison. In determining the actual sentence, the Court will consider the United States Sentencing Guidelines, which are not binding but provide appropriate sentencing ranges for most offenders.

This case is being investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Pennsylvania State Police, with valuable assistance provided by the Georgia State Patrol.

Assistant United States Attorneys Dwayne A. Brown Jr., Brock Brockington, John DeGenova, and Patrick Cespedes are prosecuting the case.

COLUMBIA, S.C. – Twelve members of a Midlands drug trafficking conspiracy have now been sentenced to federal prison, totaling just over 154 years in federal prison. Overall, more than 60 kilograms of methamphetamine, 30 kilograms of cocaine, 200 grams of fentanyl, and quantities of MDMA, crack cocaine, and marijuana were attributed to the conspiracy.

The following individuals have been sentenced to federal prison for their roles in the conspiracy:

Pearish Pierre Pretty, 41, of Columbia, was sentenced to more than 20 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

William Larry Javis, Jr., 43, of Columbia, was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a ten-year term of supervised release.

Demetrius Tyare Glenn, 34, of Lexington, was sentenced to more than 18 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Issac Christopher Bates, 53, of Columbia, was sentenced to more than 16 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Johnny Lee Dickerson, 44, of Columbia, was sentenced to more than 16 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Maynard Felder Bartlett, 39, of Lexington, was sentenced to more than 10 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Marsha Beth Gurwitch, 53, of Columbia, was sentenced to more than 10 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Billy Joe Davis, 42, of Gaston, was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Quinton Lamar Anderson, 32, of West Columbia, was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Miranda Ruth Garrett, 53, of Hopkins, was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Darwin Tramaine Sims, 34, of Columbia, was sentenced to more than six years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

Douglas Steven Raley, 41, of West Columbia, was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment, to be followed by a five-year term of supervised release.

In 2023, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the City of Columbia Police Department launched an investigation into the drug trafficking organization. Evidence identified Pretty, Javis, and Glenn as the leaders of the conspiracy. Investigators determined Pretty, Javis, Glenn, and Bates served as kilogram-level suppliers of methamphetamine and cocaine to other members, who then redistributed narcotics to others throughout Richland and Lexington counties. Between September and November 2024, investigators intercepted thousands of drug-related communications among conspiracy members. The investigation revealed several residences and hotels used to store and distribute narcotics. Agents also learned that multiple members were armed while distributing drugs and engaged in the sale and trade of firearms despite being prohibited from possessing them. In October 2024, agents executed search warrants at four locations associated with the conspiracy. They seized approximately 2,000 grams of methamphetamine, hundreds of pressed fentanyl pills, 203 grams of cocaine, 150 grams of MDMA, 400 grams of marijuana, five loaded firearms, digital scales, packaging materials, and other drug paraphernalia. Investigators also discovered that one location housed a pill press used to manufacture counterfeit pills containing fentanyl, methamphetamine, and MDMA. In total, through search warrants, controlled purchases, and traffic stops, investigators seized more than 3,000 grams of methamphetamine, along with significant quantities of cocaine, crack cocaine, fentanyl, MDMA, marijuana, and multiple firearms. United States District Judge Mary Geiger Lewis sentenced the conspiracy members to just over a combined 154 years in federal prison. There is no parole in the federal system. This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. This case was investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration, the City of Columbia Police Department, the Richland County Sheriff’s Department, the Lexington County Sheriff’s Department, and the Clarendon County Sheriff’s Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ariyana Gore prosecuted the case.

SHREVEPORT – On October 29, 2026, United States District Judge S. Maurice Hicks sentenced Marvaeya M. Anderson , 30, of Shreveport, to 180 months in federal prison for Possessing a Controlled Substance with Intent to Distribute and for Possessing a Firearm in Furtherance of a Drug Trafficking Crime, followed by four years of supervised release. Anderson pled guilty on July 20, 2026.

On October 26, 2026, Judge Hicks also sentenced Kentravious C. Kennedy , 20, of Shreveport, to 46 months in federal prison for Possession of a Firearm or Ammunition by a Convicted Felon, followed by three years of supervised release. Kennedy pled guilty on May 20, 2026.

Also on October 26, 2026, Judge Hicks sentenced Jayden Jamond Smith, 20, of Bossier City, to 20 months in federal prison for Illegal Possession of a Machinegun, followed by three years of supervised release. Smith pled guilty on June 30, 2026.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

ANDERSON According to court documents, on October 12, 2025, a Shreveport Police Department (SPD) patrol officer attempted a traffic stop on a black Dodge Challenger. The vehicle fled, leading officers on a high-speed pursuit through a residential area until it crashed. The passenger, who was later identified as Anderson, fled on foot across a field, over a fence, and then crossed all lanes of I-20 before finally being apprehended. A subsequent search of Anderson’s vehicle revealed a plastic grocery bag that contained approximately 196 grams of methamphetamine, 20.9 grams of crack cocaine, a digital scale, a handgun, and two cell phones. Anderson admitted later admitted the narcotics were for his personal use. Anderson is a previously convicted felon prohibited from possessing a firearm.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and SPD. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Allison C. Foster with assistance from Paralegal Specialist Emily Favrot.

KENNEDY According to court documents, on November 2, 2025, officers with SPD responded to a shooting at a local intersection and identified Kennedy as a suspect. Officers obtained consent to search his mother’s residence and discovered a DPMS Panther Arms A 15 rifle, an ISSC M22 pistol, multiple loaded magazines, and ammunition. The rifle contained a sixty round magazine. Photos on Kennedy’s social media accounts showed him posing with firearms that matched the ones recovered. Kennedy admitted he had a previous felony conviction and could not legally possess a firearm.

This case was investigated by ATF and SPD. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Moody with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

SMITH According to court documents, on February 8, 2025, Bossier Parish Sheriff’s Office (BPSO) deputies responded to reports of machinegun fire. Deputies recovered camera footage capturing the sound of automatic gunfire and later also obtained camera footage from nearby businesses. The footage identified an orange Dodge Charger involved in the incident. Detectives were able to discern a partial license plate number and linked the vehicle to a local high school student who admitted picking up Smith that day. The student said that Smith had possessed a Glock equipped with a machinegun conversion device (switch) and had wanted to fire it. The student said that after he and Smith drove around, they stopped, and Smith fired several automatic rounds into wooded areas between houses. Deputies obtained the student’s phone through his consent and uncovered video of Smith firing the weapon in automatic mode, along with text messages between the two discussing the weapon’s performance.

This case was investigated by ATF and BPSO. It was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert Moody with assistance from Legal Assistant Amanda Morgan.

NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA – On October 27, 2026, KEITH MORET (“MORET”) , age 30, a resident of New Orleans, pled guilty to Count 8 of the superseding indictment charging him with possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, in violation of Title 18, United States Code, Section 924(c)(1)(A)(i), announced U.S. Attorney David I. Courcelle.

Chief U.S. District Court Judge Wendy B. Vitter will sentence MORET on February 2, 2027.

Washington eventually lost control of the vehicle and crashed into the concrete steps and porch of a residence. Washington and MORET were detained. Prior to searching the vehicle, troopers noted that the car had a strong odor of marijuana coming from inside. MORET possessed a black backpack containing approximately 169.56 grams of marijuana, $11,160 in cash, several clear plastic baggies, and an unknown liquid in a prescription bottle, all of which evidenced MORET’s drug trafficking. Additionally, law enforcement located a black semi-auto F&N Model Five Seven 5.7 x 28 caliber pistol, fully loaded and with a round in the chamber, on the passenger floorboard within reach of MORET . text:
PORTLAND, Ore.— U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today that Christina Klauda, 53, of Riddle, Oregon, has pleaded guilty to one count of bank fraud and two counts of making and subscribing false federal income tax returns for a years-long embezzlement and tax fraud scheme that targeted her former employer.

According to court documents, Klauda served as the office manager and bookkeeper for Tower Timber Services, Inc., a lumber company based in Riddle, Oregon, beginning in 2014. In that role, she was responsible for payroll, accounts payable, invoicing, employee dispatch and preparation of employee tax forms.

Klauda admitted that she used her position of trust and control over the company's financial systems to systematically steal from Tower Timber from 2014 through 2023. The government estimates the company's losses at more than $1.08 million, while Klauda acknowledges losses of at least $944,371.97.

According to the plea agreement, Klauda began the scheme by increasing her hourly and overtime rates and overstating her work hours in the company's payroll system. Beginning in 2018, she created a second employee profile in the company's accounting software and arranged to receive duplicate payroll payments. Klauda received one payment through direct deposit and a second payment through paper checks that she concealed by deleting records of the transactions from the accounting software.

Klauda also admitted to using the company owner's signature stamp without authorization to issue additional checks to herself and her personal creditors. She disguised these payments as loans, reimbursements or draws, removed the transactions from company records, and failed to report the income to the Internal Revenue Service.

As part of the scheme, Klauda filed false federal income tax returns for tax years 2018 and 2019 by failing to report income she had stolen from the company. Specifically, she failed to report approximately $38,140 in income in 2018 and $74,144 in income in 2019, causing a total tax loss of $27,985.

The bank fraud charge carries a maximum sentence of 30 years in federal prison, a $1 million fine and five years of supervised release. Each tax fraud charge carries a maximum sentence of three years in federal prison, a $100,000 fine and one year of supervised release.

Klauda has also agreed to pay restitution to the victims. The parties estimate total restitution will be between approximately $972,356.97 and $1,111,771.56, including losses sustained by Tower Timber and the IRS.

The case was investigated by the IRS-Criminal Investigation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Katherine A. Rykken is prosecuting the case.

text:
ST. LOUIS – A Chinese national pleaded guilty Wednesday and admitted participating in a nationwide scam involving gift cards.

Liang Xiong, 39, pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of possession of 15 or more unauthorized access devices. From Feb. 24, 2026, through at least March 11, 2026, Xiong stole gift cards from retailers throughout the United States, according to his plea agreement. Xiong removed the strip concealing the serial number on the gift cards and recorded that number before placing the compromised gift cards back on display racks in stores in Colorado, Iowa and Missouri. Once the gift cards were purchased and activated, Xiong and others intended to steal the funds on the card by using the serial number that they’d recorded. Xiong admitted stealing 15 Amazon gift cards on March 10, 2026, from a store in O’Fallon, Missouri. The next day, he placed 16 previously stolen Apple gift cards in a display in a store in St. Charles. He was arrested that day by the St. Charles Police Department with 134 compromised gift cards from three retailers in his vehicle. The total value of the cards would have been $58,300 had the cards been purchased and activated by paying customers. All the gift cards in this case were recovered prior to any customers purchasing them, Xiong’s plea agreement says.

Court documents indicate Xiong entered the country illegally through Mexico and has a pending asylum claim.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations recommends looking out for signs that gift cards have been altered or counterfeited.

Xiong is scheduled to be sentenced on Feb. 10, 2027. The charge carries a potential penalty of up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or both prison and a fine. He will also likely be deported upon his release from prison.

The case was investigated by HSI and the St. Charles Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Karin Schute is prosecuting the case.
