CLEVELAND – A 22-year-old man has been sentenced to prison for his role during violent carjackings in Cleveland in July 2025.

Tayveonn Elliott, of Cleveland, was sentenced to 192 months (16 years) in prison and five years of supervised released by U.S. District Judge Patricia A. Gaughan after pleading guilty to: • Carjacking • Using or Carrying and Brandishing a Firearm During a Crime of Violence

Judge Gaughan also ordered him to pay $25,199.81 in restitution, jointly and severally with co-defendants Mickey Hodge, 23, and Tye Campbell, 20, both of Cleveland. Hodge is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence, and Campbell was sentenced to 12 and a half years in prison.

According to court documents, on July 16, 2025, three victims were carjacked by a coordinated group of armed assailants, later identified as Hodge, Elliott, and Campbell. The day before the carjackings, a food delivery service employee left his Honda Civic briefly to deliver food to a residence. But when he returned, his car was gone. The next morning at 4 a.m., the defendants threatened a valet at a downtown hotel and demanded the keys to vehicles she had parked. In fear of her life, she complied and the suspects took a Nissan Altima, while a third co-conspirator drove away in the Honda stolen from the delivery service driver. At about 7:30 a.m. the same morning, a woman sitting in her Toyota RAV4 was carjacked at gunpoint in a gym parking lot. Also fearing for her life, she gave the suspects the car keys and they drove off. Later, at about 6 p.m., a third victim was threatened at gunpoint, and he gave the suspects the keys to his Ford Explorer. About four hours later, law enforcement located the Honda Civic and activated lights to initiate a traffic stop. However, the Honda sped away and crashed into two other vehicles at an intersection. Several suspects, including Hodge and Elliott, got out of the car and fled on foot but were apprehended. Campbell was arrested on a later date.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Cleveland Division and the Cleveland Division of Police.

Assistant United States Attorney Scott Zarzycki led the prosecution for the Northern District of Ohio.
title: Last of Three Defendants Sentenced to 16 Years in Prison for Role in Armed Carjackings

A Rockford man has been sentenced to more than fifteen years in federal prison for trafficking cocaine and illegally possessing a loaded firearm.

WILLIAM SPEARS was arrested in June 2024 following a 4-month narcotics investigation. At the time of his arrest, Spears was in possession of three and a half grams of cocaine, which he had been planning to sell to another person. Following his arrest, law enforcement searched Spears’s residence and a storage unit he rented and discovered approximately 700 grams of cocaine, $17,000 in cash, and a loaded handgun.

Spears, 68, pleaded guilty earlier this year to possession with intent to distribute more than 500 grams of cocaine and possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. As a previously convicted felon, Spears was prohibited from possessing firearms. On Oct. 30, 2026, U.S. District Judge Iain D. Johnston sentenced Spears to 15 years and eight months in federal prison.

The sentence was announced by Andrew S. Boutros, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois, and Christopher Amon, Special Agent in Charge of the Chicago Division of the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The Winnebago County, Ill. Sheriff’s Office assisted in the investigation.

“Defendant’s actions significantly contributed to the drug problem plaguing the Rockford community,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew M. Rosati argued in the government’s sentencing memorandum. “A significant sentence is necessary to protect the public and the community from defendant’s continued drug trafficking activities.”
title: Rockford Man Sentenced to More Than 15 Years in Federal Prison for Trafficking Cocaine

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – In three separate cases, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) special agents, with the support of the Puerto Rico Police Department arrested three men indicted for child exploitation, announced Héctor Ramírez Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico.

Today, HSI special agents arrested Samuel Alexander Meléndez Pérez, a 25-year-old man from Canóvanas, PR. According to court documents, in August 2026 Meléndez Pérez knowingly transported child exploitation material in his cellular device. From on or about October 2024 through on or about August 2026, Meléndez Pérez knowingly received child pornography by electronic devices. He was also charged with possession of child pornography, including images of prepubescent minors, in a cellular phone device.

In an unrelated case, on November 3, 2026, HSI special agents arrested Carlos Javier Rosado Rosado, 21, of Vega Baja. According to the indictment, from on or about June through September 2026, Rosado Rosado received, distributed and possessed child exploitation material, including images of prepubescent minors, in a cellular phone device.

In another separate case, on October 29, 2026, HSI special agents arrested Rubén Cautiño Latoni, a 37-year-old man from Guaynabo. According to the indictment, from in or about April 2026 to in or about September 2026, Cautiño Latoni possessed child pornography in a cellular phone device. It is further alleged that prior to committing the offense alleged in this indictment, Cautiño Latoni was convicted in February of 2020 in the U.S. District Court of Puerto Rico for possession of child pornography.

Assistant United States Attorney Elba Gorbea, from the Child Exploitation and Immigration Unit, is prosecuting these cases.

“We are committed to bringing the defendants in these cases to justice and protecting every child,” said Héctor Ramírez Carbó, Acting U.S. Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico. “I would like to thank the agents and state and local partners who are relentless in their pursuit of child predators.”

“Within less than a week, HSI San Juan arrested three individuals on child exploitation charges, including one found with more than 2,500 illicit images and another previously arrested by HSI for the same offense. These cases underscore the serious and ongoing threat of child exploitation, which requires public awareness and strong collaboration with law enforcement. HSI remains committed to acting swiftly when offenders violate the law or the conditions of their supervision,” said Yariel Ramos, Acting Special Agent in Charge, HSI San Juan.

If convicted, defendant Samuel Alexander Meléndez Pérez faces a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 5 years up to 20 years; Carlos Javier Rosado Rosado faces a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 5 years up to 20 years; and Rubén Cautiño Latoni faces a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years up to 20 years. Defendants convicted of these crimes also face, after serving their term of imprisonment, an additional mandatory supervised release term of 5 years up to life and would be required to register in the Sexual Offender Registry. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The Department of Homeland Security Investigations is investigating the cases.

For more information about HSI’s efforts to protect children from online sexual abuse, visit https://www.ice.gov/topics/iGuardians .

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood , a nationwide initiative to combat the epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc.

An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

###
title: HSI San Juan Arrests 3 Men on Child Exploitation Charges

text:
DETROIT ARSENAL, Mich. – Smiles, hugs and happy tears filled the Detroit Arsenal as five people who spent decades shaping the U.S. Army Tank-automotive and Armaments Command took a permanent place in its history.
Agnes E. Holley-Smith, David W. Horton, Michele M. Moore, James “Patton” Tidwell and David L. Van Agtmael were inducted Oct. 28 into the TACOM Hall of Fame.
“These are five people who have made TACOM stronger, they’ve made our Army more ready, and they’ve made our nation more secure,” Commanding General Brig. Gen. Beth A. Behn said.
The ceremony celebrated the inductees’ contributions and enduring legacy. More than 150 people attended, including command leadership, the commanders of TACOM’s depots and arsenals, Warren Mayor Lori Stone, four previous Hall of Fame inductees and members of the workforce.
Behn highlighted the honorees’ vital role in driving readiness.
“Behind every piece of equipment that we field, behind every capability that we deliver to the point of need for Soldiers, there’s a professional behind that who’s doing that work,” she said. “The five people that we’re going to recognize today represent the very best of what we do.”
Behn described the honorees as strategic problem-solvers who thought “broadly, deeply and critically” beyond the boundaries of job titles about how to advance warfighter readiness. She said they are at the heart of TACOM’s success – and an inspiration for its future.
“All of us who are here, now, strive to live up to the standard you have set,” she said.
Each inductee had a unique and lasting impact – but all shared a deep commitment to service.
Holley-Smith broke barriers and drove collaboration throughout her career, retiring as director of Operations and Security Assistance for the TACOM Integrated Logistics Support Center.
Horton, former acting executive director of the ILSC, led critical logistics initiatives and spent time in Kuwait executing the sale of the Abrams tank. Moore brought her communications and logistics expertise to multiple roles, including director of the Army Force Generation Integration Directorate.
Tidwell’s strong dedication to the warfighter strengthened operations across Red River Army Depot, where he served as deputy commander under six commanders. Van Agtmael was at the forefront of force modernization efforts and a key architect of the logistics support structure for the Stryker Brigade.
Before the induction ceremony got under way in the auditorium of Building 200, Behn met privately with the honorees and their family members and friends. During introductions, Holley-Smith joked about inviting a large group of people.
“OK, I’m the one in the room who maybe overdid it,” she said, eliciting laughter.
“There is no such thing,” Behn replied, smiling. “You only get inducted into the hall of fame once.”
After the ceremony, the honorees and their guests gathered for a reception in the TACOM Hall of Fame in Building 230. Applause erupted when a black drape was moved away from a wall to reveal five plaques honoring the inductees.
Van Agtmael called the experience “awesomely humbling.”
Tidwell agreed. He said he felt incredibly honored to be recognized for his nearly 45 years of service to the Army, but he was quick to credit the team behind him – from his former supervisors and mentors to the men and women working on the depot’s vehicle production lines and in the rubber products shop.
“It’s really all of them who made me look good,” he said. “It takes a whole team to do what we do on a daily basis.”
As the event wound down, members of the TACOM Hall of Fame Class of 2026 enjoyed cake, reminisced with old friends and took photos with Behn, each other and their families. Horton posed in front of the plaque wall for a photo with Holley-Smith, his mentor.
“Seeing all of these people,” he said, looking around the room, “it’s a little bit like a family reunion.”
The TACOM Hall of Fame program was founded in 2024. It preserves the command’s rich history while recognizing exceptional service, achievements and dedication in support of Army readiness.
title: TACOM welcomes newest Hall of Fame inductees

SPRINGFIELD, Mo. – A Mexican national illegally residing in Reeds Spring, Mo., pleaded guilty in federal court today to firearms and immigration offenses.

Jose Guadalupe Moreno-Malagon, 43, pleaded guilty to one count of illegal possession of firearms by an illegal immigrant, and one count of unlawful entry into the United States. The plea was entered before U.S. District Judge Megan Blair Benton.

On April 20, 2026, Moreno-Malagon contacted the Stone County, Missouri Sheriff’s Office to report that he was an “illegal alien” and wished to turn himself into authorities. Deputies responded to his residence and observed several firearms but were unable to verify his immigration status. On April 21, 2026, deputies returned to the residence and arrested Moreno-Malagon for being in the United States unlawfully and for illegally possessing firearms. Deputies seized two pistols and a semi-automatic rifle from Moreno-Malagon’s residence.

Moreno-Malagon’s sentencing has been set for April 7, 2027. Under federal statutes, Moreno-Malagon is subject to a sentence of up to 15 years imprisonment for unlawful possession of a firearm in federal prison without parole, and up to six months imprisonment for unlawful entry into the United States. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of the defendant will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled after the completion of a presentence investigation by the United States Probation Office.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Tony Brown and was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Stone County, Mo., Sheriff’s Office.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities .
title: Unlawful Alien Pleads Guilty to Firearms and Immigration Offenses

CONCORD – Two men pleaded guilty in federal court for conspiring to interfere with commerce by robbery, U.S. Attorney Erin Creegan announces.

Nasaiah Johnson, 25, recently of Baltimore, Maryland, and Xiao Yu, 28, an illegal alien from China recently living in New Jersey, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Court Judge Steven McAuliffe earlier today. Johnson’s sentencing is set for February 16, 2027. Yu’s sentencing is set for February 23, 2027.

According to the court documents and statements made in court, Johnson and Yu, along with four co-conspirators, traveled from New York to New England, for the purpose of robbing a local business. Yu rented a box truck from a rental agency in Medford, Massachusetts, and purchased supplies from a hardware store there. The co-conspirators then traveled to a business in Londonderry, New Hampshire. Five individuals, including Johnson, entered the business where they threatened an employee with what appeared to be a firearm and restrained the victim. The men then proceeded to steal merchandise and goods from the business, placing those items into the box truck, which was driven by Yu. Yu left in the box truck, while the other co-conspirators fled the scene in a sedan and returned to New York.

The charge of conspiracy to interfere with commerce by robbery carries a maximum prison term of 20 years, a maximum fine of $250,000, and not more than 3 years of supervised release. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation led this investigation. The Londonderry Police Department, New Hampshire State Police, Massachusetts State Police, and New York Police Department provided valuable assistance. Assistant U.S. Attorney Matthew Vicinanzo is prosecuting the case.

Congressman Carter Celebrates Historic Elections Powered by Voters of Color
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman Troy A. Carter, Sr. (D-LA), released the following statement regarding the midterm results from November, 3, 2026:
“We’ve just witnessed a historic election night. A blue wave reached across this country powered by Black voters and other voters of color, including in places some people thought were too red to change. The American people spoke, and they entrusted Democrats with majorities in both the House and the Senate by wide margins.
“Here in Louisiana, I’m deeply grateful that the people of the Second District have placed their trust in me again. As I enter my fourth term in Congress, I do so with new responsibilities and challenges. I will continue to lead with humility and honor and fully understanding that, for whom much is given, much is required. 
“Now, it’s time to get to work. We have a duty to defend the right to vote and hold this administration accountable. We must also answer the questions families are asking at their kitchen tables: Can I afford my prescriptions? Can my children afford a place to live? Will my paycheck get me through the month? Those questions will still be there when the celebrations are over. I stand ready with my Democratic and Republican colleagues next Congress to answer them.”

PHARR, Texas- On Oct. 30, at 8 p.m., CBP officers discovered almost 1100 pounds of methamphetamine concealed within a shipment manifested as leeks.
A semi-trailer bound for McAllen, Texas was referred to secondary inspection at the Pharr Port of Entry. After a K-9 alert, officers discovered cylindrical packages hidden among a shipment of leeks. A total of 909 packages were discovered and tested positive for methamphetamine. The total weight of the narcotics was 1,082.47 pounds with a street value of $984,063.
“International drug trafficking presents a direct threat to U.S. national security, public safety and economic stability,” said Jennifer De La O, director, Laredo Field Operations. “Operation Southern Surge leverages tactical intelligence and coordinated enforcement actions to dismantle the trafficking infrastructure, intercept illicit supply chains, and bolster situational awareness across the southwest border.”
Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the dedicated men and women of CBP, alongside our law enforcement partners and with the help of the Homeland Security Task Force, are eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, human smuggling and drug trafficking networks.

text:
Congress has historically shown interest in various reserve component (RC) personnel issues, such as pay and benefits, training and readiness, and career management. The term reserve component refers collectively to the seven individual RCs of the Armed Forces: the Army National Guard of the United States, the Army Reserve, the Navy Reserve, the Marine Corps Reserve, the Air National Guard of the United States, the Air Force Reserve, and the Coast Guard Reserve. The purpose of these seven reserve components, as codified at Title 10, Section 10102, of the U.S. Code, is to "provide trained units and qualified persons available for active duty in the armed forces, in time of war or national emergency, and at such other times as the national security may require, to fill the needs of the armed forces whenever more units and persons are needed than are in the regular components." The Army National Guard and the Air National Guard also have a state role: When operating under the control of their governors, they respond to various domestic emergencies, such as disasters and civil disorders.
This report addresses how RC personnel are organized, compensated, and mobilized. It concludes with a discussion of potential issues for Congress. This report covers the military services exclusively and generally does not discuss the Coast Guard Reserve.
The Armed Forces of the United States consist of six services:
With the exception of the Space Force,2 each of these services contains two components (see Table 1): the active component (AC) contains personnel who serve full-time, while members of the reserve component (RC) generally serve in a part-time capacity.
The seven individual RCs are:
Source: 10 U.S.C §§10104-10114; 10 U.S.C §20001.
Notes: The Army and Air National Guard are part of the Army and Air Force when activated under Title 10 of the U.S. Code. When activated under a state's authority, Guard personnel report to the state's governor.
The military services staffed primarily by active-component personnel are named in statute as the "regular" Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force. In public discourse, the services commonly refer to these forces as the "active" Army, Navy, etc. This report generally uses the latter terminology.
The statutory purpose of these seven RCs is
to provide trained units and qualified persons available for active duty in the armed forces, in time of war or national emergency, and at such other times as the national security may require, to fill the needs of the armed forces whenever more units and persons are needed than are in the regular components.4
The RC can be divided into two categories: the components that are exclusively federal entities and the components that are both state and federal entities (see Table 2).
The five solely federal RCs are referred to collectively as the reserves. They are components of their respective services—the Army Reserve is part of the Army, the Navy Reserve is part of the Navy, etc.
The RCs with dual federal and state roles are referred to collectively as the National Guard. The National Guard of the United States is composed of 54 separate National Guard organizations: one for each state and one each for Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the District of Columbia.5
When under state control, these organizations are identified by their state or territorial names (e.g., the California National Guard or the Puerto Rico National Guard) and are controlled by the respective governors. Each of these organizations in turn contains an Army National Guard and an Air National Guard. (For instance, New York operates the New York Army National Guard and the New York Air National Guard.) When under federal control, they operate as part of the Army or Air Force in a manner analogous to the Army and Air Force Reserves.
Due to their dual federal and state roles, National Guard personnel can be called to duty in a variety of ways, and the mode of activation has important implications for the pay and benefits they receive.
National Guard personnel may be activated in three ways: under federal control with federal compensation, under state control with state compensation, or under state control with federal compensation (see Table 3).
The three variants of National Guard activations are discussed below.
They may also perform full-time National Guard duty (FTNGD) in Title 32 status. FTNGD may be used for full-time support activities and for federal missions of a non-military nature—such as natural disaster response, border security, or urban force presence.
Guard personnel have been activated in FTNGD to perform missions including:
Individual reservists, whether members of the reserve or the National Guard, are assigned to one of three major reserve personnel categories: the Ready Reserve, the Standby Reserve, or the Retired Reserve (see Table 4). Reservists who are assigned to the Ready Reserve are further assigned to one of its three subcomponents: the Selected Reserve, the Individual Ready Reserve (IRR), or the Inactive National Guard (ING) (see Table 4). The differences among each of these categories are explained below.
Source: Department of Defense, "Uniform Reserve, Training, and Retirement Categories for the Reserve Components," March 11, 2014, https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/121506p.pdf.
The Ready Reserve is the primary personnel pool of the RCs. Members of the Ready Reserve are typically called to active duty before members of the Standby Reserve15 or the Retired Reserve. The Ready Reserve comprises the Selected Reserve, the Individual Ready Reserve, and the Inactive National Guard, each of which is described below.
The Selected Reserve contains those units and individuals within the Ready Reserve designated as "so essential to initial wartime missions that they have priority over all other Reserves."16 Members of the Selected Reserve are generally required to perform one weekend of training each month (inactive duty for training or IDT, also known colloquially as weekend drill) and two weeks of training each year (annual training or AT) for which they receive pay and benefits.17 Some members of the Selected Reserve may be required only to complete their IDT and AT, while others may perform additional periods of service.
The IRR is primarily composed of individuals who have completed training or some period of service in the AC or Selected Reserve and "have some period of their military service obligation (MSO) or other contractual obligation remaining."18 By law, these personnel may be required to perform training, but DOD policy does not require them "to meet the same AT and IDT training requirements as Selected Reserve members."19
The ING is, for practical purposes, the National Guard equivalent to the IRR. It comprises those members of the Army National Guard who are in an inactive status. The Air National Guard does not maintain an ING.20 Members do not participate in training as do members of the Selected Reserve. However, ING members are attached to specific National Guard units and "must muster once a year with their assigned unit, but they do not participate in training activities."21 Members of the ING can be involuntarily ordered to active duty if their units are activated under Partial Mobilization or Full Mobilization.22
The Standby Reserve comprises those individuals who maintain a military affiliation but are generally not required to participate in military training. These individuals may transfer from the Ready Reserve to the Standby Reserve due to temporary disability or hardship, to ensure continuity in key federal or private civilian jobs, or for other administrative reasons.23 Members of the Standby Reserve are subject to involuntary activation only in the case of Full Mobilization.24
The Retired Reserve includes (1) reserve personnel who are receiving retired pay as a result of their reserve and/or active service and (2) reserve personnel who transfer into the Retired Reserve after qualifying for reserve retirement but before becoming eligible to receive retired pay (which typically occurs at age 60).25 Members of the Retired Reserve may be involuntarily ordered to active duty in the event of a Full Mobilization, and some members of the Retired Reserve may be ordered to active duty in the event of a recall of retirees.26 Active component personnel who are receiving retired pay are not included in the Retired Reserve.27
The Space Force does not have an RC. Current law requires that full-time and part-time Space Force personnel be managed as part of a single component.28 By contrast, the other services generally manage full-time and part-time personnel in separate components.
Current statute authorizes a category of Space Force personnel to serve in an "active status" but not on "sustained duty." These personnel may serve in a part-time capacity and may be required to drill and train periodically, in a manner analogous to members of the Selected Reserve.29 The Secretary of the Air Force may also "enter into a written agreement with a member of the Space Force not on sustained duty" that "shall specify the conditions of service."30 This statutory language may allow for individual Space Force members (known as Guardians) to transfer between full-time and part-time duty over the course of their careers. It may also allow the Space Force to rapidly adjust its force structure.
The Secretary of the Air Force may also make service agreements with Guardians serving in "inactive status."31 Such arrangements may create a category of Guardians analogous to the IRR (see "Individual Ready Reserve").
Reserve units are primarily filled by traditional reservists: members of the Selected Reserve who are usually required to serve one weekend a month and two weeks a year.32 However, some reserve units are also staffed by one or more full-time civilian and/or military employees. These employees, known as full-time support (FTS) personnel, are "assigned to organize; administer; instruct; recruit and train; maintain supplies, equipment and aircraft; and perform other functions required on a daily basis in the execution of operational missions and readiness preparations" as authorized in Title 5, Title 10, and Title 32.33
DOD regulations identify five categories of FTS personnel: active guard and reserve (AGR), military technicians (MTs), AC, Navy full-time support, and civilians.34 The distinctions among each of these categories are outlined below and in Table 5. The mix of FTS personnel in each of the RCs is intended "to optimize consistency and stability for each RC to achieve its assigned missions."35
Source: Department of Defense, "Full-Time Support (FTS) to the Reserve Components," June 5, 2020, pp. 10-11, https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/120518p.pdf?ver=2020-06-05-095821-867.
AGR personnel are members of an RC who are placed on active duty or full-time National Guard duty orders for a period of 180 consecutive days or more for the purposes of "organizing, administering, recruiting, instructing, or training the reserve components."36 They may also perform certain operational support duties (such as support for emergency preparedness programs) and may provide training to AC personnel, DOD contractors, DOD civilians, and foreign military personnel.37 Although they are serving full-time, AGR personnel are still considered members of the Selected Reserve.38
MTs, referred to in statute as "military technicians (dual status)," are federal civilian employees who provide support to reserve units either in the "organizing, administering, instructing or training of the Selected Reserve" or "in the maintenance and repair of supplies or equipment."39 Some MTs may also perform certain operational support duties and provide training to AC personnel, DOD contractors, DOD civilians, and foreign military personnel.40
MTs are generally required to maintain membership in the Selected Reserve as a condition of their employment.41 They are required to attend IDT and AT with their reserve units.42 MTs can be involuntarily ordered to active duty in the same way as other members of the Selected Reserve.
AC personnel in FTS roles are active-duty members of the military who are "assigned or attached to RC organizations or units by their respective Service to provide advice, liaison, management, administration, training, and support."43 Although they are formally members of the AC, not the RC, AC personnel may mobilize as part of the reserve units to which they are assigned.44
The Navy Reserve employs a cadre of FTS personnel who are members of the Navy Reserve but typically serve full-time in a manner analogous to their AC FTS counterparts. These personnel are comparable to AGR but are identified as a separate category in DOD regulations.45 Navy personnel and administrative regulations sometimes refer to sailors in this program as "TARs" (Training and Administration of the Reserves).46 These personnel incur an eight-year obligation, of which 48 months are "normally" served on active duty, and are administered as full-time active-duty personnel.47 Their duties involve "organizing, administering, recruiting, instructing, or training" the reserves.48
Civilians are federal civil service employees who "provide administration, training, maintenance, and recruiting support to the RCs." They are not required to hold membership in the Selected Reserve as a condition of their employment.49
Reserve personnel are entitled to a range of pay and benefits, which may vary depending on the nature of the service performed and other factors (see Table 6). In general, when reservists are ordered to federal active duty for more than 30 days, they receive pay and benefits nearly identical to those of AC personnel. When ordered to active duty for a period of 30 days or less, they receive most of the pay and benefits that AC personnel receive.50
Reservists who are not on active duty and are not in the Selected Reserve receive a different set of pay and benefits.51 Additionally, National Guard personnel in state active duty receive pay and benefits outlined in state law. Finally, the accrual of pay and benefits for IDT is calculated differently from active service.52
a. 37 U.S.C. §204 and 37 U.S.C. §206.
c. See Department of Defense (DOD), "Military Compensation and Financial Readiness," https://militarypay.defense.gov/Pay/Allowances/BAH_Types/; DOD, "Basic Allowance for Subsistence (BAS) Policy," April 23, 2007, p. 2, https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/141805p.pdf; DOD, Financial Management Regulation, vol. 7A, pp. 29-6, 30-4, and 30-5, https://comptroller.war.gov/Portals/45/Documents/fmr/Volume_07a.pdf.
d. Defense Health Agency, "TRICARE Coverage for National Guard and Reserve Members: Know Your Options," press release, July 31, 2025, https://newsroom.tricare.mil/News/TRICARE-News/Article/4260976/tricare-coverage-for-national-guard-and-reserve-members-know-your-options.
e. Department of Veterans Affairs, "Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)," https://www.va.gov/life-insurance/options-eligibility/sgli/.
g. DOD, "Service Credit for Non-Regular Retirement," https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/121507p.pdf.
Reservists activated for full-time duty under Title 10 or Title 32 generally receive one day of basic pay for each day of duty in a manner analogous to their AC counterparts. During their AT—a period of sustained training typically lasting two weeks—reservists are also usually paid for each day of duty performed.
The pay policy for reservists' IDT is more complex. When performing IDT, reservists receive the equivalent of one day of basic pay for each unit training assembly (UTA) they attend. A UTA is generally a four-hour period of instruction, and there are typically four UTAs in a weekend.53 Reservists would therefore receive four days' basic pay for two calendar days of IDT. During a typical year, a reservist who worked 38 days (14 days of AT and 24 calendar days of IDT) would receive the equivalent of 62 days of basic pay (14 days of pay for AT and 48 days of pay for IDT).
Military personnel may be eligible for special and incentive pays for performing certain types of hazardous or arduous duty, for serving in certain assignments, or for possessing certain skills.54 Reserve personnel are generally eligible for these pays when performing qualifying duty, including AT.55 They may receive a pro-rated portion of the full monthly amount corresponding to the number of days served. Reservists may also be eligible for special and incentive pays during IDT and typically receive such compensation at a rate proportional to the amount of inactive duty compensation they receive (i.e., one-thirtieth of the monthly rate for each UTA).56
Military personnel may be eligible for a housing allowance, called Basic Allowance for Housing. During AT, but not during IDT, reservists may be eligible for a housing allowance known as Basic Allowance for Housing-Reserve Component/Transit and for a subsistence allowance known as Basic Allowance for Subsistence.57 Reserve officers are also entitled to a $400 clothing allowance at the beginning of their reserve service to assist them in purchasing necessary uniform items.58 Furthermore, if they are called to active duty for more than 90 days, they are usually entitled to an additional $200 clothing allowance.59 Reserve enlisted personnel are typically issued all their uniforms, shoes, boots, and insignia and therefore do not receive a clothing allowance; however, they may be eligible for a clothing allowance if required uniform items are not provided to them.60
When ordered to federal active duty for more than 30 days, members of the National Guard and reserves are generally entitled to the same medical benefits under TRICARE as are their AC counterparts.61 When not on active duty, members of the Selected Reserve may purchase TRICARE Reserve Select, a premium-based health plan.62
Members of the Selected Reserve and IRR are generally eligible to enroll in a dental plan known as the TRICARE Dental Program.63 Reservists may also enroll their families, which increases the premium.64 The program provides up to $1,500 of coverage per year, per beneficiary, toward non-orthodontic dental services.65 There is also a benefit for orthodontic services, which has a lifetime cap of $1,750 per eligible beneficiary.66
Members of the Selected Reserve are eligible to purchase up to $500,000 of life insurance under the Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance program.67 If a reservist is covered, he or she can also purchase up to $100,000 of life insurance for a spouse. This program may also provide $10,000 of life insurance coverage per child at no additional cost.68
Military personnel and their dependents may have access to the commissary, a system of subsidized military grocery stores. They may also have access to exchanges, which provide additional goods and services to military personnel and their dependents. Per Title 10, Section 1063, of the U.S. Code, members of the Selected Reserve "in good standing" have the same level of access to the commissary and exchanges as their AC counterparts do. Reserve retirees, including those under the age of 60, have the same access as retired military personnel.69 DOD regulations further extend commissary privileges to members of the IRR and Standby Reserve and to the dependents of RC personnel.70
Reservists become eligible for retirement after 20 years of qualifying service.71 A year of qualifying service is defined as a year in which a reservist has earned at least 50 retirement points, the sum of which is used to calculate retired pay (see below).72 A reservist earns 15 retirement points per year for being a member of the Ready Reserve, one point for each UTA, one point for each day of AT, and one point for each day of active duty.73 Points can also be earned for completing certain military courses and for performing funeral honors duty.74
Earning 50 points in a given year is generally feasible for members of the Selected Reserve, because attending a full year of IDT and two weeks of AT generates 77 retirement points.75 Excluding points earned while in an active duty status (which includes AT), reservists may not earn more than 130 points per year.76 Additionally, including points earned while in an active duty status, reservists may not earn more than 365 points in a year (366 in a leap year).77
After completing 20 years of qualifying service, a reservist may apply for retirement.78 Upon reaching the retired pay eligibility age—which typically ranges between 50 and 60 depending on how many days of certain types of duty the reservist performed during his or her career79—the retired reservist is eligible to receive retired pay.
Retired pay is calculated by totaling all the points earned during all the years of service, then dividing this sum by 360. This calculation produces the number of equivalent years of active-duty service the reservist has performed. The number of equivalent years is then multiplied by 2.5% or 2.0% (depending on the date of entry to military service) to determine the retirement benefit multiplier.80 This multiplier is then applied to an amount based on the highest of the last three years of paid service, sometimes called the high-three average.81
Reservists mobilized for contingency operations are entitled to pay, benefits, and legal protections that are nearly identical to those provided to active-duty servicemembers. Specifically, they are entitled to basic pay at the same rate as active-duty personnel and, if qualified, may receive special and incentive pays including Hazardous Duty Pay, Aviation Career Incentive Pay, Hostile Fire/Imminent Danger Pay, and special pays for health professionals.82
Provided the servicemembers' orders are for more than 30 days, they are also entitled to a variety of allowances, including Basic Allowance for Housing, Basic Allowance for Subsistence, and, if separated from their families, a Family Separation Allowance.83 Medical and dental coverage for these reservists and their family members is nearly identical to that provided to active-duty servicemembers. Leave is accrued in the same manner as for active-duty personnel.84 They may use child care centers; space-available travel; and morale, welfare, and recreation services.85
Certain reservists who experience income loss while involuntarily mobilized may be entitled to a special payment of $50 to $3,000.86 Reservists who have experienced income loss become eligible for these payments in every full month of active duty following the month in which they:
The amount of compensation available under this provision is equal to the reservist's average monthly civilian income minus total monthly military compensation.88 However, payments shall be made only if the differential is at least $50 per month and may not exceed $3,000 per month. Involuntary orders to full-time National Guard duty under Title 32, Section 502(f)(1), of the U.S. Code count as qualifying duty for the purposes of this payment.89
The 111th Congress enacted a provision to minimize the income loss of civilian federal government employees who are involuntarily ordered to active duty or involuntarily retained on active duty.90 The provision provides differential pay—a payment equal to the amount by which a reservist's military pay and allowances are lower than his or her civilian basic pay. Specific eligibility criteria and the method for calculating the amount of differential pay are outlined in a 2015 memorandum issued by the Office of Personnel Management.91 This provision applies only to federal government employees, but it is not limited to cases of extended or frequent activations such as the income replacement provision discussed in the previous paragraph. Entitlement begins immediately following involuntary activation, though compensation may lag by up to eight weeks.92 Full-time National Guard duty under Title 32 does not count as qualifying duty for the purposes of this payment.93
Reservists perform federal duty under a range of statutory authorities in the U.S. Code.94 Five of these statutes are generally used to activate reservists to carry out or support military operations as part of the Armed Forces. These statutes are discussed below.
Source: Congress.gov.
Notes: The names of these mobilization authorities are taken from Department of Defense, "Accessing the Reserve Components (RC)," June 7, 2016, p. 16, https://www.esd.whs.mil/portals/54/documents/dd/issuances/dodi/123512p.pdf.
In time of war or national emergency declared by Congress, or when otherwise authorized by law, Section 12301(a) permits the service secretaries to order RC members under their jurisdiction to active duty.95 There is no limit on the number of reservists who may be activated under this provision. Reservists may be kept on active duty for the duration of the war or emergency plus six months.
In time of a national emergency declared by the President, or when otherwise authorized by law, Section 12302 permits any of the service secretaries to activate members of the Ready Reserve under presidential authority for up to 24 consecutive months. Up to 1 million members of the Ready Reserve may be called up at any one time under this provision. Congressional approval is not required for such activations.96
Under Section 12304, the President may order up to 200,000 members of the Selected Reserve and the IRR to active duty for up to 365 consecutive days. The President may activate reservists under this provision without approval from Congress. However, the President is required to notify Congress within 24 hours of such an action "in writing, setting forth the circumstances necessitating the action taken under this section and describing the anticipated use of these units or members."
Those reservists activated under this authority may not be used to suppress insurrection or enforce federal authority, nor may they be used to provide assistance to the federal government or the states for disaster response unless responding to an emergency involving the "use or threatened use of a weapon of mass destruction" or an actual or threatened terrorist attack "that results, or could result, in significant loss of life or property."97
Section 12304 also authorizes activations of reserve personnel in response to "significant cyber incidents" affecting DOD or Department of Homeland Security information systems that the relevant Secretary "determines is likely to result in demonstrable harm to the national security interests, foreign relations, or the economy of the United States, or to the public confidence, civil liberties, or public health and safety of the people of the United States" or a cyber incident or collection of related cyber incidents that "the President determines is likely to result in demonstrable harm to the national security interests, foreign relations, or economy of the United States or to the public confidence, civil liberties, or public health and safety of the people of the United States; or … a significant incident declared pursuant to section 2233 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 677b)."98
Under Section 12304a, the Secretary of Defense may order units and individuals of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force Reserves to active duty for up to 120 days "[w]hen a governor requests federal assistance in responding to a major disaster or emergency" as defined in Section 102 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. §5122).99 National Guard forces are not included in this covered group. State and territorial governors have authority to activate their National Guard forces and request support from other state and territorial National Guards under the Emergency Management Assistance Compact.100
Section 12304b allows involuntary activations of Selected Reserve units for up to 365 consecutive days of active duty in support of a combatant command.101 No more than 60,000 members of the National Guard and reserves may serve on active duty under this authority at a time. The authority to activate reservists under this provision rests with each service secretary, but it may be invoked only for a "preplanned mission in support of a combatant command" where the costs of the activations and a description of the mission are included in the service's budget materials.102
According to the committee report that accompanied the Senate version of the bill, this authority "is not designed for use for emergent operational or humanitarian missions, but rather to enhance the use of reserve component units that organize, train, and plan to support operational mission requirements to the same standards as active component units under service force generation plans in a cyclic, periodic, and predictable manner."103
Members of the Retired Reserve can be involuntarily ordered to active duty in the case of a full mobilization (see "Full Mobilization," above). Under this authority, they may be kept on active duty for the duration of the war or emergency plus six months.104 While there is no cap on the number of retirees who may be activated, a limit in this provision stipulates that "a member on an inactive status list or in a retired status may not be ordered to active duty under this subsection unless the Secretary concerned, with the approval of the Secretary of Defense in the case of the Secretary of a military department, determines that there are not enough qualified Reserves in an active status or in the inactive National Guard in the required category who are readily available."105
Additionally, the Secretary of each military department has the authority to involuntarily order certain members of the Retired Reserve to active duty at any time, but this authority applies only to members of the Retired Reserve who have a regular retirement (at least 20 years of active duty).106 There is a limit on the amount of time recalled retirees can serve and a limit on the number of officers recalled, but these limits do not apply in times of war or national emergency declared by Congress or the President.107
Congress may consider how it expects the National Guard and reserves to be employed and if the force structure and personnel policies of the reserves support Congress's intent.
Congress could evaluate the balance between the RC's strategic and operational roles. In its strategic role, the RC provides additional forces for mid- to large-scale contingency operations or other unanticipated national crises. In its operational role, the RC participates regularly in force rotations and military operations.
DOD policy indicates that the reserves maintain both operational and strategic roles.108 Congress may consider the appropriate balance between these mission sets. It may further consider whether the force structure and personnel policies of the RC supports the missions Congress intends the RC to perform.
Congress sets the authorized number of military personnel (also called the end-strength) of the Armed Forces, historically in an annual National Defense Authorization Act. Congress may consider whether RC personnel policies help or hinder the services' efforts to recruit and retain personnel to meet these end-strength goals.109 Generally, more generous RC pay and benefits may help the reserves attract recruits and retain personnel to meet end-strength goals. Generous RC benefits may also cause prospective recruits to choose the reserves over the AC—or AC personnel to switch to the reserves. This dynamic may hinder the active forces' efforts to meet their end-strength goals. Congress may consider the appropriate balance of AC and RC benefits with the structure of the total force in mind.
Congress may consider whether RC personnel policies are cost-effective, by evaluating the absolute cost of employing reserve personnel, or comparing the costs of employing active and reserve personnel.
Should Congress choose to reduce the costs of employing reserve personnel, it may adjust RC pay and benefits to achieve this goal. Congress may also adjust the AC/RC force mix for a range of reasons, including cost savings.110
title: Reserve Component Personnel Issues: Questions and Answers

DETROIT ARSENAL, Mich. – Michelle A. Link took the helm last month of the U.S. Army Tank-automotive and Armaments Command’s Integrated Logistics Support Center, leveraging decades of logistics and acquisition experience to forge future readiness.
“Ms. Link’s deep professional expertise, commitment to Army readiness and longstanding connection to the Detroit Arsenal community will serve the Integrated Logistics Support Center and the broader TACOM enterprise well,” Deputy to the Commander Brian Butler said in an announcement about her new assignment.
As TACOM ILSC executive director, Link leads an organization that provides weapons systems sustainment management and life cycle logistics support to the Soldier and ground systems enterprise. The ILSC supports more than 3,500 weapons systems.
Throughout her career, Link has led complex portfolios supporting many critical Army capabilities. She most recently served as Portfolio Management Executive Combat Sustainment, providing professional and executive management for the development, systems integration, testing, sustainment and modernization of nearly 300 programs spanning the Army’s engineer, ordnance, quartermaster and transportation equipment portfolios.
Link is a Detroit native, graduate of Michigan State University and veteran leader. Other previous roles include deputy Program Executive Officer, Ground Combat Systems and acting PEO GCS, as well as various senior positions in logistics, systems engineering and portfolio management. She has worked at U.S. Army Garrison-Detroit Arsenal since March 2009, when she joined PEO-GCS as a lead systems engineer.
In addition to her civilian service, Link is a major general in the U.S. Army Reserve. She commands the 75th U.S. Army Reserve Innovation Command at Ellington Field Joint Reserve Base in Houston, Texas.
title: Michelle Link named TACOM ILSC executive director

EPA Reaches Settlement with Colgate-Palmolive to Bring it Into Compliance with Requirements for Large-Quantity Chemical Imports
NEW YORK – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reached a settlement with the Colgate-Palmolive Corporation to correct violations of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) Chemical Data Reporting (CDR) Rule. This settlement resolves Colgate-Palmolive’s failures to report numerous chemical substances imported between 2016 and 2019. The company has certified compliance with the reporting requirements and paid a $930,000 penalty.
“EPA’s data-reporting requirements are essential to protecting human health and the environment,” said EPA Region 2 Administrator Michael Martucci. “This settlement is a great example of EPA working with a business to achieve compliance while ensuring that people have the information they need about chemicals in their communities.”
In March 2023, an EPA inspection of Colgate-Palmolive’s New Jersey facility revealed that the company had failed to report required chemical data for imports that occurred from 2016 through 2019 by the January 2021 deadline. With EPA’s assistance, it reported its chemical data in July 2023. The data showed that Colgate had imported 47 chemicals in quantities greater than the reporting threshold and that the company had failed to meet its obligation to file a report by the deadline. EPA worked with the company to bring it into compliance with the requirements and enter into a legal settlement.
Manufacturers and importers of large quantities of chemical substances listed on the TSCA Chemical Substance Inventory are required to report data on chemical manufacturing, processing, and use every four years. EPA uses CDR data to help assess the potential human health and environmental impacts of these chemicals. States, tribes, other agencies, and the public also can use CDR data to understand chemicals in commerce.

BOSTON – A Texas man pleaded guilty yesterday in federal court in Boston for his role in a scheme that involved impersonating property owners, selling their land and then laundering the proceeds. The scheme involved more than $1.5 million in fraudulent property sales.

Moshe Levi, 61, of Carrollton, Texas, pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy and money laundering conspiracy. U.S. District Court Judge Myong J. Joun scheduled sentencing for Feb. 11, 2027. Levi was charged along with two co-defendants in July 2026 .

According to court filings, Levi and his co-coconspirators executed a deed fraud scheme by identifying vacant and unencumbered real properties in Massachusetts, Georgia, Indiana and Tennessee that were owned by individuals who lived out of state. Levi and his alleged co-conspirators established email and internet telephony accounts and obtained fake identifications, including driver’s licenses and passports, all in the names of the properties’ owners. Using the fake identifications and accounts, Levi and his alleged co-conspirators impersonated the record owners of the properties in order to trick real estate professionals into listing and negotiating the sale of the properties and deeding the properties to unsuspecting buyers in exchange for payment.

In addition, Levi and his alleged co-conspirators conducted financial transactions involving the proceeds of the fraudulent sales of the properties, including by check and wire transfer, through individual and corporate bank accounts that they and others controlled, with the intent to conceal and disguise the nature, location, source, ownership and control of the proceeds. According to court documents, since approximately June 2023, Levi and allegedly others shared and attempted to share in illegal proceeds of approximately $1 million.

The charge of wire fraud conspiracy provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000, or twice the gross gain or loss from the scheme, whichever is greater. The charge of money laundering conspiracy provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $500,000 or twice the value of the financial transactions that were the object of the conspiracy. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Boston Field Office made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Seth B. Kosto, Chief of the Securities, Financial & Cyber Fraud Unit is prosecuting the case.

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The remaining defendants are presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.
title: Texas Man Pleads Guilty to Role in $1.5 Million Deed Fraud and Money Laundering Schemes

BOSTON – A New Hampshire man pleaded guilty yesterday in federal court in Boston to transporting child pornography across state lines.

Daniel Murphy, 50, of Merrimack, N.H., pleaded guilty to transportation of child pornography before U.S. Senior District Court Judge William G. Young who scheduled sentencing for Jan. 26, at 2:00 p.m. Murphy was arrested and charged in August 2026 .

In August 2025, Murphy engaged in sexualized dialogue on Facebook Messenger with a minor victim living in Massachusetts. He coerced the victim to send pornographic videos and photographs and, in turn, sent obscene material depicting himself to the victim. Over the course of several days, Murphy also repeatedly traveled to meet the minor victim in person, transporting child pornography along with him. When Murphy’s electronic devices were seized by law enforcement, they were found to contain pornographic images and video of the minor victim as well as additional videos and images of other minors constituting child sexual abuse material.

The charge of transporting child pornography provides for a sentence of no less than five years and up to 20 years in prison, at least five years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; Chief Mark Zimmerman of the North Reading Police Department; and Chief Brian K. Levesque of the Merrimack Police Department (N.H.) made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Nashua Police Department (N.H.). Assistant U.S. Attorney Eric L. Hawkins of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. The charge of making false statements relating to a health care program provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, one year of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. Court documents reflect that on July 9, 2026, the defendant was stopped and detained by a Levy County Sheriff’s deputy at a gas station because he had an active arrest warrant for violation of probation. While placing the defendant under arrest, the deputy located a fully loaded, .45 caliber firearm on the defendant’s hip, as pictured below.

Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, today announced that WINIFER ACOSTA JIMENEZ, 32, of the Bronx, New York, was sentenced yesterday by U.S. District Judge Vernon D. Oliver in Hartford to 72 months of imprisonment and two years of supervised release for a fentanyl trafficking offense.

According to court documents and statements made in court, in February 2023, the Drug Enforcement Administration arranged the controlled purchase of two kilograms of fentanyl from a wholesale supplier of narcotics with multiple distribution points in the northeastern U.S. Acosta Jimenez and her co-defendant, Ovidalis Jimenez Pujols, were arrested on February 22, 2023, after they transported the two kilograms of fentanyl from New York to a meeting location in Milford, Connecticut.

Acosta Jimenez, who was released on $100,000 bond after federal arrest on January 31, 2024, removed her GPS monitoring equipment on July 31, 2024, and absconded. She was located and arrested in New York on December 18, 2025.

Acosta Jimenez has been detained since her arrest. On February 3, 2026, she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute 40 grams or more of fentanyl.

Jimenez Pujols also pleaded guilty and, on February 19, 2025, was sentenced to 48 months of imprisonment .

This matter was investigated the Drug Enforcement Administration, with the assistance of the Connecticut State Police and the West Haven Police Department. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Stephanie T. Levick and Nathan J. Guevremont.

text:
Dear Mr. Secretary,
Since the TBAC last met in early August, Treasury markets have repriced toward a higher path for interest rates, reflecting stronger economic activity and associated financing needs, persistent energy-supply disruptions, and the Federal Reserve’s initial rate hike and projections for further increases. The selloff in rates was led by the front end of the yield curve, with two-year yields rising by roughly 50bps and ten-year yields by roughly 40bps. The move accelerated in September and early October, with ten-year yields peaking around 5.4% and thirty-year yields around 5.7% in early October. Some of that increase has since reversed.
A substantial part of the repricing reflected stronger U.S. economic activity through the summer despite higher energy prices and rising rates. Household spending remained resilient as gains in financial wealth and lower savings rates cushioned pressure on real incomes. Existing fixed-rate mortgages limited the increase in homeowners’ debt-service costs, even as higher rates on new borrowing weighed on housing activity. Meanwhile, strong investment in computing equipment, intellectual property, and data centers offset weakness in more rate-sensitive investment. The infrastructure buildout proved less sensitive to financing costs than traditional housing-led expansions. Related gains in construction and equipment manufacturing are becoming visible but have not yet generated a broad acceleration in employment.
This resilience gave the Federal Reserve greater scope to respond to persistent inflation risks exacerbated by the energy shock. Supply disruptions that began over the summer have proved more persistent than initially expected, keeping crude and refined-product prices elevated through the quarter and feeding into transportation and freight costs. Headline CPI accelerated to 3.7% in September, with gasoline alone accounting for more than half of the monthly increase. Core CPI ran at 2.6% as fuel and freight costs passed through to other categories.
The Federal Reserve responded in September by raising its target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Chairman Warsh emphasized both the strengthening economy and insufficient progress on inflation, characterizing the decision as removing accommodation rather than making already restrictive financial conditions materially tighter. The September Summary of Economic Projections reinforced the higher-for-longer message: the median policy-rate projection rose to 4.1% for both year-end 2026 and year-end 2027, compared with 3.8% and 3.6%, respectively, in June. Markets continued to price approximately three additional rate increases over the coming year even as the Fed held rates steady in October. More recently, higher borrowing costs and emerging weakness in equity and credit markets have moderated expectations for the pace of tightening but not eliminated expectations for further increases.
Several cross-market and technical developments came into play over the quarter:
- Term premium has risen less than yields this year, though the ten-year term premium showed some strain in the early fall. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s ACM model estimate of the ten-year term premium rose approximately 20bps in September. Interest rate implied volatility rose sharply, reflecting greater priced uncertainty and raising the cost of option-based protection against further yield increases. As yields rose and refinancing incentives diminished, mortgage durations extended, prompting convexity hedgers to reduce duration. Collateralized mortgage obligation floaters with coupon caps added to hedging pressures as forward-implied coupons approached their caps, likely increasing demand for intermediate-dated rates volatility. These flows likely amplified the initial selloff and increase in volatility, although the scope for further mortgage-duration extension diminished as yields moved higher.
- Stronger economic activity was also driving expectations of higher interest rates outside the United States. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan raised policy rates over the period as markets priced a broader tightening cycle across major developed economies. Developments in European sovereign markets were also relevant for Treasuries, as fiscal and political uncertainty produced a sharp widening in French government-bond spreads, adding to volatility across global fixed-income markets. Those linkages have not operated uniformly: the correlation between French and U.S. yield changes weakened in October, and more acute French stress subsequently supported safe-haven demand for Treasuries and German Bunds.
- Technology-related financing remained an additional influence on capital markets and financial conditions. Large debt offerings and prospective mega-IPOs reflected substantial private-sector financing needs. Heavy technology issuance and uncertainty over future financing needs contributed to wider spreads in the sector and increased competition for long-duration capital. Banks and asset managers also helped technology companies tap a broader pool of capital through GPU-backed loans, equipment leases, and data center project financing. Foreign investor demand to finance U.S. technology contributed to dollar strength, providing an additional channel of financial tightening alongside higher borrowing costs. Although large issuance windows may influence Treasury concessions and hedging flows at the margin, there is no evidence of a persistent deterioration in Treasury auction demand. Recent auctions remained generally resilient, though individual results varied.
- Technology news also contributed to weaker risk sentiment later in the period, helping restore demand for Treasuries. By late October, the Nasdaq 100 had fallen just over 7% from its early-October high amid greater scrutiny of the returns on increasingly debt-financed technology investment. Together with wider credit spreads, the equity pullback helped restore a safe-haven bid for Treasuries, partially reversing the earlier rise in yields.
Against that backdrop, the Committee convened for its quarterly refunding discussion. The outlook shows the funding gap widens over FY27 and increases further in FY28 and FY29. Consistent with Treasury’s cash management policy, Treasury recently published cash balance assumptions for the end of Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27 at approximately $850 billion and $1 trillion, respectively.
The Committee next addressed the first of its two charges: Super Intelligence (SI)-related issuance. Members discussed recent trends in corporate bond issuance related to SI and associated businesses. Members noted the market is in the midst of a significant technology financing cycle. Financing is also expanding beyond long-dated corporate bonds, with secured and asset-backed structures increasingly bringing issuance inside 10 years. Taken as a whole, the technology ecosystem appears to have both the capacity and incentive to sustain borrowing and investment.
Foreign demand for U.S. fixed-income assets has accelerated this year, while the broader investor base retains significant capacity to absorb additional issuance. Insurers, pensions, households, and foreign investors provide diversified sources of demand, with households and private pensions still relatively under allocated to fixed income. Even modest reallocations from cash and equities could therefore absorb a meaningful share of projected borrowing.
Treasury auction results show no evidence that 2026 technology-related issuance has crowded out long-end Treasury demand. To the extent technology investment is affecting rates, the Committee viewed the transmission as stemming from stronger growth rather than through crowding out. Higher Treasury yields have primarily reflected growth, policy expectations, and energy prices rather than an issuance-driven supply shock. Members emphasized, however, that the financing cycle remains in its early stages and recommended that Treasury continue to monitor potential effects on Treasury market demand as SI-related issuance grows.
The Committee’s second charge focused on Treasury derivatives and their growing role in the market. Since the 2022 rise in yields, asset managers have increasingly used futures to gain synthetic Treasury exposure, while liability-driven investors, including pension funds and insurers, have used interest rate swaps to manage duration. The Committee emphasized that expressing duration through derivatives enhances demand for Treasuries by broadening market access and expanding intermediation capacity.
In the context of discussing derivatives, the Committee identified several policy options that could further improve demand for cash Treasuries. These include easing regulatory constraints on balance sheet capacity, including exempting Treasuries from leverage ratios and recognizing pre-positioned discount window collateral in liquidity metrics; expanding access to repo financing; improving the availability of term repo; and enabling new entrants in repo market making. The Committee also recommended evaluation of fund accounting treatment of repo interest, tax treatment, and operational challenges. Together, these steps could broaden and diversify the base of cash Treasury holders, strengthen market intermediation, and support durable demand for Treasuries.
The Committee discussed the efficacy of the liquidity support buyback program. There is a variety of evidence that the program has supported liquidity conditions since it was introduced in 2024, and buybacks remain an effective tool for that purpose. While an effective tool, the Committee believes that any management of Treasury’s maturity profile should be done via changes to auction sizes.
To further the goal of financing the government at the lowest cost over time, the Committee continues to endorse an issuance strategy that balances expected costs and volatility of interest expense, matches issuance patterns to market demand, encourages smooth market functioning, and is regular and predictable. As members look ahead, baseline fiscal projections suggest that current auction sizes are likely to shift Treasury’s debt profile toward an increasing share of bill and shorter-term funding. The Committee believes that the market has recently been absorbing Treasury issuance well and that the bulk of recent interest rate rises reflect strong economic conditions and the monetary policy outlook rather than weak investor demand for Treasuries. The Committee discussed that real money investors, including retail and some institutional investors, have grown their demand as rates have risen and as a hedge against downward moves in economic conditions. However, the Committee also noted that money market fund assets have leveled off and the bill market has started to show some signs of price sensitivity.
In light of that outlook, for the current quarter, the Committee recommended keeping nominal coupon, FRN, and TIPS auction sizes unchanged. However, the Committee believes that given current fiscal projections, increases in coupon auction sizes will be warranted later in FY27. Looking ahead, given the projected funding gaps in FY28 and FY29, members discussed different approaches to coupon increases over the horizon. While there is broad agreement across the Committee to increase coupon auction sizes, there was considerable debate around the pace and sizing specific to the long end of the curve.
Members recommended that Treasury change its forward-guidance language and emphasized that clear communication alongside a regular and predictable operating framework remains important to help market participants adjust to future changes.
In conclusion, consistent with its past messaging, the Committee encourages Congress to act to raise or suspend the debt limit to avoid disrupting Treasury market functioning, increasing costs to the taxpayer, and constraining economic growth.
Respectfully,
Jason S. Granet
Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
E. Alexander Schiller
Vice Chair, Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
title: Report to the Secretary of the Treasury from the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee

Press Statement

Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, Spokesman Office of the Spokesman

November 4, 2026

Today, the United States is acting against a criminal network that sells fraudulent flags to the Iranian regime’s shadow fleet of ships. The United States is also targeting a Türkiye-based company that provides ground services to sanctioned Iranian airlines. The Department of the Treasury is taking these actions under Operation Economic Outcast, the Trump Administration’s campaign to cut off revenue the Iranian regime uses to fund terrorism, weapons proliferation, and its proxies across the Middle East.

For more than a decade, India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid, have formed companies that pose as the flag registries and maritime service providers of countries and jurisdictions such as Guyana, Eswatini, Aruba, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste. These companies have sold fraudulent registrations and certificates to vessels carrying illicit Iranian oil. Most of these governments have publicly disavowed the fraudulent registries.

Today’s action targets 13 individuals and companies in the Sharma network. We commend the governments that have exposed these schemes. We call on flag states, port authorities, and the maritime industry to verify vessel registrations and deny shadow fleet vessels access to their waters and ports.

The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy. For more information on today’s action, please see the Department of the Treasury’s press release .

Teneika Reynolds, 50, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Greg Kays, to aiding and assisting in the preparation of false tax returns.

Reynolds was the owner and operator of TR Tax Service, a tax preparation business operating in Kansas City. Reynolds prepared and electronically filed returns claiming false items including Schedule C business expenses, false Forms 7202, Sick and Family Leave Credits, and fictitious Household Help income for client-taxpayers for the tax years 2019 to 2023. This resulted in refunds larger than what her clients were entitled to receive.

Reynolds assisted at least 15 individuals file at least 33 false and fraudulent income tax returns for tax years 2019 through 2023. Specifically, on Feb. 8, 2022, Reynolds aided and assisted in the filing of an IRS Form 1040, U.S. Individual Income Tax Return, with the Internal Revenue Service. On that form, Reynolds included false Sick and Family Leave credits, resulting in a fraudulent refund.

Under federal statutes, Reynolds is subject to a sentence of up to three years in federal prison without parole. The maximum statutory sentence is prescribed by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes, as the sentencing of Reynolds will be determined by the court based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled after the completion of a presentence investigation by the United States Probation Office.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Rudolph R. Rhodes IV. It was investigated by Internal Revenue Service-Criminal Investigation.

Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
