From a childhood spent moving with a Coast Guard family to a career focused on occupational health and safety, Ashlyn Schmitt brings both technical expertise and a people-first mindset to the Buffalo District. As an Industrial Hygienist, she helps identify and evaluate workplace health hazards while supporting safe operations across the district.
Q: Where are you from?
Ashlyn: I was born at Cherry Point Marine Corps Air Station in Havelock, North Carolina, and moved frequently growing up because my father served in the U.S. Coast Guard. My family lived in California and Iowa before eventually settling in Northeast Ohio, where we moved to be closer to extended family after my father accepted a position at the Coast Guard station in Cleveland.
Q: What did you study, and where did you attend college?
Ashlyn: I attended The University of Akron, where I majored in chemical engineering and earned my bachelor’s degree in 2020.
Q: What is your position with the Buffalo District?
Ashlyn: I serve as an Industrial Hygienist with the Buffalo District, specializing in occupational health hazards. My work includes conducting air and noise sampling at project sites to help evaluate employee exposure levels and ensure conditions remain within appropriate limits.
Q: How did you learn about the position with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers?
Ashlyn: I was already living in the same city as the field office where I worked, so I knew the Buffalo District had a local presence. When I saw the Industrial Hygienist vacancy, I viewed it as a great opportunity because it was closer to home and allowed me to remain in Ohio.
Q: What motivated you to join the Buffalo District?
Ashlyn: Before joining the Buffalo District, I worked for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration as a Safety Engineer, conducting onsite inspections and issuing citations throughout Northeast Ohio. I was interested in transitioning into a more proactive role that focused less on enforcement and more on helping prevent workplace hazards.
Q: What do you enjoy doing outside of work?
Ashlyn: Outside of work, my husband and I spend a lot of time with our four shepherd-mix dogs. I also compete with two of them in an Akron-area frisbee league that I have participated in for the past five years. In addition, I enjoy bouldering, scuba diving, and playing trivia. One of the most memorable places I have gone scuba diving was Taiwan, and I am National Association of Underwater Instructors (NAUI)-certified with additional diving experience in quarries throughout Ohio.
With a background in engineering, safety, and field-based hazard assessment, Ashlyn plays an important role in helping protect the Buffalo District workforce. Her proactive approach to occupational health supports safe, effective mission execution across the district.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Buffalo District delivers world-class engineering solutions to the Great Lakes Region, the Army and the Nation to ensure national security, environmental sustainability, water resource management, and emergency assistance during peace and war.
For 250 years, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has been at the forefront of the nation’s engineering excellence, responding when called. From constructing fortifications during the Revolutionary War, to building the infrastructure that saw America’s strength grow militarily and economically, USACE’s mission has always been to deliver engineering solutions for our nation’s toughest challenges.
title: Meet the Team: Buffalo District Industrial Hygienist Brings Proactive Safety Focus to the Mission

Rep. Panetta’s Statement on His 2026 Reelection
Monterey, CA – United States Representative Jimmy Panetta (CA-19) released the following statement on the results of his 2026 reelection:
“I am deeply honored and humbled that the people of California’s 19th Congressional District again elected me to represent them in the United States Congress. My work in Congress has always been guided by the principle that good governing is good politics. Tonight’s overwhelming results reaffirm that belief, bolster my work, and strengthen my commitment to delivering for the people that I proudly serve.
“Over the past two years, the division and dysfunction in Washington could lead many across the nation to be disillusioned and disengage from the responsibilities of living in our democracy. However, tonight’s results demonstrate that Americans don’t cower during dark times. Instead, we face our challenges, stand together, and embrace our obligations through the democratic process of voting. By giving us robust Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the American voters also gave us a mandate to govern in the 120th Congress.
“With our agency, we must now set the agenda and provide answers for Americans when it comes to the issues of affordability and accountability.  Living up to our Constitutional responsibilities and our system of checks and balances, we will legislate to bring down the cost of living, and, at the same time, we will investigate any and all misdeeds by this Administration.  I look forward to upholding my Constitutional oath through my service in the 120th Congress, my willingness to work with anybody who helps me govern, and my will to fight anybody who threatens our democratic values.”
###
title: Rep. Panetta’s Statement on His 2026 Reelection

NASA selected three companies on Wednesday to perform work to develop Ka-band space relay capability concepts that are compatible with current missions in space, ensuring service continuity for existing spacecraft without requiring modifications to their onboard systems.
Through this work, NASA will aim to acquire end-to-end solutions that include space, ground, launch, operations, and integration elements, as one of many customers in the commercial marketplace.
The awards, under the Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships-3 Broad Agency Announcement Appendix E, are firm-fixed-price contracts that give NASA the option to provide additional funding up to the award limit to advance from initial concept development and risk reduction to an in-orbit flight demonstration. The initial period of performance runs from Nov. 4 through May 3, 2027, with additional priced options to continue work through 2029.
The contract awardees with maximum potential value inclusive of all future options are:
- Astranis Space Technologies Corp. for $264.3 million.
- Global Enterprise Solutions Inc. for $340.4 million.
- Viasat Inc. for $460.9 million.
Facilitated through the agency’s SCaN (Space Communications and Navigation) program’s Communications Services Project, this work supports NASA’s decision to gradually retire the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and adopt commercial services for future missions. In addition to the commercial capabilities currently under development by the program’s industry partners, Ka-band services are needed to support select in-orbit missions that cannot feasibly modify flight hardware or transition to non-compatible commercial services.
To learn more about NASA’s Network Extension for User Continuity and Sustainability Ka-band service acquisition, visit:

An indictment is merely an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ###

SCHOFIELD BARRACKS, Hawaii – After days of disciplined preparation and staging across the Hawaiian archipelago, U.S. Army forces and their multinational partners have officially transitioned into active, force-on-force maneuver training during Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center Rotation 27-01.
The exercise has shifted from reception, staging, and onward integration into the first battle period, testing the 25th Infantry Division's ability to seize and retain decisive terrain in a contested, multi-domain environment.
The theater is now set and established with lines of communication, and the transition to the attack is where convergence will become a reality.
" We are leveraging the condition setting and synchronization of warfighting functions to enable our Light Fighters to win in Close Combat," said Brig. Gen. Robert Bryant, 25th Infantry Division deputy commander for support.
A key component of this transition relies on distributed access and mobility.
JPMRC 27-01 involves approximately 7,000 personnel and continues to demonstrate the Army’s commitment to readiness, interoperability with allies and partners, and the ability to provide flexible, combat-credible forces to the Joint Force in the Indo-Pacific.
Operating on Maui and Oahu, elements of the French 6th Light Armored Brigade are working in tandem with the 25th Combat Aviation Brigade to secure Forward Arming and Refueling Points. This critical multinational integration extends the joint force's operational reach, allowing aviation assets to sustain continuous pressure and rapidly project combat power across the island chain.
Ground forces on Oahu and the Island of Hawaii are simultaneously maneuvering to secure initial objectives. Elements of the 2nd Mobile Brigade are applying fieldcraft, mobility, and modernized command-and-control systems to navigate demanding jungle and archipelagic terrain.
In the coming days, the 11th Airborne Division will execute a mass tactical airborne jump, known as a Joint Forcible Entry operation, into the Pōhakuloa Training Area to secure key infrastructure. This action will immediately be followed by a long-range maritime air assault conducted by the 25th Infantry Division, rapidly inserting infantry forces across the oceanic gap to reinforce the position.
These early maneuvers are setting the conditions for sustained tactical success and endurance as the exercise continues and are paving the way for massive joint integration later this week.
About the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center:
The Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center is U.S. Army Pacific’s premier regional Combat Training Center. Operating across the Hawaiian Islands, Alaska, and exportable locations throughout the Indo-Pacific, JPMRC provides realistic, live, virtual, and constructive training in complex archipelagic, jungle, and arctic environments. The center generates combat-credible forces, validates multi-domain readiness, and deepens interoperability with Joint forces, allies, and multinational partners to uphold a free and open Indo-Pacific.
About the 25th Infantry Division:
The 25th Infantry Division, "Tropic Lightning," is America's Pacific Division, headquartered at Schofield Barracks, Hawaii. As the premier land force in the Pacific, the 25th ID provides combat-ready forces capable of conducting decisive operations across the Indo-Pacific. Through rigorous training and close partnerships with allies and the Joint Force, the division remains committed to warfighting excellence, regional stability, and being a responsible steward of the ‘āina and our local communities across the State of Hawaii.
title: Tropic Lightning, Partner Forces Transition to the Close Battle at JPMRC 27-01

Parra-Rosa was sentenced by United States District Court Silvia Carreño Coll to one year probation for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute controlled substances. ALBUQUERQUE – Five defendants face federal charges alleging they used the U.S. mail, interstate travel, and electronic financial transactions to facilitate a large-scale methamphetamine and fentanyl distribution operation spanning New Mexico, Arizona, and California.

According to court documents, Cesar Antonio Huerta , 28, is alleged to have led a Hobbs, New Mexico-based drug trafficking organization that distributed large quantities of methamphetamine and fentanyl between at least June 2025 and July 2026. Investigators allege that Huerta obtained narcotics from Arizona-based supplier Jesus Landeros , 31, who coordinated shipments with the assistance of Marycruz Perez , 34, and Landero’s mother, Josefina Cabrera-Becerra , 59. Authorities allege that distribution quantities of methamphetamine and fentanyl were shipped through the U.S. mail from Arizona and Southern California to Hobbs, New Mexico, where Huerta and his girlfriend, Mariela Belen Lechuga , 24, redistributed the narcotics and collected drug proceeds.

The charging documents allege that Landeros supplied Huerta with methamphetamine and fentanyl through a network that relied on parcels mailed from Arizona and California to addresses associated with Huerta . Investigators identified at least 13 suspicious shipments between June and September 2025, including a parcel intercepted by U.S. Postal Inspectors on Sept. 11, 2025, that contained approximately 2.2 kilograms of pure methamphetamine. Investigators allege Cabrera mailed the package from Inglewood, California, while postal records, surveillance footage, and recorded jail calls linked Huerta , Lechuga , Landeros , and Cabrera to the shipment.

According to the complaint, financial records revealed that Huerta and Lechuga sent approximately $186,851 through Cash App, Zelle, and other electronic payment platforms to Landeros , Perez , and Cabrera between June 2025 and July 2026. Investigators allege the payments, often disguised as expenses for "clothes," "shoes," "rent," "food," and other ordinary items, were used to pay for narcotics shipments and conceal the source and ownership of drug proceeds.

Investigators identified additional seizures tied to the organization, including shipments intercepted in Florida that contained methamphetamine and carfentanil-laced pills, as well as a California seizure in April 2026 in which approximately 5,997 grams of fentanyl and an additional pound of methamphetamine were recovered from Cabrera .

According to investigators, Huerta and Lechuga later traveled to California to obtain narcotics directly after law enforcement intercepted several mailed shipments. Records, surveillance, and witness statements allegedly showed that the organization adapted its trafficking methods in response to law enforcement scrutiny while continuing to distribute methamphetamine and fentanyl and move proceeds through electronic payment services.

The complaint charges Huerta , Lechuga , Landeros , Perez , and Cabrera-Becerra with conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine, conspiracy to distribute fentanyl and conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted of the current charges, the defendants each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years and up to life in prison.

In addition, Huerta is charged with being a felon in possession of a firearm. Investigators allege that during a September 2026 traffic stop, agents recovered a firearm from a vehicle occupied by Huerta and Lechuga . Court records indicate Huerta had a prior felony conviction and was prohibited from possessing firearms. If convicted of the firearm charge, Huerta faces up to 15 years in federal prison, in addition to any sentence imposed for the drug trafficking offenses.

Acting U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison made the announcement today on behalf of the Homeland Security Task Force.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Renee Camacho and Judith Crews are prosecuting these cases.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

HSTF Region II CORE 7 is comprised of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Customs and Border Protection – Office of Field Operations (OFO), U.S. Border Patrol (USBP) and Air and Marine (AMO), Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), United States Department of the Interior – Bureau of Land Management (BLM), Joint Task Force North (JTF-N), United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), United States Marshal Service (USMS), Department of State, Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DSS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Texas Department of Public Safety (TXDPS), El Paso Police Department (EPPD), New Mexico State Police (NMSP), West Texas / New Mexico High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA), Albuquerque Police Department, New Mexico Sixth Judicial District, Las Cruces/Dona Ana County Metro Narcotics Agency, and the prosecution is being led by the Office of the United States Attorney for the Districts of Western Texas and New Mexico.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach and Chief Master Sgt. of the Air Force David Wolfe, accompanied by their wives, Mrs. Cindy Wilsbach and Dr. Doniel Wolfe, visited Kadena Air Base Oct. 21, to assess operational readiness and engage with Airmen projecting airpower across the Pacific.
Wilsbach, a fighter pilot with more than 6,200 flying hours, took the controls of an F-22 Raptor, gaining firsthand insight into the readiness, maintenance and operational demands of airpower in a contested environment.
Wolfe, flew aboard an HH-60W Jolly Green II combat rescue helicopter to observe personnel recovery training and survey key operational sites across Okinawa supporting joint and bilateral missions.
The senior leaders received mission briefs from the 18th Wing and 353rd Special Operations Wing on Kadena’s role in rapid contingency response and joint and bilateral operations. They also received updates on the 67th Fighter Squadron’s transition to the F-15EX Eagle II, a modernization effort that will expand the installation’s long-term airpower capabilities. Beyond flightline operations, the delegation focused heavily on base infrastructure and quality of life for service members and their families.
“We have to win, it’s all the more reason why we ought to be doing hard things together as units,” said Wilsbach. “You gotta work for it. Every single day, in constant improvement, and when it doesn’t go well – which invariably it will not, the supervisors and commanders teach, coach and mentor.”
Wilsbach and Wolfe addressed the base during an all-call, emphasizing force modernization and the vital role of deterrence driven by every airman of every specialty. The session allowed senior leaders to engage directly with Airmen, answer questions and discuss the strategic challenges and opportunities shaping today’s Air Force.
Wilsbach and Wolfe also reviewed installation revitalization efforts while touring military family housing in Stearley Heights to assess civil engineer initiatives, as well as staffing and work-order resolution efforts.
In parallel engagements, Mrs. Cindy Wilsbach and Dr. Doniel Wolfe met with spouses and base agency representatives to examine essential community support priorities, including childcare availability, spouse employment opportunities, healthcare accessibility and housing improvements across Okinawa.
Wolfe met with senior noncommissioned officers and Airmen from across the installation to discuss professional development, standards and innovation.
“We want you to have an opportunity to be the best version of yourself,” said Wolfe. “That baseline of physical fitness can really help you get there, especially over time. If you’re not there right now, good news, you can get there.
“You can decide today that you’re going to change some habits.”
The visit coincided with exercise Keen Sword, a biennial bilateral exercise that strengthens interoperability between U.S. forces and the Japan Self-Defense Forces. The exercise gave Kadena Airmen an opportunity to demonstrate integrated air defense, rapid sortie generation and their ability to operate alongside allied and joint forces.
“Kadena is built for this mission, and we showcase that every day by generating combat power and providing critical deterrence in the Pacific,” said Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander. “Our Airmen are the foundation of that capability, sustaining readiness and security in the region.”
As Kadena moves through a period of modernization, the visit underscored the Airmen behind the mission: maintaining, adapting and fortifying the capabilities needed to meet the demands of a rapidly evolving security environment.
title: CSAF, CMSAF assess Kadena readiness, modernization during Kadena AB visit

Integrated health service delivery through medical mobile units helped to reduce deaths among individuals at risk for HIV who also inject drugs
Wednesday, November 4, 2026
Integrated health service delivery through medical mobile units helped to reduce deaths among individuals at risk for HIV who also inject drugs
NIH-funded clinical trial shows mobile units may help overcome significant barriers to accessing HIV and addiction treatment, but replication is needed.
Results from a clinical trial funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in five major United States cities show that delivering integrated HIV and substance use disorder (SUD) services using peer navigation in mobile medical units reduced all-cause deaths by 71% compared to participants who received peer navigation to community-based services alone. While scientists found no difference in the use of daily, oral preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) between the groups, the secondary outcome of reduced mortality was significant.
“Injection drug use is an important contributor to HIV in the U. S. that also increases risk for other serious infectious diseases,” said Nora D. Volkow, M.D., director of NIH’s National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA), which funded the study. “Although we have effective interventions for this population, there are significant barriers to their accessibility and use. Nonetheless, these findings suggest that delivering low threshold services through mobile units could save lives.”
The trial, known as the HIV Prevention Trials Network Study 094 (HPTN 094), enrolled 409 adults without HIV, who injected drugs, had opioid use disorder, who were not taking MOUD at enrollment, and who were willing to consider MOUD. The trial took place in Houston, Los Angeles, New York City, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. One group received 26 weeks of peer navigation plus integrated PrEP, MOUD, and limited clinical and supportive services delivered on a mobile unit. The other group received 26 weeks of peer navigation services that linked participants to available non-mobile community services.
While verified PrEP use for both groups was low at 26 weeks, it was favorable compared to self-reported use among people who inject drugs. Additionally, although there was no difference in MOUD use between study arms, 14% of people used MOUD at 26 and 52 weeks, a clinically meaningful level considering none were on MOUD at study start.
“People who inject drugs often face fragmented systems, unstable housing, stigma, and other barriers that make sustained care difficult,” said Nabila El-Bassel, Ph.D., the Willma and Albert Musher Professor of Social Work at Columbia University and study co-chair. “Our findings show why we must continue developing models that meet people where they are and connect HIV prevention, addiction treatment, and supportive care in ways that are accessible and responsive to their lives.”
According to researchers, the relatively low use of oral PrEP, even in the context of structured peer navigation, underscores that PrEP uptake has major challenges for acceptance among people who inject drugs and points to the importance of evaluating long-acting PrEP formulations within this population.
Steven Shoptaw, Ph.D., the George F. Kneller Endowed Chair in Family Medicine, and vice chair for Research in the UCLA Department of Family Medicine, also served as study co-chair.
The HIV Prevention Trials Network is sponsored by NIH’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and HPTN 094 was funded by NIDA. Overall support for the trial was through awards UM1AI068619, UM1AI068617, and UM1AI068613.
About the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA): NIDA is a component of the National Institutes of Health, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIDA supports most of the world’s research on the health aspects of drug use and addiction. The Institute carries out a large variety of programs to inform policy, improve practice, and advance addiction science. For more information about NIDA and its programs, visit www.nida.nih.gov.
About the National Institutes of Health (NIH): NIH, the nation's medical research agency, includes 27 Institutes and Centers and is a component of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. NIH is the primary federal agency conducting and supporting basic, clinical, and translational medical research, and is investigating the causes, treatments, and cures for both common and rare diseases. For more information about NIH and its programs, visit www.nih.gov.
NIH…Turning Discovery Into Health®
Reference
S Shoptaw, N El-Bassel, et al. Mobile Units for Integrated Addiction and Prevention Services for People Who Inject Drugs: The HPTN 094 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2026. DOI: 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.3644.
title: Integrated health service delivery through medical mobile units helped to reduce deaths among individuals at risk for HIV who also inject drugs

COLUMBIA, Mo. – A Columbia, Mo., man has been sentenced in federal court for illegally possessing a firearm and illegal possession of a machine gun.

Caleb Devine Hunt, 28, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Steven R. Bough to 96 months in federal prison without parole for being a felon in possession of a firearm.

In November of 2023, a detective with the Columbia Police Department observed a photo on Facebook of Hunt holding a black Glock pistol with a laser and extended magazine. The detective recognized Hunt and knew he was a convicted felon and prohibited from possessing firearms. After obtaining a search warrant, the detective located multiple images and videos of Hunt possessing the same firearm and was able to read the firearm’s serial number.

On March 2, 2024, Hunt was a passenger in a vehicle pursuit with Missouri State Highway Patrol in Boone County, Mo. During the pursuit, troopers witnessed a small black object being thrown from the moving vehicle. The object was a black Glock pistol matching the serial number of the firearm Hunt possessed on Facebook. The firearm had a machine gun conversion device on it, commonly called a switch. When affixed to a Glock, the machine gun conversion device causes a single pull of the trigger to discharge rounds until the ammunition is exhausted, a malfunction occurs, or the trigger is released.

On April 24, 2024, Columbia Police Officers arrested Hunt for possession of the Glock and located three additional firearms in Hunt’s possession.

Hunt has a previous felony conviction for assault in the second degree for his participation in a 2019 shooting in downtown Columbia.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Ashley S. Turner. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and Missouri State Highway Patrol.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

PORTLAND, Ore.— A federal grand jury in Portland has returned a five-count indictment charging Cedrick Bruce Davis , 25, with assault offenses stemming from the alleged abuse of two young children and the strangulation of an intimate partner on the Warm Springs Indian Reservation, U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today.

According to court documents, Davis, an enrolled member of the Navajo Nation, is charged with two counts of assault with intent to commit murder, two counts of assault resulting in serious bodily injury, and one count of assault by strangulation.

“The conduct alleged in this indictment is shocking and deeply disturbing,” said U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford. “No child should endure this kind of abuse, and no victim should live in fear of violence in their own home. Our office remains committed to working alongside Tribal, local, and federal law enforcement partners to investigate violent crimes in Indian Country and ensure those responsible are brought to justice.”

The indictment alleges that, between Oct. 19 and Oct. 22, 2026, Davis assaulted two minor victims on the Warm Springs Reservation. Federal prosecutors allege that Davis strangled both children with the intent to commit murder and caused serious bodily injury by striking and wounding them. The indictment further alleges that Davis assaulted and attempted to strangle an adult victim.

According to an affidavit filed in support of the criminal complaint, officers with the Warm Springs Police Department responded to a residence on Oct. 22, 2026, after the adult victim called 911 seeking assistance because she did not feel safe. When officers arrived, a responding officer observed substantial injuries to both children, including facial swelling, bruising and visible trauma. The responding officer asked one of the minor victims about an injury to her face, and the child identified “Cedrick” as the person who caused it.

Court documents allege that the adult victim told investigators Davis assaulted her and the two children over several days. She reported that Davis strangled both children, struck them with his fists and a BB gun, bit them, threw them and struck their heads together. The adult victim further reported that Davis strangled her, struck her in the ribs with a BB gun and held a knife to her neck during her attempts to protect the children.

Court documents further allege that Davis waived his Miranda rights and admitted to physically assaulting the victims. Investigators reported that Davis acknowledged slapping the children in the face, striking their heads together and strangling each child on multiple occasions. According to the affidavit, Davis stated that one child lost consciousness during a strangulation assault. Davis also allegedly admitted strangling the adult victim and striking her in the abdomen.

If convicted, assault with intent to commit murder carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison. Assault resulting in serious bodily injury carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison, and assault by strangulation carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison.

The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Warm Springs Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Arin C. Heinz of the District of Oregon's Special Prosecutions Unit is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is only an accusation of a crime, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.
title: Warm Springs Man Indicted for Assaulting Two Children and Strangling Intimate Partner on Warm Springs Reservation

Tallahassee, Fla. – Frederick Allen Smith, Jr., 54, of Madison, Fla., pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The woman was still wearing her life jacket when she reached dry ground.
Chris Alley, a natural resources specialist with the USACE Little Rock District, told her she could take it off.
“Nope,” she told him. “Not until we get to that cabin.”
It was her first visit to Clearwater Lake, and it had turned into something none of the campers had planned for.
Hours earlier, the Black River had begun rising at a rate Clearwater Lake employees had never seen before. Roads into the Highway K Campground disappeared beneath the water, electricity was lost and campers who had remained on higher ground found themselves cut off from the outside world.
By the time Alley arrived at work that fateful day, the only practical way to get them out was by boat.
Getting that boat there was another matter.
The morning of July 10 began with Clearwater Lake employees watching the weather and the river gauges closely.
More than 12 inches of rain had fallen north of the lake, and the water was making its way downstream toward the project. The flooding was affecting communities throughout the region, with local authorities conducting search-and-rescue operations at other campgrounds north of the project.
Doug Stilts, a natural resources specialist who has worked at Clearwater Lake for 20 years, knew the conditions were worth watching but the speed of the rise was something different.
The river had been climbing steadily when Stilts and Operations Project Manager Robert Daniel headed toward the Highway K Bridge to check conditions. Maintenance employees had already tried to reach the area and had been stopped by floodwater, so Stilts and Daniel took a longer alternate route in hopes of finding another way through.
When they reached the area near the campground, they stopped at a local canoe concession. That was when Stilts noticed someone moving on the other side of the floodwater.
“We had thought everyone had already been evacuated,” Stilts said.
Earlier that morning, around 2 a.m., Missouri Department of Conservation game warden Caleb Neese, had been called to the area and evacuated the campers from the lower A and B sections. So, Stilts and Daniel had every reason to believe the campgrounds were empty.
But the people Stilts had spotted were still there, farther up the hill in C Section, where the water wasn't expected to reach them.
The problem was that the floodwater had cut off their access to the park entrance road.
Stilts couldn't drive across the flooded campground, so he asked the concessioner if he could borrow a kayak. He hopped in and paddled across to find out how many people were still there and what condition they were in.
The campers were not in immediate danger of being overtaken by the water. They were on a hill. The problem was that the hill had effectively become an island. If anyone needed emergency medical attention, responders could not simply drive in.
Cell service at the top of the hill was also notoriously unreliable, sometimes allowing a text message through and sometimes leaving the campers without a way to communicate.
After speaking with the campers, Stilts returned in the kayak and told Daniel what he had found.
They needed a boat and quickly.
Alley had been watching the gauges as well. After more than 25 years with USACE, he knew what rising water could mean for Clearwater Lake, particularly after heavy rain upstream.
The gauge had already jumped several feet in an hour.
Then it jumped four.
“We knew then we had something potentially historic going on here,” he said.
While Stilts paddled his way toward the campground at Daniel’s direction, Alley and volunteer Gale Wells, prepared a USACE boat at the marina in case a water rescue was needed.
The boat was a work boat designed for Clearwater Lake operations, not a specialized rescue vessel, but it had one feature that would prove especially useful: a landing craft on the front that could lower into the water and create a level platform.
The boat was ready before they knew exactly what they would be dealing with.
Then Stilts returned from the campground with the information they needed. There were campers still on the hill, including someone who used a walker, and they needed a way out.
Alley and Wells took off with the boat and headed toward the campground.
The floodwater had continued to spread by the time they arrived. Water was now running across the highway before the bridge, with about a foot of water over the road.
Alley climbed into Daniel’s truck and they drove down to assess the roadway him and Wells would have to cross with the boat.
At the bottom of the hill, Rob threw the truck in park and slowly turned to Alley and asked, “Do you think we can make it?”
Alley studied the road for a minute.
“Yeah, as long as we can see that yellow line on the road the entire time, I know the road is still there,” he said. “We’re not going to get washed away or drive into a hole.”
And in that moment, the decision was made. Alley returned to his truck and he and Wells made the crossing.
Once they reached the campground, Alley launched the boat directly from the highway into the floodwater.
Using a depth finder, he could see that the water around the campground was roughly 8 to 10 feet deep. He maneuvered toward a campsite on higher ground and lowered the boat's landing craft.
As Alley stayed at the controls, Wells walked up the hill to gather the campers and bring them down to the boat.
The platform settled at the same level as the water beside the dry ground, allowing the campers to walk directly onto the boat. Even the camper using a walker could make the step without difficulty.
For others, there was another problem: convincing them to leave.
Some campers did not want to go. They believed the water would eventually recede, and from where they were standing, they were not in immediate danger.
Alley understood why they were reluctant, but he also knew that the situation could change quickly. There was no electricity, it was sweltering hot, communications were unreliable and emergency services could not easily reach the campground.
“I understand why you want to stay,” Alley told them, “but you have to evacuate. The boat is here now. We gotta get you out of here.”
It took four or five trips to move everyone to safety.
The ride between the highway and the campground was only about 100 yards, but the landscape around them had changed completely. What had been a campground was now covered by deep, moving water.
Alley tried to keep the campers from becoming overwhelmed by the situation and set their minds at ease by bringing some levity to the situation.
“Welcome to the Black River excursion,” he joked. “I'm your tour guide, Chris.”
He reassured them that he had driven boats his entire life and that they were headed to dry ground, where a local cabin rental company had offered them cabins for the night, along with food and water.
By that time, the river was nearing its crest.
The response moved like a well-choreographed dance. Maintenance employees were shutting off power without waiting to be told. Others were handling phone calls, cancelling reservations and issuing refunds as the situation unfolded.
“Everyone worked together really well,” Stilts said. “We all knew our roles, and just got it done.”
The water itself offered no such order. The river was rising faster than the people watching it had ever seen, roads were disappearing under water and decisions had to be made while conditions continued to change.
But at Highway K, the response came together one decision at a time.
Stilts borrowed a kayak because there was no other way to reach the campers.
Alley and Wells brought a work boat into water deep enough to cover the campground.
And one crossing at a time, the campers left the rising water behind.
The Black River at Highway K crested at 28.7 feet that day, more than two feet above the previous record. Additionally, the rainfall that drove the flooding was a 1-in-1,000-year event in parts of the region.
The campers on that hill had arrived at Clearwater Lake for a camping trip and left with a story they would not soon forget.
title: The Yellow Line

Fort Drum, NY. – Soldiers assigned to 1st Brigade, 10th Mountain Division (Light Infantry), validated their readiness during Mountain Peak, Oct. 20-29, at Fort Drum, N.Y. Mountain Peak trained and validated soldiers to fight and win against America’s adversaries while also leveraging constantly evolving tactics on the battlefield.
Throughout Mountain Peak, Soldiers maneuvered through rugged terrain, conducted coordinated assaults, and worked together to secure key objectives. The exercise tested more than tactical proficiency, requiring units to ensure they are ready to fight, endure, and survive on the modern battlefield.
Throughout the training exercise, observer controller trainers, who observe, evaluate, and coach units on their performance, were present to ensure participating units are trained to standard.
“Mountain Peak is an opportunity for Soldiers to refine their techniques and put into place all the different systems they’ve been training,” said Sgt. 1st Class Michael Ranger, an observer controller trainer assigned to 2nd Battalion, 2nd Infantry Regiment. “It gives them opportunities outside of their normal routine for them to work together, war-game, and execute. We shadow and coach them so they can be effective in their mission set.”
The exercise followed a progression of tactical operations designed to replicate the demands of large-scale combat, beginning with a forcible entry before transitioning into offensive operations and ultimately defensive operations.
As the scenario evolves, Soldiers must seize and secure key terrain, maneuver against a live opposing force and establish defensive positions to protect their gains. This progression challenges the brigade in a multi-domain environment to adapt to changing battlefield conditions, synchronize its capabilities and refine its tactics while preparing to fight and win against a near-peer adversary.
In addition to testing the unit’s ability to conduct near-peer warfare, Mountain Peak provides an opportunity for medical personnel to practice prolonged field care, strengthening their ability to sustain casualties when evacuation is delayed or timely access to higher levels of treatment is limited.
The challenges they faced during Mountain Peak required medical teams to manage patients over extended periods while working with available personnel, equipment and supplies in austere field conditions.
One such capability that is being tested is Project Valkyrie; a way for medics to use compatible donors at the site for whole blood transfers for the patient.
“Project Valkyrie is setting the standard across all branches of service,” said Staff Sgt. Dominic Vigar, a combat medic specialist assigned to 1st Battalion, 87th Infantry Regiment, 1st Brigade, 10th Mountain Division (LI). “Project Valkyrie will help a lot with prolonged field medical care...if we have those donors available to us, I can start pulling from those donors, keeping the casualty alive for an extended amount of time.”
Mountain Peak serves as a proving ground for the brigade to test its tactics, evaluate its capabilities and refine how it fights against a near-peer adversary.
Along with validating readiness, the unit used Mountain Peak as an opportunity to assess developing best practices for how to employ the Multi-Functional Reconnaissance Company and integrate intelligence and coordinate fires to support maneuver operations. By identifying gaps, adjusting their approach and applying lessons in real time, units can refine their techniques and develop more effective ways to operate on the modern battlefield.
The exercise also incorporated modern battlefield technologies, including unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) and counter-UAS capabilities, allowing units to evaluate emerging threats, improve battlefield awareness and adapt to an evolving operational environment.
Mountain Peak provides the brigade with a critical opportunity to assess its overall effectiveness before its upcoming Joint Readiness Training Center (JRTC) rotation in January 2027 and for future operational requirements.
“Mountain Peak certifies us as ready to deploy whenever the nation calls,” said Capt. Connor Bryan, the commander of Charlie Company, 2nd Battalion, 22nd Infantry Regiment, 1st Brigade, 10th Mountain Division (LI). “We train here hard working on our techniques, tactics and procedures to ensure that when we go down-range, we’re a well-oiled and rehearsed fighting machine.
title: Fighting, Enduring, Surviving: Inside Mountain Peak

FORT DRUM, N.Y. (Nov. 4, 2026) -- Fort Drum community members gathered inside The Peak ballroom Nov. 4 for the monthly Community Information Exchange to learn about upcoming seasonal events, winter readiness programs, gate schedule changes and support resources.
Brig. Gen. Joseph Ewers, 10th Mountain Division (LI) and Fort Drum commanding general, said he was pleased to see company-level leaders and spouses in attendance, and asked them to relay the information to their formations and their families.
“This Community Information Exchange is a resource that ultimately informs and prepares those leaders who are going to be doing that final engagement – that final hundred yards, as they say – with our families,” he said. “We owe it to them to set the conditions for their self-reliance; that we don’t just point at them and say, ‘Be self-reliant. Be resilient.’ What are we doing to enable that resiliency? It starts with information.”
Ewers said that a key component to a great unit is having informed families, which is something he aspires to continue within the 10th Mountain Division (LI).
“Informed families start here,” he said. “We are here as their representatives. This is where the information begins. It ends at the families.”
Holiday Gate Closures
The Directorate of Emergency Services provided updates on installation access and community safety. Due to ongoing construction, the Gas Alley access control point remains closed.
The Lt. Gen. Paul Cerjan access control point and the Wheeler-Sack Army Airfield access control point continue 24/7 operations.
The Plummer Gate will observe the following holiday closure schedule:
Thanksgiving Weekend: Closes at 10 p.m. Nov. 25, and reopens at 4:30 a.m. Nov. 30.
Christmas / New Year Block Leave: Closes at 10 p.m. Dec. 19 and reopens at 5:30 a.m. Jan. 3.
Fort Drum DES is partnering with the New York State Police to host a free Child Safety Seat Installation and Inspection event starting at 10 a.m. on Nov. 21, at Fire Station 2, Bldg. 1585 on Ontario Avenue. Drivers can pull directly through the fire station bay doors in a dedicated inspection lane to have car seats inspected or properly installed.
With peak holiday shipping underway, DES advised residents to protect deliveries from porch theft by:
- Using secure drop-off lockers, counters, or local carrier pickup sites (such as UPS or FedEx Office locations).
- Enabling delivery alerts and text notifications to retrieve packages immediately upon drop-off.
- Placing carrier holds or scheduling deliveries for times when someone is home; avoiding leaving boxes unattended overnight.
To help residents navigate the weather conditions ahead, the Fort Drum Safety Office hosts a Winter Driving Course on select Tuesdays, from 2 to 3 p.m. and 5 to 6 p.m. in Bldg. 4884 on Jones Street. The Snowblower Operation course is held on alternating schedules from 3:15 to 4 p.m. and 6:15 to 7 p.m.
Class size is limited to 12 participants per session, and reservations can be made by calling 315-772-0310. Class dates can be found on the My Army Post App (MAPA). The Safety Office also offers a “train the trainer” class by unit request.
Ewers charged leaders to identify new Soldiers in their units who’ve never experienced winter weather before.
“Let’s not make this a resource that’s out there, and hope (Soldiers) get to it,” Ewers said. “Let’s identify who needs it, and then guide them to that resource.”
The Fort Drum Directorate of Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation announced an extensive slate of holiday community events and recreation opportunities to include:
- Bowl for Turkeys: Pine Plains Bowling Center will host Turkey Giveaway drawings from 5 to 7 p.m. Nov. 5-7, Nov. 12-14, and Nov. 19-21. Bowlers who roll a strike can also earn a free 7-inch one-topping pizza (limit one per person).
- Cozy Igloo Nights at The Peak: Private 75-minute reservations for up to six people inside heated, illuminated outdoor igloos opening Nov. 9. Packages include shareables, dessert samplers, and beverages. For reservations, call 315-772-6222.
- “Home for the Holidays” Thanksgiving Dinner: A free community Thanksgiving meal will be served from 1 to 4 p.m. on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26, inside The Peak. Active-duty service members, Department of the Army civilians, retirees, veterans, and their families are welcome.
- Annual Tree Lighting and Holiday Celebration: Ring in the winter season with the holiday tree lighting and family activities at 6 p.m. Dec. 4 at The Peak.
The U.S. Army Medical Department Activity-Fort Drum reminded beneficiaries that TRICARE Open Season is underway. Beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select can make plan changes for the upcoming calendar year, with changes taking effect Jan. 1.
For assistance or regional enrollment support, contact Humana Military (East Region) at (800) 444-5445 or visit www.tricare.mil/east.
Beneficiaries can also access appointment scheduling, secure messaging, and lab results via the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal, or use remote check-in for the Guthrie Clinic pharmacy by texting “Get in line” to 833-564-4369.
What Fort Drum families need to know
- Army Community Service announced that the Family Advocacy Program (FAP), Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP), and New Parent Support Program (NPSP) are transitioning offices to the main ACS facility, Bldg. 11042 on Mount Belvedere Boulevard throughout November.
- The next Parent Advisory Board meeting is scheduled from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. Jan. 21 at the Youth Center, Bldg. 10788 on Chapel Drive. Attending parents earn participation points toward CYS childcare discounts.
- The Youth Center on Chapel Drive offers free enrollment for students in grades 6–12, interested in STEM Club sessions (Nov. 5, 12, and 19 from 4:30 to 5:30 p.m.) and All-Star Indoor Softball (Nov. 6, 13, and 20 from 4 to 5 p.m.).
- Free enrollment is available for children, between 6 and 18, to participate in the Presidential Fitness Test on Dec. 4 at the CYS Youth Sports and Fitness Center, Bldg. 10790 Chapel Drive. For more information, call 315-772-6718 or visit the center.
- Transitioning families moving in or out of Fort Drum can borrow kitchen essentials, cookware, dishes, small appliances, and folding tables and chairs at the Army Community Service’s Lending Closet, Bldg. 11042 on Mount Belvedere Blvd.
And in other news
- The Transition Assistance Program will host a Career Fair from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 5 at The Peak, connecting transitioning service members and spouses with more than 90 local and national employers.
- Soldiers and family members can register through the Transition Assistance Program to attend a new “Getting Started in Cybersecurity and AI for Transitioning Veterans” class, in person or virtual. Class dates are 9 a.m. Nov. 19 and Dec. 17 in Clark Hall. To register, call 315-772-3434.
- The American Red Cross is hosting a blood drive from 9:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Nov. 13 at Guthrie Army Health Clinic; from noon to 5 p.m. Dec. 1 at the Fort Drum USO; and from noon to 5 p.m. Dec. 7 at the BOSS Center. Appointments can be made at www.redcrossblood.org. Units can sponsor a command blood drive by calling 315-317-9379 or 315-518-9982, or email katie.loffert@redcross.org.
The last Community Information Exchange of 2026 is scheduled Dec. 2, inside The Peak and livestreamed on https://www.facebook.com/drum.10thmountain/. The CIE slides are available at https://drum.armymwr.com/programs/community-and-special-event-information.
title: Fort Drum’s CIE highlights holiday events, winter readiness, family support services

OPERATION HIGHWAY SHIELD: Trump’s Transportation Department Yanks More Than 300 Dangerous Truckers, Illegals off U.S. Roads
Third wave of multiagency operation conducted 1,724 inspections in 48 hours in Arkansas
LITTLE ROCK, AR — U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced the results of the third wave of Operation Highway Shield, a Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA)-led, multiagency operation targeting unqualified big rig drivers and criminal activity on American roads.
FMCSA inspectors partnered with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Immigration & Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and the Arkansas Highway Police for a 48-hour operation to crack down on unsafe drivers, hazardous vehicles, and fraudulent practices along Arkansas highways and major freight corridors.
The operation resulted in:
- 393 drivers and vehicles placed out of service
- 183 English Language Proficiency (ELP) violations
- 74 immigration violations referred for federal immigrations enforcement
- 44 criminal arrests
- 1 stolen trailer recovered
“Gone are the days of dangerous–and many times illegal and foreign–drivers putting American lives at risk on our roads. Under the Trump Administration, we are restoring law and order,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “This latest wave of Operation Highway Shield has pulled over 300 dangerous drivers off the road including 183 foreign drivers that couldn't read road signs. We are not slowing down when it comes to keeping Americans safe on our roads.”
“Every person on the road deserves to get home safely,” said FMCSA Administrator Derek D. Barrs. “When criminal activity and unsafe vehicles creep onto our highways, it puts everyone at risk. Operation Highway Shield is about teaming up with our partners to protect everyday drivers, clear out the bad actors, and make our roads safer for everyone.”
The first wave of Operation Highway Shield resulted in 176 drivers being taken out of service, 54 of which were taken out of service for language deficiencies. Additionally, 35 individuals were arrested on criminal-related charges, and 42 individuals were taken into custody for violating federal immigration laws.
The second wave was conducted in Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, and Ohio, resulting in 51 illegal immigrants detained, 766 unsafe drivers and vehicles placed out of service, 36 English Language Proficiency test violations, and $1 million of stolen cargo recovered.
Additional Information:
In August, USDOT, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud teamed up to launch a historic interagency effort to crack down on fraud in the trucking industry. As part of the crackdown, FMCSA carried out the emergency removal of 110 commercial driver’s license (CDL) schools associated with more than 5,000 drivers who failed English language proficiency tests and put 160 more schools on notice.
Since President Trump issued the Executive Order to restore integrity to the trucking industry in April 2025, Secretary Duffy has:
- Knocked 33,000 drivers out of service who could not speak basic English or read road signs
- Revoked 31,000 illegally issued licenses to unvetted foreign drivers and
- Shut down nearly 10,000 shady driving schools
###
title: OPERATION HIGHWAY SHIELD: Trump’s Transportation Department Yanks More Than 300 Dangerous Truckers, Illegals off U.S. Roads

Ranking Member Lofgren Announces She Will Seek Chair of House Science Committee as Democrats Win Control of Congress
(Washington, DC) — This morning, Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren (D-CA) made the following statement after Democrats secured the majority of the House and Senate in the 2026 midterm election:
“Yesterday, the American people chose stability over chaos,” said Ranking Member Lofgren. “They chose people and policies that will make not only their lives better, but the lives of future generations better. Americans chose science and reason. They’ve put their trust in Democrats and our ability to deliver on our promises.
She continued: “I will be seeking the Chair of the House Science Committee. First and foremost, as Chairwoman, I will work to put a stop to Trump’s politicization of science. We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise. The oversight and investigations work we’ve been doing for the past two years in the minority will continue. We have a lot of work to do, and we’ll be ready to hit the ground running come the start of the 120th Congress, with Democrats in control of the House and Senate.
“We will also set out to fix what Trump has broken. We’ll restore and advance support for our premiere science institutions and the dedicated people who work there. We will build protections for federal science and innovation programs so Trump-era corruption cannot happen again.
“The future is unfolding before us with groundbreaking technologies like AI, quantum, and fusion energy. We need to build responsible regulations for AI while also fostering innovation. We must invest holistically in quantum to meet emerging challenges for our competitiveness in this field. This administration’s climate denialism has set us back. We need to advance climate solutions now. Fusion, with its limitless, emission-free power, will help us achieve our clean energy future. Breakthrough after breakthrough in fusion energy science has been encouraging—and we need to match this momentum with federal support.
“The U.S. research ecosystem used to be the envy of the world. People brought their ideas and energy here—and our Nation reaped the rewards of that talent in discoveries and the resulting economic growth. That is now all at risk. I will stop at nothing to earn back the trust of our allies across the globe, end the brain drain, restore scientific integrity across our agencies, and reaffirm our leadership in science. The American people deserve no less.”
title: Ranking Member Lofgren Announces She Will Seek Chair of House Science Committee as Democrats Win Control of Congress

PICATINNY ARSENAL, N.J. - The ever-evolving Unmanned Aerial Systems toolbox has grown even stronger with the introduction of the Munitions Air-dropped Lethal Effects Tool (MALET), developed by the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center.
The MALET is a kit which converts munitions so that they can be dropped as part of unmanned aerial system (UAS) deployment. Instead of having to procure purpose-built munitions on drones, Soldiers will be able to use rounds which they have in abundance already, such as 60mm and 81mm mortar rounds.
Work on MALET began in 2024 when experts at the Armaments Center’s Fuze and Mortar Divisions recognized a critical opportunity: rather than introducing new munitions to the battlefield, soldiers could benefit from a capability to safely drop existing munitions without having to perform field modifications or manually remove safety mechanisms. The team saw the project through with input from the Energetics and Warheads Directorate.
The kit adds fuze function and ensures the aerodynamic stability required for a drone drop of the cartridge. Additionally, integrating MALET is a non-destructive process, so clipping on the kit does not compromise the mortar, nor does removing the kit. As such, if a munition is not expended or mission requirements change, the kit can be removed, returning the munition back to its original state and allowing it to be fired as a conventional mortar.
According to Senior Scientific Technical Manager for Indirect Fire Munitions Ryan Gorman, the MALET architecture can be applied to munitions beyond 60mm and 81mm mortars, and the MALET Integrated Product Team (IPT) is exploring even more concepts which, while mostly close-hold for now, Gorman referred to as “unique.” Mortars were the first to be demonstrated due to their maturity and alignment with large UAS requirements.
"The MALET program is a great example of how the DEVCOM Armaments Center can leverage core competencies like fuze design, safety, and ammunition development and apply them to a dynamic, emerging space like lethal UAS to provide a unique and viable option for the warfighter," explained Gorman.
According to MALET Project Lead Brad Armstrong, test drops at multiple US Army facilities have already shown the MALET’s effectiveness, successfully maturing both the system’s fuze function and its critical safety elements. The team just recently had a successful test where they demonstrated performance of MALET with live 60mm mortars. The items were dropped from a UAS on the move; they oriented correctly and detonated within the desired target area.
The MALET IPT’s intention is to distribute the kit to major military exercises in the fall to allow for Soldier touchpoint and receive feedback. Conversations with industry partners, the User and Acquisition communities have already proven fruitful.
The Armaments Center’s efforts are meant to validate system capabilities and seamlessly transition the MALET to industry partners and the acquisition community. This strategy will allow the military to scale and field the system rapidly, while engineers at the Armaments Center continue to work on iterative improvements based on feedback from the Warfighter at tests and exercises.
title: From the foxhole to flight: Armaments Center’s MALET turns standard rounds into drone munitions

FORT SHAFTER, Hawaii — U.S. Army Pacific welcomed veterans to its headquarters on November 3, 2026, for a special event recognizing their service, sacrifice, and lasting contributions to the nation.
Gen. Ronald P. Clark, commanding general of U.S. Army Pacific, served as host and keynote speaker. He thanked the veterans in attendance for their service and their continued connection to the Army.
“It is my honor to stand with you as a veteran and recognize the contributions of our veterans here at U.S. Army Pacific headquarters,” Clark said.
Col. Richmond “Rick” Luce, commander of U.S. Army Garrison Hawaii, also spoke with veterans about his opportunities to work with veteran organizations and the importance of remaining involved in the community.
Clark emphasized the value of veteran service organizations.
“All of our veteran service organizations are about something greater than self,” Clark said. “It is the collective nature of what we do on behalf of the organizations we represent to pull all our teammates into something greater than self.”
Throughout the visit, USARPAC staff engaged with the veterans by sharing conversations, exchanging experiences, and answering questions about the command’s mission and operations across the Pacific region. These interactions strengthened connections between generations of Soldiers and highlighted the experiences and contributions of those who served before them.
Following the briefings, veterans and Soldiers gathered for a social in the headquarters courtyard, where USARPAC leadership and staff thanked the veterans personally and recognized their shared legacy of service.
USARPAC remains committed to honoring the legacy of those who served. The dedication, leadership, and commitment demonstrated by veterans continue to inspire Soldiers serving today.
title: US Army Pacific Welcomes Veterans to Headquarters, Honors Their Service

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low‑interest federal disaster loans to California businesses, private nonprofits, and residents to offset physical and economic losses from the East Oakland Apartment Fire occurring Sept. 25. The SBA issued a disaster declaration in response to an Oct. 23 request received from California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs.
The declaration covers the California counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Joaquin, San Mateo, Santa Clara, and Stanislaus.
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against fire damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofit organizations — including faith‑based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
Economic Injury Disaster Loans are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the small business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 3% for homeowners and renters, with terms up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “At these centers, our SBA specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”
Beginning Wednesday, Nov. 4, SBA customer service representatives will be at the following Disaster Loan Outreach Center to answer questions and assist with the disaster loan application process. Walk-ins are welcome, and in-person appointments can be scheduled in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The hours of operations are:
ALAMEDA COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Oakland Public Library – Melrose Branch
4805 Foothills Blvd.
Oakland, CA  94601
Opens Wednesday, Nov. 4 at Noon
Monday and Thursday, 10 a.m. – 5:30 p.m.
Tuesday and Wednesday, 10 a.m. – 6:30 p.m.
Friday, noon – 5:30 p.m.
Closed Wednesday, Nov. 11 in observance of Veterans Day
Closes Friday, Nov. 20 at 5:30 p.m.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The deadline to return physical damage applications is Dec. 28. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 27, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, the SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow, expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Offers Relief to California Businesses, Private Nonprofits, Residents Affected by East Oakland Apartment Fire

SCRANTON - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Jonathan Bishop, age 42, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on October 30, 2026, to 41 months’ imprisonment and a term of supervised release by United States District Judge Joseph F. Saporito, Jr. for conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute cocaine base and methamphetamine.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, Bishop previously admitted that between February of 2024, and June of 2025, he conspired with other members of the Jerrod Curtis Drug Trafficking Organization (“Curtis DTO”) to distribute quantities of cocaine base and methamphetamine, in Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, and elsewhere.

Seven additional co-conspirators either pled or were found guilty following a trial before Judge Saporito earlier this year. They include:

Jerrod Curtis, age 42, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, who was found guilty of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and other drug trafficking crimes following a three-week trial in September of 2026. Curtis is currently awaiting sentencing.

Paul Daniel Chavis, a/k/a “Payne”, age 57, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, who was found guilty of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and other drug trafficking crimes following a three-week trial in September of 2026. Chavis is currently awaiting sentencing.

Reneard Harris, age 68, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, who was found guilty of conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and other drug trafficking crimes following a three-week trial in September of 2026. Harris is currently awaiting sentencing.

Carlos Vasquez, age 36, of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, who previously pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and was sentenced to 40 months’ imprisonment and a term of supervised release by Judge Saporito in September of 2026.

Leroy Scriven, a/k/a “L”, age 56, of Exeter, Pennsylvania, who previously pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and his currently awaiting sentencing.

Joshua Forrester-Westad, age 44, of Plains Township, Pennsylvania, who previously pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and is currently awaiting sentencing.

Pamela Montano, age 61, of Exeter, Pennsylvania, who previously pled guilty to conspiracy to distribute controlled substances and was sentenced to 9 months imprisonment and a term of supervised release by Judge Saporito in September of 2026.

This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. Fort Myers, Florida – Thakur Sukhdeo (40, Lehigh Acres) has pleaded guilty to two counts of wire fraud and two counts of illegal monetary transactions related to COVID relief. He faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in federal prison for each wire fraud count, and up to 10 years’ imprisonment for each illegal monetary transaction count. Sukhdeo has also agreed to forfeit $413,900, which are the proceeds of the criminal offense. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court records, during the COVID pandemic, the United States Small Business Administration (SBA) offered loans to small businesses under the Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL). Beginning around April 2021, Sukhdeo engaged in a scheme to fraudulently obtain $413,900 by applying for an EIDL loan from the SBA using false pretenses and representations. To secure the loan, Sukhdeo submitted loan paperwork to the SBA claiming that he owned a handyman business that made $206,998 in 2019. However, bank records revealed the business made $19,843.50 that year. As part of the loan, Sukhdeo promised to only use the EIDL funds on business expenses. After applying for the loan, on March 24, 2022, the SBA deposited $413,900 into Sukhdeo’s personal bank account. The following day, Sukhdeo created a business account and transferred the entirety of the EIDL funds to that account. Shortly thereafter, Sukhdeo utilized the EIDL funds to purchase a luxury vehicle for $68,984.61 and a truck for $93,994.42. Sukhdeo also made numerous cash withdrawals of the EIDL funds in the amount of $172,505, as well as other personal purchases. Within one year, Sukhdeo had spent all of the EIDL funds. The FBI subsequently seized both of Sukhdeo’s vehicles and on January 13, 2025, the court ordered the civil forfeiture of both vehicles.

This case was investigated by FBI. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Matthew Redavid. The forfeiture is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney Suzanne C. Nebesky.
title: Lehigh Acres Man Pleads Guilty to Wire Fraud and Illegal Monetary Transactions

DALLAS — U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould announced that Nikolay Sapov, also known as Nikolay Georgiyevitch Sapov, was indicted by a federal grand jury on felony stalking charges after allegedly tracking a former coworker from Canada to North Texas.

The two-count indictment charges Sapov with stalking through interstate travel and stalking through electronic communications. Sapov was previously arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection on an Amtrak train entering the United States.

“No individual has the right to terrorize another human being or shatter their sense of safety inside their own home,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. “From relentless digital harassment to an international stalking campaign that spanned across the globe, this defendant went to chilling lengths to hunt down, disguise himself, and intimidate this victim. This indictment makes our position clear: predatory behavior across borders will be met with swift, uncompromising federal justice.”

“Stalking and targeted harassment can have a profound impact, disrupting victims’ lives and leaving them feeling vulnerable,” said FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock. “The FBI remains committed to identifying and holding accountable those who use threats and intimidation to instill fear. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect the members of our communities and pursue justice for victims.”

According to court filings, Sapov first met the victim several years ago while both were seasonal player services employees at the Miami Open tennis tournament. Over several years, Sapov allegedly developed an obsession with the victim, repeatedly contacting the victim outside of work hours, tracking down personal and family social media profiles, and sending unwanted gifts and correspondence to the victim’s residences.

Sapov traveled to Orlando and Plantation, Florida, to stalk her in 2023 and 2025. Court documents allege the conduct escalated in June 2026, when Sapov traveled from Toronto, Canada, to Dallas, Texas, where the victim was residing. After renting a vehicle at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, Sapov allegedly located the victim’s gated residential complex. On June 22, 2026, the victim observed Sapov loitering near their apartment building. Local law enforcement and property security responded, locating Sapov and issuing a criminal trespass warning.

Two days later, on June 24, 2026, a neighbor’s video doorbell captured an individual matching Sapov’s physical build, clothing, and footwear approaching the victim's front door while wearing a full rubber mask to conceal his face.

When confronted via the doorbell intercom, the masked suspect fled the premises. Fearing for their safety, the victim and their partner temporarily relocated to emergency hotel lodging and purchased security measures.

Despite the Dallas incident and subsequent police reports, Sapov allegedly continued to send unwanted electronic messages to the victim through August 2026, including an artificial intelligence-generated image depicting the victim posing alongside him.

On Aug. 22, Customs and Border Protection officers arrested Sapov pursuant to a Texas stalking warrant as he was traveling on an Amtrak train from Canada to into the US. Law enforcement recovered electronic equipment and two cellular devices containing maps and street names surrounding the victim’s neighborhood, photographs of women’s shoes exhibited in an apparent sexual way, and screenshots of key copying/locksmith companies. There were also explicit AI-generated photographs and videos of the adult victim.

If convicted, Sapov faces a statutory maximum penalty of five years in federal prison on each count, followed by a period of supervised release and potential financial penalties.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Dallas Field Office (Violent Crimes Task Force) investigated the case, with substantial assistance from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the Dallas Police Department, and the Tyler Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nadin-Sarah Salkić from the is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
