Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System Final Rule Fact Sheet (CMS-1844-P)
On November 4, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule that announces policy changes under the Home Health (HH) Prospective Payment System (PPS), consistent with the legal requirements to update Medicare payment policies for home health agencies (HHAs) annually. This fact sheet discusses the final rule’s major provisions.
Medicare Provider Enrollment
In its ongoing efforts to crush fraud, waste, and abuse, CMS is finalizing several provider enrollment provisions. Most of the provisions will apply to all provider types enrolled in the Medicare program. These changes will help reduce improper Medicare payments and protect beneficiaries. The provisions include, but are not limited to, the following:
- Retroactive Revocations — Under current regulations, certain Medicare enrollment revocations become effective prospectively — specifically, 30 days after the date that CMS or the CMS contractor mails notice of the revocation to the affected provider or supplier (hereafter “provider”). However, other revocations take effect retroactively to the date the provider’s noncompliance began. CMS is finalizing a policy to make all revocation grounds retroactive. This action will help CMS recover monies paid to non-compliant providers and help ensure taxpayer money is paid only to legitimate, compliant providers.
- Adding or Expanding Bases for Revocation or Denial — CMS is adding several new grounds for revocation or denial of enrollment and expanding some of its existing grounds. Among these provisions are the following:
- Change in Majority Ownership — Hospices; HHAs; and suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) must reenroll in Medicare as a new provider and undergo a survey/accreditation if they experience certain changes in majority ownership. CMS will have the authority to deny or revoke enrollment if the provider does not comply with this requirement.
- Program or License Suspension/Termination — CMS currently may deny or revoke enrollment if a provider: (1) has a suspended/revoked license in another state; or (2) is suspended/revoked from Medicaid or another federal healthcare program. We are expanding this to include similar suspensions/revocations involving the provider’s owners or managing employees/organizations.
The final revocation/denial authorities address situations noted by CMS as involving provider noncompliance and actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse. They also would allow the agency to target improper activity by those who own or operate Medicare providers.
CY 2027 Final Payment and Policy Updates for Home Health Agencies
The provisions in this final rule will help improve patient care and protect the Medicare program’s sustainability for future generations.
This rule finalizes routine, statutorily required updates to the home health payment rates for CY 2027. The CY 2027 updated rates include the final CY 2027 home health payment update of 2.1% ($365 million increase) and an estimated 0.3% increase that reflects the updated fixed dollar loss (FDL) amount ($50 million increase). CMS estimates that Medicare payments to HHAs in CY 2027 would increase in the aggregate by 2.4%, or $415 million, compared to CY 2026, based on the finalized policies.
In this final rule, CMS is also continuing its implementation of a 30-day unit of payment and of the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) case-mix adjustment methodology within the HH PPS per the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018. Specifically, it includes an analysis of the difference between assumed versus actual behavior change on estimated aggregate expenditures for home health payments linked to these changes. This rule also discusses the permanent adjustments to HH PPS payment rates applied in previous years and finalizes a temporary adjustment to the CY 2027 home health base payment rate of -3.0%.
CMS did not propose an additional permanent adjustment to the CY 2027 30-day base payment rate; however we continue to annually analyze the data through CY 2026 claims, as required by section 1895(b)(3)(D)(ii) of the Social Security Act (the Act), to determine any additional permanent adjustments to account for the impact of implementing the PDGM.
In addition, CMS finalizes the recalibrated PDGM case-mix weights; updates the FDL for outlier payments; and updates the low utilization payment adjustment (LUPA) thresholds, functional impairment levels, and comorbidity adjustment subgroups for CY 2027. This final rule also responds to comments received on the provision of palliative care services under the Medicare home health benefit and the request for information (RFI) regarding the construction of a home health specific wage index included in the proposed rule.
PDGM and Behavior Assumptions
On January 1, 2020, CMS implemented the home health PDGM and a 30-day unit of payment (previously 60 days), as required by section 1895(b) of the Social Security Act, as amended by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018. The PDGM better aligns payments with patient care needs, especially for clinically complex individuals. The law required CMS to make assumptions about behavior changes that could occur because of the 30-day unit of payment and the PDGM. CMS finalized three behavior assumptions in the CY 2019 HH PPS final rule: clinical group coding, comorbidity coding, and LUPA threshold. The law also requires CMS to annually determine the impact of differences between assumed behavior changes and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures, beginning with 2020 and ending with 2026, and to make temporary and permanent increases or decreases, as needed, to the 30-day payment amount to offset such increases or decreases.
In the CY 2023 HH PPS final rule (87 FR 66790), CMS finalized a methodology for analyzing the differences between assumed and actual behavior changes on estimated aggregate expenditures and calculated levels of actual and estimated aggregate expenditures. Based on analyses of CYs 2020 and 2021 claims data, CMS determined a permanent adjustment was needed and finalized implementing half (-3.925%) of the permanent adjustment estimated at the time (-7.85%). For CYs 2024 (88 FR 77676) and 2025 (88 FR 88373), using CY 2022 and 2023 claims, respectively, CMS similarly implemented half of the permanent adjustments estimated at those times (-2.890% out of -5.779% total for 2024 and -1.975% out of -3.95% total for 2025).
In the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (90 FR 55342), CMS finalized a policy applying the remaining permanent adjustment for claims years 2020-2022, as our analysis indicated that behavior changes after 2022 could be related to other policy factors beyond the PDGM implementation. As such, we exercised the authority expressly delegated under the statute to apply permanent adjustments “at a time and in a manner appropriate” to the remaining permanent adjustment of -1.023% to account for behavior changes associated with the PDGM implementation in CYs 2020 through 2022. We also exercised our authority to begin recouping retrospective overpayments (i.e., the temporary adjustment) for CYs 2020 through 2024 and finalized a temporary adjustment with a 3.0% reduction in CY 2026.
In the CY 2027 HH PPS final rule, similar to the policies finalized in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (90 FR 55364 through 55365), we state that behavior changes reflected in preliminary CY 2025 claims for this CY 2027 final rule may not be directly attributable to the PDGM. Other confounding factors began in CY 2023 (i.e., continued recalibration of case-mix weights, a change to the OASIS-E, and previous reductions to the home health payment rate). While we did not propose an additional permanent adjustment to the CY 2027 30-day base payment rate, this final rule continues to satisfy the statutory requirements at section 1895(b)(3)(D)(ii) of the Act as it includes our annual analysis of the data, as required by law, to determine if any additional permanent adjustments would be needed based on the impact of assumed versus actual behavior change on estimated aggregate expenditures from implementing the PDGM and the 30-day unit of payment.
In accordance with the statutory requirement to ensure that the permanent adjustments are implemented in a budget-neutral manner, we finalized our proposal to implement a temporary adjustment of -3.0% to the CY 2027 national, standardized payment rate. This finalized proposal continues recoupment of the retrospective overpayments made for CYs 2020 through 2025 through “one or more” temporary adjustments. We believe that continuing to incrementally adjust the base payment rate to account for the calculated temporary dollar amount to date may help reduce the need for a large reduction in future years.
Update to the Fixed-Dollar Loss Amount
The HH PPS allows outlier payments to be made to providers for periods of care with unusually large costs due to patient home healthcare needs. Outlier payments are made for periods of care when the estimated costs exceed a threshold amount. To determine the threshold, the 30-day period of care payment rate is multiplied by a fixed-dollar loss (FDL) ratio and then wage-adjusted to derive the FDL amount. The FDL ratio is determined so outlier payments do not exceed 2.5% of total payments (as required by section 1895(b)(5)(A) of the Act) and are annually recalibrated as part of the routine payment update. The final FDL for CY 2027 is 0.29%.
Recalibration of PDGM Case-Mix Weights
Each of the 432 payment groups under the PDGM has an associated case-mix weight and LUPA threshold. CMS’ policy is to annually recalibrate the case-mix weights and LUPA thresholds with the most complete utilization data available at the time of rulemaking. In this final rule, CMS is finalizing the recalibrated case-mix weights — including the functional levels and comorbidity adjustment subgroups — and LUPA thresholds with CY 2025 data to more accurately pay for the types of patients HHAs are serving.
Provision of Palliative Care Services Under the Home Health Benefit
CMS is interested in encouraging beneficiary access to community-based palliative care under the Medicare home health benefit and believes the Medicare home health benefit can be an important step in the care continuum when a patient needs palliative care, either during episodes of serious or progressive illness. In this rule, we respond to comments received on how to best promote access to community-based palliative care services through the Medicare home health benefit. This final rule acknowledges the role of home health in palliative care services and confirms that CMS will provide examples of such services through future sub-regulatory guidance.
Request for Information (RFI) on a Home Health-Specific Wage Index
This final rule also summarizes and responds to comments received on an RFI on the potential development of a home health-specific wage index from an alternate data source (e.g., Bureau of Labor Statistics) consistent with CMS’s statutory authority and regulatory requirements.
Durable Medical Equipment Benefit Expansion for Infusion Pumps and Drugs
CMS is amending the Medicare Part B definition of durable medical equipment (DME) at 42 CFR 414.202 to implement Section 6222(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA, 2026), which expands coverage under the DME benefit to certain external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs that would be considered appropriate for home use if certain criteria are met, such as the requirement for the drug to be administered by or under the supervision of a healthcare professional. The effective date of this provision is April 1, 2027.
Specifically, section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026, amended the definition of DME at section 1861(n) of the Act to include coverage of external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs (as defined in section 1861 (iii)(3)(C) of the Act) or other associated supplies that do not meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement applied to the definition of DME under §414.202 if the following criteria are satisfied:
- The prescribing information approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the home infusion drug associated with the pump instructs that the drug should be administered by or under the supervision of a healthcare professional.
- A qualified home infusion therapy supplier (as defined in section 1861 (iii)(3)(D) of the Act) administers or supervises the administration of the drug or biological in a safe and effective manner in the patient’s home (as defined in section 1861 (iii)(3)(B) of the Act).
- The FDA-approved prescribing information instructs that the drug should be infused at least 12 times per year —
  - intravenously or subcutaneously; or
  - at infusion rates that the Secretary determines would require the use of an external infusion pump.
The final rule does not impose any restrictions on the term “healthcare professional”, and instead interprets the term to mean any health care professional that is eligible to administer or supervise the administration of the home infusion drug and that such activities are within the professional’s scope of practice. In addition, we are finalizing that the drug should be infused “at least 12 times per year” instead of once per month, as was proposed.
Home Health (HH) Quality Reporting Program (QRP)
In the final rule, CMS summarizes potential initiatives to improve alignment between the HH QRP and expanded Home Health Value-Based Purchasing (HHVBP) Model. With respect to the HH QRP, CMS is finalizing the following:
- The HH QRP assessment data submission deadlines beginning with the CY 2027 HH QRP program year.
- The HH QRP OASIS and HHCAHPS Annual Payment Update (APU) reporting timeframes to report a calendar year of data (January 1 through December 31).
- Regulatory changes to improve digital information transfer during the HH QRP compliance reconsideration process.
Additionally, CMS acknowledges public comments on an RFI on future measure concepts for the HH QRP, specifically on a potential Advanced Care Planning measure.
Expanded HHVBP Model
CMS did not propose any expanded HHVBP Model-specific policy changes. However, CMS has included in the final rule a brief summary of the Model with context relevant to potential alignment between the HH QRP and the expanded HHVBP Model.
Improvements to the DMEPOS Competitive Bidding Program (CBP)
CMS is proceeding, through the standard Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) process, with an information collection revision that enhances the DMEPOS CBP to better inform beneficiaries and caregivers, empowering them to make well-informed healthcare decisions. CMS is revising the DMEPOS CBP reporting form, known as Form C, to include a new “country of origin” field for lead items furnished by contract suppliers. During an active round of the DMEPOS CBP, Form C collects product information such as manufacturer name, model name, and model number, which is then displayed in the Medicare Supplier Directory on Medicare.gov. The new country of origin information will be added to the Medicare Supplier Directory, giving Medicare beneficiaries and other interested parties the country of origin for their medical equipment included in the DMEPOS CBP. Suppliers can typically identify the country of origin from product markings (e.g., “Made in [Country]”), as required by U.S. Customs and Border Protection rules, or by obtaining documentation such as manufacturer certifications, commercial invoices, or customs entry records. Full details about this Form C update will be shared through official notices under OMB Control Number 0938-1408 (CMS-10744) before suppliers are required to report this information.
DMEPOS Requirements for Identical Replacement Items
CMS is finalizing the agency’s proposal to clarify that an additional comprehensive beneficiary “face-to-face” examination to gather “subjective and objective information associated with diagnosing, treating, or managing a clinical condition for which the DMEPOS is ordered” is not necessary when the item being ordered and furnished is a replacement item (for purposes of this final rule, a replacement item is an item described by the same Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System [HCPCS] code). If a claim for a replacement DMEPOS item is audited, the provider must nevertheless submit documentation from the original face-to-face encounter to demonstrate that medical necessity, billing, and coverage requirements have been satisfied. The change is consistent with the intent of 42 C.F.R. 410.38, which requires a face-to-face encounter for certain DMEPOS items and will continue to apply when the item is initially furnished; however, this clarification will make clear that the face-to-face encounter does not need to be repeated solely for replacement items.
###

Oklahoma Man Charged in Connection with Sending Threatening Letters Containing Non-Toxic White Powder to Election and Government Officials Across the Country
Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others.
“As alleged, Martin mailed letters containing white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, a calculated attempt to terrorize public servants,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These officials were left to open those letters not knowing if the powder inside could sicken or even kill them, and that was the evident intent. Intimidation like this has no place in a Nation governed by the rule of law, and the National Security Division will investigate and prosecute these cases to the fullest extent appropriate.”
“Threatening election officials and attempting to intimidate public servants is a serious federal offense and will not be tolerated,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester for the Western District of Oklahoma. “Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners, we are committed to investigating these threats and holding accountable those who seek to spread fear and intimidation in our communities.”
“Early Monday morning, the FBI conducted an operation and arrested Robin Patrick Martin – the subject who allegedly sent hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder substances to public officials around the country both before the 2024 and 2026 election,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The letters went to well over 100 locations including multiple state secretary offices, election offices, and more. The alleged subject had avoided authorities until now – as the Biden administration failed to catch him – but this FBI got it done. I want to thank our Oklahoma City Field Office and the FBI Criminal Division, as well as our USPIS, Capitol Police, and OKC PD partners who responded to the threat quickly and did outstanding work executing in this case. Every American citizen deserves a free and fair election – and anyone who attempts to undermine that process by breaking our laws and threatening public officials will be brought to justice.”
“The mailing of letters containing an unknown powdery substance across the country created unnecessary fear, diverted resources, and attempted to disrupt our nation’s democratic process,” said Special Agent in Charge Doug Goodwater of the FBI Oklahoma City Field Office. “No one should have to wonder whether a letter in the mail poses a danger, and the arrest of Robin Martin demonstrates that those who seek to spread panic and intimidation cannot expect to remain anonymous. I would like to express my gratitude to the dedicated team at FBI Oklahoma City and our partners at the US Attorney’s Offices, USPIS, USPS, U.S. Capitol Police, FBI Laboratory Division, and Oklahoma City Department for all their work in this matter.”
“The Postal Inspection Service has a long, proud, and successful history of ensuring the sanctity of election mail, safeguarding the integrity of elections, and protecting election officials from threatening and dangerous mail,” said Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS). “Utilizing our expertise in the Postal Service and mail flow, postal inspectors and our partners identified related mailings and recovered the majority of these mailings before they reached their intended recipients, keeping Postal Service customers — the American public — safe. This arrest reflects the perseverance of the Postal Inspection Service, FBI, U.S. Capitol Police, and all of our law enforcement partners to keep criminals from interfering with two trusted traditions — the election process, and the U.S. Mail.”
“Our team has been working around the clock with our law enforcement partners to put this defendant behind bars,” said U.S. Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan. “We will not tolerate anyone who attempts to use fear as a weapon.”
According to public records, on Oct. 13, 2026, the Oklahoma State Election Board notified the FBI that it had received a threatening letter containing white powder. The FBI and USPIS had been investigating threatening letters containing white powder sent to multiple state election officials — including the Oklahoma State Election Board — since 2024. The FBI and USPIS determined that this letter was part of hundreds of threatening letters, many of which had white powder, that had been sent across the country to state election boards, members of Congress, election pollsters, media organizations, and others. The white powder was later determined to be non-hazardous.
Today, Martin appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin for his initial appearance in Oklahoma City.
This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House-directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence.
This case is being investigated by the FBI, USPIS, United States Capitol Police, Oklahoma City Police Department, and Texas Department of Public Safety, including the Texas Rangers, with valuable assistance from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Oklahoma is prosecuting the case with assistance from the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.
A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Small Business Administration is reminding eligible businesses, private nonprofit organizations, homeowners, and renters in Ohio of the Dec. 1 deadline to apply for low-interest federal disaster loans to offset physical damage caused by severe storms, straight-line winds, tornadoes, flooding, and landslides occurring Aug. 10 – 22.
The declaration covers Ohio primary counties of Clermont, Franklin, Hamilton, Licking, Morgan, Muskingum, and Perry, which are eligible for both physical damage loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans from SBA. Small businesses and most private nonprofit organizations in the following adjacent counties are eligible to apply only for SBA EIDLs: Ohio counties of Athens, Brown, Butler, Clinton, Coshocton, Delaware, Fairfield, Guernsey, Hocking, Knox, Madison, Noble, Pickaway, Union, Warren, and Washington, the Indiana counties of Dearborn and Franklin, as well as the Kentucky counties of Boone, Bracken, Campbell, Kenton, and Pendleton.
Businesses and private nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Applicants may also be eligible for a loan increase of up to 20% of their physical damage, as verified by SBA, for mitigation purposes. Eligible mitigation improvements include strengthening structures to protect against high wind damage, upgrading to wind rated garage doors, and installing a safe room or storm shelter to help protect property and occupants from future damage.
“One distinct advantage of SBA’s disaster loan program is the opportunity to fund upgrades reducing the risk of future storm damage,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “I encourage businesses and homeowners to work with contractors and mitigation professionals to improve their storm readiness while taking advantage of SBA’s mitigation loans.”
Interest rates are as low as 4% for businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 3% for homeowners and renters, with terms of up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due, until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call SBA’s National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return applications for physical property damage is Dec. 1. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 2, 2027. However, after the deadline has passed, there is a 60-day grace period in which SBA will accept applications.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.

LAFAYETTE – On October 29, 2026, United States District Judge David C. Joseph sentenced Henry Nicola Meyer , 26, of Eunice, to 42 months in federal prison for Possession of Ammunition by a Convicted Felon and Possession of Five or More False Identification Documents, followed by three years of supervised release. Meyer previously pled guilty to the charges on July 9, 2026.

According to court documents, on October 9, 2025, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Eunice Police Department (EPD) executed a Louisiana search warrant at Meyer's residence when Meyer was on probation. Agents then located a padlocked bedroom containing Meyer's personal belongings and discovered a partially constructed “ghost gun” (a homemade, unregistered firearm) and 25 rounds of 9mm ammunition. Meyer admitted possessing the ammunition and acknowledged he was a convicted felon prohibited from doing so. Agents also recovered eight high-quality fake driver’s licenses bearing Meyer’s photograph, including licenses represented to be from Kentucky, Alaska, Colorado, and Georgia. Meyer admitted he knew the licenses were fraudulent and intended to use them unlawfully to misrepresent his identity.

U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller for the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.

FBI and EPD investigated this case. It was prosecuted by United States Attorney Zachary A. Keller with the assistance of Paralegal Specialist Joanne Henry-Mills.

This case was prosecuted as part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Learn more at www.justice.gov/psn.

You may find a copy of this press release (and any updates) on the website of the United States Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Louisiana at www.justice.gov/usao-wdla.

Related court documents and information may be found on the website of the District Court for the Western District of Louisiana at www.lawd.uscourts.gov or at https://www.lawd.uscourts.gov/cmecf-pacer, under Case Number 6:26-CR-00136.

WASHINGTON – Abraham Teklu Lemma, 54, a former information technology contractor at the U.S. Department of State, the U.S. Department of Justice, and the National Reconnaissance Office, pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro.

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

Senior Judge John D. Bates scheduled sentencing for April 14, 2027.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court papers, Lemma, of Silver Spring, Maryland, held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance who, from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §794. If accepted by the Court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

RENO – An Elko, Nevada, man was sentenced today by United States District Judge Miranda M. Du to 27 months in prison to be followed by three years of supervised release for assaulting a member of the Te-Moak tribe. The government recommended a sentence of 27 months in prison.

“This wasn’t a simple altercation—it was a vicious, cold-blooded attack using a deadly weapon to tear apart the safety of a community,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “By unleashing this level of brutal violence within Indian Country, the defendant showed an absolute, utter contempt for human life and tribal sovereignty. We will pursue anyone who threatens a community, and today’s sentence ensures this dangerous individual is stripped of his freedom.”

“Mr. Allison carried out a brutal, merciless attack on an innocent victim,” said Special Agent in Charge Christopher S. Delzotto for the FBI Las Vegas Field Office. “Today’s sentence underscores the unyielding commitment of the FBI, Tribal police, and our law enforcement partners to aggressively investigate and prosecute violent crime in Indian Country. Having admitted to assaulting the victim with a dangerous weapon, his fate is sealed. The message is clear: if you commit violent crimes, justice will find you.”

According to court documents, on October 30, 2025, Derrick Allison assaulted a woman within the boundaries of the Te-Moak Elko Indian Colony. He cut and stabbed the victim in the face and neck with a sharp object.

Allison pleaded guilty to one count of assault with a dangerous weapon within Indian Country.

The FBI investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Steven Rose prosecuted the case.

BOSTON – A member of the Boston Chapter of the Trinitarios pleaded guilty on Oct. 28, 2026 to racketeering drug charges, including a home invasion robbery in July 2025 in Lawrence, Mass.

Yoldari Tejeda Coronado, a/k/a “Nonoy,” 25, of Lawrence, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to conduct enterprise affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity (also known as “racketeering conspiracy” or “RICO conspiracy”). U.S. Senior District Court Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton scheduled sentencing for Jan. 27, 2027. Coronado was arrested and charged in December 2025 as part of a related case.

The Trinitarios is a violent criminal enterprise comprised of thousands of members across the United States. The Trinitarios adhere to a Magna Carta, employ an internal hierarchy to coordinate and execute violence, and undertake extensive efforts to maintain the secrecy of the organization and its members.

During the plea hearing, Coronado admitted that he was a member of the Boston Chapter of the Trinitarios. Cooperating witnesses, social media images and tattoos confirmed that he was a member since at least 2023. Coronado admitted that he conspired to commit a home invasion in Lawrence in July 2025. During the home invasion, two gunmen forced an individual into their residence and robbed the residence. Further investigation revealed that a vehicle associated with Coronado’s girlfriend was identified as being used by the robbers.

Coronado was also captured on recording, offering to conduct the robbery of a drug stash house. During that recording, Coronado discussed planning the robbery with undercover agents posing as individuals responsible for transporting a large quantity of cocaine for a Mexican drug cartel. Coronado discussed details of the planned robbery and the other individuals who would be involved and agreed to take multiple kilograms of cocaine as payment.

Additionally, Coronado was the subject of a recorded conversation involving the State Supreme, Enmanuel Paula-Cabral, a/k/a “Nelfew,” who described Coronado as having conducted a robbery of a drug dealer. Paula-Cabral discussed being contacted by the drug dealer and that he used his authority as leader of the Trinitarios to have Coronado, a subordinate member in the gang, return the drugs to the drug dealer.

In February 2025 , federal racketeering charges were unsealed against 22 leaders and members of the Trinitarios. The charges were the result of a multijurisdictional investigation, which began in the aftermath of four murders as well as a series of attempted murders and shootings that took place in Lynn in 2023, allegedly committed by the Trinitarios criminal enterprise and its members. On June 9, 2026 , additional federal racketeering and drug charges were unsealed charging 26 additional leaders, members and associates of the Lawrence, Haverhill and Boston Chapters of the gang. According to court documents, the Trinitarios have allegedly participated in five additional murders in Essex County since 2017, bringing the total of federally charged murders to 11, and the total number of federally charged defendants to 56.

The charge of conspiracy to conduct enterprise affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity provides for a sentence of up to life in prison, five years of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England; Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; Essex County District Attorney Paul F. Tucker; Massachusetts State Police Colonel Geoffrey D. Noble; and Lynn Police Chief Christopher P. Reddy made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Manchester, N.H. Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorney Philip A. Mallard of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the case.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston is comprised of agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG, DSS and CBP as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

BOSTON – A Dominican man unlawfully residing in Salem, Mass. was charged by criminal complaint allegedly unlawfully obtaining approximately $16,000 in MassHealth benefits and aggravated identity theft.

Cledis German Romero, 40, has been charged with healthcare benefit fraud and aggravated identity theft and appeared in federal court in Boston on Nov. 3, 2026. He has been detained pending further proceedings.

According to the charging documents, German Romero allegedly used the stolen identity of a U.S. citizen to obtain Massachusetts state driver’s licenses and healthcare benefits, including approximately $16,205 in MassHealth benefits. German Romero also allegedly used the stolen identity of the U.S. citizen in connection with multiple arrests and criminal convictions in Massachusetts, including resisting arrest and conspiracy to violate the controlled substances act.

The charge of making false statements relating to a health care program provides for a sentence of up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The charge of aggravated identity theft provides for a mandatory consecutive sentence of two years and one year of supervised release. The defendant is subject to deportation upon completion of any sentence imposed. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Jeff Grimming, Acting Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Investigations in New England made the announcement today. Assistant U.S. Attorney Catherine Conroy of the Major Crimes Unit is prosecuting the case.

On March 26, 2026 , United States Attorney Leah B. Foley announced the creation of the Benefit & Voter Fraud Team, a district-wide initiative established in response to the rampant fraud being uncovered across Massachusetts. Members of the public are encouraged to report suspected benefit fraud in Massachusetts by calling 1-855-SCAM-MA-1 (855-722-6621).

On April 7, 2026, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division . The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The details contained in the charging document are allegations. The defendant is presumed to be innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in the court of law.

RAPID CITY - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a Lead, South Dakota, woman convicted of Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury. The sentencing took place on October 30, 2026.

Vivian Rose One Feather, age 32, was sentenced to three years and five months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

One Feather was indicted by a federal grand jury in May 2026. She pleaded guilty on August 7, 2026.

On Valentine’s Day 2026, One Feather and her boyfriend saw a man walking alongside the road near Little Eagle, South Dakota. One Feather believed the man had wronged her boyfriend’s mother. One Feather and her boyfriend exited their vehicle and began assaulting the male. While the boyfriend used only his fists, One Feather struck the man with a metal bar and kicked him, even after he fell to the ground. One Feather only stopped when her boyfriend pulled her away. The male lost consciousness during the assault and experienced extreme pain. He required sutures and staples for several injuries to his head and experienced dizziness for months after the assault.

This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian country be prosecuted in Federal Court as opposed to State Court.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs – Office of Justice Services. Assistant U.S. Attorney Carl Thunem prosecuted the case.

One Feather was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service to serve her federal sentence.

text:
The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) is responsible for collecting nearly all of the federal revenue to fund federal government agencies and programs, as well as for enforcing taxpayer compliance with federal tax laws through taxpayer assistance and audits. According to FY2025 data, the agency processed nearly 271 million tax returns, collected $5.3 trillion in gross revenue, and issued refunds totaling nearly $358 billion.
The IRS's operating budget includes both annual appropriations and other funds. In FY2026, appropriations accounted for 67% ($11.2 billion) of the budget. The remaining 33% ($5.6 billion) came from other budgetary resources, primarily from $4.5 billion in multiyear funding provided by P.L. 117-169, the FY2022 reconciliation law commonly referred to as the Inflation Reduction Act. Smaller budgetary resources included unobligated balances from previous years, resources from other accounts, and reimbursable items.
The Administration's FY2027 appropriations request for the IRS is $9.8 billion, a 12% decrease from the FY2026 enacted amount. Requested funds include an 18% decrease in funding for both enforcement and technology and operations support activities, along with a 3% increase in funding for taxpayer services. The FY2027 request also includes $6.1 billion in other funding not provided by appropriations acts, including $4.2 billion in mandatory P.L. 117-169 funding, $1.3 billion from user fees, and several miscellaneous funding sources. Figure 1 provides an overview of the proposed FY2027 budget compared to the enacted FY2026 levels.
The IRS FY2027 appropriations request of $9.8 billion would be a $1.4 billion decrease from the FY2026 enacted amount of $11.2 billion. That decrease is driven by the IRS's workforce restructuring efforts, including a $778 million decrease to reduce staff by 4,714 full-time equivalent (FTE) positions and a $681 million reduction in related nonlabor spending (which includes costs such as contractors and equipment). These decreases are slightly offset by a $94 million and 1,132 FTE increase for customer service operations. The budget also includes a $23 million increase for the annualization of a FY2026 1.0% pay increase and an equivalent $23 million decrease due to staffing reductions to offset the cost of the pay increase.
The FY2027 budget includes $4.2 billion in P.L. 117-169 funds, accounting for 70% of other budgetary resources. P.L. 117-169 provided the IRS with $79.4 billion in multiyear funding available for obligation from FY2022 to FY2031. Of this amount, P.L. 117-169 specified $45.6 billion would be devoted to enforcement, $25.3 billion to operations support, $4.8 billion to business systems modernization (BSM), $3.2 billion to taxpayer services, $500 million for energy security, and $15 million for a study on the feasibility of a direct-file system (these funds were available through FY2023).
Approximately $53.5 billion in P.L. 117-169 funds have been rescinded, primarily enforcement funds. Congress rescinded $1.4 billion in enforcement funding in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (P.L. 118-5). Funds have also been rescinded in IRS appropriations acts, including $20.2 billion in enforcement funds in FY2024 (P.L. 118-47), $20.2 billion in enforcement funds in FY2025 (P.L. 119-4), and $11.7 billion in operations support funds in FY2026 (P.L. 119-75). An additional $371 million of unobligated balances from energy security are proposed to be canceled in the FY2027 request.
The rescissions reduced the amount of P.L. 117-169 funds available to the IRS to approximately $26 billion. By the end of the first half of FY2026, the IRS had spent $9.9 billion of $18.5 billion available for operations support and BSM, nearly all of the $3.8 billion available for enforcement, $2.8 billion of $3.2 billion for taxpayer services, $63.6 million of $500 million for energy security, and $11.6 million for the direct-file study. The IRS expects to exhaust the remaining funding for enforcement and energy security in FY2026, taxpayer services in FY2027, and operations support and BSM in FY2028.
IRS appropriations are distributed among three accounts: enforcement, taxpayer services, and technology and operations support.
This account covers the costs associated with collecting taxes owed, legal and litigation support, criminal investigations, and enforcement of tax laws. The FY2027 appropriations request for enforcement totals $4.1 billion, the largest of the three accounts. The request includes $3.3 billion for audits and collections (an 18% decrease from FY2026), $676.2 million for investigations (a 16% decrease), and $126.4 million for regulatory services (a 19% decrease).
This account pays for prefiling assistance and education, filing and account services, taxpayer advocacy services, and associated support costs. The FY2027 appropriations request for taxpayer services totals $3.1 billion, including $2.3 billion for filing and account services (a 4% increase) and $782.0 million for prefiling taxpayer assistance and education (level-funded).
This account funds the operation of the IRS's infrastructure, including research support, headquarters maintenance, information systems development and operation, and telecommunications. The FY2027 appropriations request for technology and operations support is $2.6 billion, including $1.1 billion for shared services and support (level-funded), $1.1 billion for information services (level-funded), and $331 million for infrastructure (a 63% decrease).
As Congress deliberates FY2027 funding for the IRS, it might consider the impacts of the changes in enforcement funding and the workforce in the appropriations request. The IRS anticipates the workforce restructuring efforts to "yield significant savings to the taxpayer, once fully implemented." The Congressional Budget Office previously estimated that rescissions to enforcement funding would reduce tax revenue collected. The National Taxpayer Advocate has expressed concern that reduced IRS staffing would reduce agency services and taxpayer assistance.
Another consideration is the impact of the depletion of P.L. 117-169 funding on the IRS's budget and activities. The IRS reported that, with the impending exhaustion of P.L. 117-169 funds, the IRS is in the process of reevaluating its modernization plan and investments in FY2027.

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Takquasha Beatty, age 31, of York, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on October 15, 2026, to four years in prison by United States District Judge Keli M. Neary for trafficking cocaine.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, a grand jury indicted Takquasha Beatty and others for their role in a conspiracy to traffic cocaine in York, Pennsylvania with kilograms of cocaine smuggled in from Puerto Rico into York. On March 15, 2023, law enforcement searched Beatty’s home in York where they found cocaine hidden in a children’s toy, a cash counting machine in the kitchen, $35,700 in cash, a digital scale for weighing drugs, a loaded gun, and other materials indicative of drug trafficking. Other locations linked to the drug trafficking conspiracy were searched the same day and similar evidence was recovered. Two weeks later, law enforcement intercepted 30 kilograms of cocaine shipped from Puerto Rico to York, destined for this same drug trafficking group.

At sentencing, Judge Neary emphasized the seriousness of the crime and the scope of the drug trafficking conspiracy. When imposing sentence, Judge Neary also emphasized that Beatty allowed this drug trafficking to happen in her home where her four small children lived. In March 2026, Beatty pled guilty to conspiracy to trafficking cocaine.

The following co-defendants in this case also pled guilty to conspiracy to traffic cocaine:

Juan Escalera-Carrasquillo, age 27, York, PA – pending sentencing;

Daniel Velez-Olivero, age 39, York, PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $200 fine, and $100 special assessment;

Gerald J. Calcano, age 33, York, PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $100 special assessment;

Kevin Marrero-Morales, age 31, York PA – sentenced to 120 months in prison, 5 years of supervised release, $500 fine and $100 special assessment; and

Jorge Angel Rivera-Ortiz, age 26. York, PA – sentenced to time served, three years of supervised release, $100 special assessment.

Co-defendant Reynaldo Vargas Seda pled guilty to possession of a short-barreled rifle in furtherance of drug trafficking. He is scheduled for sentencing on February 9, 2027.

Revolving loan funds (RLFs) are financial instruments frequently used to finance water, wastewater, infrastructure, brownfields redevelopment, disaster recovery, and community development activities. RLFs can also be used for economic development purposes. Federally funded economic development RLFs (ED-RLFs) are one of many tools that public agencies and nonprofit organizations may use to make loans to finance small business growth, deploy capital to underserved markets, and incentivize development activity. The main advantage of using an RLF is that the RLF can be configured in a way to be "self-replenishing," thereby reducing the need for annual appropriations or federal credit subsidies. This In Focus provides an overview of how ED-RLFs work, a summary of federal support for ED-RLFs, and a brief review of current issues.
Initial funding for the capital base and administrative expenses of an RLF may come from a variety of sources, including government agencies, foundations, or private financial markets. Federal programs may support ED-RLFs by providing grants or loans to capitalize the fund. For instance, the U.S. Economic Development Administration (EDA) and the Appalachian Regional Commission award grants through existing programs with specific guidelines for the use of funds as ED-RLFs. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) uses both grant and loan authorities to support ED-RLFs. RLF borrowers typically include for-profit businesses, nonprofit organizations, and government entities. The repayment of principal, interest, and fees can replenish RLFs so that future loans can be made to eligible borrowers and the loan fund can eventually be sustained or "revolved" without the need for continuing subsidies.
ED-RLFs are often designed to target businesses in specific industries, geographic areas, or distressed communities, or to target the unmet needs of borrowers for products and services such as microloans or gap financing. USDA funding, for example, may be used for targeted lending activities (e.g., for microloans) or for specific types of rural borrowers (e.g., to local utility organizations). ED-RLFs may also be used to finance development initiatives, such as infrastructure and revitalization projects sponsored by local government or other entities.
Many ED-RLFs report that they create some form of direct or indirect economic benefit to the region served. Directly, the ED-RLFs may increase the number of jobs created or retained, businesses expanded, or business startups created. Indirectly, ED-RLFs that finance public infrastructure or community development projects facilitate growth by supporting entrepreneurs, encouraging investment, and improving the conditions that expand facilities or amenities. The purpose of ED-RLFs typically is to supplement—not supplant—conventional lending activity where business and development credit needs are not fully addressed. ED-RLF programs can provide credit to businesses and markets that may be underserved by commercial lenders, including small or nontraditional businesses as well as businesses owned by socially or economically disadvantaged individuals. Participating in an ED-RLF program may help small or new businesses build credit and receive additional services, like technical assistance or business coaching. Some ED-RLFs serve businesses that need gap financing or microloans that may be otherwise unavailable from traditional lenders.
There are limitations and challenges associated with the creation, expansion, and maintenance of RLFs. When capitalized by grants or low-cost loans, ED-RLFs may receive lower financial returns in exchange for social or economic development outcomes. ED-RLF administrators must balance the overall demand for services, limited administrative resources, and the need to meet social or development goals while also assessing and managing risk. Loan losses are a risk to ED-RLFs and may decrease the capital base over time. Interest rates and fees have to be sufficient to cover potential loan losses, expenses, and inflation. Additionally, ED-RLFs that receive federal support may face constraints related to program regulations, including thresholds for interest rates, loan disbursements, and other requirements.
Federally supported ED-RLFs may need to raise additional capital from other government and private sources to sustain their programs or to meet nonfederal cost share requirements. High-performing ED-RLFs may need additional funds to recapitalize the fund when an ED-RLF has an active base of borrowers. The demand for ED-RLF loans can be episodic and depend on economic factors that are outside the control of ED-RLF administrators at the local, state, and regional level. Additionally, a 2026 evaluation of EDA's RLF program noted that new financial products have created more options for business loans in recent years, which could mean that ED-RLFs may face competition for borrowers.
Both borrowers and institutional intermediaries may need technical assistance to establish an RLF and to ensure the fund becomes sustainable. Thus, loans from an ED-RLF might need to be paired with technical assistance to borrowers (often at an additional cost to the funder, lender, or borrower) to facilitate businesses' financial sustainability and to protect against loan defaults.
Table 1 provides a summary of selected federal programs that support ED-RLFs. The terms, eligibility requirements, and other conditions of federally supported ED-RLFs vary based on the agency's program objectives, regulations, and statutory requirements. For instance, some ED-RLFs are administered by the federal agency directly; others are administered by an intermediary such as a local government, Indian tribe, nonprofit, utility, university, or economic development agency, including economic development districts and councils of governments. The ED-RLFs described in Table 1 often complement other forms of business capital provided by financial institutions, the Small Business Administration, and Department of the Treasury programs, such as the State Small Business Credit Initiative (SSBCI) program and the Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFI) Fund's Financial Assistance awards program. These loan, loan guarantee, and other programs offer assistance to businesses—usually through intermediaries such as community banks, CDFIs, and state economic development agencies and not included in this summary. For more information, see CRS In Focus IF12449, Connecting Constituents with Federal Assistance for Businesses.
title: Economic Development Revolving Loan Funds (ED-RLFs)

WASHINGTON — Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others.

“As alleged, Martin mailed letters containing white powder to hundreds of state and federal officials, a calculated attempt to terrorize public servants,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These officials were left to open those letters not knowing if the powder inside could sicken or even kill them, and that was the evident intent. Intimidation like this has no place in a Nation governed by the rule of law, and the National Security Division will investigate and prosecute these cases to the fullest extent appropriate.”

“Threatening election officials and attempting to intimidate public servants is a serious federal offense and will not be tolerated,” said U.S. Attorney Robert J. Troester for the Western District of Oklahoma. “Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners, we are committed to investigating these threats and holding accountable those who seek to spread fear and intimidation in our communities.”

“Early Monday morning, the FBI conducted an operation and arrested Robin Patrick Martin – the subject who allegedly sent hundreds of letters containing suspicious white powder substances to public officials around the country both before the 2024 and 2026 election,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The letters went to well over 100 locations including multiple state secretary offices, election offices, and more. The alleged subject had avoided authorities until now – as the Biden administration failed to catch him – but this FBI got it done. I want to thank our Oklahoma City Field Office and the FBI Criminal Division, as well as our USPIS, Capitol Police, and OKC PD partners who responded to the threat quickly and did outstanding work executing in this case. Every American citizen deserves a free and fair election – and anyone who attempts to undermine that process by breaking our laws and threatening public officials will be brought to justice.”

“The mailing of letters containing an unknown powdery substance across the country created unnecessary fear, diverted resources, and attempted to disrupt our nation’s democratic process,” said Special Agent in Charge Doug Goodwater of the FBI Oklahoma City Field Office. “No one should have to wonder whether a letter in the mail poses a danger, and the arrest of Robin Martin demonstrates that those who seek to spread panic and intimidation cannot expect to remain anonymous. I would like to express my gratitude to the dedicated team at FBI Oklahoma City and our partners at the US Attorney’s Offices, USPIS, USPS, U.S. Capitol Police, FBI Laboratory Division, and Oklahoma City Department for all their work in this matter.”

“The Postal Inspection Service has a long, proud, and successful history of ensuring the sanctity of election mail, safeguarding the integrity of elections, and protecting election officials from threatening and dangerous mail,” said Chief Postal Inspector Gary Barksdale of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS). “Utilizing our expertise in the Postal Service and mail flow, postal inspectors and our partners identified related mailings and recovered the majority of these mailings before they reached their intended recipients, keeping Postal Service customers — the American public — safe. This arrest reflects the perseverance of the Postal Inspection Service, FBI, U.S. Capitol Police, and all of our law enforcement partners to keep criminals from interfering with two trusted traditions — the election process, and the U.S. Mail.”

“Our team has been working around the clock with our law enforcement partners to put this defendant behind bars,” said U.S. Capitol Police Chief Michael Sullivan. “We will not tolerate anyone who attempts to use fear as a weapon.”

According to public records, on Oct. 13, 2026, the Oklahoma State Election Board notified the FBI that it had received a threatening letter containing white powder. The FBI and USPIS had been investigating threatening letters containing white powder sent to multiple state election officials — including the Oklahoma State Election Board — since 2024. The FBI and USPIS determined that this letter was part of hundreds of threatening letters, many of which had white powder, that had been sent across the country to state election boards, members of Congress, election pollsters, media organizations, and others. The white powder was later determined to be non-hazardous.

Today, Martin appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge Shon Erwin for his initial appearance in Oklahoma City.

This case is part of the nationwide National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 initiative, which is a White House-directed, interagency effort to integrate federal, state, and local partners in protecting First Amendment rights while targeting individuals and organizations engaged in political violence.

This case is being investigated by the FBI, USPIS, United States Capitol Police, Oklahoma City Police Department, and Texas Department of Public Safety, including the Texas Rangers, with valuable assistance from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Oklahoma.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Oklahoma is prosecuting the case with assistance from the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

A complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

By Staff Sgt. Kenyel Jones
4th Psychological Operations Group Public Affairs
FORT BRAGG, N.C. — Soldiers assigned to the 4th Psychological Operations Group are developing practical cooking and nutrition skills through a meal preparation program that complements the unit's newly renovated barracks kitchen.
The kitchen, which officially opened in September 2026, provides Soldiers with a functional space to prepare meals while supporting the group's efforts to improve barracks living conditions and promote healthier food choices.
Jessie Anderson, a performance dietitian supporting psychological operations Soldiers, said the renovation addressed a need for improved cooking facilities for Soldiers living in the barracks.
According to Anderson, the barracks are located far from the dining facility, and although Soldiers receive basic allowance for subsistence, they previously lacked a functional kitchen to prepare their own meals.
Anderson worked alongside unit leadership to help develop the kitchen's layout and design, creating a space where Soldiers could cook independently and participate in hands-on nutrition education.
The renovated facility also allows Anderson to move beyond office-based instruction and provide practical demonstrations of food preparation, cooking techniques and nutrition label reading.
Through the commissary tour and meal preparation class, Anderson teaches Soldiers how to make nutritious food choices, manage grocery expenses and develop sustainable eating habits.
"You have to enjoy it to sustain it," Anderson said.
The class begins at the Fort Bragg South Post Commissary, where Soldiers learn to compare food options, shop within a budget and select ingredients before returning to the renovated barracks kitchen for hands-on meal preparation.
Anderson's meal preparation roadmap outlines a goal of producing 20 meal and snack containers, including six breakfasts, 10 lunch and dinner portions and four snack containers, at an estimated grocery cost of $68 to $80.
Recipes include chia pudding overnight oats, sweet potato taco bowls, burritos and chocolate peanut butter energy bites.
For Pfc. Daniel Cedeño, assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Company, 4th Psychological Operations Group, the class provided an opportunity to develop cooking and nutrition skills he had rarely practiced before.
When asked how often he prepared his own meals before participating, Cedeño said, "Probably never."
Cedeño said the experience helped him become more aware of ingredients in food products and how some products may be marketed as healthy despite their nutritional content. He also appreciated his unit's investment in providing the renovated kitchen and nutrition program.
"It means that they care," Cedeño said. "That they support their Soldiers."
Anderson currently offers the class twice a month and hopes to expand the program as more Soldiers become aware of the opportunity. Future classes could focus on preparing individual meals while teaching Soldiers about nutrition, ingredients and cooking techniques.
Anderson emphasized that the program is designed to make preparing nutritious meals practical and manageable, helping Soldiers build confidence in the kitchen while reducing food waste and the cost of dining out.
A Soldier, assigned to Alpha Company, 9th Psychological Operations Battalion, said the renovated kitchen exceeded his expectations. Although Barnes does not reside in the barracks, he recognized the value of providing Soldiers with a functional space to prepare their own meals.
"The kitchen is very nice," Barnes said. "Six stovetops are great. I love the deep-dish sinks as well."
By combining improved barracks facilities with practical nutrition education, the 4th Psychological Operations Group (Airborne) is providing Soldiers with opportunities to develop independent cooking skills, manage food expenses and make informed decisions about their daily nutrition.
title: Fort Bragg Soldiers Build Nutrition Skills Through Renovated Barracks Kitchen, Meal Prep Program

Tallahassee, Florida – Frederick Allen Smith, Jr., 54, of Madison, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and 500 grams or more of a mixture containing methamphetamine, possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking offense, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Our state and federal law enforcement partners are cleaning up our streets and removing dangerous armed drug traffickers from our communities, and my office is backing up those efforts with aggressive prosecutions to ensure anyone who peddles deadly drugs in the Northern District of Florida is kept behind federal bars for as long as possible. Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche, we are devoting the full might of the Department of Justice toward delivering the safe, drug-free streets that our citizens deserve.”

Court documents reflect that in May 2026, law enforcement executed a search warrant at the defendant’s residence, where deputies seized 703 grams of methamphetamine, a loaded handgun, ammunition, and more than $17,000 in cash. The defendant has multiple prior felony convictions dating back to 2005 and was legally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition.

The defendant faces a minimum of 10 years’ imprisonment and up to life imprisonment on the possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine count; a minimum of 5 years’ imprisonment consecutive to other sentences on the possession of a firearm in furtherance count; and up to 15 years’ imprisonment on the possession of a firearm by a convicted felon count.

The case involved a joint investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and the Madison County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant United States Attorney Emma Schwan is prosecuting the case.

Sentencing is scheduled for November 9, 2026, at 1:00pm at the United States Courthouse in Tallahassee before United States District Judge Robert L. Hinkle.

He faces a maximum penalty of 15 years in federal prison. Zoladz will be sentenced on January 20, 2027. United States Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

DEA’s National Prescription Drug Take Back Day Safely Removes More Than 645,000 Pounds of Unwanted Medications Nationwide
More than 17,000 pounds of medications were collected across the DEA Omaha Field Division, October 24.
OMAHA, Neb. –The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), in partnership with more than 4,200 law enforcement agencies, collected 645,636 pounds of unused medications October 24, as part of ongoing efforts to prevent drug misuse. This event marked DEA’s 31st National Prescription Drug Take Back Day with 4,212 collection sites nationwide, including 64 tribal locations.
Across the five-state DEA Omaha Field Division, communities safely disposed of 17,463 pounds of unused and expired prescription medications at 142 locations spanning Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota. Since 2010, DEA’s National Prescription Drug Take Back Day has collected the equivalent of more than 10,840 tons of medications, including 371 tons from the Midwestern region.
“The importance of safely disposing of prescription medications can’t be stressed enough,” DEA Omaha Field Division Acting Special Agent in Charge Rafael Mattei said. “Whether medications are dropped off at one our Take Back Day events or taken to a year-round collection site, getting those substances out of the home helps reduce the risk of accidental overdose and drug misuse.”
More than 15,300 pharmacies, hospitals, businesses, and many police departments offer safe medication disposal year-round. For information on permanent drop boxes, visit DEA’s Every Day is Take Back Day webpage.
National Prescription Drug Take Back Day results are available at Take Back Day. Safe disposal of unused medications remains one of the simplest ways communities can help prevent drug misuse.
###
title: DEA’s National Prescription Drug Take Back Day Safely Removes More Than 645,000 Pounds of Unwanted Medications Nationwide

ATF Houston leads coordinated operation resulting in eight federal indictments and multiple arrests across East Texas
HOUSTON - What began as a firearms dealer burglary investigation in Jasper, has resulted in a coordinated, multi-agency enforcement operation across East Texas, today.

Today’s operation reflects our unwavering commitment to protecting East Texas communities from violent crime and the illegal trafficking of firearms.”
This operation highlights the impact of strong partnerships, thorough investigative work, and coordinated law enforcement efforts.

SIOUX FALLS - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier has sentenced a Sioux Falls man convicted of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. The sentencing took place on November 2, 2026.

Dakota Thorstenson, 30, was sentenced to 2 years and 6 months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Thorstenson was indicted for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person by a federal grand jury in May 2026. He pleaded guilty on August 11, 2026.

In April of this year, Thorstenson was the driver of a vehicle involved in two automobile accidents in rapid succession in southern Sioux Falls. As a result of his involvement in the two accidents, Thorstenson was taken into custody by local law enforcement. He was searched and a pistol was found on him. Thorstenson is prohibited from possessing firearms due to felony convictions for Distribution or Possession with Intent to Distribute Marijuana from 2015 in Brookings County, Simple Assault on a Law Enforcement Officer from 2015 in Brookings County, and Simple Assault, Third or Subsequent Offense from 2022 in Minnehaha County.

This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives. Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan McFall prosecuted the case.

Thorstenson was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.
title: Sioux Falls Man Sentenced to 2 years in Federal Prison for Possession of a Firearm by a Prohibited Person
