DEA New Orleans Field Division Announces Successful Fall 2026 National Prescription Drug Take Back Day Results
Arkansas Leads the Nation in Total Collection Weight with Nearly 60,000 Pounds Removed
NEW ORLEANS — The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) New Orleans Field Division, alongside 151 state, local, and tribal law enforcement and community health partners across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Arkansas, today announced that residents safely disposed of 74,059 pounds (over 37 tons) of unneeded medications during the Fall 2026 National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on October 24.
Highlighting the division’s regional success, Arkansas led the entire nation in collection weight for the 31st Take Back Day, bringing in 59,780 pounds of unneeded pharmaceuticals -- outperforming every state in the country. Combined across all four states (Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Arkansas), the New Orleans Field Division accounted for over 11.4% of the entire nation's collected pharmaceutical weight.
This semi-annual initiative provides communities with a free, safe, and anonymous way to dispose of unneeded, expired, and unwanted prescription medications, preventing drug misuse, accidental poisonings, and environmental contamination. Nationwide, DEA and more than 4,200 law enforcement partners collected 645,636 pounds of unused medications across 4,212 collection sites. Since the inception of the program in 2010, the DEA New Orleans Field Division footprint alone has safely removed over 1.15 million pounds (575 tons) of pharmaceutical waste from local households.
Across the four-state New Orleans Field Division footprint, residents turned out in high numbers across 163 dedicated collection sites to clear out home medicine cabinets:
- Arkansas: State collection operations safely removed 59,780 lbs. of unneeded medications across 118 collection sites and 193 law enforcement partners, earning the #1 ranking nationwide.
- Louisiana: 37 law enforcement partners across 41 collection sites gathered 7,567 lbs. of unneeded medications.
- Mississippi: 43 law enforcement partners across 44 collection sites gathered 4,234 lbs. of unneeded medications.
- Alabama: 33 law enforcement partners across 38 collection sites gathered 2,478 lbs. of unneeded medications.
- Regional Footprint Totals: 151 Law Enforcement Partners | 163 Collection Sites | 74,059 lbs. (Over 37 tons)
“The success of National Prescription Drug Take Back Day relies entirely on strong community leadership and active public participation,” said John P. Scott, Special Agent in Charge of the DEA New Orleans Field Division. “We are immensely proud to see Arkansas lead the entire nation in collection totals this fall, and deeply grateful to all our law enforcement officers, healthcare providers, National Guard personnel, and civic partners across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Arkansas. Removing more than 37 tons of unused prescription drugs from local homes directly prevents medication misuse and keeps our neighborhoods safer.”

BOSTON – A Holliston, Mass. man pleaded guilty on Oct. 27, 2026 in federal court in Boston to sexually exploiting a minor.

Wilson Fabian Mizhirumbay Granda, 23, pleaded guilty to one count of sexual exploitation of children. U.S. District Court Judge Allison D. Burroughs scheduled sentencing for Jan. 20, 2027. Granda was charged in September 2026 and is currently in Massachusetts state custody on an unrelated criminal case.

Between August and September 2023, Granda coerced a minor victim to travel to Massachusetts and engage in sexually explicit conduct. Granda met the minor victim on a social media site, knew she was underage and lied about his own age. Granada later recorded himself having sex with minor victim on a number of occasions.

Granda has prior state convictions in Hampshire Country Superior Court for rape of a child and enticing a child under 16, for which he was sentenced in May 2024 to four years and one day in state prison to be followed by five years of probation. Currently, Granda also has pending charges in Norfolk County for rape of child with force, rape of child and enticing a child under 16 related to another minor.

The charge of sexual exploitation of children provides for a sentence of up to 30 years in prison, a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $250,000. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Ted E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division made the announcement today. Valuable assistance was provided by the Holliston, Scituate (R.I.), Amherst, Westminster, Medway, Worcester, Millis and UMass Lowell Police Departments; and the Middlesex County, Hampshire County, Northwestern County, Norfolk County and Worcester County District Attorney’s Offices. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys David G. Tobin and Jessica L. Soto of the Criminal Division. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .
title: Holliston Man Pleads Guilty to Sexual Exploitation of Children

SAVANNAH, Georgia: Several defendants pleaded guilty in district court for charges including distribution of methamphetamine, fentanyl possession, and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.

The sentences were imposed in U.S. District Court and announced by Margaret E. “Meg” Heap, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Georgia.

Jason Chapman , a/k/a “Shane Copeland”, 50, of Waynesville, was sentenced to 102 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Distribution of More than 5 Grams of Methamphetamine.

According to court documents and testimony, in February 2025, investigators with the Drug Enforcement Administration began an investigation into drug trafficking activities of the defendant. Special agents with the DEA determined through various means of investigation that Chapman sold quantities of methamphetamine in Brantley County.

Kyle Ashley Edmunds , 44, of Augusta, was sentenced to 96 months in prison and a $2,500 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession with Intent to Distribute Fentanyl.

According to court documents and testimony, in April 2025, Edmunds was the subject of an investigation based on illegal firearms possession despite prior felony convictions when investigators determined that the defendant was actively selling illegal narcotics, including methamphetamine and fentanyl.

Keith L. Polite , 41, of Thomson, was sentenced to 57 months in prison and a $2,000 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

According to court documents and testimony, in December 2024, Polite was found in possession of a firearm, a Sterling Arms, Model 300, .25-caliber pistol and a DPMS model A-15, .223-caliber rifle. Under federal law, it is prohibited for previously convicted felons to possess firearms or ammunition.

Hunter Tucker Baxley , 32, of Evans, was sentenced to 46 months in prison and a $10,000 fine followed by three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to Possession of a Firearm by a Convicted Felon.

According to court documents and testimony, in August 2025, Baxley was found in possession of a firearm, a Fabrique Nationale, 509 Tactical, 9 mm pistol during an encounter with the Columbia County Sheriff’s Office. Under federal law, it is prohibited for previously convicted felons to possess firearms or ammunition.

There is no parole in the federal system.

“Our priority is to ensure that individuals that violate the law are removed from the streets of our community,” said U.S. Attorney Heap. “Through effective interagency cooperation with our law enforcement partners, we are ensuring those that violate the law are brought to justice.”

These cases were investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosive, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Brantley County Sheriff’s Office, Columbia County Sheriff’s Office, Richmond County Sheriff’s Office, and additional law enforcement agencies.

These cases were prosecuted for the United States by Southern District of Georgia Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jennifer J. Kirkland, Henry W. Syms Jr., and Kelsey L. Scanlon.

MARTINSBURG, WEST VIRGINIA – A former employee of the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office has admitted her role in a years‑long fraud and embezzlement scheme that targeted vulnerable individuals and public funds, U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey announced today.

Lisa Lee French, 48, of Martinsburg, admitted that between 2007 and October 2024, she conspired to steal cash payments collected by the Sheriff’s Office and to manipulate conservatorship and estate accounts overseen by the office. French acknowledged issuing fraudulent checks, forging signatures, misusing a sheriff’s signature stamp, and diverting funds for her personal benefit.

“Fraud on this scale harms not only those directly targeted, but the entire Berkeley County community. We are committed to ensuring accountability and protecting the integrity of our public offices,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

“Fraud on this scale harms not only those directly targeted, but the entire Berkeley County community. We are committed to ensuring accountability and protecting the integrity of our public offices,” said U.S. Attorney Matthew L. Harvey.

The victims include Berkeley County taxpayers, individuals under conservatorship, and the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office itself.

According to court documents, the scheme involved more than 700 fraudulent transactions, over 550 of them forged checks, connected to at least 59 conservator bank accounts. In total, the fraud amounted to nearly $3 million.

French has agreed to pay $2,737,932 in restitution to the identified victims.

A second defendant, Barbara Gail Gooden, is awaiting trial on March 23, 2027. Read the original press release here .

Senior Litigation Counsel Andrew Cogar is prosecuting the case. The investigation was conducted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office, and the West Virginia State Auditor’s Office.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the formation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”), which focuses on investigating and prosecuting fraud against the American public. This effort supports the President’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole‑of‑government initiative chaired by the Vice President to address fraud, waste, and abuse in federal benefit programs.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert W. Trumble presided.
title: Former Berkeley County Sheriff’s Office Employee Admits Guilt in Multi-Million-Dollar Fraud Scheme

Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.
Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.
“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”
“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”
“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”
According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.
Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.
During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.
Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.
On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”
According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.
The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.
The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.
title: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Cristian M. Stevens on Tuesday sentenced a convicted felon from St. Louis to 115 months in prison for shooting and wounding a man in March.

Shan Mims, 39, admitted in July that he used a stolen .380 caliber handgun to shoot the man on March 17, 2026. He also admitted that St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department officers found the gun and cocaine base in his bedroom in a court-approved search nine days later.

The shooting was captured on surveillance video at Mims’ apartment complex. The video shows Mims throwing a water bottle at the victim’s car as it drove by. Mims then approached the victim’s car with his hand inside his jacket, as if he had a gun. In response, the victim opened his car door and produced a handgun. Mims pulled his own and they exchanged gunfire. After shooting the victim, Mims ran down a sidewalk and out of view of the video camera as the victim closed his car door. Mims then circled back into view of the video camera and stood behind a tree pointing his firearm at the victim. The victim fired once at Mims before driving off.

At the time, Mims was on supervised release, having pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court to being a felon in possession of a firearm and possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance in a 2022 case. He was sentenced to 46 months in prison for those offenses.

The St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney J. Christian Goeke prosecuted the case.
title: St. Louis Felon Who Shot and Wounded Man Sentenced to 115 Months in Prison

HARRISBURG - The United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Pennsylvania announced that Tyreese Nealy, age 27, of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, was sentenced on October 22, 2026, to 60 months’ imprisonment by United States District Judge Keli M. Neary for distribution of methamphetamine.

According to United States Attorney Brian D. Miller, Nealy was sentenced for his role in the drug trafficking and firearms trafficking conspiracy that was the subject of an undercover investigation conducted by the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives in conjunction with the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General. During the investigation, undercover officers purchased over three kilograms of methamphetamine, 1,600 fentanyl pills and seven firearms from the conspirators. As a part of the investigation of the conspiracy, Nealy sold to an undercover investigator 171 grams of methamphetamine.

At sentencing, Judge Neary noted the seriousness of the crime and impact that drug trafficking has had on the Harrisburg community. The judge also recognized that Nealy lacked a significant criminal history and imposed the mandatory minimum punishment of 60 months.

Co-defendants Devonte Betts, Lamar Waters, and Rodney McMillian entered guilty pleas to drug trafficking offenses. McMillian was sentenced on October 1, 2026, to 188 months in prison. The other two co-defendants are pending sentencing.

The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General investigated the case. Assistant United States Attorney Michael A. Consiglio prosecuted the case.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

Alien from Canada Charged with Falsely Claiming to be a US Citizen to Register to Vote
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — An alien from Canada was arrested and charged with falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen to register to vote. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri made the announcement. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services assisted the investigation.
Christopher Doucet, 68, was indicted by a federal grand jury for allegedly falsely claiming U.S. citizenship to register to vote.
Doucet was born in Canada and immigrated to the United States as a child, becoming a lawful permanent resident. Lawful permanent residents are not allowed to vote in federal, state or local elections in Missouri. Doucet, knowing he was not a U.S, citizen, registered to vote in Jackson County, Missouri, on Jan. 30, 2024. On his voter registration card, Doucet answered “Yes” to the question that asked, “Are you a citizen of the United States of America?” He signed his name under the certification that read, “I hereby certify that I am a citizen of the United States.” A warning on the bottom of the voter registration card advises that a conviction for making a false statement may result in a fine or imprisonment. On April 2, 2024, Doucet voted in a general municipal election in Independence, Missouri.
The charges contained in the indictment are simply accusations and are not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must be presented to a federal trial jury that will be responsible for determining whether the defendant is guilty or not.
If convicted, Doucet is subject to a sentence of up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. The maximum statutory sentence is outlined by Congress and is provided here for informational purposes. The court will determine Doucet’s sentence based on the advisory sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.
This was investigated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Homeland Security Investigations with assistance from USCIS and is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri.
To report suspected immigration benefit fraud or abuse to USCIS, please use the USCIS Tip Form.
For more information on USCIS and its programs, please visit uscis.gov or follow us on X, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.

WASHINGTON —The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the opening of a Disaster Loan Outreach Center in Warrick County to assist businesses, private nonprofit organizations, and residents affected by severe storms, tornadoes, straight-line winds, and flash flooding occurring June 6 – 26.
Beginning Wednesday, Nov. 4, SBA customer service representatives will be on hand at the Disaster Loan Outreach Center in Warrick County to answer questions about SBA’s disaster loan program, explain the application process, and help individuals complete their application. Walk-ins are welcome, and you can schedule an in-person appointment in advance at appointment.sba.gov.
The hours of operation are listed below:
WARRICK COUNTY
Disaster Loan Outreach Center
Ohio Township Fire Headquarters Station 1
Newburgh, IN 47630
Opens at noon, Wednesday, Nov. 4
Hours: Monday – Friday, 9 a.m. – 6 p.m.
Saturday, 9 a.m. – 1 p.m.
Temporary closing: Wednesday, Nov. 11, in observance of Veterans Day
Closes permanently at 5 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 18
“When disasters strike, SBA’s Disaster Loan Outreach Centers perform an important role by assisting small businesses and their communities,” said Chris Stallings, Associate Administrator of the Office of Disaster Recovery at SBA. “At these centers, our specialists help business owners and residents apply for disaster loans and learn about the full range of programs available to support their recovery.”
Businesses and nonprofits are eligible to apply for business physical disaster loans and may borrow up to $2 million to repair or replace disaster-damaged or destroyed real estate, machinery and equipment, inventory, and other business assets.
The SBA’s Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program is available to eligible small businesses, small agricultural cooperatives, and private nonprofits — including faith-based organizations — impacted by financial losses directly related to this disaster. The SBA is unable to provide disaster loans to agricultural producers, farmers, or ranchers, except for aquaculture enterprises.
EIDLs are for working capital needs caused by the disaster and are available even if the business or private nonprofit did not suffer any physical damage. The loans may be used to pay fixed debts, payroll, accounts payable, and other bills which could not be paid due to the disaster.
Homeowners and renters are eligible to apply for home and personal property loans and may borrow up to $100,000 to replace or repair personal property, such as clothing, furniture, cars, and appliances. Homeowners may apply for up to $500,000 to replace or repair their primary residence.
Interest rates are as low as 4% for small businesses, 3.625% for nonprofits, and 2.875% for homeowners and renters with terms of up to 30 years. Interest does not begin to accrue, and payments are not due until 12 months from the date of the first loan disbursement. The SBA determines eligibility and sets loan amounts and terms based on each applicant’s financial condition.
To apply online, visit sba.gov/disaster. Applicants may also call the National Support Network Center at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov for more information on SBA disaster assistance. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
The filing deadline to return applications for physical property damage is Dec. 8. The deadline to return economic injury applications is July 9, 2027.
###
About the U.S. Small Business Administration
The U.S. Small Business Administration helps power the American dream of business ownership. As the only go-to resource and voice for small businesses backed by the strength of the federal government, SBA empowers entrepreneurs and small business owners with the resources and support they need to start, grow or expand their businesses, or recover from a declared disaster. It delivers services through an extensive network of SBA field offices and partnerships with public and private organizations. To learn more, visit www.sba.gov.
title: SBA Opens Additional Disaster Loan Outreach Center in Indiana

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Abner Estrada Cruz, 27, of Honduras, was sentenced Monday by U.S. District Judge Dale A. Drozd to 14 years in prison for conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced.

According to court documents, Cruz was a leader and organizer of a Honduran drug trafficking organization operating out of Honduras, Oakland, California, and Portland, Oregon. Through at least seven intermediaries, Cruz coordinated the sale of 14 pounds of fentanyl powder into the Eastern District of California. He was ultimately extradited from Honduras to face the charges in this case.

The Drug Enforcement Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, and the U.S. Marshals Service conducted the investigation with assistance from the Butte County Sheriff’s Office, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office, the California Highway Patrol, the California Department of Justice Division of Law Enforcement’s Bureau of Investigation, and the Yolo County District Attorney’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Cameron L. Desmond prosecuted the case.

On May 11, 2026, Cruz pleaded guilty. Below is the status of Cruz’s co-defendants in related cases:

On May 18, 2026, Carlos Samir Colindrez-Erazo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 14, 2026.

On July 27, 2026, Aronis Jose Hernandez-Aguilar pleaded guilty to distribution of at least 400 grams of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 25, 2027.

On Sept. 21, 2026, Yahir Alexander Arteaga Cruz pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute at least 400 grams of fentanyl and four counts of distribution of fentanyl. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 11, 2027.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Sacramento is composed of agents and officers from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, Northern California High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, Central Valley High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area, and the Sacramento County Sheriff’s Office with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California.
title: Leader of Honduran fentanyl trafficking ring sentenced to 14 years in prison

ATLANTA – Last week, Attorney General Todd Blanche recognized six employees of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia as recipients of the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director’s Award during a Washington, D.C. ceremony. The Atlanta-based office was the only U.S. Attorney’s Office in the country to receive multiple team awards.

“I am tremendously proud of my outstanding prosecutors and support staff who received this well-deserved national recognition,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “Their exceptional talent, unwavering dedication, and commitment to pursuing justice exemplify the highest ideals of public service and help to make our district safer.”

The Director’s Awards recognize employees of the 94 U.S. Attorney’s Offices nationwide who have distinguished themselves through extraordinary professional achievements and excellence. The Northern District of Georgia personnel were recognized for Superior Performance by a Litigation Team and Superior Performance by an Administrative Team.

Superior Performance by a Litigation Team

(From left to right: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter, Child Victim Witness Program Administrator Nicole E. Borrello, Army Criminal Investigation Division Special Agent Bryce T. Wolford, FBI Special Agent Will M. Mauk, FBI Unit Chief Johanna M. Norman, EOUSA Director Francey Hakes, Trial Attorney Eduardo A. Palomo, Assistant U.S. Attorney Leanne Marek, Litigation Support Specialist Kimberly C. Layton, U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg, Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr.)

Tampa, FL – Joel Reynolds (48, Seffner) has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Thomas P. Barber to 24 years in federal prison for production, distribution, and possession of child sexual abuse material. The court ordered the sentence to run consecutive to Reynolds’s 25-year state prison sentence. Reynolds pleaded to the federal offenses on July 9, 2026. U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe made the announcement.

According to court documents, law enforcement initiated an investigation into Reynolds after receiving a cyber tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children in November 2024. Further investigation revealed Reynolds had produced child sexual abuse material and distributed at least one such image on a social media application. Law enforcement discovered Reynolds in possession of hundreds of videos depicting minors engaged in sexually explicit conduct on his devices.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Courtney Derry.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.
Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.
“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”
“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”
“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”
According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.
Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.
During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.
Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.
On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”
According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.
The investigation was conducted by the FBI Washington Field Office.
The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.
title: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

BOSTON – A member of the violent Boston-based gang, H-Block, has pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to drug conspiracy charges. Defendant is currently an inmate at a state correctional facility where he smuggled illegal drugs into the prison.

Timothy Hearns, a/k/a “King Kill,” a/k/a “Tooly,” a/k/a “Toolman,” 36, of Roxbury; pleaded guilty on Oct. 30, 2026 to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani scheduled sentencing for Feb. 2, 2027.

Hearns was one of 10 H-Block gang members and associates charged in August 2024 following a multi-year investigation of H-Block beginning in 2021 in response to an uptick in gang-related drug trafficking, shootings and violence. According to court documents, over 500 grams of cocaine, cocaine base (crack cocaine) and fentanyl, as well as over 20,000 doses of drug-laced paper were seized during the investigation.

According to the charging documents, the H-Block street gang is one of the most feared and influential city-wide gangs in Boston. Originally formed in the 1980s as the Humboldt Raiders in the Roxbury section of Boston, the gang re-emerged in the 2000s as H-Block. Current members of H-Block have a history of violent confrontation with law enforcement, including an incident in 2015 when a member shot a Boston Police officer at point blank range without warning or provocation.

Hearns is an inmate at a state correctional institution, currently serving a 19.5 to 20-year manslaughter sentence in the Massachusetts Department of Correction. Hearns was sentenced in 2014 for committing a 2010 shooting that killed a 14-year-old at the Columbus/Heath Street basketball courts, during a time when he and other members of H-Block were engaged in a violent rivalry with Heath Street gang associates. A 15-year-old boy was also shot and struck in the chest and arm but survived.

Hearns is a long-time H-Block gang member and one of three members and associates charged with conspiring to smuggle illegal drugs into a Massachusetts prison. According to court documents, the Massachusetts Department of Correction has seen a significant increase in the smuggling of synthetic cannabinoids, a/k/a “K2,” and other dangerous substances into the prison system. A common method of introducing the drugs is by exploiting the Department of Correction’s inmate mail policies, which prohibit delivery to inmates of original copies of any materials contained in incoming mail except for legal mail, original copies of which are inspected and delivered via the U.S. postal system. Sheets of paper are saturated or sprayed with liquid narcotics, dried, printed with fake legal correspondence, and then mailed to inmates in an envelope marked as legal mail, in the hope that the drug-laced paper will be delivered undetected. It is alleged that several sheets of paper containing PCP (Phenylcyclidine) and illegal K2 were seized over the course of the investigation. It is estimated that a single sheet of such paper would be worth as much as $80,000 inside the prison. Intercepted jail calls revealed that Hearns along with his co-conspirators, conspired to introduce synthetic drugs into the facilities. Hearns is the 10th and final defendant to plead guilty in the case.

The charges of conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute PCP, MDMB-4en-PINACA and ADB-4en-PINACA provides for a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, at least three years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $1 million. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case. United States Attorney Leah B. Foley; Jarod A. Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration, New England Field Division; Special Agent in Charge Mark Comorosky of the U.S. Secret Service Boston Field Office; Ted. E. Docks, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Boston Division; Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox; and Anthony D’Esposito, Inspector General, U.S. Department of Labor, Office of Inspector General made the announcement. The investigation was supported by the Massachusetts State Police; Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office; Massachusetts Department of Corrections; and the Braintree, Quincy, Randolph and Watertown Police Departments. Assistant United States Attorney John T. Dawley of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the cases.

This case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Boston comprises agents and officers from HSI, FBI, DEA, ATF, USMS, IRS-CI, USPIS, DOL-OIG and DSS, as well as several state and local law enforcement agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.
title: Gang Member Pleads Guilty to Conspiring to Smuggle Synthetic Drugs Into Prison

Gainesville, Florida – Pablo Gomez-Sarmiento, 25, of Mexico, was sentenced to the statutory maximum sentence of two years in federal prison after pleading guilty to illegal reentry into the United States. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida.

U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This case reaffirms the absolute necessity of securing our borders against criminal illegal aliens and aggressively enforcing our immigration laws. The defendant’s rape of the child in the underlying state case was 100% preventable. That heartbreaking case is the precise reason why President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche have committed the Department of Justice to repelling the invasion of illegal immigration that took place under the prior administration, to ensure we keep criminal illegal aliens, like this defendant, out of our country.”

Court documents reflect that the defendant, a citizen of Mexico, was removed from the United States in January 2020. Thereafter, the defendant unlawfully returned to the United States, and he was arrested in Alachua County, Florida, in 2024 for impregnating a child under the age of 16. The Defendant admitted to observing the 15-year-old victim getting off a school bus and was aware that she was under 18 years old. He was convicted in 2025 and sentenced to state prison. While the defendant was serving his state sentence, the United States Immigration and Custom’s Enforcement became aware of the defendant’s presence in the United States and initiated the federal criminal charge.

“Criminal illegal aliens who prey on children will find no place to hide from the women and men of ICE” said ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston. “This criminal alien unlawfully returned to the United States after removal and then targeted a child to sexually exploit. ICE will not tolerate those who defy our immigration laws and prey on innocent victims.”

The case was investigated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Enforcement and Removal Operations and the Gainesville Police Department. Assistant United States Attorney Tyler Fleming prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

The United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Florida is one of 94 offices that serve as the nation’s principal litigators under the direction of the Attorney General. To access public court documents online, please visit the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida website. BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
A PROCLAMATION
It is America’s destiny to explore and expand our frontiers beyond Earth to the farthest depths of space. Today, my Administration reaffirms that our solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans, and that our Nation will lead the way in the exploration, development, use, and settlement of these new frontiers — forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty.
From the intrepid Apollo 11 astronauts who took humanity’s first steps on the Moon to the pioneering rovers that explored the surface of Mars, the United States has always blazed a trail into the great unknown, shattering boundaries and pushing mankind to extraordinary new heights. Behind each triumph are generations of astronauts, scientists, engineers, and workers whose tireless dedication and unmatched ingenuity turn impossible dreams into reality.
Under my leadership, the United States is once again writing a bold new chapter in space exploration. This past April, the Artemis II mission successfully carried astronauts around the Moon and farther from Earth than any human had ever traveled before. This historic voyage is only the beginning. Next summer, Artemis III will undertake one of the most complex and consequential test flight campaigns in the history of our Nation’s space program.
This proud legacy of innovation is our sacred inheritance, and our Nation bears the solemn responsibility to advance it by continuing to open new horizons of exploration and discovery. Through the landmark Executive Orders and directives I have signed, we are reinvigorating human spaceflight, unleashing a competitive and thriving commercial space industry, and ensuring American space superiority for all eternity. We will return to the Moon by 2028, lay the foundation for a permanent American lunar presence, and hasten the day when an American becomes the first human to set foot on the red dunes of Mars. Together, we will build the facilities, develop the resources, and establish a permanent presence in space to extend the reach of American exploration, preserve our frontier spirit, and strengthen our national security for centuries to come. The nation that leads in space will shape the future of humanity — and that nation will be the United States of America.
Today, we renew our solemn and righteous mission to propel humanity toward the farthest reaches of the universe. We reaffirm that the United States will lead the way in this bold endeavor, for the nation with the best scientific understanding of space, the most advanced space economy, and the greatest spacefaring citizens, will be the most prosperous nation for centuries to come. Above all, we pledge to carry our sacred values of faith and freedom wherever we journey, so that freedom may forever ring among the stars and beyond.
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the United States of America, by virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and the laws of the United States, do hereby proclaim that the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans and are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens consistent with United States law and the international obligations of the United States.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I have hereunto set my hand this third day of November, in the year of our Lord two thousand twenty-six, and of the Independence of the United States of America the two hundred and fifty-first.
DONALD J. TRUMP
title: THE AMERICAN DECLARATION OF FREEDOM IN SPACE

Release Number 9319-26
CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures
November 03, 2026
WASHINGTON — CFTC Chairman Michael S. Selig today released a statement announcing that perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities can begin trading for the first time on designated contract markets that are dually registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as notice-registered national securities exchanges to trade security futures products.
Key excerpts from Chairman Selig’s statement:
“Today, perpetual futures contracts on individual equity securities (the ‘Equity Perps’) can begin trading for the first time on CFTC-registered exchanges.
…
“This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery. I believe that bringing these types of innovative products into our regulated markets ensures that American investors and traders can access these products within the protections of the CFTC’s proven regulatory framework, rather than being forced to turn to offshore, and often unregulated, venues.
…
“The Equity Perps build on the foundation of the [Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000] and the [CFTC-SEC Memorandum of Understanding]. For too long, regulatory uncertainty left innovative products, such as security futures and equity perpetual futures, stranded in what SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins has aptly described as a regulatory ‘no man’s land’ due to a lack of harmonization between the agencies. The CFTC and SEC have turned the page on that era, and are committed to delivering regulatory clarity for innovative products and a clear path to market, rather than more casualties of jurisdictional disputes.”
Read Chairman Selig’s full statement here.
-CFTC-
title: CFTC Chairman Selig Releases Statement on Equity Perpetual Futures

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A St. Louis, Mo., man appeared in federal court today before Chief U.S. Magistrate Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. on a complaint alleging that he possessed a firearm after a prior felony conviction.

According to the affidavit filed in support of the complaint, Iseah Christopher Jackson, 23, was identified by law enforcement as having been present during a shooting in the area of Ninth Street and Walnut Street in Columbia on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. Later that day, a traffic stop was conducted on his vehicle and a loaded 9mm semi-automatic handgun was found in his glove compartment. Jackson also had a single round of 9mm ammunition in his pocket at the time of his arrest. The affidavit notes that Jackson was previously convicted of two counts of involuntary manslaughter arising out of his involvement in a shooting resulting in the death of two individuals. Due to these prior felony convictions, Jackson is not permitted to possess a firearm.

The charges contained in the complaint are accusations, and not evidence of guilt. Evidence supporting the charges must eventually be presented to a federal trial jury, whose duty it is to determine guilt or innocence.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.

Project Safe Neighborhoods

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.

text:
High losses in homeowners insurance have resulted in many state-licensed (or admitted) insurers pulling back from high-risk areas. Some homeowners have responded by seeking insurance from surplus lines (or nonadmitted) insurers, which may offer fewer consumer protections or less coverage. This dynamic has resulted in significant increases in surplus lines insurance covering, for example, personal property, which grew 20.2% in the first half of 2026. This growth has caused concerns over the relatively less regulated nature of surplus lines insurance.
Insurance in general is a highly regulated financial product, primarily at the individual state level. Unlike for banking and securities, there is no federal regulator for insurance. States generally require licenses for insurers to operate, and states regulate insurance products as well as insurer solvency and market conduct. While regulation is usually seen as important for consumer protection, it also creates barriers to entry that may reduce the available supply of insurance. Rather than requiring consumers unable to find insurance from a state-licensed insurer to simply go without insurance, states have allowed consumers to purchase insurance from surplus lines insurers as a form of safety valve for the market. Although such insurers may sell any sort of insurance, most such transactions tend to be for rarer and more exceptional risks, such as art and antiques, cyber insurance, and environmental or pollution risks.
Surplus lines insurance regulation differs from other insurance regulation both in substance and in focus. In regulating standard insurance transactions, much of the state's focus is on the insurer itself. States have licensure requirements relating to financial solvency and capital. In cases of insolvency, states have established guaranty funds to pay an insolvent insurer's policyholders. The states often regulate both the content and price of an insurance policy, with many states requiring specific state approval for changes. Surplus lines insurers are allowed to operate without being licensed in the state where they are selling insurance and thus do not follow the state regulations tied to licensure, particularly regulations on insurance policy content and rates. While surplus lines insurers report financial information, only the home states fully regulate for solvency. Surplus lines insurers also do not participate in guaranty funds.
Most surplus lines transactions are handled by insurance brokers. These brokers, in contrast to surplus lines insurers, must be licensed by the states where they operate. Thus, state requirements regarding surplus lines transactions focus on the broker. Surplus lines brokers are required to take various steps that are not required in transactions with admitted insurers. The first step is generally a diligent search of the marketplace establishing that no licensed insurer is available. Typically, this is satisfied by having some number, usually three to five, of licensed insurers decline to offer coverage.
Once establishing eligibility to use surplus lines insurance, the broker approaches various insurers seeking the coverage needed. At this point, while the consumer is outside of the admitted insurance market, the states do establish some standards to protect consumers against insurers who might be unable to pay claims. Some states establish a list of eligible surplus lines insurers, and state-licensed brokers are allowed to transact business only with insurers on that list. For non-U.S. insurers, the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) publishes a quarterly listing of eligible insurers based on financial information filed by these insurers. States also generally require that brokers provide specific disclosures detailing that surplus lines insurance is not subject to the same oversight as insurance bought from state-licensed insurers. Laws that are not tied to insurer licensure, such as those against fraud, continue to apply to surplus lines insurers.
States levy specific premium taxes on insurance to be remitted by state-licensed insurers. In surplus lines transactions, the brokers are required to collect such taxes. The situation becomes somewhat unclear, however, when the consumer, the broker, or the insured property are in different states. Such a multistate situation requires apportioning premium taxes among the different states. In the past, state laws differed significantly on the amount of such taxes and how they should be apportioned.
Varying state requirements for surplus lines insurance led to calls for greater harmonization between the states' laws and, ultimately, to federal intervention to promote uniformity through the Nonadmitted and Reinsurance Reform Act of 2010 (NRRA; Title V, Subtitle B, of P.L. 111-203). This law harmonizes surplus lines regulation and taxation. It vests the home state of the insured with the sole authority to tax a surplus lines transaction and provides for the possibility of an interstate compact to determine how taxes may be distributed; absent such a compact, the home state has the authority to determine distribution. The NRRA also preempts state laws on surplus lines eligibility that conflict with the NAIC model law and implements "streamlined" federal standards allowing a commercial purchaser to access surplus lines.
The surplus lines market has been significantly affected by general market disruptions when prices tend to increase and availability becomes more difficult. Figure 1 shows the surplus lines market compared to the regular market and the increase in total surplus lines premiums over the last 25 years. Notable growth periods include 2002 (61.7% following the 9/11 terrorist attacks), 2006 (16.3% following losses from Hurricane Katrina and other storms), and 2018-2025 (double-digit annual percentage increases following Hurricane Harvey, increasing wildfire and smaller storm losses, and the COVID-19 pandemic).
As noted above, high losses in homeowners insurance have resulted in an increasing number of homeowners seeking insurance from surplus lines insurers, although this insurance may have fewer consumer protections or less coverage. Surplus lines are still a relatively small amount of the overall homeowners insurance market (2.2%), although this percentage has more than doubled since 2015. Figure 2 shows the surplus lines share of the homeowners insurance market and the increase in surplus lines premiums for homeowners insurance.
title: Surplus Lines Insurance: An Introduction

SAGAMIHARA, Japan — Firefighters from U.S. Army Garrison Japan participated in the annual Comprehensive Disaster Preparedness Drill Oct. 25 at a joint-use area here near Sagami General Depot.
The multi-agency event brought diverse organizations together to tackle realistic emergency scenarios following a major earthquake.
During the exercise, teams responded to a simulated collapsed building to rescue two trapped victims. After a rescue dog pinpointed their location, firefighters breached the roof and deployed a ladder crane to safely extract an unconscious individual.
Ichiro Otsuka, a fire truck driver and operator assigned to USAG Japan, highlighted the value of joint operations.
“Practice doesn’t lie,” Otsuka said, emphasizing the continuous reflection and daily communication that prepared the team.
Otsuka praised the dedication of the Sagamihara firefighters, adding, “Their eyes shone with pride in protecting citizens’ lives and property. Working together gave us great motivation and exposed us to new tactical approaches and equipment.”
Acknowledging that room for improvement remains, Otsuka reaffirmed the two groups’ shared commitment to learning from one another and working tirelessly to safeguard the community.
title: USAG Japan trains alongside Sagamihara City partners to ensure community safety

Advance ticket reservations secure guaranteed seats and the best fares
WASHINGTON – As Thanksgiving approaches, Amtrak is encouraging travelers to book early to secure the best fares and guaranteed seats, as tickets are selling quickly. Thanksgiving is Amtrak’s busiest travel season and one of the busiest travel periods nationwide. In 2025, Amtrak broke ridership records during the Thanksgiving holiday with more than 1.2 million customer trips—a nearly 6% increase from 2024. Amtrak predicts another year of record ridership this holiday season and recommends travelers plan their trips early.
“Amtrak is experiencing record demand, a testament to the comfortable and convenient experience of traveling by train,” said Amtrak Interim President Byl Herrmann. “We are honored to help customers reach their holiday destinations safely and comfortably, while offering more departures, amenities and services during a time when they appreciate them most.”
Train travel offers many benefits: no waiting in long airport lines, a quick and easy boarding process, no roadway traffic, and arrival downtown, where connecting travel options are abundant.
To help accommodate the expected surge of customers during Thanksgiving week, Amtrak is expanding capacity by adding cars to select Northeast Regional trains from Nov. 20-30. Two additional Northeast Regional round trips will be added with service between Washington Union Station, New York Penn Station, and cities in between on Nov. 24-25 and Nov. 28-29. With record demand, this additional capacity is expected to fill quickly.
There’s more for customers to love at Amtrak this holiday season. The company continues to introduce additional NextGen Acela trains–providing a premium experience. Fifteen NextGen Acela trains are now in service, more than ever before.
And in the Pacific Northwest, Amtrak Cascades now features Amtrak’s brand new Airo fleet on four daily trips, providing an even more comfortable, connected, and reliable travel experience. Each of these services has enhanced food and beverage offerings, comfortable seating, picturesque views, amenities, and thoughtful touches that make holiday travel by Amtrak more enjoyable.
Purchasing tickets is fast and easy on Amtrak.com, through the Amtrak mobile app, at in-station ticketing kiosks and in-person at staffed stations, or by calling 1-800-USA-RAIL.
title: Amtrak Encourages Travelers to Book Thanksgiving Travel Early Amid Historic Demand

FORT SILL, Okla. — Apache Gate is tentatively scheduled to close Tuesday, Nov. 10, for approximately eight weeks while construction crews relocate warning lights and signal equipment to improve roadway safety.
The closure will affect Soldiers, civilian employees, families, contractors and visitors who regularly use the gate. Installation officials are coordinating alternative access routes and traffic management measures to minimize disruptions while completing the necessary improvements.
The start date and construction timeline remain subject to change as the Directorate of Emergency Services (DES), Directorate of Public Works (DPW), U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and contractors finalize project schedules.
"This project is an essential safety correction," said Ryan Clark, chief of the Physical Security Division for Fort Sill's DES.
According to Clark, warning light and signal poles were installed too close to the roadway, creating a potential collision hazard. Construction crews will remove the affected poles and install an extended overhead mast arm to provide safer clearance for vehicles.
Because the work involves removing heavy steel poles immediately adjacent to the pavement, Apache Gate must remain completely closed to vehicle and pedestrian traffic throughout construction.
"There is no safe way to perform the work under partial lane closures," Clark said.
What drivers need to know
During the closure, passenger vehicles will be redirected to alternative entrances, primarily Key Gate East and Key Gate West on Randolph Road.
All commercial delivery and contractor vehicles must use Key Gate West, Lane 3, for the duration of the project.
DES recommends commuters allow an additional 15 to 20 minutes during morning and afternoon peak travel periods. Access control staffing and operating hours are being evaluated to help accommodate the increased traffic.
Visitor processing requirements will remain unchanged, but visitors without military identification should check official Fort Sill information sources before arriving to determine the appropriate entrance.
Coordinating construction to maintain access
The Apache Gate project is being coordinated with improvements at other installation access points to avoid overlapping closures and maintain traffic flow.
Key Gate West reopened Oct. 28 following repairs to its vehicle barrier system. Work to replace the sliding gate at Scott Gate is also nearing completion, with officials working to ensure alternative entrances are operational before Apache Gate closes.
"By spacing these projects out, we ensure that there is always sufficient gate capacity to support the installation," Clark said.
DES has also reviewed and coordinated alternative routes for fire, medical and law enforcement personnel to maintain emergency response capabilities throughout construction.
Lt. Col. Chafac Mofor, Fort Sill provost marshal, emphasized the importance of completing the safety improvements while maintaining installation security and minimizing inconvenience to the community.
The project supports Fort Sill's ongoing efforts to maintain safe, reliable infrastructure for the Soldiers, civilians, families and community partners who depend on the installation.
Stay informed during construction
DES encourages drivers to plan ahead, follow designated detours and check the My Army Post App (MAPA) for current gate hours, wait times, gate status and detour information.
Updates, including any changes to the anticipated closure dates, will also be available through official Fort Sill communication channels, including the installation website and social media.
Apache Gate is expected to reopen after approximately eight weeks, pending construction progress and final safety inspections.
Fort Sill officials appreciate the community's patience and cooperation as crews complete the improvements to provide safer installation access for years to come.
Download the My Army Post App (MAPA) from your app store.
title: Apache Gate closure tentatively set for Nov. 10 for safety improvements at Fort Sill

David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, and Jarod Forget, Special Agent in Charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration for New England, today announced that DENNY GUZMAN, 34, of Hartford, NELSON TORRES, 50, of Hartford, and DOMINGO HEREDIA-SUAREZ, also known as “Daniel Heredia Suarez,” 57, a citizen of the Dominica Republic, have been charged by indictment with offenses related to the trafficking of fentanyl and cocaine.

As alleged in court documents and statements made in court, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Hartford Task Force identified Guzman, Torres, and Heredia-Suarez as being involved in a drug trafficking ring that was distributing large quantities of narcotics in Connecticut and the surrounding states. Investigators identified numerous suspicious packages that were delivered to Torres’s residence on Madison Street in Hartford and then transported to a location on Homestead Avenue in Hartford that the organization used to store, process, and package narcotics. On August 30, 2026, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service intercepted a parcel containing approximately two kilograms of cocaine that was being mailed to Torres’s residence.

It is further alleged that, on October 9, 2026, investigators observed a package delivery to Torres’s residence and then saw Guzman, Torres, and Heredia-Suarez arrive at the Homestead Avenue location with the package. The three were arrested on that date after a search of the Homestead Avenue location revealed a kilogram brick of fentanyl, narcotics processing materials, and a firearm, and a search of Torres’s residence revealed a handgun. Guzman also possessed a handgun at the time of his arrest.

On October 20, 2026, a grand jury in Hartford returned an indictment charging Guzman, Torres, and Heredia-Suarez with conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl and 500 grams or more of cocaine, and with possession with intent to distribute to distribute 400 grams or more of fentanyl. Each of these charges carries a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of 10 years and a maximum term of imprisonment of life. The indictment also charges Guzman with possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime, an offense that carries a mandatory consecutive sentence of at least five years.

Guzman, Torres, and Heredia-Suarez appeared today before U.S. Magistrate Judge Robert A. Richardson in Hartford and entered pleas of not guilty to the charges in the indictment. Torres and Heredia-Suarez are detained and Guzman is released on a $100,000 bond.

U.S. Attorney Sullivan stressed that an indictment is not evidence of guilt. Charges are only allegations, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

This investigation is being conducted by the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Hartford Task Force with the assistance of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. The DEA Task Force includes personnel from the DEA Hartford Resident Office, the Connecticut State Police, and the Bristol, Hartford, East Hartford, Enfield, Manchester, New Britain, Rocky Hill, Wethersfield, and Windsor Locks Police Departments. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Robert S. Dearington.
title: Three Men Charged with Running Hartford-Based Drug Trafficking Ring

CAMP HUMPHREYS, Republic of Korea — What began as a modest storage closet inside the Warrior Chapel has grown into a vital resource for Soldiers and families stationed overseas. On Oct. 30, 2026, the Warrior Food Pantry celebrated its grand reopening and recognition as a nonprofit organization, marking a new chapter in its mission to support the military community.
Established in November 2022 to help ease the financial and logistical burdens of an overseas assignment, the Warrior Food Pantry has provided food, diapers, and personal hygiene products to more than 880 families and 3,700 individuals.
In the spring of 2024, the USAG Humphreys Directorate of Public Works collaborated with 2nd Infantry Division / ROK-U.S. Combined Division Soldiers to transform a former mailroom into a 1,160-square-foot pantry. Using repurposed building materials like extra floor tiles and leveraging volunteer labor, the team completed the renovation for just over $200.
The pantry’s recognition as a nonprofit organization represents another step toward expanding community partnerships and sustaining its services for military families.
The pantry relies on donations and support from community organizations, 2ID/RUCD Unit Ministry Teams and Camp Humphreys Commissary. During the holiday season, Soldiers and units organize food drives, contributing thousands of nonperishable items to support fellow military families.
"Serving overseas, thousands of miles from home, brings its own set of challenges and problems," Brown said. "We miss birthdays, holidays, and important moments with the people we love. Sometimes life throws things at us that we just weren’t prepared for. That is when we lean on our spouses, our friends, and our neighbors."
Brown emphasized that taking care of service members and their families directly underpins operational readiness across the peninsula.
"In the 2ID/RUCD, we spend a lot of time talking about readiness and our ability to 'Fight Tonight,'" Brown said. "But I’ve always believed that taking care of our people is just as important as preparing them for the fight. Because when Soldiers know someone has their back, when Soldiers know their family is cared for, Soldiers and their families can face just about anything."
Under the direction of Pantry Director Cyndi Grothe, the Warrior Food Pantry operates entirely through community and American Red Cross volunteers. It provides nonperishable food, baby supplies, hygiene products and household essentials at no cost.
Services are available to command-sponsored families, active-duty service members, retirees and Department of Defense civilians stationed in Korea, regardless of rank. Eligible households may visit twice a month, with food quantities based on household size.
Located at Building 1009 on Talon Street, the Warrior Food Pantry is open Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. for services and donation drop-offs, as well as Saturdays from 12:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. for donations only. Community members interested in volunteering, partnering, or donating can contact the pantry team at warriorfoodpantrykorea@gmail.com.
For Brown, the pantry represents something greater than the food and supplies it provides; it represents a military community committed to looking after its own. "It’s not just about putting food on someone’s table. It’s about making sure a Soldier or a family going through a tough time knows they’re not facing it alone," Brown said. "We’re more than Soldiers, spouses, and neighbors. We’re a family. And family takes care of family."
title: Warrior Food Pantry strengthens community support at Camp Humphreys
