text:
The Department of Transportation's (DOT's) Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) develops and issues standards for states' testing and licensing of commercial motor vehicle (CMV) drivers. FMCSA has the authority to establish pilot programs to test changes to commercial driver licensing requirements. FMCSA established the Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot Program (SDAP) on January 14, 2022, to meet requirements in Section 23022 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58). Section 23022 required the Secretary of Transportation to submit a report to Congress in March 2026 to provide a recommendation, based on data collected, on whether the level of safety achieved by the pilot program for CMV drivers under 21 years of age was similar to or greater than the level of safety for CMV drivers aged 21 years or older, as determined by FMCSA. SDAP was the second congressionally directed pilot program for truck drivers under 21 years of age. Since 2014, there has been federal support for programs to train under-21-year-old CMV drivers due to concerns of an aging CMV workforce and employee turnover. As of 2025, workers aged 55 years or older comprised 30% of the U.S. truck transportation workforce.
FMCSA began receiving applications for SDAP first from motor carriers in July 2022, then from apprentices and experienced drivers in November 2022, and concluded the program in November 2025. Although not statutorily required, FMCSA made quarterly program enrollment data publicly available beginning in April 2023. Between November 2022 and June 2025, the program received a total of 80 applications from apprentices who were commercial driver's license (CDL) holders between 18 and 20 years of age. FMCSA approved 95% of applicants to participate in the program. Of the applicants approved, 55% completed the two required probationary periods. The program had 76 apprentice participants making up 2.5% of the 3,000 total allowed apprentice participants per Section 23022 of the IIJA. The program enrolled 62 motor carriers (29% of 211 total applications received), making up 6.2% of the 1,000 total allowed motor carriers expected by DOT. Motor carriers not enrolled either did not meet DOT's qualifications (42% of total applicants) or voluntarily withdrew their application (26% of total applicants). In 2023, DOT required interested motor carriers to meet DOT's qualifications and register their apprenticeship program with the Department of Labor (DOL). In 2024, Congress modified SDAP through provisions in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 (P.L. 118-42). As a result of the changes, DOT could no longer require motor carriers to register their apprenticeship programs with DOL or require them to use inward- or rear-facing cameras to collect safety data.
Following SDAP's conclusion, Congress may consider various policy options regarding the program. Congress could establish a permanent apprenticeship program, initiate a new pilot program, or discontinue SDAP. If Congress is satisfied with the results of SDAP, Congress could establish a permanent apprenticeship program, taking into consideration alignment between DOT and DOL to improve the administrative efficiency of apprenticeships. Alternatively, Congress could direct DOT to initiate a new pilot program based on the findings from related studies and reports. If Congress decides not to authorize a new pilot program, under 21-aged CMV drivers would not be allowed to participate in interstate commerce pursuant to existing regulatory standards. Section 5401 of the Building Unrivaled Infrastructure and Long-term Development for America's 250th Act (Build America 250 Act; H.R. 8870), a surface transportation reauthorization bill introduced and ordered reported in the House of Representatives in May 2026, would extend the apprenticeship pilot program. Some of the issues identified in this report may be addressed in congressional debates concerning the Build America 250 Act (H.R. 8870), through other legislation, or as part of committee oversight.
Congress has long been concerned about the overall adequacy of the U.S. trucking workforce and the recruitment and retention of experienced drivers to maintain that workforce in the face of aging and employee turnover. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, in 2025, workers aged 55 or older represented 30% of the U.S. truck transportation workforce.1 To attract younger drivers to the trucking workforce, Section 23022 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; P.L. 117-58), enacted in 2021, required the Secretary of Transportation to establish a three-year apprenticeship pilot program for commercial drivers. The program was intended to allow apprentices—commercial driver's license (CDL) holders between 18 and 20 years of age—to operate a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) in interstate commerce under the supervision of an experienced driver (see "Experienced Driver Applicants"). The Department of Transportation's (DOT's) Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) established the Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot Program (SDAP) on January 14, 2022, to meet the requirements of the IIJA.2 The program concluded on November 7, 2025.3 SDAP was the second congressionally directed pilot program for truck drivers under the age of 21.4
This report provides a brief overview of SDAP. The report first explains FMCSA's regulatory and administrative role, then presents SDAP enrollment data reported in 2023, 2024, and 2025.5 It also identifies policy options for congressional consideration. Congress might consider these or related issues during debates on surface transportation reauthorization, through other legislation, or as part of committee oversight. Congress included provisions to extend SDAP in the Build America 250 Act (H.R. 8870), a surface transportation reauthorization bill ordered reported in the House of Representatives in May 2026.
FMCSA was established within DOT in 2000 pursuant to the Motor Carrier Safety Improvement Act of 1999 (P.L. 106-159). FMCSA develops and issues standards—known as Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) found at Title 49, Parts 350-399, of the Code of Federal Regulations—for states' testing and licensing of CDL holders. Prior to FMCSA's establishment, the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) promulgated regulations for highway safety. In 1970, FHWA issued Title 49, Section 391.11(b)(1), of the Code of Federal Regulations requiring that CMV operators engaged in interstate commerce be at least 21 years of age, among other qualifications.
FHWA oversight of the CDL licensing process came later. In the Commercial Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1986 (Title XII of P.L. 99-570), Congress required DOT to issue regulations establishing minimum uniform standards for states' issuance of CDLs and commercial learner's permits (CLPs). States are not allowed to issue an unrestricted CDL to anyone who does not meet the driver qualifications stated in Title 49, Section 391.11, of the Code of Federal Regulations. Additionally, the act authorized the Secretary of Transportation to grant waivers and exemptions from the FMCSRs and to conduct pilot programs "to evaluate alternatives to regulations relating to, or innovative approaches to, motor carrier, commercial motor vehicle, and driver safety."6
The Under 21 Military CDL Pilot Program, the first congressionally directed pilot program for younger CMV drivers, was enacted in 2015 in Section 5404 of the Fixing America's Surface Transportation Act (FAST Act; P.L. 114-94). The FAST Act directed DOT to develop a pilot program to allow a limited number of individuals between 18 and 20 years of age to operate CMVs in interstate commerce if they received heavy-vehicle driver training while serving in the military. From 2019 to 2022, FMCSA carried out this FAST Act pilot program, which also allowed individuals receiving military-based heavy vehicle driver training to be hired by a participating motor carrier for the pilot program.7
SDAP is the second congressionally directed pilot program for CMV drivers under the age of 21.8 In contrast to the first pilot program, authorized by the FAST Act, drivers participating in SDAP must hold only an intrastate CDL to be eligible for the program. Normally, an individual between 18 and 20 years of age is issued a CDL with a "K" restriction for intrastate-only use in accordance with Title 49, Section 383.153(a)(10)(vii), of the Code of Federal Regulations. Drivers under 21 years of age cannot operate a CMV in interstate commerce without an exemption from the K license restriction. Under Section 23022 of the IIJA, Congress directs FMCSA to provide exemptions from the K license restriction through a formal pilot program process for apprentice participants aged 18-20 years. SDAP met this requirement.
Following the conclusion of SDAP on November 7, 2025, some interest groups have discussed the potential continuation of SDAP.9 On November 14, 2026, the American Trucking Associations (ATA) submitted a petition to FMCSA to extend SDAP for five years for previous apprenticeship participants. FMCSA requested comments on ATA's petition between January 28, 2026, and February 27, 2026. Several organizations, including the Commercial Vehicle Training Association, the Truckload Carriers Association, and the Next Generation in Trucking Association, expressed support for the petition as a trucking workforce development measure. The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association (OOIDA), the Truck Safety Coalition, Citizens for Reliable and Safe Highways, Parents Against Tired Truckers, and Advocates for Highway and Auto Safety, among others, opposed the petition, suggesting that the young age and inexperience of drivers in the program pose a safety risk. In its comments, OOIDA asserted that the program did not address trucking workforce concerns of driver recruitment and retention.
For motor carriers, SDAP required the completion of four tasks as part of the application process: (1) submit an application demonstrating achievement of eight safety qualifications; (2) commit to submitting monthly data on apprentices as required by Section 23022 of the IIJA; (3) register their apprenticeship program with the Department of Labor (DOL); and (4) provide their program's DOL-registered apprenticeship number to DOT.10 (See "Motor Carrier Applicants.")
On March 14, 2024, Congress enacted provisions in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 (P.L. 118-42), changing the 2023 SDAP program requirements enforced by DOT. Section 422 of the act states that "none of the funds made available by this or any other Act may be used to require the use of inward facing cameras or require a motor carrier to register an apprenticeship program with the Department of Labor as a condition for participation in the Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot Program." On May 14, 2024, FMCSA published a notice of revision to the pilot program in the Federal Register that revised motor carrier participation requirements to reflect these provisions.11 Although motor carriers were no longer required to register their apprenticeship program with DOL, they were still required to submit an application addressing the safety qualification criteria and commit to monthly data reporting.12
FMCSA made quarterly reports on SDAP publicly available beginning in April 2023.13 FMCSA began collecting motor carrier applications on July 26, 2022, and experienced driver and apprentice applications in November 2022. Applications collected by FMCSA in 2022 appear to have been reported in first quarter of 2023 data. FMCSA presented quarterly data in four categories: Motor Carriers, Experienced Drivers, Apprentice Drivers, and Apprentice Driver Progress.
The number of SDAP applications declined over the years. In 2023, the program received the most applications: 229 applications for the three roles (112 motor carriers, 81 experienced drivers, and 36 apprentice drivers). In 2024, 184 applications were received (87 motor carriers, 65 experienced drivers, and 32 apprentice drivers). FMCSA reported at the end of the second quarter of 2025 that 31 applications were received in 2025 (12 motor carriers, 7 experienced drivers, and 12 apprentice drivers). By the conclusion of the program, enrollment numbers totaled 2.5% (76 apprentices) of the maximum number of apprentice drivers allowed under the law (3,000) and 6.2% (62 motor carriers) of motor carriers allowed (1,000). Although there was a decline in the number of reported applications between 2023 and 2024, there was an increase in enrollment for the program from 2023 to 2024 (+60%). Overall reported program enrollment stayed the same between 2024 and 2025. More detailed annual data from these reports are presented in the following sections.
Pursuant to Title 49, Section 13102, and Title 49, Section 31134, of the U.S. Code, a motor carrier is an employer or person registered with DOT that provides "motor vehicle transportation for compensation." FMCSA reported receipt of 211 total SDAP applications from motor carriers between 2022 and 2025. FMCSA reported 112 applications in 2023 (53% of the total), with 84 of these applications (40% of the total) received in the first quarter of 2023. Applications dropped to 87 in 2024 and to 12 in the first half of 2025. Of the 112 applications FMCSA reported receiving in 2023, it evaluated 108 and did not evaluate 4. Table 1 provides data on motor carrier applications and application determinations reported by FMCSA from 2023 to 2025. FMCSA approved 62 (29%) of the total applications received. FMCSA did not approve of 88 (42%) motor carrier applicants because they did not meet FMCSA's safety qualification criteria. Of all motor carrier applicants, FMCSA reported that 55 (26%) voluntarily withdrew their applications by 2025.14 The remaining 6 carriers (3%) were removed from the program because of defunct operating authority.
Source: CRS based on Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), "Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot (SDAP) Program Quarterly Updates," updated August 27, 2025, https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/registration/commercial-drivers-license/sdap/safe-driver-apprenticeship-pilot-sdap-program.
Notes: FMCSA maintains a public list of approved motor carriers organized by state.15
a. FMCSA began collecting applications for motor carriers in July 2022. In April 2023, FMCSA reported applications collected in 2022 with Q1 CY2023 applications.
b. In 2025, FMCSA reported 55 applications as "voluntarily withdrawn," which include the 15 applications that were voluntarily withdrawn in 2024 and 2025 and applications that were prequalified (36) and that were not evaluated (4) by FMCSA in 2023.
c. In 2023, prequalification status was issued to motor carriers that had met qualifications for program participation in their application but had not provided their Department of Labor Registered Apprenticeship number to FMCSA for SDAP participation approval. A notice at 89 Federal Register 42054 removed this requirement for motor carrier applicants. In 2024 and 2025, FMCSA did not report prequalified applications.
d. In 2023, FMCSA reported receipt of 112 applications and evaluated 108 applications, leaving 4 applications not evaluated.
Of the 55 motor carriers that were reported to withdraw their application from the program, 96% withdrew their application by the end of 2024.16 Until 2024, motor carriers were required to meet FMCSA's safety qualification criteria and register their apprenticeship under DOL.
SDAP defined an experienced driver as an individual older than 26 years of age with a minimum of five years of experience driving a CMV in interstate commerce.17 Experienced drivers were required to apply through an approved motor carrier to participate.18 An apprentice driver was required to be accompanied by an experienced driver sitting in the passenger seat of the CMV during the apprentice's probationary periods.19 Experienced drivers were able to serve for a maximum of two years. Throughout the entirety of the service period, experienced drivers needed to hold a valid CDL, have no preventable accidents reported to DOT, and have no pointed moving violations.20
Table 2 provides data on experienced driver applications for SDAP. Of the 153 applications reported between 2023 and 2025, 141 were approved (92%) and one was disapproved (<1%). Eleven experienced drivers were disenrolled from the program before their service period ended: eight voluntarily withdrew (5%), two were removed from the carrier (>1%), and one was removed for safety reasons (<1%).21
Source: CRS based on Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, "SDAP Program Quarterly Updates," updated August 27, 2025, https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/registration/commercial-drivers-license/sdap/safe-driver-apprenticeship-pilot-sdap-program.
Notes:
a. FMCSA began collecting applications for experienced drivers in July 2022. In April 2023, FMCSA reported applications collected in 2022 with Q1 CY2023, applications.
Apprentice drivers under SDAP were individuals aged 18-20 years who held a CDL.22 Apprentice drivers were required to complete two probationary periods: a 120-hour period, which included at least 80 hours of driving time, followed by a 280-hour period, which included at least 160 hours of driving time. Both probationary periods had performance benchmarks against which an apprentice's competency was measured.23 Interested eligible drivers applied directly to an approved motor carrier for an SDAP apprenticeship position and awaited approval by FMCSA for acceptance to SDAP.24
FMCSA received a total of 80 apprentice driver applications from the end of 2022 through the middle of 2025. FMCSA approved 76 applications (or 95% of all applications received). Table 3 provides data reported by FMCSA on apprentice driver applications and determinations.
a. FMCSA began collecting applications for apprentice drivers in November 2022. In April 2023, FMCSA reported applications collected in 2022 with Q1 CY2023 applications.
b. One apprentice driver was removed from the program for safety reasons in Q4 CY2023.
Table 4 provides the reported progress through probation and completion for apprentice drivers in SDAP by the end of each year. As reported at the end of 2023, of the 36 approved applicants that year, 14 apprentices were in the process of completing both of their probationary periods (39%), 13 apprentices had completed both probationary periods (36%), and 9 apprentices did not complete both probationary periods (25%). As reported at the end of 2024, of the 66 total approved applicants, 36 apprentices had completed both probationary periods (55%), 20 did not complete both probationary periods (30%), and 10 were in the process of completing their probationary periods (15%). In 2024, the number of program participants who did not complete their probationary periods increased 120% compared with 2023. By the end of the second quarter of 2025, of the program total of 76 approved applicants, 42 apprentices had completed both probationary periods (55%), 30 had not completed both probationary periods (40%), and 4 were in the process of completing their probationary periods (5%).
Post-probationary participation status (Table 5) and the status of apprentices who did not complete both probationary periods (Table 6) are discussed below.25
a. FMCSA began collecting applications for apprentices in November 2022. In April 2023, FMCSA reported applications collected in 2022 with Q1 CY2023 applications.
b. See Table 5 for more information on apprentice drivers who completed probation.
c. See Table 6 for more information on apprentice drivers who did not complete probation because of aging out of the program, voluntarily withdrawing from the program, or being removed from their motor carrier.
In 2024, FMCSA began recording participants who aged out, voluntarily left the program, were removed from the carrier, or were removed from the program based on whether they completed both probationary periods (Table 5 and Table 6). By 2025, a total of 42 apprentice drivers had completed both probationary periods. Within this group, many apprentice drivers either remained active in the program (45%) or aged out (33%).26 In addition, 17% of apprentice drivers completed both probationary periods and voluntarily withdrew from the program.
b. Apprentices who became 21 years old while participating in the program aged out of the program.
At the end of 2023, of the 13 apprentice drivers who completed both probationary periods, 100% remained active in the program following the completion of both probationary periods. Of all years, FMCSA reported that 2024 had the most apprentice drivers who completed both probationary periods (23) and the most apprentice drivers who aged out of the program (13). In the first half of 2025, 4 of 6 apprentices who completed both probationary periods voluntarily withdrew from the program.
For each year of the program as reported by FMCSA, nearly the same number of apprentices did not complete both probationary periods (see Table 6). In 2023 and 2024, more than half of the apprentices who did not complete both probationary periods voluntarily withdrew from the program. In 2024, the largest share of apprentices who did not complete both probationary periods were removed from their carrier (45%). By 2025, there were 30 total apprentice drivers who did not complete both probationary periods. The largest share voluntarily withdrew from the program before they could complete both probationary periods (53%).
At the conclusion of the pilot program, the Secretary of Transportation is statutorily required in Section 23022(g) of the IIJA to submit a report within 120 days, addressing six items:
The program concluded on November 7, 2025. Therefore, under the provisions of the IIJA, the report was due to Congress on March 7, 2026. As of September 2026, FMCSA had not published this report. The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance and OOIDA expressed that their organizations' support of the ATA's November 2025 petition to extend SDAP for five years for previous apprenticeship participants was contingent on FMCSA's submission of a report to Congress required by Section 23022 of the IIJA that would address safety implications of the program.
DOT is to use the program participant data to make recommendations about the level of safety achieved by the pilot program compared with normal licensing conditions. In 2024, FMCSA expected to collect enough information to assess whether the conditions of SDAP promoted safe driving practices.28 DOT's assessment of safety based on SDAP participation data might not be generalizable due to the relatively small number of apprentice participants.29
This report discusses three possible policy options if Congress were to consider the status of SDAP; additional options may exist. Congress could establish a permanent apprenticeship program by statute, initiate a new pilot program, or maintain the status quo with SDAP discontinued.
If Congress is satisfied with the results of SDAP, it could create a similar permanent apprenticeship program. This could involve legislation directing DOT to promulgate regulations to provide exemptions from K license restrictions to 18-20-year-old CDL holders who participate and complete an approved apprenticeship program. Program requirements could be based on those in Section 23022 of the IIJA and the SDAP program requirements. In considering such a program, Congress might be interested in the federal administration required to carry it out. Were such a permanent program established, Congress could direct DOT to solely regulate the apprenticeship program approval process. However, because DOL regulates registered apprenticeship programs through Title 29, Section 29, of the Code of Federal Regulations, there might be potential for duplication of federal efforts between DOT and DOL. Alternatively, Congress could choose to require that motor carriers receive joint approval from DOT and DOL to carry out a registered apprenticeship program. In the 119th Congress, the DRIVE-SAFE Act (H.R. 5563) proposes to establish an apprenticeship program that would retain provisions from Section 23022 of the IIJA.
Congress could pursue a new or separate apprenticeship pilot program for CLP holders between the ages of 18 and 20. Organizations have expressed interest in offering apprenticeship opportunities for pursuers of CDLs in addition to early career CDL holders. On February 23, 2023, FMCSA announced that Pitt Ohio Express, LLC, filed an application for an exemption from the CDL requirements for SDAP participants under 21 years of age stating that the exemption would increase SDAP apprentice driver participation.30 On May 9, 2024, FMCSA announced its denial of the exemption application from Pitt Ohio Express, LLC, due to insufficient information available to determine potential safety implications.31
To provide earlier training opportunities to pursuers of a career in truck operation, Congress could direct DOT to initiate a pilot program, for example, that would offer exemptions from the entry-level driver training requirements (49 C.F.R. Part 380 Subpart F) for CLP holders under 21 years of age who complete the apprenticeship pilot program. Congress also could, for example, initiate a new pilot program that would replicate SDAP and would similarly serve as a pilot program for drivers under 21 years of age to participate in interstate commerce. In the 119th Congress, Section 5401 of the Build America 250 Act (H.R. 8870), a surface transportation reauthorization bill introduced and ordered reported in May 2026 in the House of Representatives, would extend SDAP for former apprentice participants of SDAP.
Congress could choose not to authorize a new apprenticeship program under DOT following SDAP's conclusion. If Congress chooses not to authorize a new apprenticeship program, the statutes and regulations that predate SDAP would remain, and states could continue issuing CDLs with K restrictions to individuals who are under 21 years of age. CDL holders with a K restriction because of age would follow their state's process to remove the restriction upon reaching 21 years of age if the driver pursues interstate commerce.
If Congress wishes to maintain the status quo, registered apprenticeship programs may exist as a legacy of SDAP. In 2023, at least 34 motor carriers had registered programs with DOL in accordance with Title 29, Section 29, of the Code of Federal Regulations.32 Congress may wish to ensure that any registered apprenticeship programs established as part of SDAP also are deactivated by directing DOL to terminate those programs. As an alternative to terminating the registered apprenticeship programs, Congress may direct DOL, in consultation with DOT, to verify that such programs can operate in compliance with federal CDL laws after SDAP's termination.
title: Safe Driver Apprenticeship Pilot Program: In Brief

Media Note

Office of the Spokesman

November 3, 2026

The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America and the Republic of Portugal on the occasion of the 53rd meeting of the U.S.-Portugal Standing Bilateral Commission. Begin Text: The Governments of the United States of America and the Portuguese Republic convened the 53rd meeting of the Portugal-United States Standing Bilateral Commission (SBC). The dialogue focused on the following priorities:

Defense and Security Cooperation: The delegations reaffirmed NATO’s central role in Euro-Atlantic security and their shared commitment to allied defense investment in line with commitments made at the 2025 NATO Summit in The Hague. Recognizing the strong bilateral defense relationship and the successful collaboration on defense equipment programmes, both sides welcome the continued expansion of cooperation between their respective armed forces. They highlighted the ongoing implementation of the State Partnership Program between Portugal and the Illinois National Guard, including activities already underway and further engagements planned to strengthen interoperability, readiness, and the exchange of expertise.

Cooperation in the Azores/Lajes: Both sides praised the growing U.S. engagement with the Autonomous Region of the Azores. The delegations committed to expanding economic opportunity and people-to-people ties that benefit Azorean communities. The delegations acknowledged the U.S. Air Force’s efforts in environmental remediation.

Economic security/CEO Forum: The delegations reaffirmed their strong commitment to reinforcing economic ties between Portugal and the United States. Building on the 52nd SBC meeting commitments and the October 8 meeting between Secretary Rubio and Foreign Minister Rangel in Lisbon, the two governments confirmed the inaugural CEO Forum Plenary Meeting to be held on November 10, 2026, in Lisbon. With this initiative, both sides aim to identify new opportunities for trade and investment, while facilitating job creation and promoting economic growth and security, to the benefit of both the United States and Portugal.

The United States congratulated Portugal on its election to the UN Security Council for the 2027-2028 term. Both delegations agreed to cooperate within the Council to address the pressing topics of the global agenda.

The delegations reaffirmed their sustained interest in continuing and deepening the bilateral strategic partnership.

The 54th SBC will meet in Lisbon, in 2027. End Text.

BOSTON – Two men have been indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston for allegedly conspiring to distribute cocaine.

Eduardo Gomez-Santana, 50, of Providence, R.I. and Isaac Marrero, 33, of Middleboro, Mass. were indicted on one count each of conspiracy to distribute 500 grams or more of cocaine and distribution of 500 grams or more of cocaine. Both defendants were arrested and charged in September 2026. Gomez-Santana is currently detained pending trial and Marrero was released on conditions.

According to the charging documents, in August 2026, a cooperating witness allegedly met with Gomez-Santana outside a restaurant in Pawtucket, R.I. and purchased approximately 250 grams of cocaine. Ahead of that sale, it is alleged that Gomez-Santana was seen meeting with a black Mercedes registered to Marrero.

A few weeks later, the cooperating witness allegedly arranged to meet with Gomez-Santana again, this time to buy approximately 1.5 kilograms of cocaine. On Sept. 29, 2026, Gomez-Santana allegedly met the cooperating witness in the parking lot of a shopping plaza in Taunton, Mass., before directing the cooperating witness to a gas station in Berkley, Mass. There, Gomez-Santana allegedly met with Marrero, who handed Gomez-Santana a bag containing approximately 1.5 kilograms of cocaine. It is alleged that Gomez-Santana then provided the cocaine to the cooperating witness in exchange for cash.

The charges of conspiracy to distribute and distribution of 500 grams or more of cocaine each provide for a sentence of no less than five years and up to 40 years in prison, at least four years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $5 million. Due to a prior conviction for conspiracy to distribute drugs (for which he was sentenced to 90 months), Gomez-Santana faces an enhanced maximum penalty of penalty of life, with a mandatory sentence of at least 10 years in prison, at least eight years and up to a lifetime of supervised release and a fine of up to $8 million. Sentences are imposed by a federal district court judge based upon the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and statutes which govern the determination of a sentence in a criminal case.

United States Attorney Leah B. Foley and Thomas Greco, Special Agent in Charge of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives made the announcement. Valuable assistance was provided by the Massachusetts State Police and the Pawtucket (R.I.) and Bridgewater (Mass.) Police Departments. Assistant U.S. Attorney John J. Reynolds III of the Organized Crime & Gang Unit is prosecuting the cases.

The details contained in the charging documents are allegations. The defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.
title: Two Men Indicted for Drug Conspiracy and Distribution

Defense and Aerospace Contractors ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace Agree to Pay $13M to Resolve Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations
Defense and aerospace companies ILC Dover LP and ILC Astrospace LLC, of Frederica, Delaware, have agreed to pay $13 million to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by failing to comply with cybersecurity requirements in their contracts with the Department of the Army, the Missile Defense Agency, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
“To protect sensitive information from cyber threats, defense and aerospace contractors must comply with the cybersecurity requirements in their federal contracts and subcontracts,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. “We will continue our efforts to hold accountable government contractors and subcontractors that fail to meet their cybersecurity commitments.”
Today’s settlement resolves allegations that from January 2018 to October 2024, ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace (collectively, ILC) submitted false or fraudulent claims for payment on contracts with the Army, Missile Defense Agency, and NASA, and that those claims were false or fraudulent because ILC knew it had not complied with those contracts’ cybersecurity requirements. The settlement resolves allegations that:
- From February 2023 to October 2024, ILC allegedly used a third-party company to store controlled unclassified information in the cloud without requiring and ensuring that the third party met security requirements equivalent to the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) Moderate baseline and complied with Department of Defense (DoD) requirements for cyber incident reporting, malicious software, media preservation and protection, access to additional information and equipment necessary for forensic analysis, and cyber incident damage assessment.
- From January 2018 to March 2022, and from September 2022 to October 2024, ILC allegedly did not develop, document, and periodically update a system security plan for each of its covered information systems, as required by DoD and NASA contracts, describing system boundaries, system environments of operation, how security requirements are implemented, and the relationships with or connections to other systems.
- From January 2018 to October 2024, ILC allegedly had not fully implemented all cybersecurity controls in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publications (SP) 800-171 and 800-53, including controls that, if not implemented, could lead to significant exploitation of the network or exfiltration of controlled defense information and controls that, if not implemented, could have a specific and confined effect on the security of the network and its data.
- From January 2018 to May 2019, and from January 2022 to September 2024, ILC allegedly had not developed and implemented plans of action and milestones designed to correct deficiencies and reduce or eliminate vulnerabilities in ILC’s systems.
- From November 2020 to October 2024, ILC Astrospace allegedly had not submitted to DoD any current assessment of its implementation of NIST SP 800-171 cybersecurity controls, and ILC Dover allegedly had not submitted an assessment that was current, based on the entity’s review of a system security plan associated with covered contractor information systems, and conducted in accordance with the NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment Methodology.
“The best response to cyberattacks is to prevent them from happening in the first place,” said U.S. Attorney Benjamin L. Wallace for the District of Delaware. “The obligations that ILC violated exist to prevent bad actors from taking advantage of the United States’ technical innovation. My office is committed to ensuring that cybersecurity requirements in contracts are honored and that America’s leadership in aerospace is protected.”
“Cybersecurity lapses place critical defense information at risk,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jessica Herrington of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General, Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), Northeast Field Office. “DCIS remains committed to ensuring that companies entrusted with sensitive data fully meet the security obligations outlined in their federal contracts. This settlement reflects our continued efforts to safeguard the Department of Defense’s information and hold contractors accountable when they fail to uphold required cybersecurity standards.”
“This case should send a clear message to anyone conducting business with the Department of the Army: If you engage in fraudulent or illegal activity, the Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division (CID) will vigorously pursue those responsible and work tirelessly to bring them to justice,” said Special Agent in Charge Joel Kirch, of Army CID’s Northeast Field Office.
“Strict compliance with federal cybersecurity standards is non-negotiable for any company doing business with NASA,” said Robert Steinau, Assistant Inspector General for Investigations at the NASA Office of Inspector General. “Those who jeopardize America’s space program by ignoring government protocols will incur steep financial penalties. We are grateful to whistleblowers who do right by reporting these wrongs.”
The settlement resolves a lawsuit filed under the whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act, which permit private parties to sue on behalf of the government when they believe that a defendant has submitted false claims for government funds and receive a share of any recovery. The settlement in this case provides for the whistleblower, Philip Root, ILC’s former Director of Cybersecurity, to receive a $2.35 million share of the settlement amount. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel. Root v. ILC Dover LP, et al., No. 25-cv-70 (D. Del.).
This year the Administration launched the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division to enhance the Administration’s war on fraud, waste, and abuse in federal programs. When unscrupulous actors exploit these programs for their own financial gain, they defraud the government, harm the people these programs are designed to aid and protect, and undermine American businesses that play by the rules. The Civil Division’s FCA enforcement plays a critical role in combatting such fraudulent schemes, recovering billions of dollars for the American taxpayers, and holding wrongdoers accountable. FCA matters will continue to be on the forefront of the battle against fraud, and the Civil Division’s FCA work will support and advance the mission of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud and the National Fraud Enforcement Division.
The settlement announced today was the result of a coordinated effort between the Civil Division’s Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Delaware, with assistance from NASA OIG, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, Army CID’s Northeast Field Office, the Navy Criminal Investigative Service, the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, and the General Services Administration Office of Inspector General.
The matter was handled by Assistant Director Christopher Terranova in the Civil Division’s Commercial Litigation Branch (Fraud Section) and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Dylan Steinberg and Jacob Laksin for the District of Delaware.
The claims resolved by the settlement are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability.
title: Defense and Aerospace Contractors ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace Agree to Pay $13M to Resolve Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations

Coast Guard detains MSC Poesia in Port of Miami
Southeast Public Affairs - Southeastpublicaffairs@gmail.com
MIAMI — A U.S. Coast Guard Miami Port State Control team detained MSC Poesia on Sunday after identifying deficiencies during an inspection at the Port of Miami.
“The Coast Guard cannot currently comment on the specifics of an ongoing Port State Control Examination, but we have identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel that we are addressing with MSC,”  said Capt. Frank Florio, Commander, U.S. Coast Guard Sector Miami.
The vessel remains detained at the Port of Miami until the deficiencies are corrected and it is cleared for departure.
Through its Port State Control program, the Coast Guard inspects foreign-flagged commercial vessels visiting U.S. ports to verify compliance with applicable safety, security, and environmental requirements. When substantial noncompliance is identified, the Coast Guard may detain a vessel until the deficiencies that prevent its departure are corrected.
- USCG -

Baltimore, Maryland – A Maryland man pled guilty in federal court to tax and COVID-related fraud charges. This prosecution is part of the Trump Administration’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud.

Dekwii Woah-Tee, 43, of Rosedale, pled guilty to conspiracy to submit false, fictitious, and fraudulent claims to the Internal Revenue Service; wire-fraud conspiracy in connection with Unemployment Insurance (UI) claims for benefits; and aggravated identity theft stemming from a scheme to fraudulently obtain UI benefits during the COVID-19 Pandemic.

Kelly O. Hayes, U.S. Attorney for the District of Maryland, announced the guilty plea with Executive Special Agent in Charge Kareem Carter, Internal Revenue Service – Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI), Washington D.C. Field Office; Inspector General Anthony P. D’Esposito, U.S. Department of Labor - Office of Inspector General (DOL-OIG); and Joseph V. Cuffari Ph.D., Inspector General, Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS-OIG).

According to the plea agreement, beginning in January 2018, and continuing until December 2024, Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirators conspired to defraud the United States and the Department of the Treasury by filing fraudulent Form 1040s seeking tax refunds from the IRS through false claims. The co-conspirators identified and recruited individuals to become customers of their tax-return business and obtained tax documentation and personal identifiable information from those individuals seeking tax-return preparation assistance.

Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirators used the information obtained from those individuals to prepare tax filings with the IRS. Then he and his co-conspirators filed or caused the filing of false tax returns, which contained fabricated information regarding the taxpayer’s dependents, income, education expenses, and eligibility for the Earned Income Tax Credit.

The co-conspirators caused the IRS to deposit funds into bank accounts or to deliver treasury checks to addresses that they controlled. As a result, the co-conspirators obtained tax refunds they were not entitled to in connection with submitting tax returns in which they illegally sought at least $3.5 million in refunds.

Dekwii Woah-Tee pleaded guilty to wire fraud, wire fraud conspiracy, and aggravated identity theft arising out of his scheme to unlawfully obtain UI benefits during the COVID-19 Pandemic. Dekwii Woah-Tee and his co-conspirator Daiwor Woah-Tee, who pled guilty to charges connected to his role in the conspiracy in June 2026, submitted UI applications to the Maryland Department of Labor on behalf of victims, often without the victim’s knowledge, falsely stating that the applicant was entitled to UI benefits. As a result, the co-conspirators caused the Maryland Department of Labor to deposit UI benefits into bank accounts that they controlled, allowing them to withdraw the funds for their own personal use. The co-conspirators received UI benefits in excess of $550,000.

As part of the plea, Dekwii Woah-Tee agreed to restitution to the Internal Revenue Service of $3.5 million and restitution to the Maryland Department of Labor of at least $550,000. Dekwii Woah-Tee also agreed to a forfeiture of approximately $250,000.

If convicted, Dekwii Woah-Tee faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison for conspiracy to submit false, fictitious, and fraudulent claims to the Internal Revenue Service. He is also facing 20 years for wire-fraud conspiracy in connection with Unemployment Insurance claims for benefits and a mandatory two years for aggravated identity theft.

Actual sentences for federal crimes are typically less than the maximum penalties. A federal district court judge determines sentencing after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The District of Maryland Strike Force is one of five strike forces established throughout the United States by the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate and prosecute COVID-19 fraud, including fraud relating to the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (“CARES”) Act. The CARES Act was designed to provide emergency financial assistance to Americans suffering the economic effects caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. The strike forces focus on large-scale, multi-state pandemic relief fraud perpetrated by criminal organizations and transnational actors. The strike forces are interagency law enforcement efforts, using prosecutor-led and data analyst-driven teams designed to identify and bring to justice those who stole pandemic relief funds.

For more information on the Department’s response to the pandemic, please visit justice.gov/coronavirus . Anyone with information about allegations of attempted fraud involving COVID-19 can report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud (NCDF) Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form .

U.S. Attorney Hayes commended the IRS-CI, DOL-OIG, and DHS-OIG for their work in the investigation. Ms. Hayes also thanked Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jared W. Murphy and Matthew P. Phelps who are prosecuting this federal case.

For more information about the Maryland U.S. Attorney’s Office, its priorities, and resources available to report fraud, visit justice.gov/usao-md and justice.gov/usao-md/report-fraud .

title: Maryland Man Pleads Guilty to Role in Tax and COVID-Fraud Conspiracy

DEA-Led HSTF Investigation Results in Historic New Mexico Fentanyl Seizure, Arrest of State Employee
ALBUQUERQUE - Angel Ramirez, from Albuquerque, New Mexico, faces federal drug trafficking and firearm offenses following her arrest during a DEA-led Homeland Security Task Force investigation.
"During this operation, DEA agents working alongside our Homeland Security Task Force partners seized more than 40 kilograms of fentanyl powder, representing over 3 million potentially deadly doses destined for our communities," said DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda. "This is the largest single seizure of fentanyl powder in DEA New Mexico's history and a significant step towards saving American lives.”
On October 29, 2026, agents and officers executed a federal search at Ramirez’s residence where they located multiple duffel bags containing large quantities of narcotics that field tested positive for fentanyl and heroin, bulk U.S. currency, and numerous firearms.
In total, agents and officers recovered approximately 43.75 kilograms of fentanyl powder, 90,000 fake pills containing fentanyl, 4.4 kilograms of heroin, and an additional 1,036 grams of fentanyl, which was in a separate container within the home. Agents and officers also recovered 29 firearms and assorted ammunition.
According to court documents, Ramirez was employed as a paralegal with the State of New Mexico’s Department of Justice, a position of public trust, at the time of her arrest. It is alleged that Ramirez leveraged her government employment, clean criminal history, and internal access to the justice system to create a veneer of legitimacy while her residence operated as a distribution hub for narcotics, drug proceeds, and firearms.
“More than 40 kilograms of fentanyl powder in a single Albuquerque home tells us just how serious the drug trafficking problem has become in New Mexico,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison. “This is a tremendous accomplishment by the agents who got these drugs off our streets, but it is no cause for celebration. With fentanyl overdose deaths on the rise in New Mexico, we have a lot more work to do. We will continue targeting the organizations bringing these drugs into our state and aggressively prosecuting those responsible.”
Ramirez is charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl and using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime. She will remain in custody pending trial. If convicted, Ramirez faces at least 15 years and up to life in prison.
First Assistant U.S Attorney Ryan Ellison and DEA El Paso Division Special Agent in Charge Robert “Eric” Castañeda made the announcement on behalf of the HSTF. U.S. Attorneys Mark Probasco, Timothy Piatt, and Oliver Stephanez are prosecuting the case.
The Sandoval County Sheriff’s Office, Bernalillo County Sheriff’s Office, Rio Rancho Police Department and Pueblo of Pojoaque Tribal Police Department provided invaluable assistance in this arrest.
This arrest is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States.

text:
Text of Letter (PDF)
Washington, D.C. — Representative Becca Balint (VT-AL), a member of the House Subcommittee on the Administrative State, Regulatory Reform, and Antitrust and U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) demanded answers from McDonald’s President and CEO Chris Kempczinski about how the company generates AI-driven pricing recommendations, whether McDonald’s pressures franchisees to follow them, and how the company assesses the technology’s potential harm to consumers and competition. The letter came after reports that the company is using artificial intelligence (AI) to determine the “optimal price” for individual menu items at each of its locations and pushing franchisees to adopt these AI-based prices.
“We are concerned that McDonald’s may be using AI to squeeze consumers into paying higher prices, and that its AI pricing tools may facilitate collusion between franchisees who should be operating as competitors,” wrote the lawmakers. 
U.S. Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Jesús “Chuy” García (D-Ill.), and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.) also signed the letter.
According to recent reports, McDonald’s has developed an AI-based pricing tool that it may be using to recommend specific prices for each individual store, building off the massive trove of consumer data that Amazon has collected through its loyalty program and mobile app. For example, two McDonald’s-operated restaurants just two miles apart in Fresno, California reportedly charged prices that differed by as much as 21 percent for the same menu items. The lawmakers raised particular concerns about McDonald’s use of AI-based pricing at a time when food prices are rising nationwide and particularly at McDonald’s. One report found that certain McDonald’s menu prices doubled between 2014 and 2024, rising more than three times as fast as overall inflation and driving away customers who previously relied on McDonald’s for an affordable meal.
“We are concerned that McDonald’s is using its extensive consumer data and algorithmic pricing tools to unfairly raise prices on consumers who are already struggling with high food and dining costs,” wrote the lawmakers.
The lawmakers also questioned McDonald’s for reportedly putting pressure on franchisees to adopt its pricing recommendations, including through new business standards and potential consequences for franchise renewals. They warned that encouraging competing franchisees to rely on a shared pricing tool informed by nonpublic data could undermine independent pricing decisions and raise antitrust concerns.
“While McDonald’s asserts that using data and analytics to inform pricing is a standard business practice, pressuring competing franchisees to use a shared AI pricing tool built on nonpublic data is not a standard business practice, but rather a potential antitrust issue,” continued the lawmakers.
The lawmakers requested answers by November 16, 2026, on the data and algorithms used to generate pricing recommendations, the extent to which franchisees adopt those recommendations, the pressure McDonald’s places on franchisees to comply, and the company’s assessment of potential antitrust risks. 
###
title: Balint, Warren, Colleagues Demand Answers from McDonald’s on Whether AI Pricing Tools are Raising Prices and Facilitating Collusion

U.S. Marshals Task Forces Arrest Massachusetts Fugitive Wanted for Assault to Murder
For immediate release
Dennis Matulewicz, Acting U.S. Marshal
BOSTON – The U.S. Marshals Service (USMS) Districts of Massachusetts and Connecticut today announced the arrest of a Massachusetts fugitive wanted for Assault to Murder in Hartford, Connecticut, on November 3, 2026.
Sanedlly Santana, 26, was arrested in connection with a stabbing incident that occurred in New Bedford, Massachusetts on October 10, 2026. Specifically, during a fight at a local bar, a male victim was stabbed in the chest, and a female victim was stabbed in the neck. Both victims were transported to a local hospital and survived their injuries.
On October 13, 2026, an arrest warrant was issued for Santana out of the New Bedford District Court on charges of Assault to Murder, Assault and Battery by Means of a Dangerous Weapon, and Assault and Battery, in connection with the stabbing of the female victim.
Investigators with the USMS Massachusetts Fugitive Task Force (MAFTF) developed information that Santana was in Connecticut. Through collaboration between the two districts, members of the USMS District of Connecticut Fugitive Task Force arrested Santana without incident in Hartford, CT.
Santana is being held on a fugitive from justice charge in Connecticut and is awaiting extradition to Massachusetts to face the charges in New Bedford District Court.
“One of the greatest strengths of the U.S. Marshals Service is our extraordinary nationwide network of law enforcement partnerships,” said Dennis Matulewicz, Attorney General-designated U.S. Marshal for the District of Massachusetts. “This arrest demonstrates our ability to seamlessly coordinate across state lines, our unwavering commitment to protecting the communities we serve, and our determination to bring violent fugitives to justice. Our thoughts are with the victims of this violent attack, and we wish them both a full and speedy recovery.”
John Iverson, Acting U.S. Marshal for the District of Connecticut, said, “The collaborative investigation by the Massachusetts and Connecticut Fugitive Task Forces ensured this apprehension occurred quickly and highlights the strong partnerships throughout the region. New England presents a unique landscape with close borders, leading violent criminals to flee the state, believing they may evade law enforcement. This case is a strong reminder that the U.S. Marshals Service will find and apprehend those charged with violent crimes, no matter where you abscond.”
USMS MAFTF participants include the USMS District of Massachusetts, Massachusetts State Police, Boston Police, Brockton Police, Cambridge Police, Chicopee Police, Hampden County Sheriff’s Department, Haverhill Police, Lowell Police, Middlesex Sheriff’s Department, New Bedford Police, Plymouth County Sheriff's Department, Quincy Police, Randolph Police, Rochester Police, Springfield Police, Suffolk County Sheriff’s Department, West Springfield Police, Worcester Police, Massachusetts National Guard Counter Drug Program, Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, and the Drug Enforcement Administration.
The USMS and its law enforcement partners remain committed to identifying, locating, and apprehending violent fugitives, developing actionable intelligence, and working collaboratively to enhance public safety throughout Massachusetts and across the nation.
The USMS reminds the public that criminal charges and allegations are accusations, and a defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.
If you have any information regarding the whereabouts of any state or federal fugitive, please contact the USMS at 1-877-WANTED2 or submit information via the USMS Tips App.

ALBUQUERQUE – A McKinley County man pleaded guilty to assaulting a woman after offering her a ride in his car, then driving her toward a remote residence and repeatedly groping her along the way, despite her repeatedly ordering him to stop.

According to court documents, on March 23, 2026, Barton Rico Cooeyate , 41, offered the victim a ride while she was walking along a road within the exterior boundaries of the Zuni Pueblo. After the victim accepted, Cooeyate suggested they drive to a location in Vanderwagen, New Mexico. Instead, Cooeyate drove past the turnoff and headed toward a rural residence approximately 15 miles away. During the drive, Cooeyate repeatedly touched the victim’s breasts and thighs over her clothing and attempted to kiss her despite her telling him she did not want to be touched. The victim ultimately escaped Cooeyate ’s car and hid until a Zuni Pueblo Tribal Ranger stopped Cooeyate for an unrelated DWI investigation. The victim suffered injuries, including a contusion to her left forearm.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today.

American Man Extradited from Germany to Face Charges of Defrauding U.S. Consumers in Fake Psychic Mailing-Fraud Scheme
Mael Chemla, 61, a U.S., French, and Israeli national, previously residing in Aventura, Florida, was extradited to the United States from Germany and made his initial appearance in Miami federal court yesterday to face charges for his role in operating a mailing fraud scheme.
According to the indictment, unsealed yesterday, Chemla allegedly conspired with others to send letters to victims throughout the United States that appeared to be personalized communications from psychics. The letters falsely informed victims that the psychic had learned of an imminent financial windfall the victim was entitled to receive, and the victim needed to send a payment in order to receive the financial windfall. Chemla opened U.S. bank accounts in the names of the purported psychics, deposited checks from victims of the scheme into those accounts, then wired the victim funds to European bank accounts controlled by a co-conspirator. From September 2016 through November 2020, Chemla and his co-conspirator collected more than $4 million from thousands of victims in the United States, many of whom were elderly and otherwise vulnerable.
Chemla is charged with conspiracy, mail fraud, and wire fraud. If convicted, Chemla faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison on all counts.
The U.S. Postal Inspection Service is investigating the case.
Trial Attorneys Ann Entwistle and Charles Dunn of the Criminal Division’s White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section are prosecuting the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant support in the litigation before the German extradition court, and once extradition was granted, coordinated with the U.S. Marshals to arrange the defendant’s transport to the United States.
An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Former Airline Employee Sentenced to 16 Months in Federal Prison for Participating in a “Waivers And Favors” Scheme to Defraud Three Major Airlines
A former airline employee was sentenced yesterday to 16 months in federal prison for participating in a scheme to defraud three major airlines, resulting in total revenue losses of over $600,000.
Chaculvin Hayes, 37, of Jacksonville, Florida, was sentenced by United States District Judge John F. Walter, who also ordered him to pay $602,886.18 in restitution.
Hayes pleaded guilty in June 2026 to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.
According to his plea agreement, Hayes and co-conspirators participated in a scheme to fraudulently upgrade tickets, alter bookings, and issue travel vouchers, causing more than $600,000 in losses to three major airlines.
During the period between January 2017 and December 2019, Hayes and his co-conspirators worked for GAT Airline Ground Support, a contractor that provided ticketing and ground support services at Hollywood Burbank Airport and other locations. Through their job, the group had access to airline reservation systems for United and Delta and could also book American flights through airline agreements.
Hayes and his co-conspirators exploited a ticketing accommodation process known as "waivers and favors," which is intended to allow authorized customer service employees to make special booking changes when necessary. During the scheme, Hayes used his access to upgrade tickets (for example, from economy to first class) without charging the proper fees; change travel dates and itineraries without required fees; and create unauthorized Electronic Travel Coupons (ETCs) that could be used like vouchers.
Hayes admitted using an alias, "Neeve Andrews," to sell heavily discounted airline tickets obtained through fraudulent reservation modifications and accepted payments from customers. Hayes also admitted to using his employee credentials to modify hundreds of Passenger Name Records (PNRs) and issue dozens of unauthorized vouchers.
Through hundreds of PNR modifications and through the issuance of fraudulent ETC vouchers, Hayes and his co-conspirators caused combined losses totaling approximately $602,886.18.
The FBI investigated this matter.
This case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Amanda Elbogen of the Major Crimes Section for the Central District of California.
title: Former Airline Employee Sentenced to 16 Months in Federal Prison for Participating in a “Waivers And Favors” Scheme to Defraud Three Major Airlines

MISSOULA – An Indiana man who traveled to Montana to have sex with a minor, and had explicit images of her on his phone, was sentenced today to 15 years in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release, U.S. Attorney Scott Twito said.

Brandon Cole Stoliby, 33, pleaded guilty in July 2026 to traveling with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct and transportation of child pornography.

U.S. District Judge Donald W. Molloy presided.

The government alleged in court documents that Stoliby met a 15-year-old Montana girl through Snapchat, exchanged sexually explicit messages and photos with her, and then traveled from Indiana to Missoula with his wife and children to pick up the girl and take her back to his home in Indiana.

Stoliby and the girl met over Snapchat in March 2025. She presented herself as 18 and Stoliby quickly showed sexual interest in her, sending her explicit messages and persuading her to send him explicit images. Those images were later found on Stoliby’s phone when he was eventually arrested in Montana.

By April 2025, the two had made plans for Stoliby to travel to Montana to pick her up and move her back to Indiana. Stoliby and the girl made plans for her to sell explicit images of herself to help cover the costs of the trip and the move. He arrived in Missoula County on April 6, 2025, and picked the girl up from her home. On the trip back to Indiana, while still in Montana, the two engaged in sexual intercourse. Law enforcement removed the girl from Stoliby’s custody, telling him she was 15 years old. Despite this knowledge, Stoliby again tried to transport the girl to Indiana and retained Child Sex Abuse Material depicting the girl.

Stoliby was eventually arrested and admitted in interviews with law enforcement to exchanging sexually explicit images with the girl, engaging in a sexual relationship with her, and keeping explicit photos she had sent him.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Lowney prosecuted the case. Homeland Security Investigations and the Missoula County Sheriff’s Department conducted the investigation.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOs, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC .

ICE requests transfer of criminal illegal aliens, California jail chooses lockdown instead
SALINAS, Calif. — On Oct. 27, six ICE agents arrived at the Monterey County Jail in Salinas requesting custody transfer of three suspected criminal illegal aliens. What should have been a simple, routine operation quickly went sideways.
The agents were there to recover Eduardo Castro-Lopez, also known as Jordan Eduardo Yac; Jose Luis Quinones, also known as Jose Manuel Garcia; and Angelina Ramirez-Sepulveda. The suspects have prior arrests for multiple offenses including DUI, drug offenses and providing false identification.
The officers waited outside the jail and cordoned off the area with yellow tape to facilitate the targeted operation. A crowd of protesters began to form, and Monterey County Sheriff Tina M. Nieto opted to place the facility on lockdown.
The lockdown lasted approximately three hours. During that period, new bookings and inmate releases were suspended, and public visitor doors were closed, though the jail continued regular operations and published an online custody log.
“None of the suspects were turned over to ICE during the lockdown,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “A local county supervisor told the ICE officers that the sheriff would not release the inmates to them. It’s borderline obscene that a facility that’s there to protect the public would go on lockdown to protect criminal illegal aliens from the consequences of violating federal immigration law.”
By the next day, the online custody log showed that Castro-Lopez had been released from custody and Quinones was no longer shown as being in custody. Ramirez-Sepulveda remained in custody.
“Two of the individuals ICE sought were reportedly released from custody. This is where we are: Criminals are being protected in sanctuary cities and states, and a law enforcement facility is siding with CRIMINALS instead of cooperating with federal law enforcement," ICE posted on social media.
Under President Trump, ICE is focused on its core mission: enforcing immigration law and protecting the American people.
Learn more about ICE’s public safety mission on X, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, Bluesky and Truth Social.
If you have information about foreign fugitives or illegal aliens, contact ICE by calling the ICE Tip Line at (866) DHS-2-ICE (3472423). You can also file a tip online by completing ICE’s online tip form.

SAN DIEGO – Ivan Alonso Rodriguez of El Cajon pleaded guilty in federal court today, admitting that he failed to report the death of a former coworker to the government, and pocketed almost $300,000 in federal benefits intended for the deceased man.

Rodriguez and the deceased coworker, identified in court documents as R.J.W., had worked together as police officers at Naval Base San Diego Security Department until R.J.W.’s retirement. In his plea agreement, Rodriguez admitted that in 2013, R.J.W. designated him as the sole trustee of his living trust, gave Rodriguez power of attorney over his affairs, and added Rodriguez as a co-signatory to the bank account where R.J.W. was receiving retirement benefit payments from the Social Security Administration and the Office of Personnel Management.

In 2016, R.J.W. died in Baja California, and despite receiving news about the death, Rodriguez did not report it to either the government or the bank. As a result, the Social Security Administration and Office of Personnel Management continued to make payments intended to benefit R.J.W. that would otherwise have ceased at the time of R.J.W.’s death. From May 2016 through September 2025, Rodriguiez received more than $200,000 in Retirement Insurance Benefits, $85,000 in Federal Employees Retirement System benefits, and $3,200 in Economic Impact Payments intended to benefit R.J.W. Rodriguez admitted in his plea agreement that he converted this stolen public money to his own use and benefit.

Rodriguez is scheduled to be sentenced on February 12, 2027, at 8:30 a.m. before U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta.

This case was prosecuted by Special Assistant United States Attorney Jeffrey D. Hill.

Receipt, Concealment, and Retention of Stolen Public Money – Title 18, U.S.C., Section 641

FRESNO, Calif. — Ron Cook, 58, of Fresno, has been indicted on multiple charges of making false statements to the federal government, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and money laundering for running a nearly $65 million fraud scheme through his company, Corporate America Lending (CAL), U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced today.

Cook was arrested at his office this morning and will make his initial court appearance this afternoon.

According to court records, CAL is a lending company based in Fresno that originates loans for farmers, ranchers, and others who work in the agriculture industry. Once CAL originates the loans, it sells the interest in them to others, including investors, financial companies, and the Federal Agricultural Mortgage Company (Farmer MAC). Farmer MAC is a company backed by the federal government that provides increased access to affordable financing for the agriculture industry.

Beginning in 2023, the borrowers of a $58 million loan that Cook had originated and sold to one financial company refinanced the loan with another financial company. The first financial company did not know about the refinancing. Cook then made several misrepresentations to the borrowers, the first financial company, and the second financial company so that he would receive the $58 million refinance amount without the first financial company becoming aware and could keep the money for himself. When the first financial company found out about the refinancing, Cook transferred the money to his friends and associates to conceal its location. It was these transfers that resulted in the money laundering charges.

During this period, Cook also defrauded his other customers and investors. He defrauded his customers by stealing their identities and taking out loans in their names from Farmer MAC without their knowledge, and he defrauded his investors by selling them interests in loans that did not actually exist. It was Cook’s stealing his customers’ identities to get loans from Farmer MAC that resulted in the false statements to the federal government charge against him.

Cook obtained at least $64 million through his fraud scheme. He used the money to pay for his lifestyle and to pay debts that he owed to some of his customers and investors who had detected the fraud and threatened to file criminal charges against him. He also used the money to make political donations.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Arelis Clemente and Joseph Barton are prosecuting the case.

If convicted, Cook faces 30 years in prison and a $250,000 fine for the making false statements to the federal government charge. He faces 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for each of the wire fraud and money laundering charges. Finally, he faces a mandatory two years in prison, consecutive to the sentence he receives for any other charges, for each of the aggravated identity theft charges. Any sentence, however, would be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables. The charges are only allegations; the defendant is presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
title: Fresno Executive Indicted for $65 Million Fraud Scheme that Defrauded Farmer MAC and Others

Stamford Man Sentenced to Additional Prison Time for Distributing Crack Prior to Reporting to Prison
STAMFORD, Conn. - David X. Sullivan, United States Attorney for the District of Connecticut, announced that DANNY TURKVAN, also known as “Smooth” 55, of Stamford, has been sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stefan R. Underhill in Bridgeport to an additional 14 months of imprisonment for distributing crack cocaine after he had been sentenced in another federal case and prior to reporting to prison.
On August 13, 2025, Turkvan was sentenced in Hartford federal court to 46 months of imprisonment and three years of supervised release for his participation in a southwestern Connecticut narcotics trafficking conspiracy. Turkvan, who was released on a $150,000 bond, was ordered to report to prison on October 16, 2025. An investigation revealed that Turkvan continued to distribute narcotics after his August 2025 sentencing. Stamford Police arrested Turkvan on state charges on October 11, 2025, and seized crack cocaine that he intended to distribute.
Turkvan has been detained since his arrest. On July 8, 2026, he pleaded guilty in federal court to possession with intent to distribute cocaine base (“crack”).
This investigation was conducted by the Stamford Police Department and the Drug Enforcement Administration. The case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Patricia Stolfi Collins.

SYRACUSE, N.Y.— The Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Financial Management and Comptroller, Jake Fischer, recently visited Syracuse University to strengthen the Army’s longstanding academic partnership and explore opportunities to develop the next generation of financial management leaders.
The visit included engagements with Army ROTC cadets, students enrolled in the Defense Comptrollership Program (DCP), and senior faculty from the Whitman School of Management and Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs.
During his visit with DCP students, Fischer emphasized the evolving role of financial management professionals as the Army accelerates its modernization efforts. As emerging technologies and super intelligence reduce the burden of routine financial transactions, the Army must increasingly leverage its workforce’s knowledge, analytical expertise, and judgment to inform senior leader decisions.
These discussions reinforced priorities outlined in the Army’s FY27 Financial Management Strategy and Transformation Plan, including the Fiscal Frontline financial dashboard, Army Audit Acceleration, and ongoing efforts to modernize how the Army allocates resources.
When meeting with Army ROTC cadets, Fischer discussed Army transformation, leadership, and the importance of financial accountability in supporting warfighter readiness.
A tour of Syracuse’s National Veterans Resource Center highlighted the university’s extensive support to service members, veterans, and transitioning Soldiers, including educational opportunities, professional certifications, and career transition programs.
Dialog with university leadership explored new opportunities for academic collaboration, particularly in artificial intelligence, strategic resource management, and executive communication. These efforts emphasized strengthening the workforce’s ability to translate complex financial information into clear, actionable recommendations.
The visit underscored the Army’s continued commitment to investing in its people and leveraging academic partnerships to build a more agile, analytically capable financial management workforce—one prepared to transform financial information into decision advantage for the warfighter.
title: Army PDASA FM&C Jake Fischer strengthens partnership with Syracuse University to modernize workforce
