VICENZA, Italy – California National Guard members worked alongside Armed Forces of Nigeria partners during an engagement in Abuja, Nigeria, Aug. 15-22, integrating the California Military Department into the AFN's ongoing air-to-ground integration efforts.
By directly addressing AGI integration, this collaboration made substantial progress on the California Guard’s top priority with Nigeria, its partner in the National Guard’s State Partnership Program since 2006.
The primary objectives of this meeting involved assessing current capability gaps in integrating Nigeria’s joint terminal attack controllers — commonly referred to as “JTACs” — into combat operations, analyzing existing force generation and training pipelines, and developing a mutually beneficial, long-term partnership roadmap, as well as future training pathways.
JTACs operate on front lines in wartime scenarios, directing combat aircraft to provide close-air support and other offensive air operations. This collaborative event was a significant step forward in strengthening interoperability between the California Guard and the AFN.
“The engagement built working relationships among the California Guard, U.S. Embassy Abuja, the Nigerian military’s Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre, and Nigerian Air Force personnel while establishing shared training priorities,” said U.S. Air Force Lt. Col. Daniel Kempf, commander of the 146th Logistics Readiness Squadron, 146th Airlift Wing, California Air National Guard. “We also set conditions for joint curriculum development, virtual instruction, in-person training and evaluator development, which will pave the way for further development and engagements,” Kempf said.
Nigeria’s Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre is the primary training institution responsible for certifying JTACs across its military. Once certified, the controllers report to active theater commands to support tactical operations. The AWDC oversees the standardization of training and continuous evaluation of its graduates, while also ensuring that those graduates maintain their skills.
“Working together, we identified JTAC training, sustainment and ground-force integration gaps, and we produced a roadmap for building a more capable, sustainable program,” Kempf said. “That program will also support safer operations and stronger civilian-harm mitigation, improving the AFN’s abilities as a regional security provider and a partner to the California National Guard.”
According to Kempf, the AFN intends to train and maintain a mission-appropriate level of certified JTACs for each of its active combat theaters to ensure a healthy operational rotation, while lowering risks faced by friendly forces and local populations. As of August 2026, the AWDC graduated two training cohorts toward meeting this long-term goal.
“While the California State Partnership Program can’t directly provide or procure operational military hardware, our capabilities are perfectly aligned to support training, curriculum development and institutional capacity building,” Kempf said. “We’ve already identified and agreed on key areas to drive long-term improvements.”
U.S. Africa Command leads “Flintlock” and “African Lion,” which are major, multinational training exercises that take place annually in Africa, focusing on improving security and cooperation with partner nations. Kempf explained that future training that further integrates the California Guard and AWDC personnel into regional exercise frameworks would involve these events, among others.
“Additional potential events include virtual ground force commander instruction, practical training in Maiduguri, Nigeria, advanced JTAC-evaluator training, as well as Nigerian JTAC and air-to-ground-integration refresher exchanges in California,” Kempf said.
Planning these training opportunities not only helps further develop working relationships between partners, they also prepare reaction forces for unexpected tasks, which can involve wartime scenarios or missions involving disaster response.
“In peacetime, we concentrate on training, doctrine, airspace management and civilian-harm mitigation,” Kempf said. “In combat or contingency operations, the focus in these engagements can improve air-to-ground coordination and reduce risks to friendly forces and civilians.”
Along with augmenting Nigerian readiness, Kempf emphasized how the engagement benefited the Golden State's warfighting trainers.
“This visit strengthened our own readiness by providing practical experience assessing a partner force’s doctrine, training pipeline, equipment limitations and security constraints,” Kempf said. “Continued engagements will provide further valuable context for the California Guard to analyze tactics, techniques and procedures currently used in active combat environments in the region.”

title: California Guard, Nigerian state partners improve air-to-ground integration

HOUSTON, TX — Representative Christian D. Menefee (TX-18) has joined the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC) as an Associate Member, bringing the Caucus to a historic 86 Members of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, its largest membership since its founding.
“Houston is one of the most diverse cities in the nation. The strength and resilience of our many cultures, including our Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities, are woven into the fabric of our district. I’m proud to join the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. More than 40,000 AANHPI residents call TX-18 home, and I’m committed to making sure our community has a seat at the table. Thank you to Chair Meng for the warm welcome. I look forward to being an ally in this fight,” said Rep. Christian D. Menefee.
“I am thrilled to welcome Congressman Christian Menefee as CAPAC’s new Associate Member,” said Rep. Grace Meng, Chair of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus. “We need allies in Congress who are committed to fighting for the needs of Asian Americans, Native Hawaiians, and Pacific Islanders across the country—including right in the heart of Houston. Rep. Menefee will be a strong advocate for our communities, and we are proud to have him as the newest member of our ever-growing caucus.”
Founded in 1994, the bicameral Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus is composed of 86 Members of Congress who advocate on behalf of Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander communities. The Caucus is led by Congresswoman Grace Meng, who was elected CAPAC Chair in 2024.
###
title: Congressman Menefee Joins the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus

April Nikkel, 37, from Sioux City, Iowa, was sentenced on October 29, 2026, to 168 months’ imprisonment. Nikkel pled guilty on May 18, 2026, in federal court in Sioux City to one count of conspiracy to distribute methamphetamine and one count of distributing methamphetamine within 1,000 feet of a protected location.

Evidence at the plea and sentencing hearings showed Nikkel was involved in a conspiracy from January 2025 through November 2025 that distributed more than three pounds of methamphetamine. On at least three occasions Nikkel distributed and helped another distribute a total of over 190 grams of pure methamphetamine to individuals cooperating with law enforcement. These distributions occurred within 1,000 feet of Fairmount City Park and Cecillia City Park in Sioux City.

United States District Court Judge Leonard T. Strand sentenced Nikkel to 168 months’ imprisonment and eight years of supervised release. There is no parole in the federal system. Nikkel remains in custody of the United States Marshal until she can be transported to a federal prison.

The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Shawn S. Wehde and was investigated by Tri-State Drug Task Force based in Sioux City, Iowa, that consists of law enforcement personnel from the Drug Enforcement Administration; Sioux City, Iowa, Police Department; Homeland Security Investigations; Woodbury County Sheriff’s Office; South Sioux City, Nebraska, Police Department; Nebraska State Patrol; Iowa National Guard; Iowa Division of Narcotics Enforcement; United States Marshals Service; South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation; and Woodbury County Attorney’s Office.

Court file information at https://ecf.iand.uscourts.gov/cgi-bin/login.pl .

The case file number is25-4063. Follow us on X @USAO_NDIA.
title: Sioux City Woman to Federal Prison for Meth Distribution Conspiracy

MONTGOMERY, Ala. — Today, the United States Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Alabama, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), the Montgomery Police Department, and the Montgomery County District Attorney’s Office announced the indictment of a Montgomery teacher on drug trafficking and firearms charges.

On October 29, 2026, a federal grand jury returned an indictment charging Langston Fremont Carter, 30, of Montgomery, Alabama, with two counts of possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute and two additional counts related to the unlawful possession of a firearm.

According to the charging documents, the alleged offenses occurred on October 22, 2026, at L.E.A.D. Academy in Montgomery. Carter, who was employed as a teacher at the school, is accused of possessing controlled substances, including oxycodone and marijuana, with the intent to distribute them. He is also charged with possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime and possessing a firearm within a school zone.

Carter made his initial appearance in federal court on October 29, 2026. His arraignment is scheduled for November 3, 2026.

If convicted on all charges, Carter faces a maximum sentence of 20 years' imprisonment on the drug trafficking charges. In addition, the charge of possessing a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime carries a mandatory minimum sentence of five years' imprisonment, which must be served consecutively to any sentence imposed on the other counts. A federal district judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. There is no parole in the federal system.

The ATF and Montgomery Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Joel Feil is prosecuting the case for the Middle District of Alabama.

An indictment or criminal complaint is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
title: Montgomery Teacher Facing Federal Drug Trafficking and Firearms Offenses

PORTLAND, Maine: A Maryland woman, formerly of Westbrook, was sentenced today in U.S. District Court in Portland for aiding and abetting the presentation of a counterfeit government check to her credit union.

U.S. District Judge John A. Woodcock, Jr. sentenced Palwasha Shir , 36, to 24 months in prison to be followed by three years of supervised release. Shir was also ordered to pay $290,947 in restitution. Shir pleaded guilty on June 23, 2026.

According to court records, Shir was the sole owner of The Selfie Room LLC, a business Shir registered in Maine. Shir opened a checking account for The Selfie Room at a credit union in Maine. In July 2024, Shir caused a counterfeit Treasury check made payable to The Selfie Room in the amount of $291,203 to be deposited in the account. In August 2024, Shir caused a counterfeit Treasury check made payable to The Selfie Room in the amount of $193,107 to be deposited in the account. The serial numbers and amounts on the checks matched those of genuine tax refund checks issued by the IRS to entities other than The Selfie Room and unrelated to Shir. The counterfeit checks changed the payee and address to make the checks payable to The Selfie Room. When a representative of the credit union called Shir to discuss the checks, Shir falsely claimed that she received the checks from the IRS.

IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case.
title: Maryland Woman Sentenced for Aiding and Abetting Deposit of Counterfeit Treasury Check

Reps. Castro, Vasquez, Cisneros Introduce Resolution Recognizing Hispanic and Latino Servicemembers
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Reps. Joaquin Castro (TX-20), Congressional Hispanic Caucus Vice Chair of Diversity and Inclusion, Gabe Vasquez (NM-02), and Gil Cisneros (CA-31) introduced a resolution recognizing the contributions of Hispanic and Latino servicemembers in the United States Armed Forces and calling for stronger Hispanic and Latino leadership across every branch of the military. Between 2017 and 2025, Hispanic representation in the military grew by 6.8 percent, and Hispanic servicemembers now make up 20.81 percent of the force across all branches. They remain underrepresented in leadership. Hispanic servicemembers hold only about 3 percent of general and flag officer positions and less than 10 percent of officer positions in any branch.
“San Antonio, known as Military City, USA, is home to generations of military heroes,” said Congressman Castro. “Latino servicemembers have proudly served in every major war in our nation’s history, and today they are the fastest-growing segment of our armed forces. Yet their contributions have not been equally honored. I’m proud to join Congressman Cisneros in honoring and supporting these servicemembers, and in pushing for leadership that reflects the people who serve.”
“I’m honored to recognize the generations of Latino servicemembers who have served our nation with valor,” said Congressman Cisneros. “But honoring their contributions also means acknowledging the work that needs to be done. While Hispanic and Latino servicemembers account for the largest growing population across the military, they are too often overlooked for leadership roles, and that needs to improve. Our forces are at their best when they reflect our nation’s diversity.”
“The Hispanic community has proudly demonstrated its pride and willingness to serve our nation for decades, diversifying our ranks and strengthening our national defense,” said Congressman Vasquez. “In New Mexico, that tradition runs deep — we are a state of proud Americans who answer the call. This is a reminder that diversity at all ranks makes us stronger as a nation and reflects who we are.”
Read the full text of the resolution here.
###
title: Reps. Castro, Vasquez, Cisneros Introduce Resolution Recognizing Hispanic and Latino Servicemembers

PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Rosebud, South Dakota, woman convicted of Involuntary Manslaughter. The sentencing took place on October 26, 2026.

Crystal McCloskey, age 34, was sentenced to two years and four months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

McCloskey was indicted by a federal grand jury in January 2026. She pleaded guilty on July 29, 2026.

On June 14, 2025, McCloskey was under the influence of alcohol and controlled substances and drove her vehicle at a high rate of speed. McCloskey missed a curve near Rosebud and drove off the road. The vehicle rolled, throwing McCloskey and her passenger out of the vehicle. The passenger died as a result of her injuries in the crash. The offense occurred in the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation.

This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in Federal court as opposed to State court.

This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services, the Oglala Sioux Tribe Department of Public Safety, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kimberly Zachrison prosecuted the case.

McCloskey was ordered to self-surrender to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service on November 10, 2026.
title: Rosebud Woman Sentenced to Federal Prison for Involuntary Manslaughter

NEWPORT NEWS, Va. – Ex-Enterprise (CVN 65) began its final transit this morning, departing Newport News Shipbuilding for Mobile, Alabama, where the ship will be dismantled.
Commissioned in 1961, the USS Enterprise served the nation for more than 50 years. A technological milestone in naval history, the world’s first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier played a central role in U.S. naval operations during the Cold War, Vietnam War, and post-9/11 conflicts, including Operations Enduring Freedom and Iraqi Freedom.
“Enterprise will always be remembered for her proud legacy of service, a legacy made possible by the Sailors and support personnel whose dedication kept her mission-ready,” said Kevin Cormier, Deputy Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maritime for Aircraft Carriers. “All who served aboard and sustained this historic ship should take pride in the vital role they played in supporting the fleet. Their dedication ensured that Enterprise remained a lasting example of naval excellence. Fair winds and following seas.”
Following Enterprise’s inactivation in December 2012, the Navy completed defueling of the ship’s reactor plants in 2017. Enterprise was decommissioned during a ceremony in the ship’s hangar bay on Feb. 3, 2017. The ceremony marked the end of the ship’s nearly 55-year career and the first decommissioning of a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.
The eighth naval vessel to bear the name Enterprise, the ship was built by Newport News Shipbuilding and christened Sept. 24, 1960, by Bertha Irene Franke, wife of former Secretary of the Navy William B. Franke. The ship entered service in 1961 and safely steamed more than 1 million nautical miles under nuclear power during its operational career. Enterprise’s legacy will continue with the future Ford-class aircraft carrier, Enterprise (CVN 80), the ninth U.S. Navy ship to carry the name.
The Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Maritime is the single accountable organization for delivering surface ships for the U.S. Navy. This centralized organizational construct will empower leaders with broader scope and greater authority to accelerate delivery of combat capability and ensure acquisition speed and discipline are driven by what the warfighter needs—when they need it.
title: Ex-Enterprise (CVN 65) Begins Final Voyage

text:
The Social Security program pays monthly cash benefits to retired or disabled workers and their family members and to the family members of deceased workers. Social Security's receipts and expenditures are accounted for through two federal trust funds: the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund and the Federal Disability Insurance (DI) Trust Fund. The trust funds represent funds dedicated to pay current and future Social Security benefits.
The OASI and DI programs each have three sources of income: payroll tax revenues, federal income taxes paid by some beneficiaries on a portion of their benefits, and interest income from the investment of asset reserves in U.S. government securities. Payroll tax revenues provide about 90% of program income, federal income taxes on Social Security benefits provide about 5% of program income, and interest provides about 5% of program income. By law, Social Security tax revenues must be invested in U.S. government obligations (debt instruments of the U.S. government). The OASI and DI programs each have three sources of cost: monthly benefits, administrative costs, and costs associated with the Railroad Retirement Board interchange. Monthly benefits typically account for over 99% of program costs. The interactions between these revenues, costs, and trust fund balances (i.e., accumulated excess revenues from previous years) determine each program's ability to pay full scheduled benefits on time.
According to the 2026 annual report of the Social Security Board of Trustees, the OASI trust fund has been operating under an annual deficit—total costs exceeding total revenues—since 2021. Furthermore, the Social Security trustees project this financial shortfall to continue indefinitely. Specifically, the trustees show that while OASI's total revenues are increasing, the program's total costs are increasing more rapidly. This trend can exist, with the OASI program able to pay full benefits, only so long as a positive trust fund balance exists to cover the shortfall.
Under their intermediate assumptions and current law, the Social Security trustees project that the OASI trust fund will become depleted (i.e., insolvent) in 2032, whereas the DI trust fund will not become depleted in the 75-year projection period. The two trust funds are legally distinct and do not have authority to borrow from each other. However, Congress has authorized the shifting of funds between OASI and DI in the past to address shortfalls in a particular fund. For this reason, and because of the projected insolvency of the OASI trust fund, the two trust funds are often considered on a combined (i.e., OASDI) basis. The trustees project that the combined Social Security trust funds would become depleted in 2034. At the point of trust fund depletion, a program's (e.g., OASI's) incoming revenue would be sufficient to pay only a fraction of the benefits scheduled to be paid under current law. Trust fund insolvency does not mean that Social Security will be unable to pay any benefits.
If a trust fund were to be depleted and current receipts were insufficient to cover current expenditures, there would be a conflict between two federal laws. Under the Social Security Act, beneficiaries would still be legally entitled to their full scheduled benefits. However, the Antideficiency Act prohibits government spending in excess of available funds, so the Social Security Administration (SSA) would not have legal authority to pay full Social Security benefits on time.
The Social Security Act does not stipulate what happens to benefit payments if a trust fund becomes depleted. Thus, it is unclear what specific actions SSA would take if a trust fund were insolvent. After depletion, a trust fund would continue to receive tax revenues from which a portion of scheduled benefits could be paid. One option would be to pay full benefits on a delayed schedule; another would be to make timely but reduced payments.
Eliminating OASI's financial shortfall would require reductions in Social Security benefits, increases in tax revenues, or some combination of the two. The sooner that Social Security policy changes are undertaken, the less abrupt the changes would need to be, because they could be spread over a longer period and would therefore affect a larger number of workers and beneficiaries. Enacting adjustments to Social Security policy sooner, rather than later, would give workers and beneficiaries more time to plan and adjust their work and savings behavior.
Known collectively as Social Security, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) and Disability Insurance (DI) programs provide monthly cash benefits to eligible retired or disabled workers and their dependents, and to the eligible survivors of deceased insured workers.1 The programs, referred to on a combined basis as OASDI, are authorized under Title II of the Social Security Act and are administered by the Social Security Administration (SSA).2
Workers obtain insurance by working for a sufficient number of years in jobs covered by Social Security. A worker's job is considered covered if the earnings derived from that job are subject to the Social Security payroll tax and are thus creditable for program purposes. In 2026, an estimated 185 million people (or about 94% of all workers) will work in paid employment or self-employment covered by Social Security.3 In August 2026, more than 71 million people collected Social Security benefits.4 Approximately 77% of those beneficiaries are retired workers, and another 10% of those beneficiaries are disabled workers.
Monthly Social Security benefits are based on a retired or disabled worker's career-average earnings in jobs covered by Social Security. The monthly benefits are designed to replace a portion of the income lost to a family due to the retirement, disability, or death of the worker. In August 2026, the average monthly benefit for retired workers was $2,088, whereas the average monthly benefit for disabled workers was $1,636.5 Family members of retired, disabled, or deceased workers accounted for the remainder of the benefit population (about 13%) and collected an average monthly benefit of $1,325.
Social Security's receipts and expenditures are accounted for through two federal trust funds: the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund and the Federal Disability Insurance (DI) Trust Fund. The trust funds represent funds dedicated to pay current and future Social Security benefits. The OASI and DI programs' ability to pay the full amount of scheduled monthly benefits depends on the relationship between the revenues, costs, and asset reserves held in the respective trust fund.
Each year when the Social Security trustees release their annual report, attention is focused on the projected year in which the Social Security trust funds will become depleted (i.e., the year in which the amount of asset reserves falls to zero). In their 2026 report, the trustees project that the OASI trust fund will become depleted in 2032, whereas the DI trust fund is not projected to become depleted at any time in the next 75 years.6 The trustees project, on a hypothetical combined basis, that the OASDI trust fund would be depleted sometime in 2034. These projections, and the projections presented in this report, are based on the trustees' intermediate assumptions, which reflect their best understanding of the status of the Social Security trust funds at the start of 2026.7 These projected depletion dates indicate a financial shortfall that, absent a change to current law, would compromise the program's ability to pay full scheduled benefits.
Social Security is the federal government's largest benefit program. Moreover, among aged individuals, Social Security is the most common source of income (90% of aged individuals receive Social Security benefits) and also the largest source of income (Social Security supports over one-quarter of aggregate income for aged individuals).8 Some people mistakenly believe that if the trust funds were depleted, Social Security would be unable to pay benefits at all. However, in 2032, the first year of the projected depletion of the OASI trust fund, ongoing revenues are expected to pay approximately 78% of scheduled benefits.9
To examine the Social Security trust funds and the projected financial shortfall, this report (1) discusses what the Social Security trust funds are and how they are used; (2) defines Social Security's sources of income and cost, and analyzes their respective performance (cash flow and annual balances); (3) discusses the effects of these balances on trust fund asset reserves and the ability of each program to pay full benefits; and (4) focuses on what would happen if a trust fund were to be depleted.
Within the U.S. Treasury, numerous accounts are in place for internal accounting purposes. Although all the monies within the U.S. Treasury are federal monies, the designation of an account as a trust fund allows the government to track revenues dedicated for specific purposes (as well as expenditures). In addition, the government can affect the level of revenues and expenditures associated with a trust fund through changes in the law.
Social Security program revenues (i.e., income or receipts) and costs (i.e., outgo or expenditures) are accounted for in two separate trust funds authorized under Title II of the Social Security Act: (1) the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund and (2) the Federal Disability Insurance (DI) Trust Fund.10 The OASI trust fund was created by the Social Security Act Amendments of 1939 (P.L. 76-379) and superseded the Old-Age Reserve Account established by the original Social Security Act in 1935 (P.L. 74-271).11 The DI trust fund was established as part of the Social Security Amendments of 1956 (P.L. 84-880).12 The trust funds have existed on a hypothetical combined basis since the DI fund was first credited with receipts and debited for expenditures in 1957.
In the federal accounting structure, a trust fund is an accounting mechanism used by the Department of the Treasury to track and report receipts dedicated for spending on specific purposes, as well as expenditures made to beneficiaries that are financed by those receipts, in accordance with the terms of a statute that designates the fund as a trust fund.13 The OASI trust fund records receipts and expenditures associated with retired workers, their dependents, and survivors of deceased insured workers. The DI trust fund records receipts and expenditures associated with disabled workers and their dependents. Under current law, the two trust funds are legally distinct and do not have authority to borrow from each other. However, several times in the past, lawmakers have authorized the reallocation of the Social Security payroll tax rate and have authorized interfund borrowing to preserve the solvency of the two trust funds.14 This precedent is important given projections showing that the asset reserves held by the OASI fund will be depleted in 2032, whereas the asset reserves held by the DI fund are not projected to be depleted at any time during the next 75-year period.15 Because of the prior authorization to shift funds between OASI and DI, analysts often treat the two funds collectively on a hypothetical basis as the combined OASDI trust funds.
A government trust fund has different attributes than private sector trust funds. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) notes the following:
In the federal budget the meaning of the term "trust" differs significantly from its private sector usage. In the private sector, a person creates a private trust fund using his or her own assets to benefit a stated individual(s). The creator of the trust names a trustee who has a fiduciary responsibility to manage the designated assets in accordance with the stipulations of the trust. In the federal sector, the Congress creates a federal trust fund in law and designates a funding source to benefit stated groups or individuals. However, in contrast to a private trust fund, the federal government does not have a fiduciary responsibility to the trust beneficiaries, and it can raise or lower future trust fund collections and payments or change the purposes for which the collections are used by changing existing laws. Moreover, the federal government has custody and control of the funds as well as the earnings of most federal trust funds.16
As opposed to the General Fund, which finances the daily and long-term operations of the federal government as a whole, a trust fund—such as the two Social Security trust funds—is required to be available for a specific program or use.17 Under current law, monies held in the Social Security trust funds may be spent only on program costs. In the case of Social Security, costs are largely synonymous with benefit payments. It is argued that the decision to tie a program to a trust fund signals a long-term political commitment: "The trust fund device is meant to provide assurance that policy promises, once made, will be kept."18 Upon creation of the OASI trust fund, President Franklin D. Roosevelt remarked, "We put those pay roll contributions there so as to give the contributors a legal, moral, and political right to collect their pensions and their unemployment benefits. With those taxes in there, no damn politician can ever scrap my social security program."19
Although usage of the trust fund mechanism may reflect a political commitment, it does not represent a legally binding one. While Social Security has been referred to as an intergenerational compact—between workers of one generation and beneficiaries from another—it has also been argued that "a trust fund is only as secure as its beneficiaries are powerful."20 Congress has the right to change the compact at any point by altering the tax revenue supplied by workers or the benefits collected by beneficiaries.
The Secretary of the Treasury is required by law to invest Social Security revenues in securities backed by the U.S. government (i.e., special U.S. government obligations).21 These securities are held in the Social Security trust funds, and the trust funds receive interest on these holdings. Each U.S. government security issued by the U.S. Treasury for purchase by the Social Security trust funds must be a paper instrument in the form of a bond, note, or certificate of indebtedness.22
Any interest or proceeds from the sale of U.S. government securities held by the Social Security trust funds must be paid in the form of paper checks from the General Fund of the Treasury to the Social Security trust funds.23 The interest rates paid on the securities issued to the Social Security trust funds are tied to market rates. Specifically, for any newly-issued security, the average yield is calculated as the average market yield on any marketable interest-bearing security of the federal government that is not due or callable until after four years from the last business day of the prior month, rounded to the nearest eighth of one percent.24
For internal federal accounting purposes, when special U.S. government obligations are purchased by the Social Security trust funds, the U.S. Treasury is shifting surplus Social Security revenues from one government account (the Social Security trust funds) to another government account (the General Fund). The special U.S. government obligations are physical documents held by SSA, not the U.S. Treasury. The securities held by the Social Security trust funds are redeemed on a regular basis. These special U.S. government obligations, however, are not resources for the federal government because they represent both an asset and a liability for the government.25
For federal budget purposes, on-budget status generally refers to programs that are included in the annual congressional budget process, whereas off-budget status generally refers to programs that are not included in the annual congressional budget process.
Social Security's receipts and most of its outlays are designated by law as off-budget. The off-budget designation has no practical effect on program funding, spending, or operations. The annual congressional budget resolution, in its legislative language, separates the off-budget totals from the on-budget totals. The report language accompanying the congressional budget resolution usually shows the unified budget totals (which combine the on- and off-budget amounts) as well as the separate on- and off-budget totals. The President's budget tends to use the unified budget measures when referring to the budget totals. The President's budget documents also include the totals for the on- and off-budget components, as required by law. The Congressional Budget Office uses the unified budget numbers in its analyses of the budget; it generally does not include on- and off-budget data in its regular annual reports.
The unified budget framework is important because it includes all federal receipts and outlays, providing a more comprehensive picture of the size of the federal government and the federal budget's impact on the economy. In the unified budget, the Social Security program is a large source of both federal receipts and federal outlays.26 For purposes of the unified budget, the annual Social Security cash flow surplus or deficit is counted in determining the overall federal budget surplus or deficit.27
As part of the annual congressional budget process, the level of federal debt (the federal debt limit) is established for the budget by Congress. The federal debt limit includes debt held by the public, as well as the internal debt of the U.S. government (i.e., debt held by government accounts). Borrowing from the public and the investment of the Social Security trust funds in special U.S. government obligations both fall under the restrictions of the federal debt limit. As a result, the balance of the Social Security trust funds has implications for the federal debt limit.28
Social Security program financing determines the program's ability to pay benefits to current and future beneficiaries. Revenues for the OASI and DI programs are credited to their respective trust funds, whereas costs for the OASI and DI programs are debited from their respective trust funds.
Social Security has three sources of income or revenue: (1) payroll tax revenues, (2) tax revenues from the taxation of benefits, and (3) interest earned on asset reserves held in the trust funds. Taken together, payroll tax revenues and tax revenues from the taxation of benefits are referred to more generally as tax revenues or non-interest income. Interest earned on asset reserves held in the trust funds is commonly referred to as interest income.
Payroll taxes provided under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) and Self-Employment Contribution Act (SECA) are the primary source of financing for both the OASI and DI programs.29 FICA taxes are paid by both employers and employees, but it is employers who remit the taxes to the U.S. Treasury. Employers remit FICA taxes on a regular basis throughout the year (e.g., weekly, monthly, quarterly, or annually), depending on the employer's level of total employment taxes (including FICA and federal personal income tax withholding). For past FICA and SECA tax rates, see Table A-1.
Under current law, the FICA tax rate is 7.65% of covered earnings for each employees and employers (i.e., each party pays 7.65%, yielding a combined 15.3% payroll tax).30 The FICA tax has two components: 6.2% of covered earnings for Social Security and 1.45% of covered earnings for Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI).31 The SECA tax rate is 15.3% of covered earnings for self-employed individuals, with 12.4% of covered earnings for Social Security and 2.9% of covered earnings for Medicare HI.32
The Social Security portions of FICA and SECA taxes are split between the two Social Security trust funds. FICA taxes are divided, with both employees and employers paying 5.3% of covered earnings to the OASI trust fund (i.e., combined 10.6%) and 0.9% of covered earnings to the DI trust fund (i.e., combined 1.8%). SECA taxes are also divided, with self-employed individuals paying 10.6% of covered earnings to the OASI trust fund and 1.8% of covered earnings to the DI trust fund.33
The Social Security portions of FICA and SECA taxes are applied to covered earnings up to an annual limit. The annual limit, known formally as the contribution and benefit base (CBB), is indexed to national average wages and is only adjusted in years for which a cost-of-living adjustment is payable.34 Consequently, the CBB generally increases each year.35 While the CBB can remain the same as the previous year, it is protected from decreasing.36 Table A-2 provides a historical record of CBBs.
In aggregate nominal dollars, revenues from payroll taxes have generally increased each year and are projected to increase in each future year37—a result of, among other things, a generally increasing number of workers, generally increasing wages, and a generally increasing CBB (i.e., taxable maximum).38 Table 1 shows the previous five years of payroll tax revenues for each trust fund and the combined trust fund, as well as the projected payroll tax revenues for each under the trustees' intermediate assumptions for the next five years.
Table 1. Payroll Tax Revenues for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
In billions of dollars
Source: Board of Trustees, The 2026 Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Federal Disability Insurance Trust Funds, June 8, 2026, Tables IV.A1, IV.A2, and IV.A3, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf.
Notes: Individual trust fund values may not sum to the combined (OASDI) total due to rounding.
The second type of tax revenue credited to the Social Security trust funds is revenue from the taxation of benefits.39 Beginning in 1984, up to 50% of Social Security benefits became subject to federal income tax for beneficiaries whose provisional income exceeds $25,000 and couples whose provisional income exceeds $32,000.40 The proceeds from taxing up to 50% of Social Security benefits are credited to the trust funds. Beginning in 1994, up to 85% of Social Security benefits became taxable if provisional income exceeds $34,000 for single-filing beneficiaries and $44,000 for couples. Proceeds from taxes on the first 50% of Social Security benefits are credited to the trust fund (e.g., OASI or DI) from which they were paid. Proceeds from taxes on Social Security benefits that exceed 50% are credited to the Medicare HI trust fund, regardless of whether benefits were paid from the OASI or DI trust funds.41
The two sets of thresholds mentioned above are fixed in law. That is, unlike the CBB (i.e., taxable maximum), they are not indexed. Because the thresholds are fixed, the share of Social Security beneficiaries subject to income taxation of a portion of their Social Security benefits is expected to increase as overall economy-wide wages and monthly benefit amounts increase.42 Recent projections suggest that more than half of Social Security beneficiaries will be subject to federal income taxes on a portion of their Social Security benefits each year between now and 2050.43
Table 2 shows the previous five years of revenues from the taxation of Social Security benefits for the two Social Security trust funds, and the combined trust funds, as well as the projected revenues from the taxation of Social Security benefits for each under the trustees' intermediate assumptions for the next five years. In aggregate nominal dollars, revenues from the taxation of benefits have generally increased each year and are projected to increase in each future year.44 This increase results from, among other things, a generally increasing number of beneficiaries and generally increasing average benefits.45

Under current law, asset reserves held in the Social Security trust funds are invested in nonmarketable federal public debt obligations known as special issues.46 These securities—like other federal debt obligations—are interest-bearing and, thus, provide a source of income to the Social Security program. The amount of interest income earned for the trust funds depends on the trust fund having a positive balance (i.e., the trust fund must have asset reserves upon which interest is earned) and the interest, or coupon, rate.47 For a list of historical interest rates, see Table A-3.
On a combined OASDI basis, revenues from interest income have generally decreased in recent years and are projected to decrease in each future year, in aggregate nominal dollars. 48 This decrease results from, among other things, a decreasing amount of excess reserves held in the trust funds.49 On an individual fund basis, this holds true for the OASI trust fund but not the DI trust fund (as discussed above, the DI trust fund is not projected to become depleted at any time in the next 75 years). As shown in the table, total trust fund revenues have grown and are projected to continue to grow on an individual and combined basis. This is largely due to growth in payroll taxes (the largest source of revenue for each trust fund).

This includes reimbursements for (1) the cost of payroll tax credits provided to employees in 1984 and self-employed persons in 1984-1989 by P.L. 98-21; (2) payroll tax revenue forgone under the provisions of P.L. 111-147, P.L. 111-312, P.L. 112-78, and P.L. 112-96; and (3) transfers of a portion of proceeds from repayments of loans authorized under P.L. 116-136.
Social Security has three sources of cost: (1) monthly benefits, (2) administrative costs, and (3) costs associated with the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB) interchange. On a combined basis, monthly benefits typically account for over 99% of program costs.50 Conversely, when taken together, administrative costs and transfers required for the RRB interchange account for less than 1% of program costs.
The Social Security program pays benefits on a monthly schedule to all program beneficiaries. Retirement benefits and survivors benefits are paid out (i.e., debited) from the OASI trust fund; disability benefits are paid out (i.e., debited) from the DI trust fund.
In aggregate nominal dollars, the amount paid in monthly benefits has increased in every year of the program's history.51 The total amount of monthly benefits can be thought of as the product of average benefits and the number of beneficiaries, both of which are projected to increase in future years. (Figure A-1 and Figure A-2 show the intermediate projections for the number of beneficiaries and initial monthly benefits by earnings level.) As such, the total amount of scheduled benefits (i.e., benefits calculated under current law) are projected to increase as well.
Social Security Benefit Calculation
Social Security benefits for retired and disabled workers are calculated using the same benefit computation process. The computation process includes three main steps. First, a summarized measure of lifetime Social Security-covered earnings is computed. This measure is called the average indexed monthly earnings, or AIME. Second, a progressive benefit formula is applied to a worker's AIME to compute his or her primary insurance amount, or PIA. The PIA is commonly referred to as the basic monthly benefit (i.e., the monthly benefit before any adjustments are applied). Third, adjustments are applied to the worker's PIA. The two most common adjustments are cost-of-living adjustments and adjustments for claiming age. Benefits for eligible dependents and survivors are based on a worker's PIA. For a detailed explanation of Social Security benefits, including example calculations, see CRS Report R46658, Social Security: Benefit Calculation.
Table 5. Aggregate Monthly Benefits for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
Expenses incurred by SSA and the Department of the Treasury in administering the OASI and DI programs and associated provisions of the Internal Revenue Code are debited from their respective trust funds.52 Nearly all of SSA's administrative expenses are funded by appropriations to its limitation on administrative expenses account, and almost all of the funding for this account is provided each year as part of the annual appropriations process.53

To ensure the OASI and DI trust funds maintain the same financial position in which they would have been if railroad employees had always been covered by Social Security, the Railroad Retirement Act requires an annual financial interchange between the OASI and DI programs with the Railroad Retirement program.54

Table 8 shows the previous five years of total costs for each trust fund and the combined trust funds, as well as the projected total costs for each under the trustees' intermediate assumptions for the next five years. As shown in the table, total trust fund costs have grown, and are projected to continue to grow, on an individual and combined basis. As the largest individual source of costs, growth in total costs is attributable to the growth in scheduled benefits.
Table 8. Total Costs for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
Comparing OASI and DI revenues and costs helps to illustrate the financial position of each program. The differences between costs and revenues can be analyzed on a cash flow basis (i.e., noninterest revenues less cost) and on an annual basis (i.e., total revenues less cost). When either measure results in a positive balance, the program operates under a surplus according to that measure. When either measure results in a negative balance, the program operates under a deficit.
Cash flow balances show the difference between the OASI and DI programs' current revenues and current costs. This measure does not consider interest income earned on asset reserves held in the respective trust funds, as these are generally earned based on accumulated excess revenues from prior years. When noninterest income (i.e., tax revenues) exceeds total cost, the program has a cash flow surplus. When noninterest income (i.e., tax revenues) is less than total costs, the program has a cash flow deficit. If either program operates a cash flow deficit, it may use interest income or accumulated holdings in its trust fund to help cover costs. Table 9 shows that the OASI program has operated cash flow deficits (i.e., negative cash flow balances) for the past five years and is projected to do so for the next five years. Under the intermediate assumptions, the trustees project the OASI program will experience cash flow deficits indefinitely.55 Conversely, the DI program has operated cash flow surpluses in each of the past five years, a trend that is expected to continue in the next five years (as shown in Table 9) and in each of the next 75 years.56 On a hypothetical OASDI basis, the combined trust funds are projected to experience cash flow deficits in each of the next 75 years.57
Operating with Cash Flow Deficits
When a trust fund (e.g., OASI) operates with annual cash flow deficits, the U.S. Treasury can continue to pay benefits scheduled under current law as long as the accumulated balance in the trust fund is sufficient to cover the costs. This is because the Social Security program has budget authority to pay benefits in full and on time if there is a positive balance in the designated account. However, if Social Security cannot cover benefits, the U.S. government must raise the funds necessary to pay back the bonds held in the trust funds. To do this, the government can increase taxes or other income, reduce non-Social Security spending, borrow from the public (i.e., by replacing bonds held by the trust funds with bonds held by the public), or a combination of these measures.
Table 9. Cash Flow Balances for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
Source: Congressional Research Service (CRS) using the 2026 Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Federal Disability Insurance Trust Funds, June 8, 2026, Tables IV.A1, IV.A2, and IV.A3, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf.
The occurrence of cash flow deficits—total costs exceeding noninterest revenues (i.e., tax revenues)—does not necessarily indicate an inability of a trust fund to pay full scheduled benefits (i.e., remain solvent).
In fact, in a perfectly pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) financing approach, with the assets in the trust fund maintained consistently at the level of a "contingency reserve" targeted at one year's cost for the program, the program might well be in a position of having negative cash flow on a permanent basis. This would occur when the interest rate on the trust fund assets is greater than the rate of growth in program cost. In this case, interest on the trust fund assets would be more than enough to grow the assets as fast as program cost, leaving some of the interest available to augment current tax revenue to meet current cost.58
If a trust fund's total revenues (i.e., noninterest income plus interest income) were to exceed total cost, the program would be operating an annual surplus. On one hand, a program could operate simultaneous cash flow deficits and annual surpluses, wherein the cash flow deficits were offset by interest income, allowing for full scheduled benefits to be paid.
On the other hand, the ability of a trust fund to pay full benefits could be weakened by sustained annual deficits where total revenues (i.e., noninterest income plus interest income) are less than total cost. A trust fund experiencing sustained cash flow deficits large enough to result in declining trust fund reserves would eventually threaten a program's ability to remain solvent. That is, a trust fund cannot sustain continued cash flow deficits and annual deficits.
Table 10 shows the annual balances for the OASI, DI, and combined trust funds for the previous five years and the next five years under the intermediate assumptions. As shown in Table 10, the OASI program has had annual deficits—interest income was not enough to offset negative cash flows—for the past five years and is projected to have annual deficits for the next five-years. This is projected to continue in each of the next 75 years as well.59 Although the DI program has had, and is projected to continue to have, annual surpluses, the status of the combined OASDI trust fund is expected to mimic that of the OASI program.
Table 10. Annual Balances for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
Source: The 2026 Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Federal Disability Insurance Trust Funds, June 8, 2026, Tables IV.A1, IV.A2, and IV.A3, https://www.ssa.gov/OACT/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf.
When a trust fund spends more than it receives in tax revenue and interest income, as it would under an annual deficit, it can redeem accumulated assets to pay scheduled benefits. Essentially, an annual deficit can be offset by drawing from accumulated assets (i.e., excess revenues accrued during years of annual surpluses). This process—redeeming assets reserves (i.e., bonds) held in the trust funds—results in a decrease in trust fund balances and can only occur when a positive trust fund balance exists.
Table 11 shows the trust fund balances for the OASI, DI, and combined trust funds for the previous five years and for the next five years under the intermediate assumptions. As shown in Table 11, the OASI program's annual deficits resulted in decreasing trust fund balances for the 2021 through 2025 period and are projected to continue for the next five years. Moreover, because costs are projected to grow faster than revenues, the trustees estimate that the continuing annual deficits will require increasing amounts of asset reserve redemption leading to asset reserve depletion in 2032. The combined trust funds' experience will closely resemble that of the OASI trust fund; the trustees estimate that on a combined basis, the OASDI trust funds assets would be depleted sometime in 2034. This combined result, an extension of overall program solvency by about two years, relies on the annual surpluses and a growing trust fund balance of the DI trust fund. As previously discussed, any transfer or borrowing from one trust fund to another would require a change in law.
Table 11. Asset Reserves for the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI), Disability Insurance (DI), and Combined OASDI Trust Funds
The trust funds have run annual surpluses in most years. Except for the first decades of the program and a few years beginning in the late 1960s, these annual surpluses were typically small relative to the size of the trust funds' expenditures. Beginning in 1975, the combined trust funds ran annual deficits. The trust funds made up the difference between revenues and cost during these years by redeeming some of the bonds accumulated in earlier years.
The Social Security program experienced significant financial difficulties during the mid-1970s through the early 1980s. A combination of high inflation, high unemployment, and slow real wage growth during this period caused the program's costs to exceed its income, which eroded the balances of the Social Security trust funds. To address these challenges, Congress passed a series of legislative measures aimed at mitigating program costs and increasing revenues.60
Near-Insolvency of the OASI Trust Fund in the Early 1980s

ICE Houston deports criminal illegal alien and accused child rapist who was granted conditional permanent resident status by Biden administration
HOUSTON — ICE officers removed Christian Ruvalcaba-Salas, a 28-year-old criminal illegal alien and accused child rapist, to his home country of Mexico Oct. 16. He was granted conditional permanent resident status by the Biden administration.
“This dangerous criminal alien, who is accused of doing unspeakable things to an innocent child in Mexico, was able to use the immigration status that the Biden administration gave him to allegedly slip into Mexico, brutalize a helpless child and then flee back into the U.S. through the port of entry to evade prosecution,” said ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Houston Field Office Director Bret Bradford. “That same status then allowed him to remain free in the community for years endangering public safety, despite the fact that he was wanted in Mexico for raping a child and had been arrested for numerous criminal offenses in the U.S. Thankfully, our officers were able to track him down after he attempted to flee and repatriate him to Mexico to face prosecution for his alleged crimes.”
Ruvalcaba-Salas was turned over to Mexican authorities to face prosecution for allegedly raping a child in Aguascalientes, Mexico, in 2022.
Ruvalcaba-Salas has been arrested for numerous crimes in the U.S., including assaulting a peace officer, unlawfully carrying a weapon, criminal trespass and twice for resisting arrest. On July 21, 2025, he pleaded no contest to resisting arrest and received deferred adjudication.
"Criminal illegal aliens who are child predators and sex offenders represent the very worst of the worst and they have no place in the United States,” said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock. “ICE will relentlessly pursue these violent predators and remove them, making our communities and neighborhoods safer and more secure.”
Ruvalcaba-Salas was admitted into the U.S. as a nonimmigrant in January 2020, near Laredo. Under the terms of his admission, he was required to leave the U.S. by July 6, 2020, but he failed to depart and remained in the U.S. illegally. On March 4, 2021, the Biden administration granted his petition for conditional permanent resident status. On March 28, 2023, the First Judicial District in the State of Aguascalientes, Mexico, issued a warrant calling for his arrest for allegedly raping a child on Nov. 24, 2022. While the U.S. does not track departures through the ports of entry to Mexico, U.S. Customs and Border Protection encountered him reentering the U.S. three days after the alleged rape on Nov. 27, 2022.
On May 20, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services denied his petition to remove conditions on his residence and terminated his conditional permanent resident status. He was thereafter placed in removal proceedings, and on July 7, an immigration judge ordered him removed from the U.S. in absentia. On Oct. 3, ICE officers successfully tracked him down and took him into custody during a targeted enforcement operation in Giddings.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — One day before his scheduled jury trial, Cole Martin, 42, of Vallejo, pleaded guilty today to being a felon in possession of a firearm, U.S. Attorney Eric Grant announced.

According to court documents, Martin was a parolee at large who had absconded from supervision in late 2023 after serving more than nine years in state prison for a felony robbery conviction. On Aug. 14, 2025, parole agents located Martin living at a residence in Vallejo and executed a warrant to apprehend him. While inside the residence, agents arrested Martin but noticed firearm parts, ammunition, and suspected drug residue inside the house. They received court authority to search the house and discovered the two guns charged in this case: a loaded Springfield 9 mm firearm, and a loaded KelTec .32-caliber gun, as well as other contraband.

The Solano County Sheriff’s Office, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation conducted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Nicole M. Vanek and Jason Hitt are prosecuting the case.

Martin has been detained on the federal charge since September 2025. He will remain detained pending his sentencing.

Martin is scheduled to be sentenced by U.S. District Judge William B. Shubb on March 8, 2027. Martin faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The actual sentence, however, will be determined at the discretion of the court after consideration of any applicable statutory factors and the federal Sentencing Guidelines, which take into account a number of variables.

Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: Violent Vallejo felon pleads guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm on eve of trial

NEWARK, N.J. – A New Jersey man who obtained more than $2.1 million in fraudulent COVID-19 relief funds was sentenced on October 28, 2026 to 78 months in prison, three years’ supervised release, and ordered to pay $2,131,747 in restitution, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced.

Following a four-day jury trial in May 2026 before U.S. District Judge Michael A. Shipp in Trenton federal court, Nikenson Jean Mathurin, aka “Nik Mathurin,” aka “Jean Mathurin,” 46, of Sparta, New Jersey, was convicted of three counts of wire fraud and one count of money laundering.

According to documents in this case and evidence at trial:

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic impact, Congress authorized emergency funding that small businesses could use to help keep their businesses afloat and employees on payroll.

Beginning in April 2020, Mathurin participated in a scheme to defraud lenders and the Small Business Administration to obtain federal COVID-19 emergency relief money by submitting fifteen fraudulent PPP and EIDL applications on behalf of businesses he claimed to own. Mathurin’s fraudulent applications included false information concerning, among other things, the applicant entities’ average monthly payroll, gross revenue, and number of employees, and fake supporting tax documents and payroll records. As a result of his fraudulent applications, Mathurin unlawfully obtained more than $2.1 million in federal COVID-19 emergency relief money.

U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer credited special agents the IRS – Criminal Investigation, under the direction of Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan, with the investigation.

The government is represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Matthew Stark and Fatime Meka Cano of the U.S. Attorney’s Office Criminal Division in Newark.

The District of New Jersey COVID-19 Fraud Enforcement Strike Force is one of five strike forces established throughout the United States by the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate and prosecute COVID-19 fraud. The strike forces focus on large-scale, multi-state pandemic relief fraud perpetrated by criminal organizations and transnational actors. The strike forces are interagency law enforcement efforts, using prosecutor-led and data analyst-driven teams designed to identify and bring to justice those who stole pandemic relief funds.

The Department of Justice has established the National Fraud Enforcement Division. The core mission of the National Fraud Enforcement Division is to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars. The National Fraud Enforcement Division will fulfill that mission by coordinating with agencies responsible for administering benefit programs; partnering with federal, tribal, state, territorial, and local law enforcement on fraud-fighting efforts; developing systems and processes that ensure efficient identification of fraud against taxpayer dollars; and equipping prosecutors and law enforcement with state-of-the-art tools and resources needed to bring criminal actors to justice. The attorneys in the National Fraud Enforcement Division will work every day to protect the financial integrity of our government and the tax system that supports it.

Anyone with information about allegations of attempted fraud involving COVID-19 can report it by calling the Department of Justice’s National Center for Disaster Fraud Hotline at 866-720-5721 or via the NCDF Web Complaint Form at: https://www.justice.gov/disaster-fraud/ncdf-disaster-complaint-form .

ATLANTA - Brady Lum, the former chief operating officer of the High Museum of Art, has been sentenced to one year in federal prison for stealing more than $600,000 from the museum by doctoring invoices and approving transactions for personal purchases. Before today’s sentencing hearing, Lum paid full restitution to the museum and reimbursed its $500,000 of investigative expenses and legal fees.

“Lum brazenly pilfered hundreds of thousands of dollars from a beloved civic institution to pay for his high-end guitars and other personal items. His appalling breach of trust damaged not only the High Museum but also the larger art community,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “Lum repaid the High Museum by covering its losses and expenses, and now he will pay his debt to society from prison.”

“We expect leaders of one of our communities’ historic institutions to serve as stewards, not loot it,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “Brady Lum manipulated internal processes to steal hundreds of thousands of dollars. The FBI is committed to uncovering and stopping this kind of greed and fraud.”

According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the charges, and other information presented in court: Lum served as the High Museum of Art’s chief operating officer from January 2, 2019, until his resignation on December 9, 2025. Prior to working at the High Museum, Lum held leadership positions at the Coca-Cola Company and Special Olympics International.

During his tenure as the High Museum’s COO, Lum repeatedly purchased non-business items and services for himself, including expensive guitars and other music equipment, personal music lessons, and woodworking equipment, through direct supplier invoicing and the High Museum’s corporate credit card reimbursement process. Lum started to siphon money from the museum in September 2019, less than nine months after he started his COO job, and continued through the discovery of the fraud in November 2025.

Lum concealed the nature of his transactions in several ways, including by submitting altered invoices, using his position to approve expenses, and using accounting adjustments to spread his expenses across different cost centers. Over the course of his scheme, Lum stole more than $600,000 from the High Museum.

Today, U.S. District Judge Michael L. Brown sentenced Brady Lum, 60, of Atlanta, Georgia, to one year in prison to be followed by one year of supervised release. As part of his plea agreement, Lum paid full restitution of $607,688.18 to the High Museum. Lum also voluntarily paid approximately $500,000 to the High Museum to cover costs the museum incurred while uncovering and investigating his criminal activity.

This case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicholas N. Joy prosecuted the case.

For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga .
title: High Museum of Art's Former Chief Operating Officer Sentenced to Federal Prison for Embezzlement

NEW BERN, N.C. – A federal judge sentenced Murad Terrell Taylor, 26, of Garner, to over eleven and a half years in federal prison for possessing a gun as a convicted felon. Taylor pleaded guilty on July 15, 2026.

“This gun toting convicted felon will no longer terrorize the Johnston County community. His long rap sheet is proof of his disregard for the law and the families and children in this community,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle. “By the grace of God, he didn’t kill his victim, even though he tried. He can spend the next eleven and a half years peering through the cold bars of a federal prison cell to think about behaving in society.”

“This gun toting convicted felon will no longer terrorize the Johnston County community. His long rap sheet is proof of his disregard for the law and the families and children in this community,” said U.S. Attorney Ellis Boyle. “By the grace of God, he didn’t kill his victim, even though he tried. He can spend the next eleven and a half years peering through the cold bars of a federal prison cell to think about behaving in society.”

On September 5, 2025, Johnston County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded to a report that a driver fired a gun at another car traveling along Veterans Parkway in Garner in a road rage frenzy. The bullet smashed through the front passenger door and, thankfully, did not injure the other driver. The victim provided deputies with the suspect vehicle’s license plate number.

“This case demonstrates what local and federal partners achieve together for Johnston County. From response to prosecution, it was a team effort, and I thank the District Attorney’s Office and Dangerous Offenders Task Force for holding this offender accountable,” said Johnston County Sheriff Steve Bizzell. “Following his state trial for shooting at a victim, Taylor’s 137-month federal sentence adds crucial accountability. Cooperation between state and federal authorities remains one of our strongest tools against violent crime, ensuring those who endanger our community are taken off the streets.”

“This case demonstrates the Johnston County District Attorney’s Office’s commitment, through our Dangerous Offenders Task Force, to pursuing every appropriate avenue to protect the public. Following a Johnston County trial, Taylor received a lengthy active prison sentence for shooting at an innocent victim, and his federal firearms conviction represents an additional measure of accountability,” said Johnston County District Attorney Jason Waller. “Cooperation between state and federal authorities is an important tool in addressing violent crime. Our priority is keeping those who pose the greatest threat off our streets and making our communities safer for all.”

Ellis Boyle, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of North Carolina made the announcement after sentencing by U.S. District Judge Louise W. Flanagan. The ATF and Johnston County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case.

A copy of this press release is located on our website . Related court documents and information can be found on the website of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina or on PACER by searching for Case No. 5:25-CR-269-FL.
title: Garner Convicted Felon Sentenced to Almost Twelve Years in Prison for Gun Possession After Multi-County High Speed Chase

PHILADELPHIA – United States Attorney David Metcalf announced that Donald Michael, aka “Baseball Fun,” 49, of Queen Creek, Arizona, was sentenced to 330 months in prison, 15 years of supervised release, and various financial penalties, including $137,933 in restitution to victims, by United States District Judge Mark A. Kearney for online child sexual exploitation. In addition, Michael is required to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act and Megan’s Law, as well as state law.

The defendant was charged by indictment in July 2024 with one count of conspiracy to manufacture child pornography, one count of conspiracy to receive and distribute child pornography, one count of distribution and attempted distribution of child pornography, and two counts of receipt of child pornography. He pleaded guilty to all the charges against him in April of last year.

As detailed in court filings and statements, Michael, who served as a baseball coach of minor boys for more than two decades, engaged in an online child exploitation catfishing scheme for over 18 months with co-conspirators Andrew Wolf , a former teacher at Springside Chestnut Hill Academy (“SCH”), and Kray Strange, of Carthage, New York, both of whom were previously convicted and sentenced.

Michael conspired with Wolf and Strange to target minor boys who were Wolf’s current and former students at SCH and to coerce and induce them to produce sexually explicit images and send them to the defendant and his co-conspirators over the internet. They did so by creating multiple fake online profiles where they pretended to be teenaged girls, engaging each of their victims in sexually explicit and graphic chats, and distributing child pornography to the minor boys, in an effort to get them to reciprocate with their own images.

When the boys refused to continue to engage, Michael and his co-conspirators used blackmail and extortion to manipulate them into continuing to produce images. After Wolf and Strange were arrested and incarcerated, this defendant continued his catfishing scheme by targeting and victimizing minor boys who were Little League World Series players.

“Cloaked in the anonymity that the internet provided them, Michael and his co-conspirators manipulated young boys into taking and sending explicit images of themselves,” said U.S. Attorney Metcalf. “These men are predators, plain and simple, and deserve every day of the lengthy sentences they’ve received. Protecting children from sexual exploitation will always be a priority for my office and our partners at the FBI.”

“The sexual exploitation and extortion of children remains one of the most devious crimes the women and men of the FBI investigate,” said Wayne A. Jacobs, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Philadelphia. “This sentencing serves as a reminder how seriously the FBI and our partners take the online victimization of minors. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to work tirelessly to protect young people from exploitation and ensure those who prey on them are brought to justice.”

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by United States Attorneys’ Offices and the Criminal Division’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit projectsafechildhood.gov .

The case was investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys Kelly Harrell and Michelle Rotella.
title: Arizona Man Sentenced to 27½ Years in Prison for Child Exploitation Offenses in Connection With Catfishing Scheme That Targeted Young Boys

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Madobox, S.A. de C.V. (Madobox), located in the city of Uruapan in the state of Michoacán, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The U.S. request for review follows an RRM petition received from a Mexican labor union alleging that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Madobox facility, which produces boxes for commercial use.
Background
The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 30, 2026, the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores y Empleados de la Industria del Comercio, Alimenticia, Textil, Automotriz, Metalúrgica, Servicios y Distribución “Generalísimo José María Morelos y Pavón”—a Mexican labor union affiliated with the Confederacion Central Nacional (COCENA)—filed a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) petition alleging a denial of rights at Madobox. The petition alleges that Madobox is interfering with union activity at the facility, including by unlawfully arranging a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that was negotiated without workers, by coercing and misinforming workers about the CBA and their union rights, and by unlawfully dismissing workers in retaliation for union activity. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.
After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Madobox are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Madobox.
Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.
A copy of the request for review can be found here.
A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.
Information about previous requests can be found here.

title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Madobox
